conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Posterior STEMI → RCA or circumflex. These anterior-lead changes are the mirror image of true posterior ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does the MONA mnemonic stand for in immediate ACS management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin. A memory aid only — aspirin 300 mg is for all, but oxygen (only if SpO₂<94%), nitrates and morphine are conditional, not routine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must oxygen be given only if SpO₂ is below 94% in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction and worsens infarct size, so supplemental oxygen is reserved for genuine hypoxia (SpO₂ <94%).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In which two situations should nitrates be used with caution in ACS, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: If the patient is hypotensive, or has an inferior MI with RV involvement — nitrates reduce preload and can precipitate severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What dose of aspirin is given in acute ACS, and how should it be taken for fastest effect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 300 mg stat, chewed or crushed for rapid absorption.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is morphine used cautiously in ACS beyond its sedative/respiratory risks?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Morphine delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption (slowing antiplatelet onset). It's reserved for severe pain and given with an anti-emetic such as metoclopramide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A STEMI is confirmed and aspirin given. PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes. What is the reperfusion strategy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Primary PCI — the preferred reperfusion method when available within 120 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A STEMI is confirmed but PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes. What is the alternative, and name agents used.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Fibrinolysis — e.g. alteplase or streptokinase, plus an antithrombin (fondaparinux/enoxaparin) and a second antiplatelet (clopidogrel — ticagrelor/prasugrel are reserved for primary PCI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: After fibrinolysis, when is the ECG repeated, and what indicates failure requiring rescue PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Repeat the ECG at 60–90 minutes. Persistent ST elevation indicates failed lysis → proceed to rescue PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which second antiplatelet is given alongside aspirin for a patient going for primary PCI, and what is the exception?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Prasugrel 60 mg (or ticagrelor 180 mg). Use clopidogrel instead if the patient is on an oral anticoagulant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What stent type and arterial access are preferred in primary PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A drug-eluting stent, via radial access (preferred over femoral).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: List the '6 A's' of secondary prevention after ACS.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Aspirin (75 mg OD indefinitely), Another antiplatelet (ticagrelor/clopidogrel for 12 months = DAPT), Atorvastatin (80 mg OD), ACE inhibitor (e.g. ramipril), Atenolol/beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol), and Aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone if HF post-MI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the role of a beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol) in secondary prevention post-MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Titrated up to reduce adverse ventricular remodelling (and improve prognosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is an aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone) indicated after an MI, and what must be monitored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Indicated if there is clinical heart failure post-MI. Monitor potassium, as it causes hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is renal function and potassium monitoring essential when combining an ACE inhibitor with an aldosterone antagonist?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both drugs cause hyperkalaemia and can impair renal function, so U&Es must be monitored when used together.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Beyond drugs, what additional steps are arranged as part of post-MI secondary prevention?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: An echocardiogram (to assess LV function), cardiac rehabilitation, and a diabetes/lipid review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why does an NSTEMI cause subendocardial rather than transmural ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: NSTEMI results from partial coronary occlusion. The subendocardium is the most distal, watershed region of perfusion, so it is the first to become ischaemic when flow is only partially reduced — sparing the outer wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What ECG findings are typical of an NSTEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG. By definition there is no ST elevation and no new LBBB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What single investigation distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina, and how?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Troponin — it is elevated in NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis) but normal in unstable angina (ischaemia without infarction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which risk-stratification tool is used in NSTEMI, and what decision does it guide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The GRACE score — it stratifies risk and guides the urgency/timing of coronary angiography.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: On the GRACE score, what threshold indicates the need for early angiography, and within what timeframe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A GRACE score >3% indicates early angiography, performed within 72 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What does the BATMAN mnemonic stand for in NSTEMI / unstable angina management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: B – Base on GRACE score (risk-stratify for angiography/PCI timing); A – Aspirin 300 mg stat; T – Ticagrelor 180 mg stat; M – Morphine (if severe pain + anti-emetic); A – Antithrombin (fondaparinux/enoxaparin); N – Nitrate (sublingual/IV GTN for ongoing pain).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In the BATMAN approach, what does the 'B' represent and what does it determine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: B = Base on GRACE score — risk-stratification that determines angiography and PCI timing (>3% → early angiography within 72h).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What loading dose of aspirin is given in NSTEMI/UA, matching the 'A' in BATMAN?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Aspirin 300 mg stat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In BATMAN, what is the standard second antiplatelet and its dose, and what are the alternatives?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Ticagrelor 180 mg stat (first-line in NSTEMI). Prasugrel only once coronary anatomy is known and proceeding to PCI; clopidogrel 300 mg if high bleeding risk or on an anticoagulant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which antiplatelet is preferred in NSTEMI/UA if the patient has a high bleeding risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Clopidogrel 300 mg (instead of ticagrelor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What antithrombin agents are used in NSTEMI/UA, and which is preferred?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Fondaparinux is preferred; enoxaparin (LMWH) is the alternative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In the BATMAN protocol, when are nitrates given and by what route?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Nitrates (sublingual or IV GTN) are given for ongoing chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the defining feature of unstable angina in terms of myocardial damage?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Partial coronary occlusion causing ischaemia WITHOUT infarction — there is no myocyte necrosis, so troponin remains normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What ECG findings can be seen in unstable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: ST depression, T-wave inversion, or a normal ECG — the same range as NSTEMI, with no ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Describe the three classic symptom patterns that define unstable angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 1) New-onset chest pain, 2) angina occurring at rest, or 3) rapidly progressive (crescendo) exertional angina.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How does the initial management of unstable angina compare with that of NSTEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is the same — the BATMAN protocol, with GRACE-score risk stratification to guide angiography timing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient describes stable exertional angina that has suddenly become more frequent and easily provoked over the past few days. What does this progression suggest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Crescendo (rapidly progressive) angina — a presentation of unstable angina, indicating an unstable plaque and warranting ACS workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the fundamental mechanism of pain in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A fixed atheromatous plaque causes flow-limiting stenosis, so myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply (demand > supply) during exertion. The plaque is intact — no rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What three features define 'stable' in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is predictable, brought on by exertion, and relieved by rest or GTN (typically within ~5 minutes).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Name the three characteristics used in the typicality ladder for angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: 1) Constricting central/retrosternal pain ± radiation, 2) brought on by exertion or stress, 3) relieved by rest or GTN within ~5 minutes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How many of the three angina features are needed to classify chest pain as typical, atypical, or non-anginal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Typical = all 3 features; atypical = 2 of 3; non-anginal = ≤1 of 3 (unlikely to be cardiac ischaemia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: A patient has constricting central chest pain on exertion that settles with rest, but with no radiation noted. How is this classified on the typicality ladder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Atypical angina — 2 of the 3 features present (exertional + relieved by rest, but pain character/radiation criterion not fully met).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What distinguishes the plaque behaviour in stable angina from that in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: In stable angina the plaque is intact (fixed stenosis → ischaemia only on increased demand). In ACS the plaque ruptures → thrombus → partial or complete occlusion → ischaemia at rest, unpredictable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why does stable angina produce subendocardial (not transmural) ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The fixed stenosis limits flow only when demand rises; the subendocardium — the watershed area — becomes ischaemic first, but the plaque does not occlude the vessel completely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must LFTs be checked before starting a statin in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: To establish a baseline, as statins can affect liver enzymes; LFTs are rechecked at 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Is troponin a routine test in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: No — troponin is only sent if there is an unstable or acute presentation, not in routine stable angina assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What can a resting ECG show in stable angina, and what is its main value?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is often normal between episodes, but may show old Q waves (previous MI), ST depression or T-wave changes. It is done in all patients mainly to help exclude other diagnoses.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: According to NICE, what is the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected cardiac origin with no known CAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: CT coronary angiography (CTCA) — a non-invasive scan that identifies plaque burden and degree of stenosis, with an excellent negative predictive value for ruling out significant CAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the main strength of CTCA that makes it the first-line investigation for stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Its excellent negative predictive value — it effectively rules out significant coronary artery disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Give three examples of functional imaging used in stable angina, and when they are used.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Stress echocardiography (exercise/dobutamine, wall motion), stress cardiac MRI (adenosine perfusion), and myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI, nuclear). Used if CTCA is non-diagnostic or to assess the functional significance of a stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the role of invasive coronary angiography in stable angina, and what does FFR add?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is the gold standard for coronary anatomy/severity and allows simultaneous PCI. Fractional flow reserve (FFR) measures the functional significance of a stenosis to guide whether to intervene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: The stable angina management framework has three parallel arms. What are they?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Arm 1 — secondary prevention (modify risk / prevent MI); Arm 2 — acute symptom relief (GTN); Arm 3 — prophylactic symptom control (anti-anginal ladder).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: How does antiplatelet therapy in stable angina differ from that in ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Stable angina uses a SINGLE antiplatelet (aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely, or clopidogrel if aspirin-intolerant). ACS uses DAPT (aspirin + a P2Y12 inhibitor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What statin and dose is used for secondary prevention in stable angina, and what is its mechanism of benefit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg ON (high-intensity) — lowers LDL and stabilises plaque. Check LFTs at baseline and 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is an ACE inhibitor specifically indicated in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: If there is co-existing diabetes, hypertension, CKD or heart failure — it is cardioprotective and reduces afterload/vascular tone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which single risk-factor modification is considered the most important in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Smoking cessation. Other targets: BP control (<140/90; <130/80 if diabetes/high CV risk), glycaemic control in diabetes, weight, exercise and diet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Describe the mechanism by which sublingual GTN relieves angina.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: It is a nitric oxide donor causing venodilation → reduced preload → reduced myocardial oxygen demand; it also dilates the coronary arteries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What is the patient-education GTN protocol for an acute angina attack?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Sit down and use GTN spray/tablet → wait 5 minutes → repeat dose if pain persists → wait 5 minutes → call 999 if still no relief (possible ACS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the common side effects of GTN, and how should the spray be stored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Headache (vasodilation), flushing and hypotension. Store away from light/heat; GTN tablets expire ~8 weeks after opening, whereas the spray is stable for ~2–3 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: What are the two first-line options for prophylactic symptom control in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: A beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol, atenolol — reduces HR and contractility, lowering O₂ demand) OR a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (diltiazem, verapamil) if a beta-blocker is contraindicated/not tolerated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: If first-line monotherapy fails to control angina, what is the safe second-line combination, and which combination must be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Safe: beta-blocker + amlodipine (a dihydropyridine CCB). Never combine a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem — risk of heart block/sinus arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why is the combination of a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem dangerous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Both suppress AV conduction and heart rate, so together they risk bradycardia, complete heart block or sinus arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Name three add-on anti-anginal options beyond beta-blockers and CCBs, with a brief mechanism for each.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Long-acting nitrate (ISMN — isosorbide mononitrate, venodilation); ivabradine (If-channel inhibitor, lowers HR, sinus rhythm only, if beta-blocker intolerant); nicorandil (K-ATP channel opener + nitrate); ranolazine (late sodium-channel inhibitor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Why must rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) be avoided in HFrEF, and what is the alternative?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: They are negative inotropes — reducing contractility can precipitate decompensation. Use amlodipine instead if a CCB is needed in heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Under what circumstances is revascularisation considered in stable angina?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: For significant stenosis confirmed on imaging, or refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: When is PCI a suitable revascularisation choice, and what does it require afterwards?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: PCI (angioplasty + drug-eluting stent) suits single or discrete vessel disease — less invasive, shorter recovery. It requires DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for ~6 months post-stent in stable angina (adjust for bleeding/ischaemic risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: In which scenarios is CABG favoured over PCI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: Left main stem disease, severe/multivessel disease, diabetes mellitus, and poor LV function (EF <30%) — CABG gives better long-term outcomes in complex disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.front: Which bypass graft is the gold standard, and how do its patency rates compare with a saphenous vein graft?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Corona.back: The LIMA (left internal mammary artery) → LAD graft is gold standard, with >90% patency at 10 years, versus ~50% patency for saphenous vein grafts at 10 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Define chronic heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: A clinical syndrome resulting from a structural or functional cardiac abnormality, leading to an inability to maintain adequate cardiac output at normal filling pressures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction defines HFrEF, and what is the underlying problem?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≤40% — systolic dysfunction with impaired contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction range defines HFmrEF, and why is it clinically important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF 41–49% — a distinct ESC 2021 category (mildly reduced EF). It behaves more like HFrEF and often responds to HFrEF drugs; increasingly examined at finals.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What ejection fraction defines HFpEF, and what is the underlying problem?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≥50% — diastolic dysfunction with impaired filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is high-output heart failure, and name its causes.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Normal or raised cardiac output that is unable to meet the body's demands. Causes: anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, pregnancy, thiamine deficiency (beriberi), and a large AV fistula.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the most common cause of chronic heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Ischaemic heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the main aetiologies of chronic heart failure (excluding high-output causes).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Ischaemic heart disease (most common), hypertension (chronic pressure overload), valvular disease (aortic stenosis common), arrhythmias (AF common), cardiomyopathy (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive), and myocarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: In the pathophysiology of heart failure, what is the role of neurohormonal activation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: RAAS activation causes Na/water retention (raising preload), and SNS activation causes tachycardia and vasoconstriction (raising afterload).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Describe the sequence of ventricular remodelling in heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Hypertrophy → dilatation → worsening dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Outline the broad pathophysiological cascade of heart failure from injury to fluid accumulation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Cardiac injury (reduced stroke volume/cardiac output) → neurohormonal activation (RAAS + SNS) → ventricular remodelling → fluid accumulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does fluid accumulation differ between left and right heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Left HF → pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary oedema. Right HF → systemic venous hypertension → peripheral oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class I heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: No limitation — symptoms only on extreme exertion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class II heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Mild limitation — comfortable at rest, symptoms on moderate exertion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class III heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Marked limitation — symptoms on less than ordinary activity; comfortable at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What does NYHA Class IV heart failure describe?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Symptoms at rest — unable to carry out any activity without symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the symptoms and signs of LEFT heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea (breathless lying flat — ask about pillows), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (PND), cough with frothy white/pink sputum, displaced apex beat (lateral + downward), S3 gallop (always pathological >40 yrs), and bibasal crackles (pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: List the symptoms and signs of RIGHT heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Raised JVP, peripheral pitting oedema (ankles → sacrum), congestive hepatomegaly, positive hepatojugular reflux, ascites (when severe), and fatigue.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why is an S3 gallop significant in suspected heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It is always pathological in patients over 40 years and is part of the classic HF triad (S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is orthopnoea, and how do you elicit it in the history?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Breathlessness when lying flat — ask the patient how many pillows they need to sleep.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Why is NT-proBNP raised in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Ventricular wall stretch triggers BNP release, which causes vasodilation and natriuresis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How do NT-proBNP levels guide the timing of echocardiography?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: <400 = HF unlikely; 400–2000 = echo within 6 weeks; >2000 = echo within 2 weeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Is NT-proBNP sensitive or specific for heart failure, and what else raises it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Sensitive but NOT specific — it is also raised in PE, CKD, sepsis and AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for heart failure, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Echocardiogram — it measures EF, wall motion and valves, classifies HF (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF), and guides treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What can a 12-lead ECG show in heart failure, and what does a normal ECG imply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It may show LVH, LBBB, AF or ischaemia, helping to guide aetiology. A normal ECG makes heart failure less likely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the CXR features of heart failure (ABCDE)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, upper lobe Diversion, and pleural Effusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which blood tests are sent in heart failure, and why check U&E in particular?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: U&E (renal function before starting drugs), FBC, TFTs, HbA1c, LFTs and cholesterol.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the 'four pillars' of HFrEF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist), and SGLT2 inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does modern practice approach starting the four pillars of HFrEF treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It favours early initiation of all four pillars together (or in rapid sequence) rather than strict sequential step-up — per current ESC/NICE guidance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the role of an ACEi/ARB in HFrEF, and what must be monitored?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: E.g. ramipril (or losartan if cough). Inhibits angiotensin II, increases bradykinin → vasodilation, reduces RAAS-driven remodelling, with a mortality benefit. Monitor potassium and renal function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which beta-blockers are licensed for HFrEF, and which are NOT used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Bisoprolol, carvedilol or nebivolol only. NOT atenolol or metoprolol. Start low and titrate slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: How does a beta-blocker benefit HFrEF mechanistically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: It blocks chronically activated SNS → reduces heart rate and produces anti-remodelling effects.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the mechanism and key risk of an MRA (e.g. spironolactone/eplerenone) in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Blocks aldosterone → reduces fibrosis and potassium loss. Key risk is hyperkalaemia — monitor potassium and renal function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure, and what makes them unique?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin reduce glucose reabsorption → osmotic diuresis and cardioprotection. They are the only class with evidence in HFpEF, and are given regardless of diabetes status.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the role of loop diuretics in heart failure, and the crucial exam point about them?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Furosemide/bumetanide for congestion/fluid retention — they reduce preload and relieve oedema and dyspnoea. Key point: NO mortality benefit (purely symptomatic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) used, and what is the critical safety rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Replaces an ACEi if the patient is still symptomatic with EF ≤35%. It prevents breakdown of natriuretic peptides. A 36-hour washout from the ACEi is required to avoid angioedema risk if combined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the criteria for adding ivabradine in HFrEF, and its mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Sinus rhythm >75 bpm + EF ≤35% on maximal beta-blocker. It blocks the If (funny) current in the SA node → reduces heart rate without affecting contractility or BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is digoxin used in heart failure, and what are its key cautions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: HFrEF with coexisting AF (rate control). A positive inotrope (Na/K-ATPase inhibitor) that improves symptoms and reduces hospitalisations but has NO mortality benefit. Narrow therapeutic index — toxic in CKD/hypokalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: When is hydralazine + ISMN indicated in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: In Afro-Caribbean patients intolerant of ACEi/ARB — it provides vasodilation via a different pathway (A-HeFT trial evidence).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the indications for an ICD in heart failure (primary and secondary prevention)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Secondary prevention: EF ≤35% + previous VT/VF. Primary prevention: EF ≤35% on optimal therapy ≥3 months. It continuously monitors rhythm and shocks VF/VT back to sinus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What are the criteria for CRT in heart failure, and how does it work?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: EF ≤35% + QRS ≥130 ms (especially LBBB) + NYHA II–IV. A biventricular (triple-chamber) pacemaker with RA, RV and LV leads resynchronises ventricular contractions → increases cardiac output. CRT-D adds ICD function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What vaccinations and surgical options are offered in heart failure beyond drugs and devices?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Annual influenza vaccine + a one-off pneumococcal vaccine, and surgical correction of underlying valvular disease where indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: What is the classic auscultation triad of heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.front: Which heart failure drug classes do NOT confer a mortality benefit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.back: Loop diuretics (symptomatic relief only) and digoxin (improves symptoms/reduces admissions but no mortality benefit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the mechanism of acute heart failure (AHF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: An acute event renders the LV unable to efficiently pump blood into the systemic circulation → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs → pulmonary oedema (lung tissue and alveoli fill with interstitial fluid).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is de novo acute heart failure, and what are its typical causes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: A first-ever presentation with no prior HF diagnosis. Often caused by a new MI, hypertensive emergency, or acute valve rupture. It requires a full diagnostic workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is decompensated chronic heart failure, and how common is it relative to de novo AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Known HF that is acutely worsened by a trigger — it is the more common form. Management involves identifying and treating the trigger while optimising chronic therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: How does the acute management of de novo AHF differ from decompensated AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: The acute management is the same, but de novo AHF additionally needs a full diagnostic workup to find the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: List the common triggers that precipitate decompensated chronic heart failure.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: MI/ACS, new AF or arrhythmia, hypertensive emergency, sepsis/infection, iatrogenic IV fluids, non-compliance with medications, anaemia/PE, and valvular rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the SYMPTOMS of acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Acute shortness of breath (worse lying flat, improves sitting up), cough with frothy white/pink sputum, raised respiratory rate with reduced O₂ sats, and extreme anxiety / sense of impending doom.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the SIGNS of acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Tachycardia and tachypnoea, a 3rd heart sound, bilateral basal crackles, hypotension in severe cases (cardiogenic shock), signs of the underlying cause (chest pain in ACS, fever in sepsis, palpitations in arrhythmia), and — if right-sided HF too — raised JVP and peripheral oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does hypotension signify in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: It occurs in severe cases and indicates cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the role of an ECG in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: To look for arrhythmias (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI) and LBBB — it helps identify the trigger.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Which bloods are sent in acute heart failure, and what is each looking for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: FBC (anaemia), U&E (renal function), BNP/NT-proBNP, troponin, and CRP/cultures (sepsis). D-dimer only if PE is clinically suspected (not routine).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the role of an arterial blood gas (ABG) in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: To assess the degree of hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV or intubation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does echocardiography assess in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: LV function and structural abnormalities — it identifies the cause (e.g. valve rupture, wall motion abnormality).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What level of care does acute heart failure require, and when is HDU/ITU needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: It requires hospital admission. Severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock warrants HDU or ITU.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does the SODIUM mnemonic stand for in first-line AHF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: S – Sit up; O – Oxygen; D – IV Diuretic; I – IV fluids stop; U – Underlying cause (treat the trigger); M – Monitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the SODIUM approach, why is sitting the patient up beneficial?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Gravity moves fluid to the lung bases, clearing the upper/mid zones for gas exchange.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the oxygen target in AHF, and what is added if it is not achieved on oxygen alone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Give oxygen only if hypoxic, targeting SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of CO₂ retention). Escalate to CPAP/NIV if refractory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What IV diuretic and dose is used in AHF, and how does it help?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: IV furosemide 40–80 mg — it increases urine output and reduces circulating volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Why are IV fluids stopped in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: The patient is fluid-overloaded; all IV fluid infusions should be stopped (the 'I' in SODIUM).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does 'Monitor' (M in SODIUM) involve in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Monitoring urine output, observations, U&E, and fluid balance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is >100 mmHg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Vasodilator-led: IV GTN (or nitroprusside) — reduces preload/afterload. Add CPAP/NIV for respiratory failure. (BNP is a diagnostic biomarker, not a treatment.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is 90–100 mmHg?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Inotrope-led with cautious vasodilator: dobutamine, adding low-dose GTN only under continuous BP monitoring (or a PDE inhibitor if poor response).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In the BP-stratified approach to AHF, what is the strategy when SBP is <85 mmHg (cardiogenic shock)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support: dobutamine (↑contractility, ↑CO), noradrenaline (vasopressor, ↑SVR), and consider IABP or LVAD if no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: Why is IV morphine no longer routinely recommended in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Although historically used for anxiolysis and preload reduction, evidence shows harm (increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries). Avoid unless in a palliative context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the role of NIV/CPAP in acute heart failure, and when is invasive ventilation needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Use NIV/CPAP early if oxygen alone is insufficient — it reduces work of breathing, decreases preload and improves oxygenation. Invasive ventilation is reserved for refractory cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: In which specific situations is IV GTN indicated in acute heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Hypertensive AHF (SBP >100) and ACS-triggered AHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: How does fluid management in cardiogenic shock differ from septic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: In cardiogenic shock do NOT give fluids (unlike septic shock) — instead give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are dobutamine and noradrenaline each used for in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility, ↑CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR). IABP or LVAD is considered if there is no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the definition of acute heart failure (AHF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Rapid onset or worsening of symptoms/signs of HF requiring urgent therapy — includes de-novo AHF and acute decompensation of chronic HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the six clinical presentations of AHF (ESC classification)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Acute decompensated HF; hypertensive AHF; pulmonary oedema; cardiogenic shock; isolated right HF; ACS + AHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Tissue hypoperfusion due to cardiac failure: SBP <90 mmHg + signs of low output (cold/clammy, oliguria, altered consciousness) despite adequate filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the key bedside findings in pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Severe dyspnoea, tachypnoea, orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, widespread crepitations, hypoxia — life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What does the chest X-ray show in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: ABCDE: Alveolar oedema (bat-wing); Kerley B lines; Cardiomegaly; upper-lobe Diversion (vascular redistribution); Effusion (pleural).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the first-line acute pharmacological treatment for AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: IV loop diuretics (furosemide) — reduce preload; IV/SL nitrates if hypertensive; O₂ if SpO₂ <94%; opiates no longer routinely recommended.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: When is non-invasive ventilation (NIV/CPAP) used in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Pulmonary oedema with respiratory failure unresponsive to O₂ — reduces need for intubation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What inotropes are used in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Dobutamine (first-line); noradrenaline if vasodilated shock; levosimendan (calcium sensitiser) — bridge to intervention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is the Killip classification?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Killip I: no HF; II: mild HF (S3/creps); III: pulmonary oedema; IV: cardiogenic shock — post-MI mortality predictor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What is BNP/NT-proBNP used for in AHF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Diagnosis (rules out if low) and prognosis — elevated BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL supports AHF; guides discharge.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: What are the precipitants of acute decompensation in chronic HF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: FAILURE: Forgot medications; Arrhythmia (AF); Ischaemia/Infection; Lifestyle (salt/fluid); Uraemia; Reduced EF progression; Embolism (PE).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.front: EXAM PEARL: What distinguishes cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.back: Cardiogenic: elevated PCWP (>18 mmHg), elevated BNP, cardiac cause — vs ARDS (non-cardiogenic): normal PCWP, lung injury cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why does rhythm classification matter so much in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Rhythm classification determines the entire management pathway: shocking a non-shockable rhythm wastes time, while delaying adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm loses the only treatment that works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two SHOCKABLE arrest rhythms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless VT (pVT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two NON-SHOCKABLE arrest rhythms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe ventricular fibrillation (VF) and its ECG appearance.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Chaotic, disorganised electrical activity — the ventricles quiver with no coordinated contraction. The ECG shows erratic fibrillatory waveforms with no discernible QRS complexes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is pulseless VT (pVT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Organised ventricular tachycardia (wide QRS, rate >100) but with no palpable pulse — it is too fast for effective cardiac output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why does defibrillation work in VF/pVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A single high-energy shock simultaneously depolarises the entire myocardium → brief asystole → the intrinsic pacemakers can then restart a coordinated rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Organised electrical activity on the monitor (it looks like a rhythm) but with no palpable pulse — the electrical system is intact but mechanical function has failed. It is almost always caused by a reversible 4H/4T.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the defining feature of PEA on the monitor?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: It can look like any organised rhythm — the defining feature is the absence of a palpable pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is asystole, and what determines its outcome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A flat line — no electrical activity. It is terminal unless an underlying cause is identified and reversed rapidly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why is defibrillation ineffective in PEA and asystole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: There is no disorganised electrical activity to 'reset.' Defibrillating PEA or asystole does not help and wastes critical time.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the first intervention for a shockable rhythm vs a non-shockable rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: 1 shock → CPR for 2 minutes. Non-shockable: CPR for 2 minutes + adrenaline as soon as possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the main outcome driver in shockable vs non-shockable arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: early defibrillation. Non-shockable: finding and fixing the reversible cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the monitored arrest exception to the standard ALS sequence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: If the arrest is witnessed in a monitored environment (CCU, cath lab, ICU) and a defibrillator is immediately available, give 3 quick stacked shocks first, then begin the standard ALS cycle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the initial steps of the ALS algorithm before assessing the rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Confirm unresponsive + not breathing normally → call the resuscitation team / ambulance → start CPR 30:2 and attach the defibrillator/monitor → assess the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in CPR before the airway is secured?
In the shockable arm, what is the shock energy and why must it NOT be synchronised?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 shock, unsynchronised, 120–150 J biphasic. It must not be synchronised because there is no R wave to lock onto in VF/pVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: After delivering a shock in VF/pVT, what is done immediately?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes — do NOT pause to check the pulse after the shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In the shockable arm, when are adrenaline and amiodarone first given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: After the 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV (once compressions are restarted) and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is adrenaline repeated in the shockable arm after the first dose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (every alternate cycle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is the second dose of amiodarone given in the shockable arm, and what dose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: After the 5th shock: amiodarone 150 mg IV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In the non-shockable arm, what is done immediately after identifying PEA/asystole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes and give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as IV/IO access is obtained — do not delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does the timing of the first adrenaline dose differ between shockable and non-shockable arrests?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: adrenaline after the 3rd shock. Non-shockable: adrenaline immediately, as soon as IV/IO access is obtained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is adrenaline repeated in the non-shockable arm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (every other cycle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the two things NOT done in the non-shockable arm, and what replaces them as the priority?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: No defibrillation and no amiodarone. The priority instead is to identify and treat the reversible causes (the 4Hs and 4Ts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How often is the rhythm reassessed during an ALS cycle, regardless of arm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Every 2 minutes — both arms loop back to the rhythm check every 2 minutes until ROSC or a decision to stop.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Summarise the adrenaline 1 mg timing in shockable vs non-shockable arrest.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable (VF/pVT): after the 3rd shock, then every 3–5 min. Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): immediately, then every 3–5 min.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Summarise the amiodarone timing across shockable and non-shockable arrest.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Shockable: 300 mg after the 3rd shock and 150 mg after the 5th shock. Non-shockable: never given.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When should a thrombolytic be considered in cardiac arrest, and what does this change about CPR duration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Consider a thrombolytic if PE is suspected — and if given, continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after administration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the target depth and rate for high-quality chest compressions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Depth 5–6 cm (not deeper — risks injury) and rate 100–120/min (faster reduces perfusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why is full chest recoil between compressions important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Allowing complete chest recoil lets the heart refill — incomplete recoil reduces venous return and perfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the key quality rules for chest compressions regarding interruptions and compressor fatigue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Minimise interruptions (no pause >5 seconds), rotate the compressor every 2 minutes (fatigue rapidly degrades quality), and use a hard flat surface with hands in the centre of the sternum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why should the compressor be rotated every 2 minutes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Fatigue rapidly degrades compression quality (depth and rate), so swapping every 2 minutes maintains effectiveness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe Step 1 of airway progression in CPR.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Basic airway: head tilt–chin lift or jaw thrust, with a two-rescuer 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Describe Step 2 of airway progression (supraglottic airway).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Insert a supraglottic airway (LMA, iGel) without stopping CPR, then attempt ventilation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Once an endotracheal tube is secured, how does ventilation change?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Switch to continuous compressions (no pauses) and ventilate at 10 breaths/min (no ratio). Confirm tube placement immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is endotracheal tube placement confirmed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Waveform capnography (the gold standard), 5-point auscultation, and a CXR when the patient is stable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the first-line vascular access in CPR, and the key practical points?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: IV first-line: a large-bore peripheral cannula, antecubital fossa preferred, flushing drugs with a 20 mL bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is intraosseous (IO) access used, and how does it compare to IV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: IO is used if IV fails (sites: tibial, sternal, humeral). It is equally effective for all ALS drugs and rapid to insert under CPR conditions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does waveform capnography confirm correct ETT placement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A CO₂ waveform being present confirms the tube is in the trachea.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ETCO₂ value indicates adequate chest compressions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: ETCO₂ >2.0 kPa indicates adequate compressions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How does waveform capnography flag the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A sudden rise in ETCO₂ during CPR suggests ROSC — stop and check the pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What capnography finding is a poor prognostic marker in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A persistently very low ETCO₂ (<1.3 kPa / ~10 mmHg after 20 minutes of ALS) is a marker of poor prognosis — used only as one part of a multimodal assessment, never alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What can point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) identify during the pulse-check window in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Pericardial effusion/tamponade, cardiac motion (organised vs fine VF), IVC filling, and pneumothorax — all without interrupting CPR for more than the pulse-check window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why are the reversible causes (4Hs & 4Ts) so central to managing a non-shockable arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Non-shockable rhythms are won by finding and fixing the reversible cause — drugs alone will not restart the heart. In shockable rhythms you also search simultaneously, as failure to find the cause leads to re-arrest after ROSC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: List the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (reversible causes of cardiac arrest).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 4 Hs: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/Hyperkalaemia & metabolic, Hypothermia. 4 Ts: Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOXIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: low SpO₂, cyanosis, poor bag-mask seal, obstructed airway, inadequate ventilation. Treat: ensure the airway is open and patent, high-flow O₂, confirm ETT position, suction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOVOLAEMIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, haematemesis, AAA. Treat: rapid IV/IO fluids, blood products early, control the haemorrhage source (surgery/IR if needed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is hyperkalaemia recognised and treated during cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: known renal failure, peaked T waves / broad QRS / sine wave on ECG. Treat: calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV (also sodium bicarbonate if severe acidosis or TCA overdose).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How are hypoglycaemia and hypomagnesaemia treated in the metabolic 'H' of cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Hypoglycaemia: 10% glucose IV. Hypomagnesaemia: magnesium. (Calcium chloride is for hyperkalaemia; sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis or TCA overdose.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is HYPOTHERMIA recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: cold patient, core temp <30°C, J-waves (Osborn waves) on ECG, drowning/exposure. Treat: warm IV fluids, external warming (warm blankets, warmed humidified O₂), and ECMO for deep hypothermia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ECG finding is characteristic of hypothermia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: J-waves (Osborn waves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is coronary THROMBOSIS recognised and treated as a cause of arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: preceding chest pain, STEMI on ECG, known CAD. Treat: CPR whilst arranging PCI (primary PPCI) post-ROSC; thrombolysis if PCI is unavailable and PE is also suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is pulmonary THROMBOSIS (PE) recognised and treated as a cause of arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: PE risk factors, RBBB pattern, no other cause found, sudden arrest. Treat: thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV) — and continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after; surgical embolectomy if available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: If a thrombolytic is given for suspected PE in arrest, how long should CPR continue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For 60–90 minutes after administration, to allow the thrombolytic time to work.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: unequal/absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation (late), traumatic arrest, ventilated patient. Treat: immediate needle decompression → 2nd ICS midclavicular line → confirm with finger thoracostomy → chest drain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How is cardiac TAMPONADE recognised and treated in cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Recognise: penetrating chest trauma, known pericardial disease, Beck's triad (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds), POCUS showing a pericardial effusion. Treat: US-guided pericardiocentesis, or emergency thoracotomy if it is a traumatic arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is Beck's triad, and which reversible cause of arrest does it indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Raised JVP, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds — indicating cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: How are TOXINS recognised as a cause of cardiac arrest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Known ingestion/exposure, a brady- or tachyarrhythmia, miosis/mydriasis, and the history.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Match each specific antidote to its toxin in cardiac arrest: organophosphates, opioids, local anaesthetic toxicity, digoxin.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Organophosphates → atropine; opioids → naloxone; local anaesthetic toxicity → 20% lipid emulsion; digoxin → digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Activated charcoal only if alert and within 1 hour.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is UNSYNCHRONISED defibrillation used, and why is no synchronisation possible?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For VF / pulseless VT. There are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the device delivers the shock immediately on the button press.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What energy is used for unsynchronised defibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 120–150 J biphasic for the first shock, escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Where are the defibrillator pads placed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Right infraclavicular + left lateral (V5/apex position), or an anterior-posterior configuration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When is SYNCHRONISED cardioversion used, and how does the device behave?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: For an organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse. The device waits for the R wave, then shocks — avoiding delivery during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T → VF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: Why must a synchronised shock avoid the T-wave?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Delivering a shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T) can induce VF, so the device synchronises to the R wave.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What energies are used for synchronised cardioversion in AF vs flutter/SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: AF: 120–150 J biphasic. Flutter/SVT: 70–120 J biphasic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the defibrillation safety drill?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: 'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m from patient) · All clear · Shock' — visually confirm all personnel are clear before each shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the immediate (minutes) priorities of post-ROSC care?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: ABCDE reassessment, SpO₂ 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia), aim for normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa), IV fluid if hypotensive with vasopressors if needed, and a 12-lead ECG (STEMI → emergency PCI).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the oxygen saturation target post-ROSC, and why avoid hyperoxia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: SpO₂ 94–98%. Hyperoxia is harmful (oxidative injury), so 100% oxygen is weaned to this target range.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the target PaCO₂ post-ROSC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Normocapnia — PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What does targeted temperature management involve post-ROSC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Prevent fever (target 36°C), and consider cooling to 33°C for comatose survivors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What ongoing (ICU) post-ROSC measures are undertaken beyond temperature management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Identify and treat the cause (4Hs/4Ts, CTPA, echo, coronary angiography), neuroprotection with seizure monitoring and glucose control, and prognostication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: When should neurological prognostication be performed post-ROSC, and why the delay?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment, so early prognostication is unreliable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In what situations should CPR NOT be started?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: A valid DNACPR order in place, injuries incompatible with life, or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What are the criteria for stopping CPR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: ROSC achieved, all reversible causes excluded, prolonged ALS without ROSC (>20–30 min in most cases), and team-leader consensus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the hypothermic arrest exception to stopping CPR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Continue CPR until the core temperature is >35°C or ECMO is available — 'not dead until warm and dead'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the 'adrenaline timing trap' and why is it the most-tested ALS fact?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Non-shockable → give adrenaline immediately. Shockable → give adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st). The differing timing is the most commonly tested ALS point.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: In which arrest arm is amiodarone used, and where is it never used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Amiodarone is ONLY for the shockable arm. Never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is magnesium 2 g IV specifically indicated for in arrest, and is it routine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: It is the specific treatment for torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT). Magnesium is NOT routine in all cardiac arrests.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.front: What is the most time-critical post-arrest intervention if the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG shows a STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.back: Emergency PCI — a STEMI after ROSC mandates the most time-critical post-arrest intervention (emergency coronary intervention).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is tachycardia defined, and what is the first and most important ECG step?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A heart rate >100 bpm. The first and most important ECG step is to measure the QRS duration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What QRS duration defines a narrow-complex tachycardia, and what does it imply about origin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QRS <120 ms — a supraventricular origin, because the impulse uses the normal His-Purkinje system.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What QRS duration defines a broad-complex tachycardia, and what is the key rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QRS ≥120 ms — treat as ventricular until proven otherwise. It is the QRS width, not the origin, that triggers this rule.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of a REGULAR narrow-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sinus tachycardia, AVNRT (re-entry within the AV node), AVRT (re-entry via an accessory pathway), atrial tachycardia, and atrial flutter with fixed block (e.g. 2:1).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of an IRREGULAR narrow-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter with variable block, and multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of a REGULAR broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Ventricular tachycardia (VT — most likely), SVT with aberrant conduction (BBB), and SVT with pre-excitation (WPW).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the causes of an IRREGULAR broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF — dangerous), torsades de pointes / polymorphic VT, and AF with BBB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the key rule for any broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad-complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise. Never assume SVT with aberrancy without senior review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does a narrow QRS guarantee a supraventricular origin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A narrow QRS means the ventricles are being activated normally via the His-Purkinje system, so the rhythm must originate at or above the AV node ('narrow = safe').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) so dangerous, and what must be avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It can cause a broad, irregular tachycardia that mimics VF. Do NOT give AV nodal blockers — blocking the AV node forces conduction down the accessory pathway, which can precipitate VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the ECG diagnostic framework, what makes Step 2 (QRS width) a 'hard fork'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad-complex rhythms go directly to the VT feature checklist, not to P-wave analysis — the QRS width determines the entire management pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: On a tachycardia ECG, what do a completely irregular rhythm vs an irregular-with-a-pattern rhythm suggest?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Completely irregular (no pattern) → AF or multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT). Irregular with a pattern (e.g. varying groups) → atrial flutter with variable block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In narrow-complex P-wave analysis, what does a normal P wave before each QRS indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sinus tachycardia — treat the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In narrow-complex P-wave analysis, what do absent P waves with a chaotic baseline indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial fibrillation (fibrillatory f-waves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG finding of a sawtooth baseline at ~300 bpm indicates, and where is it best seen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial flutter — best seen in leads II, III, aVF and V1.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: A buried P wave producing a pseudo-R' in V1 and pseudo-S in II/aVF on a narrow-complex tachycardia points to which diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVNRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: A P wave after the QRS with RP < PR on a narrow-complex tachycardia points to which diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVRT (accessory pathway).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Abnormal P-wave morphology at a rate of 100–250 bpm on a narrow-complex tachycardia suggests what?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: When you identify a broad QRS, why must you NOT proceed to P-wave analysis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad QRS = VT until proven otherwise; instead of P-wave analysis you check for VT features.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is AV dissociation, and why is it diagnostic of VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: P waves march through independently of the QRS complexes — the atria and ventricles are beating independently, which is diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are capture beats and fusion beats, and what do they indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Capture beats = rare narrow QRS amid the broad complexes; fusion beats = hybrid morphology. Both are diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does 'concordance' mean on a broad-complex tachycardia ECG, and what does it favour?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: All the V (chest) leads deflect in the same direction — this favours VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the features that favour VT in a broad-complex tachycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats, concordance (all V leads same direction), atypical BBB morphology (doesn't match classic LBBB/RBBB), and structural heart disease / prior MI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: If uncertain whether a broad-complex tachycardia is VT or SVT, how should it be treated, and what must never be given?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat as VT. Never give verapamil to a broad-complex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the stability override principle in tachycardia management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Regardless of the rhythm diagnosis, haemodynamic instability = immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (or defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF). Do not delay to identify the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What features define an 'unstable' tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Hypotension (SBP <90), reduced consciousness (confusion, syncope, GCS drop), ischaemic chest pain (not palpitations alone), and acute pulmonary oedema (severe breathlessness, crepitations).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Do palpitations, anxiety or mild breathlessness count as instability in tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — the threshold for instability is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse, not symptoms like palpitations or mild breathlessness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does management differ between a stable and an unstable tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Stable → time to identify the rhythm, consider pharmacological options and vagal manoeuvres. Unstable → call for help, IV access, synchronised DC shock, sedation if conscious.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the central conceptual question for any stable tachycardia, and why does it matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 'Is the AV node in the circuit?' — it determines whether AV nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem) will terminate, slow, or endanger the patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which tachycardias have the AV node IN the re-entry circuit, and what do nodal blockers do?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AVNRT and AVRT (orthodromic) — the node is part of the circuit, so nodal blockers TERMINATE the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: For which rhythms do AV nodal blockers provide rate control only (not termination)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AF (atria sustain it; the node is gatekeeper), atrial flutter (macro re-entry in the atria only), atrial tachycardia (ectopic atrial focus), and sinus tachycardia (treat the cause). The node conducts but doesn't sustain the circuit, so blockers slow the rate but don't terminate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In which rhythms is the AV node NOT in the circuit, making nodal blockers dangerous or useless?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: VT (may cause arrest), pre-excited AF (WPW — blocking the AV node forces all conduction down the accessory pathway → VF), and antidromic AVRT (use procainamide/flecainide instead).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Give the key mnemonic linking narrow/regular/no-pre-excitation tachycardia to adenosine safety.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Narrow + regular + no pre-excitation → AV-node-dependent → adenosine is safe and likely terminates. Any broad-complex tachycardia → treat as VT; never give verapamil to a broad-complex rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the Resus Council adult tachycardia algorithm, what are the four life-threatening (unstable) features, and what is the treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and severe heart failure. Treatment: synchronised DC shock up to 3 attempts (sedation/anaesthesia if conscious); if unsuccessful, amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min then repeat the shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable narrow-complex REGULAR pathway, what is the first manoeuvre, and what drug follows if ineffective?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Vagal manoeuvres first. If ineffective, give adenosine (6 mg rapid IV bolus → 12 mg → 18 mg if needed) with continuous ECG monitoring; if still ineffective, verapamil or a beta-blocker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable narrow-complex IRREGULAR pathway (probable AF), how is rate controlled and when is anticoagulation considered?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Control rate with a beta-blocker; consider digoxin or amiodarone if there is evidence of heart failure. Anticoagulate if the duration is >48 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable broad-complex REGULAR pathway, what drug is given if it is VT or uncertain rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–60 min. If there is a previous certain diagnosis of SVT with BBB/aberrant conduction, treat as for a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: In the stable broad-complex IRREGULAR pathway, what are the possibilities and how is polymorphic VT (torsades) treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Possibilities include AF with BBB (treat as for irregular narrow-complex) or polymorphic VT (e.g. torsades de pointes) → give magnesium 2 g over 10 min.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What should be assessed and done in the initial ABCDE approach to any tachycardia, per the Resus algorithm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Give oxygen if SpO₂ <94%, obtain IV access, monitor ECG/BP/SpO₂ and record a 12-lead ECG, and identify/treat reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte abnormalities, hypovolaemia causing sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What three features do all irregular narrow-complex tachycardias share?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Narrow QRS (<120 ms), an irregularly irregular rhythm, and no consistent P–QRS relationship. The AV node is a bystander, not part of the circuit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the defining ECG features of AF among the irregular narrow-complex tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No P waves, a chaotic fibrillatory baseline (f-waves, best seen in V1), and completely irregular R-R intervals.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features distinguish variable-block atrial flutter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm (best in II, III, aVF), an irregular ventricular response (varying block ratio), and no isoelectric baseline.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features define multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
