conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead, varying PR intervals, and an irregular rhythm with a rate typically 100–150 bpm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the underlying mechanism of atrial fibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Disorganised atrial electrical activity driven by multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets — there is no single focus and no coordinated atrial contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three key consequences of atrial fibrillation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Haemodynamic (loss of atrial kick → cardiac output drops 10–20%, worse in diastolic dysfunction), thromboembolic (stasis in the left atrial appendage → thrombus → stroke/TIA, risk ×5 vs general population), and tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy if a sustained fast rate is untreated for months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: By how much does AF increase stroke risk compared with the general population?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Approximately five-fold (×5).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Define paroxysmal and persistent AF.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Paroxysmal = self-terminating <7 days (usually <48h), with sinus rhythm restored spontaneously. Persistent = duration >7 days; requires cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Define long-standing persistent and permanent AF.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Long-standing persistent = >12 months, with rhythm control still being attempted. Permanent = cardioversion abandoned; rate control and anticoagulation only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What distinguishes valvular from non-valvular AF, and why does it matter for anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Valvular AF = AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve. It matters because valvular AF requires warfarin (a VKA) — DOACs are contraindicated. All other AF is non-valvular → DOACs preferred.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does the SMITH mnemonic for the causes of AF stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: S – Sepsis, Surgery (post-op AF, esp. cardiac), Sleep apnoea; M – Mitral valve disease (MS/MR dilate the LA); I – IHD/MI, Inflammation (pericarditis, myocarditis), Idiopathic (lone AF); T – Thyroid (hyperthyroidism — always check TFTs in new AF); H – Hypertension (most common modifiable cause worldwide).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most common modifiable cause of AF worldwide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is 'holiday heart syndrome'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Binge drinking (alcohol) triggering paroxysmal AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Name additional causes of AF beyond the SMITH mnemonic.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Alcohol (holiday heart syndrome), PE, COPD/pneumonia, obesity, HF/cardiomyopathy, and caffeine/stimulants (minor risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the hallmark ECG feature of AF, and what is the atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An irregularly irregular rhythm (no two R-R intervals are equal) is the hallmark. The atrial rate is 350–600 bpm, with absent P waves replaced by fibrillatory f-waves (best in V1 and lead II).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the typical untreated ventricular rate in AF, and why is it slower than the atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Typically 100–160 bpm untreated — the AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses, so only some conduct to the ventricles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is unstable (haemodynamically compromised) AF managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of onset time — do not delay for anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the first-line rate-control agents in stable AF, and the key cautions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol) first-line, but avoid in decompensated HF. CCBs (diltiazem/verapamil) if beta-blockers are contraindicated, but avoid in HFrEF. Digoxin for sedentary patients or HF with AF (poor rate control on exertion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the heart rate targets for rate control in AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: HR <110 bpm at rest (lenient strategy); <80 bpm if symptomatic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: When can a patient with AF be cardioverted safely without prolonged anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: If onset is <48 hours (or they have been anticoagulated for ≥3 weeks) → cardiovert safely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is AF of >48h or unknown onset managed before cardioversion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Either perform a TOE to exclude a left atrial appendage thrombus, OR anticoagulate for ≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks after cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which chemical cardioversion agents are used in AF, and when is each chosen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Flecainide if there is no structural heart disease; amiodarone if there is structural heart disease or HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the energy for electrical cardioversion of AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Synchronised DC shock, starting at 120–150 J biphasic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the CHA₂DS₂-VASc factors and their point values.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: C – Congestive HF (or LVEF <40%) = 1; H – Hypertension = 1; A – Age ≥75 = 2; D – Diabetes = 1; S₂ – Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism = 2; V – Vascular disease (prior MI, PAD, aortic plaque) = 1; A – Age 65–74 = 1; Sc – Sex (female) = 1.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How do CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores translate into anticoagulation decisions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Score ≥2 (male) / ≥3 (female) → anticoagulate (benefit clearly outweighs risk). Score 1 (male) / 2 (female) → consider anticoagulation (clinical judgement). Score 0 (male) / 1 (female) → no anticoagulation (risk too low to justify bleeding risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which anticoagulant is preferred in non-valvular AF, and which is required in valvular AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) are preferred for non-valvular AF. Warfarin (VKA) is required for valvular AF (mechanical valve, moderate-to-severe MS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the macro re-entry circuit responsible for typical atrial flutter, and what is the critical slow zone?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A macro re-entry circuit circulating around the tricuspid annulus. The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — tissue between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava — is the critical slow zone; ablating it breaks the circuit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of atrial flutter, including the typical atrial rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial rate ~300 bpm (range 250–350), sawtooth flutter waves (inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1), and no isoelectric baseline between flutter waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does AV block ratio affect the appearance of atrial flutter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Variable AV block → irregular ventricular response. Fixed 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150, regular (which then appears as a regular narrow-complex tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does anticoagulation and cardioversion in atrial flutter compare with AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds — the stroke risk is equivalent. The same <48h / >48h anticoagulation rule applies. Flutter is often more cardioversion-responsive than AF, needing lower energy (50–100 J biphasic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the curative treatment for typical atrial flutter, and how effective is it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: CTI (cavotricuspid isthmus) ablation — curative in ~95% of typical flutter; first-line for recurrent or persistent flutter.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is cardioversion ineffective in multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: MAT is caused by multiple ectopic atrial foci firing chaotically — it is NOT a single re-entry circuit, so there is no circuit to interrupt with a shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the cornerstone of MAT management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat the underlying cause — oxygen for hypoxia, optimise COPD, and correct Mg²⁺ and K⁺.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the preferred rate-control agent in MAT, and what is avoided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A CCB (verapamil or diltiazem) is preferred; avoid beta-blockers in bronchospasm (MAT is often associated with COPD).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Does MAT require routine anticoagulation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — MAT does not carry the same stroke risk as AF/flutter; it is not a re-entry rhythm with atrial stasis in the same way.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What three features do all regular narrow-complex tachycardias share?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Narrow QRS (<120 ms), regular R–R intervals, and a rate >100 bpm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Into which three groups are the regular narrow-complex tachycardias divided by AV-node involvement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Group A — re-entry with the AV node IN the circuit (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT); Group B — AV node a bystander (atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter with fixed 2:1); Group C — normal pacemaker (sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the '150 bpm trap' in regular narrow-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly ~150 bpm should be assumed to be atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block until proven otherwise. P (flutter) waves may be hidden in the T waves; give adenosine to unmask them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the shared treatment principle for Group A (AV-node-dependent) tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The AV node is an essential part of the re-entry circuit, so blocking it (vagal manoeuvres or adenosine) terminates the arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is AVNRT, how common is it, and who does it affect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrioventricular Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia — the most common paroxysmal SVT. It affects young adults, more commonly women, with abrupt onset and offset (an 'on-off switch').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Describe the mechanism of AVNRT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Two pathways within the AV node — slow (longer ERP) and fast (shorter ERP). A premature atrial beat finds the fast pathway refractory, travels down the slow pathway, and re-enters up the fast → a sustained loop. Atria and ventricles are activated nearly simultaneously (P buried in or just after the QRS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Rate 140–280 bpm, regular, narrow QRS. P waves are buried in the QRS or immediately after → pseudo-R' in V1 (most useful sign) or pseudo-S in II/III/aVF. Short RP interval (RP < PR). Abrupt onset, often triggered by a PAC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most useful ECG sign of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A pseudo-R' in V1 (from the P wave buried just after the QRS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the stepwise acute treatment of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Step 1: vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva with legs elevated, or carotid sinus massage — terminates ~25%). Step 2: adenosine IV (6 mg rapid bolus → 12 mg → 18 mg). Step 3 if adenosine fails: verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV (not if broad complex/pre-excitation) or metoprolol IV; synchronised DC cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does adenosine work in AVNRT, and what must the patient be warned about?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It transiently blocks the AV node → terminates the circuit. Warn the patient about flushing, chest tightness and brief asystole (seconds). It is contraindicated in asthma and high-degree AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the long-term/recurrent management of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Flecainide or a beta-blocker for prevention; slow-pathway catheter ablation is curative (>95% success, low risk of AV block).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is orthodromic AVRT, and what is the path of conduction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Re-entry using an accessory pathway (e.g. Bundle of Kent in WPW). Orthodromic = conduction down the AV node and up the accessory pathway → narrow QRS (normal ventricular activation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Rate 150–250 bpm, regular, narrow QRS. P wave after the QRS → RP < PR (inverted P in II/III/aVF), but a longer RP than AVNRT (P clearly visible after the QRS, not buried). In sinus rhythm, look for a short PR + delta wave (WPW).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How does the P-wave position differ between AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In AVNRT the P is buried in/just after the QRS (very short RP). In orthodromic AVRT the P is clearly visible after the QRS (longer RP, though still RP < PR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG hallmarks of WPW in sinus rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A short PR interval and a delta wave (δ) — the diagnostic hallmark of pre-excitation, caused by the accessory pathway pre-exciting the ventricle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does orthodromic AVRT produce a narrow QRS while antidromic AVRT produces a broad QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Orthodromic (~95%): antegrade down the AV node → His-Purkinje → ventricles activated via normal wiring → narrow QRS. Antidromic (~5%): antegrade down the accessory pathway straight into ventricular muscle, bypassing His-Purkinje → abnormal sequential spread → broad QRS (mimics VT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What do 'orthodromic' and 'antidromic' refer to in AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 'Ortho' = correct direction (antegrade down the AV node); 'anti' = opposite direction (antegrade down the accessory pathway). The pathway taken determines the QRS width.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the treatment of orthodromic AVRT, including the definitive option?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Same stepwise approach as AVNRT — vagal manoeuvres → adenosine → verapamil/beta-blocker → DC cardioversion if unstable. Definitive: accessory pathway ablation (curative). Long-term, avoid AV nodal blockers if WPW is present in sinus rhythm (risk of pre-excited AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why must antidromic AVRT be managed differently from orthodromic AVRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Antidromic AVRT (conduction down the accessory pathway, up the AV node) is a broad-complex tachycardia, so it is treated differently (as per the Regular Broad section), not with AV nodal blockers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the shared principle for Group B (AV node a bystander) tachycardias?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The AV node conducts the impulse to the ventricles but is not part of the sustaining circuit. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction → unmasks the underlying atrial activity (diagnostic) but does not terminate. Manage with rate control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism and rate of atrial tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An ectopic atrial focus firing faster than the sinus node (enhanced automaticity or micro re-entry), at a rate of 100–250 bpm, regular.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the 'warm-up' phenomenon in atrial tachycardia, and what does it distinguish it from?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The rate gradually accelerates at the start ('warm-up'), which distinguishes it from AVNRT/AVRT, both of which have an abrupt onset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of atrial tachycardia (P wave and PR interval)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Abnormal P-wave morphology (differs from the sinus P in the same lead; P axis depends on focus location), and a normal or prolonged PR interval (because the AV node is not part of the circuit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the causes of atrial tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Structural heart disease, digoxin toxicity, alcohol, and hypoxia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is atrial tachycardia treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat the underlying cause (especially digoxin toxicity — stop digoxin), rate control with beta-blockers or CCBs, rhythm control if needed (flecainide, amiodarone), and focal catheter ablation if recurrent and drug-refractory. Adenosine may transiently block the AV node and reveal atrial activity but rarely terminates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Atrial rate ~300 bpm with fixed 2:1 AV block → ventricular rate ~150 bpm, regular. Sawtooth flutter waves (inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1), with no isoelectric baseline. Flutter waves may be hidden in the T waves at 2:1 — look carefully.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the '150 bpm rule' for atrial flutter, and how can adenosine help?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Any regular narrow tachycardia at ~150 bpm → consider flutter first. Adenosine increases AV block transiently → the flutter waves become visible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is fixed 2:1 atrial flutter managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Rate control with beta-blockers, CCBs or digoxin (same as AF); anticoagulation using the same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds as AF; cardioversion (highly effective, often lower energy than AF, 50–100 J); CTI ablation (curative ~95%).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the key principle about sinus tachycardia (Group C)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sinus tachycardia is always a response to something — it is physiologically appropriate. Never rate-block it without identifying and treating the cause, as slowing the rate without addressing the driver can be dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the ECG features of sinus tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Rate 100–160 bpm (rarely >200 in adults), a normal upright P wave before every QRS (identical morphology throughout), a normal PR interval (0.12–0.20 s), gradual onset and offset (not abrupt), and rate that varies with respiration and activity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What does the PIRATES mnemonic for the causes of sinus tachycardia stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: P – Pain, PE, Pneumothorax; I – Infection/Sepsis, Inflammation; R – Respiratory failure (hypoxia); A – Anaemia, Anxiety, Alcohol withdrawal; T – Thyrotoxicosis, Tamponade; E – Exercise, Electrolyte imbalance; S – Shock (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive), Stimulants.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is sinus tachycardia managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat the underlying cause. Beta-blockers or CCBs may be used symptomatically in specific contexts (e.g. inappropriate sinus tachycardia, thyrotoxicosis) but only after the cause is established.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the three-way treatment split for regular narrow-complex tachycardias by the unifying question.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The unifying question is 'Is the AV node part of the circuit?' Yes → terminate (Group A: vagal/adenosine/ablation). No, but conduction via it → rate control (Group B: beta-blockers/CCBs/digoxin; adenosine is diagnostic only). No, physiological → treat the cause (Group C: sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the 'Golden Rule' for any regular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Treat every regular broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise. Misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) can be fatal; treating SVT as VT is always safe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three causes of a regular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 4A — Ventricular tachycardia (origin in ventricle; most common cause; default assumption); 4B — SVT with aberrancy (SVT + bundle branch block; pre-existing or rate-related; looks broad but isn't VT); 4C — SVT with pre-excitation (antidromic AVRT in WPW; conducts down the accessory pathway; rare but important).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is a broad QRS defined, and what three factors guide the diagnosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Broad QRS = ≥120 ms (3 small squares), rate >100 bpm, regular R–R intervals. History, ECG morphology, and haemodynamic context guide the diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does VT produce a wide QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: The impulse originates below the His bundle in ventricular myocardium and spreads cell-to-cell (not via the His-Purkinje system) — this slow, abnormal depolarisation produces a wide QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the most common substrate for VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Re-entry around scar tissue from a prior MI or ischaemic heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is monomorphic VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: VT with the same QRS morphology throughout, arising from a stable re-entry circuit. (Polymorphic VT / torsades is covered under irregular broad tachycardias.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is a history of ischaemic heart disease or prior MI critical when assessing a broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In any patient with known IHD or prior MI, a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT until definitively proven otherwise — the scar provides the re-entry substrate, raising the pre-test probability of VT to >95%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Does haemodynamic stability rule out VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: No — patients can be in VT and remain haemodynamically stable. This is a common and dangerous trap.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the ECG features with HIGH specificity for VT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS march independently — pathognomonic), capture beats (occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles), fusion beats (hybrid QRS when sinus and ventricular impulses collide), and concordance (all precordial leads V1–V6 point the same direction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the supportive (less specific) features favouring VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Very broad QRS (>140 ms — the wider, the more likely VT), extreme axis deviation (north-west axis / 'no man's land', −90° to ±180°), RS interval >100 ms in any precordial lead (Brugada criterion), an RBBB-like pattern but with a dominant S in V6 (not a tall R), and an LBBB-like pattern but with Q or R in V1 (not a pure negative deflection).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What defines 'unstable' VT requiring immediate cardioversion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Any of: hypotension, shock, syncope, pulmonary oedema, or ischaemic chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is UNSTABLE VT managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious — midazolam/propofol). If pulseless, treat as VF — unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR (arrest algorithm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is STABLE VT managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min (first-line UK), then 900 mg over 24h maintenance. Correct electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺). Procainamide or lidocaine are alternatives. Prepare for cardioversion if drug therapy fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of SVT with aberrancy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: A supraventricular rhythm (AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia) conducts normally to the AV node, but below the AV node conduction is blocked or delayed in one bundle branch. The ventricle depolarises via the opposite bundle — slow spread → broad QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the difference between pre-existing BBB and rate-related (phase 3) BBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Pre-existing BBB is present at baseline with the same morphology in sinus rhythm. Rate-related (phase 3) BBB appears only at faster rates when the bundle's refractory period is exceeded.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What ECG features help distinguish SVT with aberrancy from VT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology (not atypical), no AV dissociation (no capture or fusion beats), P waves visible and 1:1 with QRS, identical morphology to a prior 12-lead (if pre-existing BBB), a narrow QRS at a slower rate on a previous ECG (if rate-related), and termination/slowing with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the clinical bottom line for using adenosine in a suspected SVT with aberrancy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Adenosine is useful diagnostically — but only if you are confident this is NOT VT (old 12-lead showing BBB, no structural heart disease, haemodynamically stable, classic SVT history). When in doubt, treat as VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Describe the classic RBBB vs LBBB morphology used to identify aberrancy.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: RBBB: rSR' in V1 and qRs in V6. LBBB: rS in V1 and R in V6. SVT with aberrancy shows one of these classic patterns — atypical morphology favours VT instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is antidromic AVRT, and what is its conduction path?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In WPW, the accessory pathway conducts both ways. Antidromic: the impulse travels antegrade DOWN the accessory pathway, then retrograde UP the His-AV node. The ventricle depolarises entirely via the AP → maximally pre-excited → very broad, slurred QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How common is antidromic AVRT, and what are its ECG/clinical features?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Uncommon — ~5–10% of AVRT in WPW patients. ECG: broad, maximally pre-excited QRS (may resemble LBBB or be atypical), regular tachycardia ~150–250 bpm, NO AV dissociation (the AV node is part of the circuit retrogradely). A history of WPW or a δ-wave on the baseline ECG is a diagnostic clue.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in antidromic AVRT / pre-excited WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) block retrograde AV conduction, which may force all conduction antegrade down the accessory pathway → risk of VF. Use flecainide or procainamide instead (or DC cardioversion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What happens if AF develops in a patient with WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: It becomes pre-excited AF — a life-threatening irregular broad-complex tachycardia (covered under the irregular broad section).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the ECG/clinical features that FAVOUR VT in the VT-vs-SVT decision.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: AV dissociation (pathognomonic), capture or fusion beats, concordance in precordial leads, QRS >140 ms, extreme/north-west axis, known IHD or prior MI, structural heart disease, and atypical BBB morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the features that FAVOUR SVT with aberrancy in the VT-vs-SVT decision.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology, P waves clearly 1:1 with the QRS, no AV dissociation/capture/fusion, identical to a prior ECG with BBB, young patient with no structural heart disease, termination with adenosine, and a prior history of SVT with no syncope.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three safety rules summarising VT-vs-SVT management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 1) Stability first — unstable → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of diagnosis. 2) Doubt = VT — if you cannot confidently exclude VT, treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex tachycardia. 3) The unifying question — 'Could this be VT?' If yes, treat as VT; step down only with clear evidence and specialist input.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the danger instinct to instil for any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Irregular + broad → think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise. Never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers — it can be fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three causes of an irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 5A — Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF; very fast, varying width; the lethal trap); 5B — Polymorphic VT / Torsades (twisting QRS morphology, long QT substrate, can degenerate to VF); 5C — AF with BBB (ordinary AF + block, fixed BBB morphology, managed as AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is a broad QRS defined for the irregular broad tachycardias, and why does distinguishing them matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: ≥120 ms, rate >100 bpm, irregular R–R intervals. Distinguishing the three causes determines whether you give a nodal blocker or avoid it entirely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of pre-excited AF in WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: In WPW the accessory pathway (AP) bypasses the AV node. When AF develops, the chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the AP — bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating — so the ventricles are bombarded at near-atrial rates (300–600 bpm atrial, often >200 bpm ventricular).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why does the QRS width vary beat-to-beat in pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Each beat may conduct via the AP, the AV node, or both — producing fusion beats with varying QRS width from one beat to the next.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Irregular R–R intervals (underlying AF), broad QRS (conducted via AP), very fast (ventricular rate often >200 bpm), varying QRS width (beat-to-beat fusion), no organised P waves, and — if seen prior — a short PR + delta wave on the baseline WPW ECG.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why must AV-nodal blockers NEVER be given in pre-excited AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin block the AV node and force all conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme rate acceleration → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is UNSTABLE pre-excited AF managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious). If it has degenerated to VF → unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is STABLE pre-excited AF managed pharmacologically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Flecainide IV (first-line if no structural heart disease) or procainamide IV (alternative, safe with structural disease). Both work by slowing AP conduction, not by blocking the AV node. Consider early cardioversion if the drug response is slow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is polymorphic VT, and what defines torsades de pointes specifically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Polymorphic VT is VT with continuously varying QRS morphology and axis — irregular, 'twisting around the baseline'. Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism linking a prolonged QT to torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Prolonged QT → prolonged repolarisation → spontaneous depolarisation in some cells (early after-depolarisations) → triggered VT. It is typically self-terminating but can degenerate to VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the ECG signature of torsades de pointes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: An irregular broad-complex tachycardia where the QRS complexes twist around the isoelectric baseline — amplitude waxes and wanes over 5–20 beats. The preceding sinus rhythm shows a long QT (key diagnostic clue). Rate typically 160–250 bpm; may self-terminate, recur, or degenerate to VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is the QT interval measured, and what QTc values count as prolonged?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: QT is measured from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave. Corrected QT (QTc) >440 ms (men) or >460 ms (women) is prolonged.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Name the congenital causes of a prolonged QT interval.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Long QT syndrome (LQTS — a channelopathy), Romano-Ward (autosomal dominant), and Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (associated with deafness).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: List the high-yield drug causes of a prolonged QT.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antidepressants (citalopram, TCAs), antibiotics (macrolides — erythromycin, clarithromycin), antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone), and antimalarials (chloroquine, quinine).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Which electrolyte abnormalities cause a prolonged QT, and which is the most common?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Hypokalaemia (the most common electrolyte cause), hypomagnesaemia, and hypocalcaemia — all impair repolarisation and lengthen the QT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is unstable or pulseless torsades managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Unsynchronised defibrillation (polymorphic morphology makes synchronisation unreliable). If pulseless → arrest algorithm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the first-line treatment for stable torsades de pointes, and the key point about it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — first-line even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal, because it stabilises cardiac membranes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Beyond magnesium, what are the management steps for stable torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Correct electrolytes (K⁺ >4.5 mmol/L; Mg²⁺ >1 mmol/L; Ca²⁺), stop all QT-prolonging drugs immediately, treat the underlying cause, consider temporary (overdrive) pacing — which shortens the QT, ICD if recurrent/congenital LQTS, and avoid amiodarone (it itself prolongs QT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Why is the distinction between sotalol and other beta-blockers important in torsades?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades — do not confuse it with other beta-blockers, which are safe and actually used in congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What is the mechanism of AF with BBB, and why is it the 'less scary' irregular broad rhythm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB. The AF provides the irregularity and the BBB provides the broad QRS. The AV node is intact and still rate-limiting (ventricular rate rarely >180 bpm) — it's just AF that looks broad.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How do you distinguish pre-excited AF from AF with BBB on rate, QRS width, history and treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Pre-excited AF: rate >200 bpm, QRS width varies beat-to-beat, history of WPW/δ-wave, treat with flecainide/DC. AF with BBB: rate typically <180 bpm, fixed BBB morphology, known BBB/structural disease, treat with rate control + anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: How is AF with BBB managed once pre-excited AF is confidently excluded?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker / CCB / digoxin) and anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. If in doubt, treat as pre-excited AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: Summarise the discriminating features of pre-excited AF, torsades, and AF+BBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: Pre-excited AF: very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, history of WPW/δ-wave, no clear BBB pattern. Torsades: twisting QRS, preceding long QT, drug/electrolyte history, self-terminating but recurrent. AF+BBB: slower rate (<180 bpm), fixed BBB morphology, classic RBBB/LBBB, known BBB or structural disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.front: What are the three safety rules for any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.back: 1) Stability first — unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF). 2) No AV-nodal blockers — never give adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers or digoxin until pre-excited AF is excluded. 3) Deterioration risk — both pre-excited AF and torsades can degenerate to VF, so have a defibrillator immediately available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFrEF = EF <40% — pump failure (systolic dysfunction). The 'classic' HF treated with the 'fantastic four'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFpEF = EF ≥50% with symptoms and diastolic dysfunction. Common in elderly, hypertensive, obese, diabetic patients. Fewer proven therapies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the 'fantastic four' in HFrEF management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: ACE inhibitor (or ARB/ARNI), beta-blocker, MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone), SGLT2 inhibitor — all reduce mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What does ARNI stand for and what is the example?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor — sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto). Replaces ACE inhibitor in HFrEF if still symptomatic — reduces hospitalisation and mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the role of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Dapagliflozin/empagliflozin reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF (and increasingly HFpEF) — even in non-diabetics. Diuretic-like effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are indications for cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: HFrEF (EF ≤35%) + LBBB with QRS ≥130 ms + NYHA II–IV despite optimal medical therapy — restores synchronised ventricular contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are indications for ICD in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Primary prevention: EF ≤35% + NYHA II–III + >3 months optimal therapy — ICD reduces sudden cardiac death from VT/VF.
I: No symptoms; II: Symptoms on moderate exertion; III: Symptoms on mild exertion; IV: Symptoms at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are the causes of HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Ischaemic cardiomyopathy (most common — post-MI), dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertension, valve disease, arrhythmia (tachycardia-induced), toxins (alcohol, chemotherapy).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What are loop diuretics used for in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Symptom relief — reduce fluid overload (oedema, pulmonary congestion). Furosemide is first-line. Do NOT reduce mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: Why are CCBs (except amlodipine/felodipine) contraindicated in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Negative inotropes — worsen systolic function. Amlodipine/felodipine are vascular-selective and safe if needed for angina/hypertension in HFrEF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the role of digoxin in heart failure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Rate control in AF + HF (no longer first-line for sinus rhythm HFrEF). Reduces hospitalisation but no mortality benefit. Narrow therapeutic window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: What is the target heart rate in heart failure on beta-blocker?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: Resting HR 50–70 bpm on beta-blocker. Evidence-based doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25–50 mg, nebivolol 10 mg.
Right heart failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension from lung disease — RV hypertrophy/dilatation. Causes: COPD, PE, OSA, pulmonary fibrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the single most important prognostic intervention in HFrEF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.back: ACE inhibitor (or ARNI) + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i = the fantastic four — ALL reduce mortality independently. Start all four at lowest doses and uptitrate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Anticoagulate — DOAC first-line (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
Structural heart disease (IHD, HF, LVH) — proarrhythmic
TFTs + LFTs every 6 months + CXR annually (pulmonary fibrosis) + eye exam (corneal deposits)
Atrial ~300bpm, ventricles 150bpm (2:1 block) — sawtooth F waves in II, III, aVF
Infrequent paroxysmal AF + no structural heart disease + well-tolerated episodes — flecainide
Shock on R wave — avoids T wave (vulnerable period) → prevents VF induction
Minimum 4 weeks regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc — atrial stunning
Rhythm control under therapeutic anticoagulation cover (LMWH/heparin or a DOAC — NOT antiplatelets) — can cardiovert pharmacologically (flecainide/amiodarone) or electrically.
3 weeks anticoagulation OR TOE to exclude LAA thrombus
Adenosine · Digoxin · Beta-blockers · Rate-limiting CCBs — all block AV node → forces conduction via accessory pathway → VF
Idarucizumab (Praxbind) — monoclonal antibody fragment
Andexanet alfa — for rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban
<80bpm at rest (lenient: <110bpm acceptable in stable patients per RACE II)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Digoxin: best for rate control in?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Sedentary/elderly patients. Ineffective during exercise (purely vagotonic).
5mg BD (reduce to 2.5mg BD if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60kg, Cr ≥133 μmol/L)
Catheter ablation of PV ostia — eliminates ectopic triggers. Success ~50–80% paroxysmal AF at 1 year.
<48h (usually <24h)
Cardioversion not pursued — rate control only by patient and clinician choice

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Fall risk: threshold to withhold anticoagulation in AF?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Patient must fall ~295 times/year to offset stroke benefit — falls alone are NOT a contraindication
Rate control = rhythm control for mortality. Rhythm control had more hospitalisations. Use based on symptoms.
Curative for typical atrial flutter (>95% success)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: AF + HFrEF: rate control drug of choice?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol) — NOT diltiazem/verapamil (negatively inotropic)
Prolonged uncontrolled tachycardia (AF) → reversible cardiomyopathy. Rate control → EF improves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Warfarin target INR for non-valvular AF?

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Supraventricular tachycardia — any tachyarrhythmia (HR >100 bpm) originating above the bundle of His. Includes AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the most common form of paroxysmal SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: AVNRT (AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia) — accounts for ~60% of SVTs. Due to dual AV nodal pathways forming a re-entrant circuit.
AV re-entrant tachycardia — re-entrant circuit using AV node + accessory pathway (bypass tract). Divided into: orthodromic (narrow complex) and antidromic (wide complex).

Pre-excitation syndrome — congenital accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypassing the AV node. ECG: short PR interval + delta wave + wide QRS. Risk of AF conducting rapidly via accessory pathway → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the ECG appearance of AVNRT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Narrow complex tachycardia (HR 150–250 bpm), regular rhythm, P waves buried in or just after QRS (retrograde — 'pseudo-r' in V1), abrupt onset/offset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the first-line treatment for acute SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) — first-line. Then IV adenosine (6 mg, 12 mg, 18 mg). If haemodynamically unstable: DC cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: Why is adenosine used in SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Adenosine blocks AV node conduction temporarily — terminates re-entrant SVTs depending on the AV node. Causes transient asystole/bradycardia. Very short half-life (10 seconds).
Asthma (bronchoconstriction), WPW (may enhance accessory pathway conduction causing AF → VF), sick sinus syndrome, second/third-degree AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the long-term treatment for recurrent SVT?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Catheter ablation (radiofrequency) — first-line for recurrent symptomatic SVT. Curative in >95% of AVNRT. Medical: beta-blocker or flecainide as second-line.
Patient-initiated flecainide or propafenone taken at onset of SVT — for infrequent, well-tolerated episodes. Avoids need for daily prophylaxis.

Regular atrial tachycardia at ~300 bpm with 2:1 (or variable) AV block → ventricular rate ~150 bpm. ECG: sawtooth flutter waves (negative in II, III, aVF). Re-entrant circuit in right atrium around tricuspid annulus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: What is the ECG appearance of atrial flutter with 2:1 block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Regular narrow complex tachycardia at ~150 bpm with sawtooth flutter waves at 300 bpm — 'think atrial flutter when rate is exactly 150 bpm'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: How is WPW treated acutely if AF develops?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: DC cardioversion or procainamide/flecainide (avoid adenosine, digoxin, verapamil — these block AV node and may increase accessory pathway conduction → VF).
Forced expiration against closed glottis — increases vagal tone → slows/blocks AV node → terminates AVNRT. Modified: strain then leg raise (more effective). First-line non-pharmacological treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.front: EXAM PEARL: What 3 findings on ECG suggest WPW?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.back: Short PR interval (<120 ms) + delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) + wide QRS — the WPW triad. If AF occurs with WPW: irregular wide complex tachycardia (pre-excited AF) = emergency DC cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why is hypertension called the 'silent killer'?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It is a sustained elevation of BP that is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is hypertension diagnosed, and why is the confirmation step needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Via clinic measurement, then confirmed with ABPM or HBPM (ambulatory/home) to exclude the white-coat effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic BP and ABPM/HBPM thresholds for Stage 1 hypertension, and when is it treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic ≥140/90, ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85. Treat if <80 yrs with end-organ damage, CV risk >10%, or T2DM/CKD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the Stage 2 hypertension thresholds, and what is the treatment rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic ≥160/100, ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95. Offer treatment regardless of other factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What defines Stage 3 / Severe hypertension, and what is the action?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic ≥180/120. Same-day assessment for end-organ damage; if present → hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: State the key diagnostic rule linking clinic BP to confirmation and treatment threshold.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic BP 140/90–180/120 → confirm with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing. Treat to the lower ambulatory threshold. White-coat hypertension is common — ABPM prevents over-treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What proportion of hypertension is primary/essential, and what characterises it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: ~90%. No identifiable cause; polygenic (multiple genes + lifestyle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: List the risk factors for primary hypertension.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Age, obesity, high salt diet, alcohol, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, family history.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the proposed mechanism of primary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Increased RAAS activity, sympathetic overdrive, and impaired renal sodium excretion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the commonest category of secondary hypertension, and which renal causes are included?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Renal (commonest, ~80% of secondary) — CKD, renovascular disease (RAS — especially if treatment-resistant), polycystic kidney disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: List the endocrine causes of secondary hypertension.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism), phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, acromegaly, hypothyroidism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which 'other' (non-renal, non-endocrine) causes of secondary hypertension are listed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Coarctation of the aorta (young patients), pre-eclampsia, OSA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which drugs can cause secondary hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: NSAIDs, oestrogen (OCP), alcohol, liquorice, cocaine, ciclosporin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: When should you 'think secondary' hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Young, Resistant (≥3 drugs), or Sudden onset — especially patients under 40, those with refractory HTN, or an identifiable clinical clue (e.g. hypokalaemia → Conn's; episodic headache/sweating/palpitations → phaeochromocytoma).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Is primary hypertension symptomatic, and what do symptoms usually signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It is largely asymptomatic; symptoms usually signify end-organ damage or an underlying secondary cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the neurological red flags of accelerated/malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Headache (occipital, morning), visual disturbance, seizures, confusion, encephalopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What retinal red flag confirms malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages, exudates — confirm malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cardiac and renal red flags of malignant hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Cardiac: chest pain (ACS / aortic dissection), breathlessness (acute LVF). Renal: haematuria, oliguria — AKI from malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Renal/RAS as a secondary cause: what symptoms/signs and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms/signs: renal bruit, peripheral oedema, resistant HTN. Clue: rising Cr on ACEi, asymmetric kidneys on USS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Conn's syndrome as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms: muscle weakness, polyuria, cramps. Clue: hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Phaeochromocytoma as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor. Clue: paroxysmal BP spikes; 24h urinary catecholamines / metanephrines.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Cushing's as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms: central obesity, striae, buffalo hump, moon face. Clue: 24h urinary free cortisol / overnight dexamethasone suppression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Coarctation as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms: young patient, radiofemoral delay, weak femoral pulses. Clue: BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Pre-eclampsia as a secondary cause: what symptoms and what clue?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Symptoms: HTN after 20 weeks, oedema, proteinuria, headache. Clue: pregnancy — screen for HELLP (haemolysis, raised LFTs, low platelets).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: On fundoscopy, how does a normal optic disc differ from papilloedema, and what does papilloedema indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Normal optic disc has a sharp disc margin; papilloedema has a blurred disc margin. It indicates severely raised ICP from a hypertensive emergency — grade IV Keith-Wagener retinopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What fundoscopy features make up hypertensive retinopathy, and which grade signifies a hypertensive emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Haemorrhage (grade III), hard exudates (lipid deposits), soft exudates (cotton-wool spots = micro-infarcts), microaneurysms; grade III/IV = hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 of diagnosis — how is the clinic measurement performed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic measurement ≥140/90: use a validated device, average of 2 readings, confirm on a second visit unless ≥180/120.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How are ABPM and HBPM performed, and which threshold is used to diagnose?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: ABPM: average of readings during waking hours. HBPM: 2 readings morning + evening for 4–7 days. Diagnose using the lower ambulatory threshold (≥135/85 Stage 1).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In the work-up, what are the two parallel goals?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Assess end-organ damage, and identify secondary causes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which investigations assess end-organ damage in hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Urine ACR (nephropathy/proteinuria); U&E/Cr/eGFR (CKD, baseline before ACEi); ECG (LVH — Sokolow-Lyon criteria, AF); fundoscopy (retinopathy grading — Keith-Wagener); fasting glucose/HbA1c (T2DM); lipid profile (CV risk assessment).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which investigations help identify secondary causes of hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: U&E (low K+ suggests Conn's or Cushing's); aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn's if low K+ or resistant HTN); 24h urinary catecholamines/metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma); renal USS ± Doppler (RAS, polycystic kidney disease); overnight dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's); TFTs (hypo/hyperthyroidism).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is QRISK3 used in hypertension management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Calculate the 10-year cardiovascular risk. If >10% → offer atorvastatin 20 mg (primary prevention). If already diagnosed with CVD → statin regardless of risk score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why is drug choice in hypertension driven by age and ethnicity?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: They predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Explain the renin logic that makes the ACD algorithm memorable.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Younger/Caucasian = high-renin → RAAS-dependent → ACEi/ARB works. Older/Black African/Caribbean = low-renin → volume-dependent → CCB or diuretic works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 monotherapy: what is first-line for a patient <55 yrs and not Black African/Caribbean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: A — ACEi or ARB (e.g. ramipril or losartan); a high-renin state where RAAS blockade is most effective. T2DM at any age/ethnicity → A.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 1 monotherapy: what is first-line for a patient ≥55 yrs or Black African/Caribbean (any age)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: C — calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine, a dihydropyridine); a low-renin state where volume/vascular tone reduction is most effective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the Step 2 (two-drug) combination in hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: A + C (preferred), or A + D if a CCB is not tolerated / there is fluid overload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the Step 3 (three-drug) regimen, and what must be done before escalating?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: A + C + D — confirm adherence before escalating.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 resistant HTN (still ≥140/90 on A+C+D, adherence confirmed): what is added if K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Add spironolactone 25 mg (aldosterone antagonist); check U&E before and 1 month after — risk of hyperkalaemia. Especially effective if a Conn's component is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 resistant HTN: what is added if K+ >4.5 mmol/L?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Add an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers are less preferred due to metabolic side effects. Seek specialist advice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What non-pharmacological measures apply at all stages of hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Salt restriction (<6g/day), DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week, weight loss, limit alcohol, stop smoking.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class A — ACEi: give examples, key side effects, and key contraindications/cautions.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Examples: ramipril, lisinopril, perindopril. Side effects: dry cough (10–15%), hyperkalaemia, angioedema (rare but serious), 1st-dose hypotension, raised Cr. CI/caution: bilateral RAS, pregnancy, aortic stenosis; caution in CKD (acceptable if Cr rise <30%); monitor U&E.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class A — ARB: examples, key side effects, and contraindications.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Examples: losartan, candesartan, valsartan. Side effects: hyperkalaemia, raised Cr (no cough — use if ACEi cough). CI: bilateral RAS, pregnancy; same CI profile as ACEi.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class C — CCB (dihydropyridine): examples, key side effects, and caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Examples: amlodipine, felodipine. Side effects: ankle oedema (most common), flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia. Caution: heart failure with reduced EF (peripheral vasodilators).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Class D — thiazide-like diuretic: examples, key side effects, and key CI/caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Examples: indapamide, chlortalidone. Side effects: low K+, low Na+, raised urate (gout attacks), raised glucose, raised cholesterol, impotence. CI/caution: gout (relative CI); caution in T2DM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Step 4 — aldosterone antagonist: example, key side effects, and key CI/caution.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Spironolactone 25–50 mg. Side effects: hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity. CI/caution: K+ >4.5 before starting; eGFR <45 → caution; monitor U&E.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Alpha-blocker in hypertension: example, key side effect, and when it is useful.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Doxazosin. Side effect: postural hypotension (1st dose), dizziness. Useful if BPH co-exists; caution with urinary incontinence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Beta-blocker in hypertension: examples, key side effects, and cautions.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Bisoprolol, atenolol. Side effects: fatigue, cold extremities, impotence, raised glucose, masks hypoglycaemia. Caution: asthma/COPD (relative); avoid abrupt cessation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which antihypertensives are used in pregnancy, and which classes are absolutely contraindicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Use labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa. ACEi and ARBs are teratogenic — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic and ABPM/HBPM BP targets for patients <80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic <140/90; ABPM/HBPM <135/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the clinic and ABPM/HBPM BP targets for patients ≥80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Clinic <150/90; ABPM/HBPM <145/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What is the clinic BP target for patients with CKD / Diabetes / CVD?
Why is the BP target less aggressive in the elderly (>80 yrs)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope, and hypoperfusion. Target 150/90 in clinic unless there is significant CVD/CKD where tighter control is warranted.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: How is a malignant / accelerated hypertensive emergency defined?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: BP ≥180/120 + evidence of end-organ damage. Severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the encephalopathy/ICH features and the investigation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Headache, confusion, seizures, focal neurology — CT head urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what retinal damage is seen and how is it confirmed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Papilloedema, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots — fundoscopy confirms malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the ACS/aortic dissection features and management trigger?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Chest pain — ECG, troponin, CXR. If dissection → IV labetalol urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: In a hypertensive emergency, what are the AKI / acute LVF features and investigations?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Raised Cr, haematuria, pulmonary oedema — U&E, CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Why must BP be lowered slowly in a hypertensive emergency, and what is the target rate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion. Aim to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then cautiously to 160/100 over 2–6 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Which IV agents are used in a hypertensive emergency (ITU/HDU setting)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Labetalol IV (α and β blocker; first-line for most emergencies including dissection and pregnancy); GTN infusion (ACS/acute LVF component); sodium nitroprusside (highly titratable; thiocyanate toxicity risk); nicardipine IV (CCB; useful in post-stroke/neurological presentations).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What assessment and monitoring is done in a hypertensive emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Same-day referral to specialist centre; fundoscopy (grade retinopathy, confirms malignant); U&E, Cr (baseline + AKI); urinalysis / ACR (renal damage); ECG (LVH, ischaemia); CXR (pulmonary oedema, widened mediastinum for dissection); CT head if neurological symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: On fundoscopy, what do cotton-wool spots represent and which retinopathy grade do they mark?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Soft exudates from retinal micro-infarcts due to arteriolar occlusion; a hallmark of grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy in a hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cerebrovascular complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), TIA, vascular dementia, hypertensive encephalopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the cardiac complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: LVH → heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF, sudden cardiac death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the renal complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: CKD, nephrosclerosis, proteinuria — HTN is the 2nd commonest cause of ESRD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: What are the retinal and vascular complications of untreated hypertension?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Retinal: hypertensive retinopathy (grades 1–4) — grade 3/4 = malignant HTN. Vascular: PAD, AAA, aortic dissection, accelerated atherosclerosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: why does ACEi-induced dry cough occur, and what is the switch?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: ACEi dry cough in 10–15% → switch to ARB (same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: why is an ACEi contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: It reduces GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.front: Exam pearl: which electrolyte/clinical combination should make you think Conn's, and what is the screening test?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.back: Low K+ + HTN → think Conn's (primary hyperaldosteronism). The aldosterone:renin ratio is the screening test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is infective endocarditis, and what is its pathological hallmark?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Infection of the endocardium and valves. The pathological hallmark is the vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Contrast acute IE and subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) by tempo, valve and organism.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Acute IE: fulminant (hours–days), on normal or damaged valves, classically Staph aureus. Subacute SBE: insidious (weeks–months), on damaged valves, classically Strep viridans.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the strongest risk factor for infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Previous IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the in-hospital mortality of IE, and what proportion require surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: In-hospital mortality is 20–30%, and surgery is required in roughly 50% of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which layer of the heart does infective endocarditis infect?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: The endocardium — the innermost lining of the heart (and the valves).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism causes acute IE on a normal or damaged native valve, and IE in IVDU?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Staph aureus (the most common overall).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism classically causes IE after poor dental hygiene or a dental procedure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep viridans.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism causes prosthetic valve IE within 2 months of surgery (perioperative)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococcus).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organisms cause prosthetic valve IE more than 2 months after surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep viridans and Staph aureus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organism links IE to colorectal cancer, and what investigation does it mandate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Strep bovis ('bovis = bowel') → send for colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the causes of culture-negative IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Bartonella, Brucella, and prior antibiotics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What causes non-infective / sterile vegetations?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: SLE → Libman-Sacks endocarditis; malignancy → marantic endocarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the valve and patient risk groups for IE, with approximate proportions?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Normal valves (~50%, often mitral), rheumatic valve disease (~30%), prosthetic valves, congenital heart disease, and IVDU (→ tricuspid / right-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which valve does IE affect in IV drug users, and why does this matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: The tricuspid valve (right-sided IE), because injected organisms reach the right heart first — leading to septic pulmonary emboli.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Outline the mechanism by which a vegetation forms in IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Endothelial damage → a platelet-fibrin thrombus forms → pathogens seed it during bacteraemia → a vegetation forms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the three consequence streams that explain almost every sign of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 1. Local destruction, 2. Embolisation, and 3. Immune complex deposition.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the LOCAL DESTRUCTION stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Valve regurgitation → heart failure, annulus / aortic root abscess → AV block (an ECG red flag), and fistula / leaflet perforation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Why is a new AV block on ECG in IE an important red flag?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: It signals an aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the EMBOLISATION stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Left-sided emboli to brain, spleen, kidneys, coronary arteries; right-sided (IVDU) septic pulmonary emboli; and Janeway lesions (painless infarcts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the features of the IMMUNE COMPLEX stream in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Small-vessel vasculitis, Osler's nodes (painful nodules), Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, and glomerulonephritis (with a raised rheumatoid factor).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the systemic infection features of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Fever (the most consistent sign), malaise, night sweats, weight loss, anaemia of chronic disease, and (late/subacute) splenomegaly and clubbing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the most consistent clinical sign of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Fever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the cardiac (local destruction) clinical features of IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A new or changing murmur (in ~85%), signs of heart failure, and an aortic root abscess → AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the embolic / vascular phenomena of IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Janeway lesions (painless, palms & soles), stroke/TIA (left-sided), splenic and renal infarcts, conjunctival haemorrhages, and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the immune / vasculitic phenomena of IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Osler's nodes (painful, finger/toe pulps), Roth spots (retinal, pale centre), splinter haemorrhages (subungual), glomerulonephritis (haematuria, casts), and a raised rheumatoid factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the classic exam discrimination between Janeway lesions and Osler's nodes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Janeway = painless = embolic infarcts (palms & soles). Osler's = Ouch = painful = immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Why are blood cultures the cornerstone investigation in IE, and how are they taken?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 3 sets from different sites, taken before antibiotics. ≥2 sets positive with a typical organism is a major Duke criterion; persistent bacteraemia is characteristic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: How many blood culture sets are taken in IE, and what makes them a major Duke criterion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 3 sets from different sites before antibiotics; ≥2 sets positive with a typical organism meets a major Duke criterion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the role of TTE vs TOE in IE, and which is more sensitive?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: TTE first (less sensitive). TOE if TTE is negative but suspicion is high, or for a prosthetic valve, poor window, or complications. A normal echo does NOT exclude IE — do TOE if clinical suspicion is strong.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Does a normal echocardiogram exclude infective endocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: No — a normal echo does not exclude IE. If clinical suspicion is strong, proceed to TOE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the characteristic echo finding in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What ECG change is monitored for in IE, and what does it signify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: A new AV block → an aortic root abscess (a surgical emergency); a prolonging PR interval is a red flag, so ECGs are serially monitored.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What blood and urine abnormalities are seen in IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Normocytic anaemia, raised ESR/CRP, leucocytosis, raised creatinine with haematuria and red cell casts, a raised rheumatoid factor and immunoglobulins, and serology for culture-negative organisms (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: How is 'definite IE' established under the Modified Duke criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What are the two MAJOR criteria of the Modified Duke criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: 1. Positive blood cultures (a typical organism — Staph aureus, Strep viridans, Enterococcus, HACEK — in ≥2 sets, or persistently positive ≥12h apart). 2.
