Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What does the 'BE TIMER' mnemonic cover for the Duke MINOR criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Bacteriological evidence not meeting major, Echo findings not meeting major, Temperature (fever >38°C), Immune phenomena (GN, Osler's, Roth spots, +RF), Microvascular/vascular phenomena (Janeway, infarcts), Echo minor, and a Risk factor / predisposing condition.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the management principle in IE, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics — poor vascular penetration of the avascular vegetation requires high drug concentrations for weeks. Take blood cultures first and discuss with microbiology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the blind/empirical antibiotic regimen for native-valve IE (and the penicillin-allergy/MRSA alternative)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Amoxicillin (± gentamicin); if penicillin-allergic or MRSA: vancomycin + gentamicin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for native-valve MSSA Staph aureus IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for 4–6 weeks (vancomycin + rifampicin if penicillin-allergic/MRSA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for prosthetic-valve MSSA Staph IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Flucloxacillin + rifampicin + gentamicin (vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic/MRSA).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for sensitive Strep viridans IE (MIC <0.1)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Benzylpenicillin for 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin); vancomycin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for Enterococcus IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Amoxicillin + gentamicin for 4–6 weeks (vancomycin + gentamicin if penicillin-allergic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: What is the regimen for MRSA IE?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Vancomycin for 6 weeks (daptomycin is an alternative).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: List the indications for surgery in IE.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Severe HF (acute aortic/mitral regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise), valve destruction (leaflet perforation, fistula), aortic root/annulus abscess (especially if causing AV block), recurrent systemic emboli despite antibiotics (especially vegetations >10mm), resistant organisms (fungi, highly resistant bacteria), prosthetic valve dehiscence or persistent bacteraemia despite treatment, and worsening renal failure from immune complex disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Which organisms causing IE are an indication for surgery due to resistance?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Fungi and highly resistant bacteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what does the 'Osler's = Ouch' / 'Janeway = painless' distinction encode?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Osler's nodes are painful, on the finger/toe pulps, from immune complex vasculitis. Janeway lesions are painless, on the palms/soles, from embolic micro-infarcts.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what does Strep bovis IE mandate, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Always send for colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma ('bovis = bowel').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what does Staph epidermidis IE classically indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: Prosthetic valve IE within the first 2 months (perioperative contamination).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what is the IVDU → IE pattern and its imaging finding?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: IVDU → tricuspid / right-sided IE → septic pulmonary emboli → cavitating lung lesions on CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.front: Exam pearl: what does a new AV block on ECG in IE mean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.back: An aortic root abscess until proven otherwise — warranting urgent surgical review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Define an abdominal aortic aneurysm, including the size threshold and the normal diameter.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta >3 cm (normal ~2 cm). Most are infrarenal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How do most AAAs present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: The vast majority are asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the two exam anchors for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Size thresholds (when to watch vs when to cut — pure recall) and ruptured AAA (the high-stakes emergency scenario).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How does the aetiology of AAA compare with thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection) and is kept separate; AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Smoking.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: List the risk factors for AAA.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Smoking (strongest modifiable RF), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, male sex (4:1 male:female), age >65, family history (first-degree relative), atherosclerosis, connective tissue disease (Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos), inflammatory (Takayasu's aortitis), infection (rare).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the pathological mechanism of AAA formation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → MMPs degrade elastin + collagen in the aortic wall → progressive wall weakening → dilatation. Atherosclerosis is associated, not directly causative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Which major cardiovascular risk factor is protective against AAA, and why is this notable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Diabetes is protective — the only major cardiovascular risk factor that reduces AAA risk. Counterintuitive → frequently examined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What symptoms can occur when an unruptured AAA becomes symptomatic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Non-specific abdominal/back/loin pain; distal embolisation → limb ischaemia; aortoenteric fistula → GI bleed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What might be found on examination of a symptomatic unruptured AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus; rarely, signs of retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the main mimic of a ruptured AAA, and what is the key teaching?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Renal colic — back pain + collapse in an older man = rupture until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: List other differentials for a symptomatic AAA besides renal colic.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Diverticulitis, IBD, appendicitis; GI haemorrhage, ovarian torsion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the differential for an epigastric mass?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: AAA, gastric CA, pancreatic pseudocyst/tumour; pyloric stenosis, transverse colon CA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the National AAA Screening Programme, and who is screened?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A one-off abdominal ultrasound for all men at age 65. Women are not routinely screened (lower risk); consider USS if >70 with risk factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and action for an aorta <3 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Normal — no further action.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and surveillance for a 3.0–4.4 cm aorta?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Small AAA — yearly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and surveillance for a 4.5–5.4 cm aorta?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Medium AAA — 3-monthly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On AAA screening, what is the classification and action for an aorta ≥5.5 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Large AAA — refer vascular surgery, consider repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the driving rules for AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: AAA >6 cm → inform DVLA. AAA >6.5 cm → disqualified from driving.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the first-line investigation for AAA, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Abdominal USS — first-line for diagnosis and surveillance. Cheap, no radiation, repeatable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: When is CT angiogram used in AAA, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm). Gives anatomy for EVAR suitability planning; also used in stable rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: On ultrasound, how is the AAA distinguished from the IVC?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: The AAA is round, pulsatile and thick-walled (on the left); the IVC is ovoid, collapsible and thin-walled (on the right); the vertebral body shadow lies below.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What conservative measures apply to all AAA patients to slow progression?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Smoking cessation (biggest modifiable factor); BP control (target <140/90); statin + aspirin; weight loss + exercise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the three indications for surgical repair of an AAA (any one of)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Diameter ≥5.5 cm; growth >1 cm/year (rapid expansion regardless of absolute size); symptomatic (pain or tenderness in an otherwise fit patient).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: When might surgical repair be delayed despite a diameter ≥5.5 cm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: In unfit/high-risk patients repair may be deferred with continued surveillance, balancing rupture risk against elective operative mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the open repair technique for AAA.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Midline laparotomy or transverse incision; clamp the aorta proximally + iliac arteries distally; remove the segment → prosthetic graft replacement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the advantages and disadvantages of open AAA repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: More durable long-term, but a bigger operation with longer recovery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Describe the EVAR (endovascular) repair technique.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: A graft is introduced via the femoral arteries; the stent is fixed across the aneurysm under fluoroscopy, excluding the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the advantages and disadvantages of EVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Lower 30-day mortality + shorter hospital stay, but a higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: State the examinable trade-off between EVAR and open repair.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: EVAR = better short-term (lower peri-op mortality); Open = better long-term durability. Both are valid repair options.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the overall mortality of a ruptured AAA, and how do rupture sites differ in prognosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: 80% overall mortality. 80% of ruptures are retroperitoneal (posterior — may be temporarily contained); 20% into the peritoneal cavity (anterior — very poor prognosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the presentation of a ruptured AAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Severe abdominal/back/flank pain (sudden onset, may radiate to groin); syncope/collapse (haemodynamic instability: tachycardia + hypotension); a pulsatile expansile mass above the umbilicus (present in ~50%); vomiting; tenderness on palpation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the classic triad of a ruptured AAA, and in what proportion is it present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass — present in 50% of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Why might high-flow O₂ be given in a ruptured AAA despite a normal-looking SpO₂?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: SpO₂ may be falsely normal (remaining Hb fully saturated) — still give O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is the initial resuscitation in a ruptured AAA regarding access and bloods?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: 2× large-bore IV cannulae; urgent bloods (FBC, U&Es, clotting); crossmatch ≥6 units.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is permissive hypotension in ruptured AAA, what is the target, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Aim SBP <100 mmHg — do NOT over-resuscitate. Raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot → torrential haemorrhage. (A favourite exam question.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: How is a ruptured AAA managed differently in an unstable versus stable patient?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Unstable: immediate transfer to theatre, open repair (no time for imaging), do NOT delay with CT. Stable: CT angiogram first, assess anatomy + EVAR suitability, EVAR if suitable / open if not.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: After transfer to a vascular unit, how is a ruptured AAA triaged?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: By haemodynamic stability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What is an endoleak, and what is its mechanism and consequence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Incomplete seal around the graft → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → the sac re-expands → risk of rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: What are the key points about endoleaks following EVAR?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Usually asymptomatic; any post-EVAR sac expansion → investigate for endoleak; classified by mechanism (Types 1–5) — beyond most finals requirements.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.front: Briefly outline the endoleak types.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.back: Type 1 — leak at graft ends (inadequate seal); Type 2 — back-fill from branch vessels (most common in AAA); Type 3 — graft fabric defect; Type 4/5 — porosity/endotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define aortic dissection.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: A tear in the aortic intima → blood forces its way between the intima and media → creates a false lumen that propagates along the aortic wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why is aortic dissection a time-critical emergency, and what determines management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery. Everything hinges on Stanford A vs B — this determines management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How are acute and chronic aortic dissection defined by time?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Acute = <14 days; subacute = 14–90 days; chronic = >90 days.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What complications arise from anterograde propagation of a dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Anterograde → iliac arteries → limb ischaemia, renal/mesenteric malperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What complications arise from retrograde propagation of a dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Retrograde → aortic root → aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does aortic dissection link to AAA/TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: A 'dissecting aneurysm' refers to an aneurysm complicated by dissection — the same connective-tissue thread (Marfan, bicuspid AV) runs through all three aortic pathologies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Which classification matters clinically for aortic dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: The Stanford classification — it directly determines surgical vs medical management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define Stanford Type A dissection and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending) — a surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Define Stanford Type B dissection and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Does NOT involve the ascending aorta (distal to the left subclavian) — medical management (if uncomplicated).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the mnemonic for the Stanford classification?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: A = Ascending = surgery (Aaargh, operate!); B = Below/Beyond subclavian = medical (Best managed medically).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type I and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type I = ascending + arch + beyond = Stanford A.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type II and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type II = ascending only = Stanford A.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: In the DeBakey classification, what is the extent of Type III and its Stanford equivalent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type III = descending only (IIIa above diaphragm; IIIb below) = Stanford B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the most important modifiable risk factor for aortic dissection, and which transient surges are especially dangerous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Hypertension. Transient surges are especially dangerous: cocaine use, heavy weightlifting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Which connective tissue diseases predispose to aortic dissection, and what is notable about thresholds?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 — weak media) and Ehlers-Danlos — operate at lower thresholds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does a bicuspid aortic valve predispose to dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What demographic profile is typical for aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Male sex, age 50–70, atherosclerosis — a shared risk profile with TAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the cardinal symptom of aortic dissection, and how does it differ from MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain — maximal at onset (unlike MI, which builds).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does the pain location differ between Type A and Type B dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Type A → anterior chest pain (ascending aorta); Type B → interscapular/back pain (descending aorta).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What causes a pulse deficit in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse — the false lumen occluding a branch.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What does a >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference indicate in dissection, and what is the teaching?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Subclavian involvement — the classic discriminating sign. Check both arms in every chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why might a new AR murmur appear in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation (an early diastolic murmur).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What does hypotension/tachycardia in a dissection signify, and what classification should be assumed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Blood loss, cardiac tamponade, or severe AR — haemodynamic instability = Type A until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: List the end-organ malperfusion effects when the false lumen occludes branches.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Stroke (carotid/cerebral), paraplegia (spinal artery occlusion), limb ischaemia (iliac/femoral), AKI (renal artery), mesenteric ischaemia (gut ischaemia), MI (coronary ostium involvement).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How can aortic dissection mimic MI/ACS, and why is this critical?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement — never thrombolyse or anticoagulate a suspected dissection. Getting this wrong is fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does PE differ from dissection in pain quality and signs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: PE: acute chest pain + haemodynamic compromise, but pain is usually pleuritic with no inter-arm BP difference.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does pericarditis differ from dissection in pain character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Pericarditis: sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, with no tearing quality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How does MSK back pain differ from dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: MSK back/interscapular pain has gradual onset, is positional, with no haemodynamic instability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: State the safety rule about excluding dissection before anticoagulation.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Exclude dissection before anticoagulating for suspected MI/PE — CT angiogram first if any dissection features present (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the role of ECG in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Often normal or non-specific — used to exclude/identify MI. May show ischaemia if coronary involved. A normal ECG in severe chest pain raises dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What bloods are taken in suspected aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: FBC, U&Es, clotting, troponin (coronary involvement), crossmatch ≥4 units, G&S.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the gold-standard/first-line definitive investigation for aortic dissection, and what does it show?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: CT angiogram — shows the intimal flap, true/false lumen, extent, branch vessel involvement. Used for classification and surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: When is TOE used in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: If the patient is too unstable for CT, or to assess aortic valve/root involvement. Sensitive for proximal dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What CXR findings occur in aortic dissection, and what is the key caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Widened mediastinum (classic), double/irregular aortic contour, pleural effusion (haemothorax). May be normal — does not exclude dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What immediate measures apply to all patients with aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: High-flow O₂, large-bore IV access × 2; analgesia (IV morphine); catheterise (strict fluid balance); crossmatch ≥4 units blood; careful resuscitation (target cerebral perfusion, avoid over-filling); senior review / cardiothoracic referral immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the target SBP in aortic dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Target SBP 100–120 mmHg — to reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) and limit propagation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the first-line agent for BP & HR control in dissection, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: IV labetalol (beta-blocker) — lowers both BP and HR simultaneously.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is used for BP/HR control if a beta-blocker is contraindicated in dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: IV calcium channel blocker (diltiazem/verapamil).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: Why must vasodilators not be used alone in aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Vasodilators alone (e.g. nitroprusside) increase HR → worsen shear stress — always cover with a beta-blocker first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What is the surgical management of a Stanford A dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Emergency sternotomy + excision of the ascending aorta; replacement with a synthetic Dacron graft ± arch reconstruction; Bentall procedure if the aortic root is involved (graft + prosthetic aortic valve + reimplantation of coronary ostia). Without surgery, mortality ~1–2%/hour in the acute phase.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: How is an uncomplicated Stanford B dissection managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Bed rest + strict BP control; IV beta-blocker first-line; transition to oral antihypertensives; surveillance imaging at 1, 3, 12 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: When is TEVAR indicated in a Stanford B dissection, and what does it do?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Complicated Type B (malperfusion — limb/renal/gut, rupture or impending rupture). TEVAR = a covered stent seals the entry tear, re-expands the true lumen and thromboses the false lumen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the long-term management measures after aortic dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Lifelong antihypertensives; surveillance CT/MRI at 1, 3, 12 months then annually; avoid isometric exercise/heavy lifting; genetic counselling if CT disease (Marfan, EDS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the complications of a Type A (retrograde + proximal) dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Cardiac tamponade (pericardial haemorrhage), acute aortic regurgitation, MI (coronary ostium dissection), stroke (carotid involvement), death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.front: What are the complications of a Type B (anterograde + distal) dissection?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.back: Aneurysm formation (commonest long-term complication), rupture, malperfusion (renal AKI, mesenteric, limb), paraplegia (spinal artery).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How is bradycardia defined, and what is the clinically important distinction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A heart rate <60 bpm. The clinically important distinction is symptomatic vs incidental — symptomatic bradycardia causes haemodynamic compromise (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) and needs treatment, whereas incidental bradycardia in an athlete or during sleep is physiologically normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the central organising principle for understanding bradycardias and heart block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The anatomical level of the block determines everything — the escape rate, QRS width, escape reliability, response to atropine, and whether pacing is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of a block at the SA node level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome. Escape ~60 bpm, narrow QRS, and atropine works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of a block at the AV node level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree block and Mobitz I. Junctional escape 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, usually benign, and atropine works.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the features of an infranodal (His-Purkinje) block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Mobitz II and complete heart block (CHB) with a broad escape. Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, and atropine is INEFFECTIVE — the patient must be paced.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: State the key principle linking the level of block to the escape rhythm.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape rhythm — and the less reliable it is.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why is atropine ineffective in an infranodal block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it. An infranodal (His-Purkinje) block is below the AV node, so atropine cannot improve conduction there — pacing is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How does QRS width relate to the level of a bradycardic block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Higher blocks (SA node, AV node) preserve a narrow QRS because the His-Purkinje system still conducts normally; infranodal blocks produce a broad QRS as the escape arises below the His-Purkinje system.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Define sinus bradycardia on the ECG.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: HR <60 bpm with P waves of normal morphology preceding every QRS — the SA node fires, just slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In which physiological situations is sinus bradycardia expected and not treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: In athletes (enhanced vagal tone) and during sleep — no treatment is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the drug (extrinsic) causes of sinus bradycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Beta-blockers, digoxin, rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), and amiodarone/lithium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the systemic (extrinsic) causes of sinus bradycardia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Hypothyroidism (myxoedema), hypothermia, raised ICP (Cushing's reflex — bradycardia + hypertension + irregular respirations), and cholestasis (bile salts are vagotonic on the SA node).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is Cushing's reflex, and what triad does it produce?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A response to raised intracranial pressure producing the triad of bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respirations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the intrinsic (within the heart) causes of sinus bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Acute ischaemia / inferior MI (the RCA supplies the SA node in ~60%; also vagally mediated), and sick sinus syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why does an inferior MI commonly cause sinus bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: The right coronary artery supplies the SA node in ~60% of people, and inferior MI is also vagally mediated — so RCA-territory infarction frequently produces bradycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is sick sinus syndrome, and what patterns does it encompass?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: SA node dysfunction encompassing idiopathic degenerative fibrosis (commonest; elderly), persistent symptomatic sinus bradycardia, prolonged pauses (SA exit block / sinus arrest), and brady-tachy syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the most common cause of sick sinus syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node, typically in the elderly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is brady-tachy syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A form of sick sinus syndrome with alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter — treating the tachy component can worsen the brady.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the therapeutic dilemma in brady-tachy syndrome, and how is it resolved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Antiarrhythmics used to treat the AF worsen the bradycardia. The resolution is to pace first — then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics. Anticoagulation is also given for the AF component.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How is sick sinus syndrome managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Treat the reversible cause (stop offending drugs, replace thyroid hormone), give atropine for acute symptomatic episodes, and implant a permanent pacemaker if symptomatic and the cause is not reversible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the V1 and V6 morphology of RBBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: RBBB shows an RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the V1 and V6 morphology of LBBB.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: LBBB shows a deep S (dominant downward deflection) in V1 and a broad/notched R wave in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the key discriminator for classifying AV blocks, beyond just the degree?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal. This determines the escape rhythm, atropine response and need for pacing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe first-degree AV block and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: PR >200 ms, fixed, with every P conducting to a QRS. It is at the AV node level, benign, and needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets. It is at the AV node level, with a narrow QRS, and is usually benign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe Mobitz II second-degree AV block and its key risks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A fixed PR interval with a sudden dropped QRS (no warning). It is INFRANODAL with a broad QRS, carries a HIGH risk of progression to complete heart block, and requires a pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe third-degree (complete) heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: P waves and QRS complexes are fully dissociated, with the ventricles driven by an escape rhythm only. A wide QRS escape indicates an infranodal (unreliable) origin. A pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the PR interval across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree: fixed, prolonged >200 ms. Mobitz I: progressive lengthening. Mobitz II: constant (may be normal). 3rd degree (CHB): no P–R relationship.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the dropped-QRS pattern across the AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree: none — all P waves conduct. Mobitz I: dropped after maximal PR, then resets. Mobitz II: sudden, no warning. 3rd degree: all P waves fail — escape rhythm only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare QRS width and conduction level across the AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree: narrow, AV node. Mobitz I: narrow, AV node. Mobitz II: broad (usually), infranodal. 3rd degree (CHB): narrow if His-level escape, broad if Purkinje-level; AV node or infranodal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the asystole risk across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree: none. Mobitz I: low. Mobitz II: HIGH. 3rd degree (CHB): HIGH if there is a broad escape.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In which AV blocks is atropine useful, and in which is it not?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Mobitz I: yes. 1st degree: N/A. Mobitz II: no. 3rd degree (CHB): only if there is a narrow escape and the situation is acute. Atropine works at the AV node, not below it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the treatment across the four AV blocks.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: 1st degree: none. Mobitz I: monitor / treat the cause. Mobitz II: pacemaker. 3rd degree (CHB): pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the memory hook for Mobitz II regarding atropine?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Fixed PR then sudden drop = INFRANODAL = atropine INEFFECTIVE. Atropine increases the atrial rate but cannot improve conduction below the AV node — it may paradoxically worsen the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why can atropine paradoxically worsen an infranodal block?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine increases the atrial (sinus) rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so a greater proportion are blocked — worsening the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: In complete heart block, what does ventricular output depend on, and what determines its reliability?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: It depends entirely on a spontaneous escape rhythm arising below the block. The anatomical level of that escape determines its reliability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the features of a NARROW escape (His bundle) in complete heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Rate 50–60 bpm, narrow QRS (<120 ms), a reliable pacemaker, often from inferior MI / a reversible cause, may respond to IV atropine acutely — but still usually needs permanent pacing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Describe the features of a BROAD escape (His-Purkinje) in complete heart block.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Rate <40 bpm, broad QRS (>120 ms), unreliable (may fail without warning), causes Stokes-Adams attacks, atropine ineffective, and a permanent pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is a Stokes-Adams attack?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A sudden loss of consciousness from complete heart block due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion. The patient goes pale then flushes as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: How can a Stokes-Adams attack be distinguished from an epileptic seizure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: By the rapid, complete return to normal (no post-ictal confusion), no tongue-biting and no incontinence, with pallor then flushing as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Is bundle branch block a bradycardia, and what causes the wide QRS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: No — BBB is a conduction delay, not a bradycardia. The AV node and His bundle conduct normally; the delay is in one bundle branch, producing a wide QRS (>120 ms) with characteristic morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does the WiLLiAM mnemonic describe for LBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: LBBB = WiLLiAM: a W in V1 (deep QS or rS wave) and an M in V5/V6 and I (broad notched R wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the additional features and significance of LBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: QRS >120 ms with left axis deviation. It is always pathological — causes include aortic stenosis, hypertension, IHD and cardiomyopathy. New LBBB with chest pain is a STEMI equivalent → primary PCI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does the MoRRoW mnemonic describe for RBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: RBBB = MoRRoW: an M in V1 (RSR' pattern, 'rabbit ears') and a W in V5/V6 and I (broad slurred S wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the additional features and causes of RBBB?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: QRS >120 ms with an rSR' ('M') pattern in V1 and a normal cardiac axis (right axis deviation suggests an additional left posterior fascicular block or RVH). Can be a normal variant in young people; other causes include PE (acute RV strain), RVH and congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the clinical significance of a new LBBB with chest pain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: It is treated as a STEMI equivalent, warranting the primary PCI (PPCI) pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the four adverse features in bradycardia that signify haemodynamic instability requiring immediate treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion), syncope (LOC from reduced cardiac output), myocardial ischaemia (chest pain or ECG ischaemia related to the bradycardia), and heart failure (breathlessness, pulmonary oedema from low output).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the four high-risk-of-asystole situations that warrant aggressive treatment even if the patient is currently stable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: (1) Recent asystole, (2) Mobitz II, (3) complete heart block with a broad QRS, and (4) ventricular pauses >3 seconds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What does Step 1 (stabilise) of the peri-arrest bradycardia algorithm involve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: ABCDE assessment, oxygen, IV access, a 12-lead ECG, continuous monitoring, and identifying/treating reversible causes (electrolytes, hypoxia, hypothermia, drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If adverse features are present in bradycardia, what is the first-line drug, dose and regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg total.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the mechanism of atropine, and when is it ineffective?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: It is an antimuscarinic that blocks vagal slowing of the SA/AV node. It is ineffective for Mobitz II, CHB, or a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If atropine gives an inadequate response in bradycardia, what interim escalation measures are available?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Isoprenaline 5 mcg/min IV, adrenaline 2–10 mcg/min IV, aminophylline, transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge that needs sedation), and glucagon if the cause is a beta-blocker or CCB overdose.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is glucagon the specific antidote for in refractory bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Beta-blocker and CCB overdose causing bradycardia, when atropine and pacing are insufficient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is transcutaneous pacing, and what are its drawbacks?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Defibrillator pads on the chest delivering pacing — it is fast but painful and needs sedation. It is a bridge only, used until a more definitive measure is available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is transvenous pacing, and how does it compare to transcutaneous?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A pacing wire passed via the subclavian/femoral/IJV to the right ventricle. It is more reliable than transcutaneous pacing and is used as a bridge to a permanent device (seek expert help).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the definitive treatment for persistent/irreversible bradycardia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: A permanent pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: If a bradycardic patient has NO adverse features, how is management decided?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Assess asystole risk. If high (Mobitz II, CHB + broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable. If low risk → observe and monitor with regular review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What are the two forms of temporary pacing, and the role of each?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Transcutaneous (defibrillator pads on the chest — fast, painful, needs sedation, bridge only) and transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV — more reliable, used while awaiting a permanent device).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: List the indications for a permanent pacemaker.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia (reversible causes excluded), sick sinus syndrome, Mobitz II AV block, complete (3rd-degree) heart block, bifascicular/trifascicular block with symptoms, and recurrent Stokes-Adams attacks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: What is the difference between a VVI and a DDD pacemaker?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: VVI paces and senses the ventricle only. DDD paces both the atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (the atrial kick), which is important in impaired LV function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why is a permanent pacemaker indicated in Mobitz II regardless of symptoms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Mobitz II (fixed PR then sudden dropped beat) carries a HIGH risk of progression to complete heart block, so a permanent pacemaker is indicated even if the patient is asymptomatic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Compare the prognosis and escape rhythm of complete heart block in anterior MI vs inferior MI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Anterior MI + CHB = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing; worse prognosis. Inferior MI + AV block = AV nodal level, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine and resolves with reperfusion; less alarming than anterior.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.front: Why does complete heart block complicating an anterior MI carry a worse prognosis than with an inferior MI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.back: Anterior MI damages the His-Purkinje system, giving a broad-QRS, unreliable escape (30–40 bpm) that needs urgent pacing. Inferior MI affects the AV node, giving a narrow-QRS, usually transient block that often responds to atropine and resolves with reperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is myocarditis, and what are its three main consequences?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Inflammation of the myocardium leading to myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Describe the typical clinical course of myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: A viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia) → days to weeks later → cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the key clinical flag for myocarditis over ACS?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: A young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → think myocarditis before ACS. Troponin is raised but the coronaries are normal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the commonest cause of myocarditis in the UK, and overall?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Viral — and Coxsackie B is the most common overall. Other viruses include adenovirus, parvovirus B19, CMV, EBV, HIV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How does HIV cause myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Through direct infection plus immunosuppression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: List the bacterial, spirochaete and protozoal causes of myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Bacteria: diphtheria (toxin-mediated), Clostridia. Spirochaete: Lyme disease (Borrelia). Protozoa: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), toxoplasmosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which protozoal infection causes myocarditis, and where is it common?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) — common in South America.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which drugs and toxins cause myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Doxorubicin (dose-dependent cardiotoxicity), immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab — a high-yield emerging cause), and cocaine, alcohol, radiation, clozapine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why are immune checkpoint inhibitors an important emerging cause of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Pembrolizumab and nivolumab can cause fulminant myocarditis; management is to stop the drug and give high-dose steroids urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the autoimmune and infiltrative causes of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis; giant cell myocarditis (rare, aggressive); and eosinophilic myocarditis (drug hypersensitivity).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is giant cell myocarditis clinically important?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is rare but aggressive, with high mortality, and is a poor prognostic factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: The clinical features of myocarditis arise from which two overlapping processes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: The inflammatory process itself, and secondary myocardial dysfunction (heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the inflammatory symptoms of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: A recent viral prodrome (fever, rash, GI upset, myalgia, arthralgia), chest pain (sharp/stabbing, may be pleuritic), and dizziness/syncope (arrhythmia). It can overlap with pericarditis → myopericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the heart failure / muscle dysfunction symptoms of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Dyspnoea on exertion → orthopnoea, fatigue, ankle oedema, biventricular failure (an acute dilated picture), and palpitations (VT/VF risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is myopericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocarditis overlapping with pericarditis — both components (e.g. pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes) are present and both are treated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the examination signs of myocarditis related to ventricular dysfunction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Tachycardia (often disproportionate), soft/muffled heart sounds, an S3 gallop (ventricular dysfunction), and bibasal crackles (LHF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What examination signs of right heart failure and systemic illness occur in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Raised JVP and oedema (RHF), hypotension (if fulminant), fever and signs of viral illness, and a pericardial rub (if myopericarditis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What blood markers indicate myocyte damage and ventricular dysfunction in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Raised troponin / CK-MB (myocyte damage — mimics ACS) and raised BNP / NT-proBNP (ventricular dysfunction).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What additional blood tests are done in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Raised ESR, CRP, WCC (inflammation), viral serology (paired titres), and an autoimmune screen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the key ECG findings in myocarditis, and how do they differ from STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Diffuse non-specific ST/T changes — the key difference from STEMI (which is territory-based). Also sinus tachycardia, heart block, VT/AF; it can mimic STEMI with widespread ST elevation. Serial ECGs are important.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is the ST change distribution useful in distinguishing myocarditis from STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocarditis causes diffuse (widespread) non-specific ST/T changes, whereas STEMI changes are territory-based (in a coronary distribution).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does echocardiography show in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Ventricular dilatation, reduced ejection fraction, wall motion abnormalities, a pericardial effusion (if myopericarditis), and it excludes structural/valve pathology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What are the CXR findings in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Cardiomegaly (significant LV dilatation), pulmonary oedema / pleural effusions if in heart failure, and it may be normal in early/mild disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is cardiac MRI the key modern test for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is the non-invasive gold standard in clinical practice: late gadolinium enhancement shows myocardial inflammation/fibrosis, the Lake Louise criteria are used for diagnosis, and it guides prognosis and risk stratification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI indicate in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Myocardial inflammation/fibrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Which criteria are used for the cardiac MRI diagnosis of myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: The Lake Louise criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the pathological gold standard for diagnosing myocarditis, and which criteria are used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Endomyocardial biopsy — using the Dallas criteria (an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes/neutrophils + myocyte necrosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is endomyocardial biopsy rarely performed, and when is it reserved for use?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is rarely done due to the risk vs benefit. It is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, suspected giant cell / eosinophilic myocarditis, or an unclear diagnosis after non-invasive workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What does endomyocardial biopsy histology show, and what does it identify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: An inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes/neutrophils) + myocyte necrosis (the Dallas criteria), identifying the aetiology (viral, giant cell, eosinophilic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the mainstay of management for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Supportive care — most cases are self-limiting. Treat the underlying cause where possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What supportive measures are used in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Hospital admission + cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk), bed rest, treating heart failure (diuretics, ACEi/ARB, beta-blockers once stable), anti-arrhythmics if needed with a defibrillator on standby, and IABP or LVAD in fulminant/cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is cardiac monitoring required for myocarditis inpatients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Because of the arrhythmia risk (VT/VF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How is heart failure managed in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Diuretics, ACEi/ARB, and beta-blockers (once stable).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: How are specific underlying causes of myocarditis treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Bacterial: IV antibiotics (Lyme: doxycycline/ceftriaxone). Chagas': benznidazole. Drug-induced: stop the offending agent immediately. Autoimmune: steroids/immunosuppression. ICI-associated: high-dose steroids and hold the checkpoint inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the treatment for Chagas' myocarditis and for Lyme myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Chagas': benznidazole. Lyme: doxycycline or ceftriaxone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why must strenuous exercise be avoided in myocarditis, and for how long?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It risks haemodynamic deterioration and life-threatening arrhythmia. Abstain from competitive sport for a minimum of 3–6 months (or until MRI/echo confirms resolution); it is a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Why is myocarditis significant in young athletes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, which is why competitive sport is avoided for ≥3–6 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What is the prognosis of myocarditis in the majority of cases?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Good — most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously, with full recovery of cardiac function over weeks–months; a viral cause with mild dysfunction has an excellent outlook.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: List the poor prognostic factors in myocarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Fulminant presentation / cardiogenic shock, giant cell myocarditis (aggressive, high mortality), progression to dilated cardiomyopathy, sudden cardiac death (young athletes, arrhythmia), and persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months → transplant consideration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: What happens if LV dysfunction persists at 6 months in myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It prompts consideration of cardiac transplantation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: what triad should make you think myocarditis, and what are the troponin/angiography findings?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → think myocarditis. Troponin is raised but the coronaries are normal on angiography.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: what are the commonest causes of myocarditis in the UK and in South America?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: UK: Coxsackie B. South America: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: which is the key non-invasive diagnostic test and which is the pathological gold standard for myocarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: Cardiac MRI is the key non-invasive diagnostic (late gadolinium enhancement); endomyocardial biopsy is the pathological gold standard (rarely done).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: how do you recognise and manage myopericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: An overlap with pericarditis: a pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes — treat both components.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.front: Exam pearl: why is myocarditis important regarding cardiomyopathy and young people?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.back: It is an important cause of dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death in young people — avoid exercise for ≥3–6 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Define atherosclerosis and its end consequences.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Chronic arterial wall inflammation → lipid deposition → fibrous plaque formation → arterial stiffening, stenosis, and plaque rupture → MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Walk through the cellular sequence of atherosclerosis from LDL entry to plaque development.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: LDL particles enter the intima → monocytes adhere via adhesion molecules and differentiate into macrophages → engulf LDL → form macrophage foam cells → chronic inflammation and plaque development.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the goal of primary prevention in atherosclerosis, and which tool/threshold is used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: No prior CVD event — calculate risk and intervene before disease manifests. Tool: QRISK3 (10-year stroke/MI risk); threshold ≥10% → atorvastatin 20 mg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the goal of secondary prevention, and what is the regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Post-CVD event (MI, stroke, PVD) — prevent recurrence. Atorvastatin 80 mg + the 4 A's, regardless of baseline cholesterol.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why does the primary vs secondary fork matter so much in lipid management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: It drives everything: statin dose, antiplatelet choice, and beta-blocker use all differ between the two arms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: List the non-modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Age, male sex, family history of premature CVD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: List the modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Raised cholesterol, smoking, alcohol, poor diet, physical inactivity, obesity, poor sleep, stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which comorbidities increase atherosclerosis risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Diabetes, hypertension, CKD, inflammatory disease (RA, SLE), atypical antipsychotics (increased metabolic risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Is hyperlipidaemia usually symptomatic, and what do clinical signs indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Usually asymptomatic — picked up on routine bloods or screening. Signs indicate severe/longstanding disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are tendon xanthomata, where are they found, and what are they pathognomonic of?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Hard nodules of cholesterol deposition. Sites: knuckles (extensor tendons), Achilles tendon. Pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is xanthelasma, and what is its association with lipids?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Yellowish plaques on the eyelids; associated with dyslipidaemia but may occur with normal lipids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is corneal arcus, and when does it suggest a lipid disorder versus being normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A grey-white ring at the corneal periphery. Premature (<45 years) = lipid disorder; normal in the elderly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which lipid abnormality can precipitate acute pancreatitis, and at what level?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis — a serious complication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the dietary targets for lifestyle optimisation in lipid disorders?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Total fat <30% of caloric intake; saturated fat <7% of calories; reduce sugar and refined carbohydrates; 5-a-day fruit and vegetables; ≥2 portions oily fish per week; reduce salt (especially if hypertensive).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What exercise and habit changes are advised in lipid disorders?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: 150 min moderate OR 75 min vigorous aerobic exercise/week, plus 2× strength/resistance training/week; smoking cessation (single most effective CVD intervention); alcohol ≤14 units/week spread across ≥3 days; treat comorbidities (HTN, diabetes, obesity).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which single lifestyle change is the most effective CVD intervention?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Smoking cessation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Outline the primary prevention pathway using QRISK3.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Calculate QRISK3 (10-year cardiovascular risk); ≥10% risk → offer atorvastatin 20 mg nocte after lifestyle discussion; recheck lipids at 3 months — aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Which patients qualify for an automatic statin without needing a QRISK calculation — CKD criteria?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3): atorvastatin 20 mg regardless of QRISK; CKD independently multiplies CVD risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the automatic statin criteria for Type 1 diabetes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Atorvastatin 20 mg if >40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy; no QRISK calculation needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: When and what statin is started for secondary prevention, and what accompanies it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: After any CVD event (MI, stroke, TIA, PVD): start atorvastatin 80 mg + the 4 A's, regardless of baseline cholesterol level.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the secondary prevention 4 A's, what does the first A (atorvastatin) involve?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg — high-intensity statin nocte; target ≥40% reduction in non-HDL. (Note: 20 mg in primary prevention.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, what is the antiplatelet regimen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Aspirin 75 mg OD (indefinite); post-MI DAPT = aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor for 12 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, why is atenolol / a beta-blocker used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Bisoprolol or atenolol — rate control, reduce cardiac remodelling post-MI, reduce sudden death risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the 4 A's, what is the role of the ACE inhibitor?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Ramipril/perindopril — BP control, cardioprotection, remodelling prevention post-MI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: State the key contrast between primary and secondary prevention regimens.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Primary = atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); Secondary = atorvastatin 80 mg + antiplatelet + beta-blocker + ACEi.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the mechanism of statins, and why are they taken at night?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis → upregulate LDL receptors → reduced LDL. Taken at night because hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: In the cholesterol synthesis pathway, which enzyme do statins block and what conversion does this prevent?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate and reducing downstream cholesterol production.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What baseline bloods are checked before starting a statin?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Fasting lipids, LFTs, CK, TFTs, HbA1c — to establish a baseline before starting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is checked at 3 months on a statin, and what is the target/stopping rule?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Fasting lipids + LFTs. Aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL. If ALT/AST >3× ULN → stop the statin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is monitored at 12 months on a statin, and what transaminase rise is acceptable?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: LFTs. A mild transaminase rise is acceptable; >3× ULN → stop.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is checked if a patient on a statin develops muscle pain, and what level signals rhabdomyolysis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Check CK. CK >5× ULN = rhabdomyolysis → stop immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Describe the myopathy → rhabdomyolysis side effect of statins, including the emergency sign.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Muscle pain/weakness → check CK. CK >5× ULN = rhabdomyolysis → stop statin. Dark urine (myoglobinuria) = emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the T2DM risk associated with statins, and how does it affect prescribing?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A modest increase in diabetes risk — but the benefit vs CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What stroke-related consideration applies to statins?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: A small increased risk of haemorrhagic stroke — a relevant consideration in patients with prior haemorrhagic stroke.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Why should a statin be held during macrolide antibiotic use?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Macrolides (clarithromycin, erythromycin) cause CYP3A4 inhibition → increased statin levels → increased myopathy risk, so hold the statin while on them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the mechanism of ezetimibe, and how is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 inhibitor); used as an add-on to a statin or in statin-intolerant patients; well tolerated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are PCSK9 inhibitors, how are they given, and who are they for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Evolocumab, alirocumab — monoclonal antibodies, subcut every 2–4 weeks. Prevent LDL receptor degradation → profound LDL reduction. For FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is the role of omega-3 / fibrates in lipid management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Fibrates (fenofibrate) — for severe hypertriglyceridaemia. Omega-3 fatty acids — adjunct for triglyceride lowering.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the key features of familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Autosomal dominant — LDL receptor mutation (or ApoB/PCSK9 variants); very high cholesterol from birth, dramatically accelerating atherosclerosis; untreated → MI in the 4th–5th decade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What are the Simon Broome criteria for familial hypercholesterolaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L (or LDL >4.9); tendon xanthomata in the patient or a first-degree relative; FHx premature CVD (MI <60 in 1st-degree, <50 in 2nd-degree relative); DNA mutation in LDL receptor/ApoB/PCSK9 = definite diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: Outline the management of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Urgent specialist referral; genetic testing; high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg); add ezetimibe if target not met; PCSK9 inhibitor for refractory cases; cascade screening — test all first-degree relatives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.front: What is cascade screening in familial hypercholesterolaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.back: Testing all first-degree relatives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Death (necrosis) of body tissue due to failure of blood supply, infection, or both. Classified into dry, wet, gas, and Fournier's types.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is dry gangrene and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Ischaemic necrosis without infection — occlusion of arterial supply (atherosclerosis, embolism, diabetes). The tissue desiccates and mummifies. Features: black/brown shrivelled tissue, well-demarcated line, minimal pain (nerves infarcted), no systemic upset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is wet gangrene and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Ischaemic necrosis + secondary bacterial infection. Features: swollen, blistered, malodorous, moist tissue; poorly demarcated; systemic sepsis (fever, tachycardia). Diabetics and immunocompromised are at highest risk. Surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: How does dry gangrene differ from wet gangrene clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry: black/mummified, demarcated, no systemic upset. Wet: swollen/malodorous, poorly demarcated, systemic sepsis. Wet is the surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What organism causes gas gangrene, and what is its key feature?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Clostridium perfringens (Gram-positive anaerobe). Key feature: gas in tissues → crepitus on palpation / gas bubbles on XR. Rapidly progressive, life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the mechanism of tissue destruction in gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: C. perfringens produces alpha-toxin (lecithinase) → destroys cell membranes → rapid tissue necrosis + gas production (CO₂ + H₂) → crepitus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What are the clinical features of gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Rapid-onset severe pain out of proportion to appearance; bronze/brown discolouration of skin; crepitus (gas in tissues); sweet/offensive odour; systemic toxicity (high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion). Rapid progression to death within hours if untreated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: How is gas gangrene treated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Surgical emergency: wide surgical debridement / amputation. High-dose IV penicillin G (+ metronidazole). Hyperbaric oxygen — adjunct (inhibits anaerobic growth). No role for delayed surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is Fournier's gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva. Polymicrobial (aerobic + anaerobic). Affects diabetics, immunocompromised, obese men. Rapidly fatal if untreated. Emergency debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam + metronidazole).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is necrotising fasciitis and how does it relate to gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Deep infection of the fascia causing spreading necrosis of fascia, subcutaneous tissue, and overlying skin. Gangrene of the skin overlies the fasciitis. Classified as Type I (polymicrobial) or Type II (Group A Streptococcus / 'flesh-eating').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the hallmark clinical sign of necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Pain out of proportion to appearance + 'dishwater' (grey/brown) fluid on incision. Also: woody induration, rapid spreading erythema, skin necrosis, and crepitus (if gas-forming).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the LRINEC score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis — uses CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose. Score ≥6 = high risk. Used to prompt urgent surgical exploration, not to delay it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the commonest precipitant of limb gangrene in clinical practice?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Diabetic foot — peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed trauma) + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity → infection + ischaemia → wet gangrene or neuropathic ulcer leading to gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the role of ABPI in the assessment of gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: ABPI (ankle-brachial pressure index) quantifies peripheral ischaemia. <0.5 = severe ischaemia; <0.3 = critical ischaemia (tissue loss/rest pain/gangrene). Guides revascularisation decisions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the definitive management of established limb gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Revascularisation (bypass/angioplasty) if viable tissue remains. Amputation if revascularisation is not possible or has failed. Wet/gas gangrene: debridement first + antibiotics, then revascularisation/amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: At what ABPI level is critical ischaemia and tissue loss expected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: ABPI <0.3 — critical ischaemia. Features: rest pain, non-healing ulcers, gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What blood test is an early marker of tissue ischaemia and necrosis in gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Raised serum lactate (anaerobic metabolism from ischaemia); also raised CRP, WCC (if infected), creatinine (AKI from sepsis), clotting (DIC risk in gas gangrene).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the four types of gangrene.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry = ischaemia, no infection, mummified, demarcated. Wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, sepsis. Gas = Clostridium, crepitus, fatal. Fournier's = perineal necrotising fasciitis, polymicrobial.
