conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key distinguishing feature of gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Crepitus (gas in tissues) from Clostridium perfringens — surgical emergency. Wide debridement + IV penicillin + hyperbaric O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: Pain out of proportion to appearance — what must be excluded?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Necrotising fasciitis / gas gangrene — requires immediate surgical exploration. Do not be reassured by normal-looking overlying skin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the diabetic foot triad that leads to gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed injury) + peripheral arterial disease (impaired healing) + immunosuppression (infection) = diabetic foot gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What are the two main types of gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry gangrene (ischaemic — peripheral arterial disease) and wet gangrene (infected — bacteria, often in diabetics).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Rapidly spreading myonecrosis caused by Clostridium perfringens — crepitus (gas in tissue), severe systemic toxicity, very high mortality. Surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What organism causes gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Clostridium perfringens (anaerobe) — produces exotoxins (alpha toxin) causing rapid tissue destruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is Fournier's gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia — polymicrobial synergistic infection, diabetics and immunocompromised at highest risk. Surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Rapidly spreading infection along fascial planes — polymicrobial or Group A Streptococcus. 'Woody-hard' induration, disproportionate pain, skin necrosis. Mortality 20–40%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the LRINEC score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis — uses CRP, WBC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose to risk-stratify soft tissue infections. Score ≥6 = high risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What imaging is most useful in suspected necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: CT with contrast — shows gas along fascial planes, fascial thickening, fluid collections. Does NOT delay surgical exploration if clinical suspicion high.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the definitive treatment for necrotising fasciitis/gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Emergency surgical debridement (source control) + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin ± metronidazole). Reconstruction later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the role of hyperbaric oxygen in gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Adjunct treatment (not first-line) — hyperoxic environment inhibits anaerobe growth and promotes healing. Used after surgical debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: Why is gangrene common in diabetics?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Peripheral vascular disease (macroangiopathy) + peripheral neuropathy (painless injury) + impaired immunity → infection progresses unnoticed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the classic appearance of dry gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Dry, black, shrunken, mummified tissue with sharp demarcation line — usually toes/foot. Cold, pulseless. Represents ischaemic infarction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the classic appearance of wet gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Moist, oedematous, foul-smelling, rapidly spreading necrosis — blurred margins. Associated with systemic sepsis. Requires urgent debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the surgical treatment of dry gangrene of the toes?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Amputation — level depends on blood supply (digital → forefoot → below-knee → above-knee). Revascularisation first if possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What investigations are needed when gangrene is suspected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Bloods: FBC, CRP, cultures; Imaging: X-ray (gas in soft tissue), CT (extent); Ankle-Brachial Index; Doppler USS; Arteriography for revascularisation planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What triad points to gas gangrene?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: (1) Rapid onset after trauma/surgery; (2) crepitus in tissue; (3) profound systemic toxicity — emergency debridement + IV penicillin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What distinguishes necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis clinically?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: NF: disproportionate pain, woody-hard induration, systemic sepsis, skin necrosis, rapid progression — cellulitis does not have crepitus, necrosis or this severity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the most common causative organism in Type 1 necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Polymicrobial (mixed aerobic + anaerobic — e.g. E. coli, Bacteroides, Streptococcus). Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus — commonest monomicrobial).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What antibiotics are used for necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Broad-spectrum IV: piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem + clindamycin (inhibits toxin production) ± IV immunoglobulin for streptococcal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.front: What is the mortality of gas gangrene if untreated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.back: Near 100% untreated. Even with surgery + antibiotics, mortality is 20–30%. Speed of surgical debridement is the key prognostic factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is acute pericarditis, and where does it sit in the broader disease spectrum?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Inflammation of the pericardium. It is part of a spectrum: acute pericarditis → effusion → tamponade, and separately → constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the commonest infective cause of pericarditis, and which organisms?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Viral is commonest — Coxsackievirus B, enteroviruses, EBV, CMV. Bacterial causes include TB (suspect with any exudative effusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Which infective cause of pericarditis should be suspected with any exudative effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Tuberculosis (TB).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Distinguish the two post-MI causes of pericarditis by timing and mechanism.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Early (1–3 days): fibrinous pericarditis from direct irritation. Late (weeks–months): Dressler's syndrome — an autoimmune process with fever + pleurisy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Dressler's syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A late (weeks–months) post-MI autoimmune pericarditis presenting with fever and pleurisy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: List the systemic/inflammatory causes of pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: SLE, RA and other connective tissue diseases; uraemia (pericardial rub in renal failure); hypothyroidism; and malignancy (lung, breast).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the single largest group of pericarditis cases by aetiology?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Idiopathic — the largest single group, presumed viral. Other 'other' causes include radiotherapy and trauma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the defining symptom of acute pericarditis, and its character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Chest pain — sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal, worsened by deep inspiration and movement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does positioning affect the chest pain of pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Relieved by sitting/leaning forward (lifts the inflamed pericardium away from the diaphragm) and worse lying flat — the latter being a key feature distinguishing it from ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why does leaning forward relieve pericarditic chest pain?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It lifts the inflamed pericardium away from the diaphragm, reducing irritation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Where does pericarditic pain radiate, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: To the neck and left shoulder, due to phrenic nerve irritation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the cardinal clinical sign of acute pericarditis, and its character?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A pericardial friction rub — scratchy/squeaking, high-pitched, heard at the left sternal edge.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How is the pericardial friction rub best heard, and what is its classic timing pattern?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Best heard leaning forward, in end-expiration. It may be triphasic (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastole).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What happens to the pericardial friction rub if a large effusion develops?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It is transient — it disappears once a large effusion develops, because the fluid separates the two inflamed layers.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What systemic features may accompany acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Fever (especially viral/infective), malaise and myalgia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis, and how many are needed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Chest pain (sharp, pleuritic, positional, relieved leaning forward), friction rub, ECG changes (widespread saddle ST + PR depression), and pericardial effusion on echo. ≥2 of the 4 = diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is TTE (echo) recommended in all suspected cases of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: To exclude a pericardial effusion and assess for myocardial involvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Describe the ST elevation seen in acute pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation, widespread (most leads — I, II, aVL, aVF, V2–V6), with a concave upward 'saddle/smiley' morphology that returns to baseline as inflammation resolves, and NO reciprocal ST depression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is PR depression important in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It is highly specific for pericarditis, reflecting atrial epicardial involvement in the inflammation. There is PR elevation in aVR (the mirror image), and PR depression may precede the ST changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: In which lead is PR ELEVATION seen in pericarditis, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: aVR — it is the mirror image of the PR depression seen in the other leads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What other (non-ST/PR) ECG findings occur in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Sinus tachycardia is common, and low voltage if an effusion develops.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the ST shape and distribution in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericarditis: concave (saddle/smiley), widespread (most leads). STEMI: convex (tombstone/frowning), territorial (leads facing the infarct).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare reciprocal changes and the PR interval in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericarditis: no reciprocal changes, with PR depression (highly specific). STEMI: reciprocal changes present, with a normal PR interval.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare Q waves and ECG evolution in pericarditis vs STEMI.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericarditis: no Q waves; diffuse ST → returns to baseline. STEMI: pathological Q waves develop; hyperacute T → ST rise → T inversion → Q wave.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does troponin differ between pericarditis and STEMI?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericarditis: may be mildly raised (indicating a myopericarditis component). STEMI: significantly raised.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the two hallmark ECG changes of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation and PR depression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What blood tests are relevant in acute pericarditis, and what do they assess?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: FBC (raised WCC), CRP/ESR, U&E (uraemia), TFTs, ANA/dsDNA, and troponin (myocarditis component).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What CXR findings may occur in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It may be normal; an enlarged cardiac silhouette (if effusion) or a pleural effusion (Dressler's) may be seen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When are CT/MRI used in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain, or to assess pericardial thickening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for acute pericarditis, including doses and duration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600 mg TDS or aspirin 750–1000 mg TDS) for 1–3 months, plus colchicine 0.5 mg BD added to the NSAID to reduce recurrence, continued for 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What does colchicine add to NSAID therapy in pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: It reduces (roughly halves) the risk of recurrence; it is continued for 3 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why should NSAIDs/colchicine be tapered rather than stopped abruptly in pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Both are tapered on symptom resolution and not stopped abruptly to avoid rebound/recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What lifestyle advice accompanies pericarditis treatment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Rest and avoid strenuous exercise until asymptomatic and CRP has normalised.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When are systemic corticosteroids used in pericarditis, and what is the caution?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: For an autoimmune cause (SLE/RA) or NSAID failure — used with caution, as corticosteroids increase the recurrence risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why are NSAIDs contraindicated post-MI, and what is used instead?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: They risk myocardial rupture, so aspirin is used only at anti-inflammatory doses (for Dressler's syndrome).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the caution regarding anticoagulation in acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Use with caution due to the risk of haemopericardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: List the high-risk features that warrant admission in acute pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Fever >38°C, large effusion or tamponade, elevated troponin (myopericarditis), immunosuppression or anticoagulation, and subacute onset or failure to respond to NSAIDs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the complications of acute pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericardial effusion (most common), constrictive pericarditis (chronic, especially TB), recurrent pericarditis (>15% without colchicine), and myopericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the headline exam pearl distinguishing pericarditis from STEMI on ECG?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericarditis: concave ST, widespread, PR depression, no reciprocal changes. STEMI: convex ST, territorial, reciprocal changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What positional chest-pain pattern should be treated as pericarditis until proven otherwise?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Chest pain relieved by leaning forward and worse lying flat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial effusion, and where does it sit in the disease spectrum?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. It can result from any cause of pericarditis and is the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is a pericardial effusion often asymptomatic?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Especially if accumulation is slow — the pericardium stretches to accommodate the fluid gradually.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What examination findings suggest a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: An obscured apex beat (fluid insulates and displaces the heartbeat), soft/muffled heart sounds, and dullness to percussion at the left base (Ewart's sign in large effusions — dullness below the left scapula).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Ewart's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Dullness to percussion below the left scapula, seen in large pericardial effusions due to compression of the left lung base.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What ECG findings occur in a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Low-voltage QRS complexes, electrical alternans (the QRS axis alternates beat-to-beat as the heart swings in the fluid — specific for a large effusion), and sinus tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is electrical alternans, and what does it indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The QRS axis/amplitude alternates beat-to-beat as the heart swings within the fluid. It is specific for a large pericardial effusion (and tamponade until proven otherwise).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the classic CXR finding in a pericardial effusion, and the threshold?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A globular (water-bottle) heart — a flask-shaped cardiac silhouette when the effusion is >250 mL. The lung fields are clear (unlike heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why are clear lung fields on CXR a useful discriminator in pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: They distinguish a pericardial effusion (globular heart, clear lungs) from heart failure (where pulmonary congestion would be expected).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for a pericardial effusion, and what does it show?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Echo — it shows an echo-free space surrounding the heart, quantifies the size, and guides pericardiocentesis. It must be done urgently if tamponade is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why does the RATE of fluid accumulation determine the haemodynamic impact of an effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Slow accumulation lets the pericardium stretch to accommodate 1–2 L with little effect, whereas rapid accumulation of even 150–200 mL can cause tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the mainstay of managing a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Treat the underlying cause — most effusions resolve with this alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When is pericardiocentesis indicated for an effusion, and what is done with the fluid?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If symptomatic or large: echo-guided pericardiocentesis (aspiration). Fluid is sent for culture, cytology/histology, and PCR (for TB) — highest yield with large effusions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial window, and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Excision of a pericardial segment to allow ongoing drainage — used if an effusion recurs or the fluid is loculated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is cardiac tamponade, and why is it a medical emergency?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericardial fluid accumulates faster than the pericardium can stretch → rising intrapericardial pressure compresses all four chambers → impaired diastolic filling → reduced cardiac output → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest if untreated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Hypotension (reduced cardiac output → shock), raised JVP (impaired venous return into the compressed heart), and muffled heart sounds (fluid surrounding and insulating the heart).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is pulsus paradoxus, and what is the threshold in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg. On inspiration, increased RV volume pushes the interventricular septum into the LV, impairing LV output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: On inspiration, venous return to the RV increases; with a fixed total cardiac volume, the increased RV volume pushes the interventricular septum into the LV, impairing LV filling and output → a fall in systolic BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Besides Beck's triad and pulsus paradoxus, what additional features occur in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Compensatory tachycardia and dyspnoea, cool peripheries (reduced cardiac output), an absent JVP y descent (heart volume fixed; venous inflow cannot increase in diastole), and absent Kussmaul's sign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is the JVP y descent ABSENT in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The heart volume is fixed by the surrounding fluid, so venous inflow cannot increase in early diastole — abolishing the y descent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the significance of Kussmaul's sign being absent in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Its absence distinguishes tamponade from constrictive pericarditis (where Kussmaul's sign is present).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the classic ECG triad of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Electrical alternans + low voltage + sinus tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the most sensitive echo sign of tamponade, and what does echo also guide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Diastolic collapse of the RA and/or RV is the most sensitive sign. Echo also guides pericardiocentesis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the definitive treatment of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis — needle aspiration of the pericardial fluid. Cardiac arrest occurs if not performed; immediate haemodynamic improvement is expected after even small volumes are drained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: When is a surgical pericardial window used in tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: If the effusion recurs or the fluid is loculated (fluid analysis: culture, cytology/histology, PCR for TB).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is constrictive pericarditis, and the most important cause worldwide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A chronic consequence of recurrent or persistent pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes a rigid fibrotic cage preventing diastolic filling. TB is the most important cause worldwide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why does constrictive pericarditis produce a right-sided heart failure picture?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The rigid pericardium traps raised venous pressure that cannot go forward, causing raised JVP, dependent oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites, pleural effusions, SOB/exercise intolerance, and (late) AF from atrial dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is Kussmaul's sign, and why does it occur in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The JVP paradoxically RISES on inspiration, because the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate the increased venous return that inspiration would normally allow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is a pericardial knock, and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A loud early S3 heard in constrictive pericarditis, caused by the abrupt cessation of ventricular filling as the ventricle hits the rigid pericardium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: How does the JVP waveform differ between constriction and tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Constriction: prominent x AND y descents. Tamponade: y descent absent (x descent prominent) — the y descent is the key contrast.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why is the apex beat normal/impalpable in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: The rigid pericardium restricts outward movement of the heart, so the apex beat is not displaced or thrusting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Why can constrictive pericarditis not be clinically distinguished from restrictive cardiomyopathy?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: They share the same haemodynamic profile, so imaging is essential to distinguish them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the pathology and onset of tamponade vs constrictive pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Tamponade: fluid in the pericardial space, acute onset (minutes–hours). Constriction: a rigid fibrotic pericardium, chronic onset (months–years).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare Kussmaul's sign and pulsus paradoxus in tamponade vs constriction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Tamponade: Kussmaul's absent, pulsus paradoxus present (>10 mmHg). Constriction: Kussmaul's present, pulsus paradoxus usually absent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the heart sounds, CXR heart size and calcification in tamponade vs constriction.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Tamponade: muffled sounds, enlarged (globular) heart, no calcification. Constriction: pericardial knock (loud early S3), normal heart size, calcification may be present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Compare the definitive treatment of tamponade vs constrictive pericarditis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Tamponade: pericardiocentesis. Constriction: pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the key CXR findings in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A normal heart size plus pericardial calcification (best seen on the lateral film — strongly supports the diagnosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the gold-standard imaging for diagnosing constrictive pericarditis and planning surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: CT/MRI — demonstrating pericardial thickening and calcification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What echo findings are seen in constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Septal bounce, a dilated IVC, and preserved systolic function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the 'square root sign' on cardiac catheterisation, and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A dip-plateau pattern in the ventricular pressure trace, seen in constrictive pericarditis — used when imaging is inconclusive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What is the only definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis, and its risk?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Pericardiectomy (surgical excision) — reserved for severe/progressive cases, with a perioperative mortality of 5–15%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: What are the medical/supportive measures in constrictive pericarditis alongside surgery?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Diuretics for symptomatic fluid overload (a bridge to surgery), treat the underlying cause (e.g. full anti-tuberculous therapy ± corticosteroids for TB to reduce fibrosis), and rate control for AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: what does electrical alternans signify until proven otherwise?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: A large pericardial effusion / tamponade — the QRS axis alternating beat-to-beat reflects the heart swinging in the fluid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: what does pericardial calcification on CXR/CT indicate, and what is the surgical caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Constriction. Pericardiectomy cures constriction, but there is no surgical fix for restrictive cardiomyopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: which bedside signs best discriminate tamponade from constriction?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: Kussmaul's sign is present in constriction and absent in tamponade; pulsus paradoxus is present in tamponade and absent in constriction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.front: Exam pearl: why always check a TB screen in an exudative effusion of unknown cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis.back: TB is the most important cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide, so it must be excluded in any exudative effusion without a clear cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is a pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. Causes range from infection to malignancy to metabolic disorders. The clinical significance depends on the rate of accumulation, not just the volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid → impaired ventricular filling → reduced cardiac output. It is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Beck's triad?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds. The classic triad of cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: Why does rapid accumulation cause tamponade at a low volume?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch acutely. 150–200 mL accumulating quickly can cause tamponade; a chronic effusion may reach >1 L before tamponade because the pericardium slowly distends.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is pulsus paradoxus?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: An exaggerated fall in systolic BP of >10 mmHg on inspiration. Mechanism: inspiration → RV expands → interventricular septum shifts left → LV filling reduced → BP falls.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the ECG findings in cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Low-voltage QRS complexes + electrical alternans (beat-to-beat variation in QRS axis as the heart swings in the effusion). Sinus tachycardia is also typical.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What does electrical alternans indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Cardiac tamponade — the swinging movement of the heart within the effusion causes beat-to-beat variation in the QRS axis and amplitude.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What does CXR show in a large pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Globular/flask-shaped ('water-bottle') cardiac silhouette. Lung fields are typically clear (differentiates from pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the most sensitive investigation for pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Echocardiography — detects even small effusions and assesses for tamponade physiology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the earliest echocardiographic sign of tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Right atrial collapse (late diastole/early systole) — the RA is the lowest-pressure chamber, so it is the earliest and most sensitive sign. Right ventricular diastolic collapse appears later but is more specific.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the common causes of pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Viral pericarditis (commonest); malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma — commonest in large effusions); TB; uraemia; post-MI (Dressler's); hypothyroidism; autoimmune (SLE, RA); aortic dissection (haemopericardium); post-cardiac surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: Which cause of tamponade is a contraindication to pericardiocentesis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Aortic dissection — the haemopericardium is tamponading the dissection site. Draining it removes the protective tamponade and can cause fatal exsanguination. Requires emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the emergency treatment for cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration) — urgent, life-saving. Subxiphoid approach, needle aimed towards left shoulder at 45°. Even a small drain (30–50 mL) dramatically improves haemodynamics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is a pericardial window and when is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Surgical creation of a communication between the pericardial sac and the pleural/peritoneal space to allow continuous drainage. Used for recurrent effusions not amenable to repeated aspiration (malignancy, post-surgical).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: How does tamponade differ from constrictive pericarditis on examination?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Both cause raised JVP and reduced cardiac output. Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises on inspiration) is seen in constrictive pericarditis but NOT in tamponade (JVP falls in tamponade). Pulsus paradoxus is prominent in tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Kussmaul's sign and in which pericardial condition is it seen?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration. Seen in constrictive pericarditis and right heart failure — NOT in cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What supports the diagnosis of tamponade on echo beyond the effusion itself?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: RV diastolic collapse; RA systolic collapse; dilated IVC with <50% inspiratory collapse (elevated RA pressure); interventricular septal shift/bounce.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is uraemic pericardial effusion and how is it managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Caused by uraemic toxins irritating the pericardium. Managed by urgent dialysis — pericardiocentesis is reserved for tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Dressler's syndrome?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Post-MI or post-cardiac surgery pericarditis (immune-mediated) occurring weeks to months later — can cause a pericardial effusion. Treated with NSAIDs/colchicine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the Beck's triad and its immediate management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Beck's triad = hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds → tamponade → urgent pericardiocentesis. Do not wait for echo if haemodynamically compromised.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the ECG hallmark of tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Electrical alternans + low voltage + sinus tachycardia = tamponade until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is pericardiocentesis contraindicated in aortic dissection causing tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: The haemopericardium is sealing the dissection. Draining it removes the tamponade effect and precipitates fatal haemorrhage — patient needs emergency surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: Rate of accumulation vs volume — which matters more?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Rate. 150 mL rapidly → tamponade. 1 L slowly → no tamponade. The stiff fibrous pericardium cannot accommodate rapid filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: EXAM PEARL: How does CXR differentiate large effusion from pulmonary oedema?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Large effusion = globular heart + CLEAR lung fields. Pulmonary oedema = normal/enlarged heart + bilateral infiltrates/bat-wing shadowing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the symptoms of pericardial effusion / tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Small effusion: often asymptomatic. Larger/tamponade: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, chest heaviness, fatigue, syncope. Severe tamponade: hypotension, confusion, cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the pathophysiology of cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Fluid in the pericardial space → increased intrapericardial pressure → external cardiac compression → reduced ventricular filling → reduced cardiac output → shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Beck's triad?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds — the classic triad of cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is pulsus paradoxus?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Exaggerated fall in SBP >10 mmHg on inspiration — the key sign of tamponade physiology. Occurs because inspiration increases RV filling at the expense of LV filling in a fixed pericardial space.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the first-line imaging in pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Echocardiography — quantifies effusion, assesses tamponade physiology (RV collapse, RA collapse, IVC plethora, respirophasic changes).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the ECG finding in cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Electrical alternans — alternating QRS amplitude/axis due to the heart swinging in the effusion. Plus: sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the treatment for cardiac tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Emergency pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration guided by echo/X-ray) — even small fluid removal dramatically improves haemodynamics. Surgical pericardiectomy for recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the major causes of pericardial effusion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Idiopathic/viral (most common); tuberculosis (commonest worldwide); malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma); uraemia; autoimmune (SLE, RA); post-cardiac surgery; trauma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is the minimum fluid volume that causes tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Tamponade depends on rate of accumulation — 200 mL of rapidly accumulating fluid can cause tamponade; 2000 mL of slowly accumulating fluid may not.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is haemopericardium?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Blood in the pericardial space — causes include aortic dissection (most serious), trauma, cardiac rupture post-MI, iatrogenic (pacemaker/ablation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: Why is aortic dissection a contraindication to pericardiocentesis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Drainage may release tamponade effect that was tamponading the dissection — fatal rebleeding. Emergency surgery is required instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What are the echocardiographic signs of tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: RV diastolic collapse + RA systolic collapse + IVC dilatation without respiratory collapse + >25% respirophasic variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What fluid is sent from pericardiocentesis aspirate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Cytology (malignancy), microbiology (culture + AFB for TB), LDH + protein (exudate vs transudate), pH, glucose.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is chronic constrictive pericarditis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Fibrotic, calcified, rigid pericardium constraining ventricular filling — late complication of TB, post-cardiac surgery, radiation. Treated by pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: How does constrictive pericarditis differ from tamponade?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Both: raised JVP, low CO, peripheral oedema. Constrictive: Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises on inspiration — paradoxical), calcification on X-ray, gradual onset. Tamponade: pulsus paradoxus, acute.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.front: What is Kussmaul's sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial.back: Paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration — seen in constrictive pericarditis (and restrictive cardiomyopathy). Normally JVP falls on inspiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Define peripheral arterial disease (PAD).
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs — the 'CAD of the legs.' It presents on a spectrum from stable claudication to limb-threatening emergencies.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe intermittent claudication — symptom, ABPI range, and Fontaine stage.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Crampy pain on walking, relieved by rest. ABPI 0.5–0.9. Fontaine II.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe critical limb ischaemia — features, ABPI, Fontaine stage, and urgency.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Rest pain + ulcers + gangrene. ABPI <0.5. Fontaine III–IV. Needs urgent referral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe acute limb ischaemia — cause, key feature, time frame, and category.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Sudden occlusion; the 6 P's; hours to save the limb; an emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the key framing message about claudication patients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Claudication patients don't lose their legs — they die of MI and stroke. PAD is a systemic atherosclerosis marker; treat the whole patient, not just the leg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How is the ABPI calculated, and where is it used?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index = ankle systolic BP ÷ brachial systolic BP. Used at every stage of PAD assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI >1.2 indicate, and what is the caveat?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Calcified/stiff arteries — falsely high. Common in diabetes and advanced age — do not rely on ABPI alone; use the toe-brachial index or duplex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What ABPI range is normal, and what does it mean?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: 1.0–1.2 = normal — no significant PAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI of 0.5–0.9 indicate and how is it managed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Claudication — conservative management, supervised exercise, risk factor modification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What does an ABPI <0.5 indicate and what action is required?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Critical ischaemia / rest pain — urgent vascular referral for revascularisation or amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What ABPI value must be checked before applying venous compression, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: ABPI ≥0.8 is required before full compression bandaging — always check first; 0.5–0.8 needs reduced/modified compression under specialist guidance, and <0.5 (ischaemic leg) must not be compressed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What inspection findings are seen in PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Pallor, cyanosis, dependent rubor (reactive hyperaemia); muscle wasting, hair loss, dry skin; poor wound healing, ulcers, gangrene; scars (amputation, sternotomy, calf vein harvest from prior bypass).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What palpation findings occur in PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Weak or absent pulses (femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial); reduced skin temperature, prolonged capillary refill; reduced sensation (late sign — neuropathy or ischaemia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe Buerger's test and what the angle signifies.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Elevate the limb → pallor (ischaemia); hang the leg down → dependent rubor (reactive hyperaemia). Buerger's angle <20° = severe ischaemia (the angle at which pallor appears on elevation).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the classic triad of Leriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Buttock/thigh claudication, absent femoral pulses bilaterally, and erectile dysfunction (internal iliac involvement). A high-yield exam eponym.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does intermittent claudication present (Fontaine II)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Cramping pain on walking, relieved by rest within minutes; a predictable claudication distance that reproducibly reproduces symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does the site of claudication map to the level of arterial disease?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Calf = femoropopliteal; thigh = iliac; buttock = aortoiliac (Leriche).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What investigations are used in intermittent claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: ABPI (0.5–0.9 in claudication; baseline and follow-up); duplex ultrasound (first-line imaging — identifies stenosis site and severity); MRA/CTA (before surgical intervention — full anatomical map of disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the first-line imaging in claudication, and what does it identify?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Duplex ultrasound — identifies the stenosis site and severity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What conservative (first-line) management applies in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Supervised exercise programme (2 hr/week × 3 months — first-line; improves walking distance); smoking cessation (most important intervention); diet, weight loss, glycaemic control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What medical management is used in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg (established CVD — secondary prevention); clopidogrel 75 mg (first-line antiplatelet; aspirin if intolerant); naftidrofuryl (vasodilator for claudication if the exercise programme fails); optimise BP and diabetes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is the first-line antiplatelet in PAD, and the alternative if intolerant?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Clopidogrel 75 mg first-line; aspirin if intolerant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: When is naftidrofuryl used in claudication?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: It is a vasodilator for claudication if the exercise programme fails.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: When is surgery considered in claudication, and what are the two main options by lesion type?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Lifestyle-limiting only (after conservative + medical have failed and symptoms severely limit life). Angioplasty ± stent — short lesions (<10 cm), aortoiliac preferred; bypass/endarterectomy — long/multifocal disease (>10 cm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How is critical limb ischaemia (Fontaine III–IV) defined?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Defined by any of: rest pain >2 weeks requiring opiates; ischaemic ulceration; gangrene; ABPI <0.5.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe the rest pain of critical limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Worse at night (loses gravity-assisted perfusion when supine); the patient hangs the foot off the bed for relief; requires opiates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What tissue loss and limb signs occur in critical limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Tissue loss: ischaemic ulcers (punched-out, distal) and gangrene — the end-stage of untreated CLI. Limb signs: pale, cold, absent pulses; atrophic shiny skin; absent hair; poor capillary refill.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Outline the management of critical limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Urgent vascular referral (same-day if acute deterioration); revascularisation (angioplasty/stent, bypass/endarterectomy, intra-arterial thrombolysis); amputation (if the limb is unreconstructable or there is extensive necrosis/sepsis/limited life expectancy).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Define acute limb ischaemia and the signs that mean irreversible ischaemia is imminent.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Sudden arterial occlusion threatening limb viability within hours. Paralysis + paraesthesia = irreversible ischaemia imminent — act immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What are the 6 P's of acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Pain (severe, sudden — worse on elevation); pallor (skin white/waxy vs the other limb); pulselessness (absent distal pulses — confirm with handheld Doppler); perishing cold (poikilothermia — limb temperature = environment); paraesthesia (numbness/tingling — early nerve ischaemia, threatened limb); paralysis (motor loss — LATE sign of irreversible ischaemia, urgent surgery).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Which two of the 6 P's signal a threatened or irreversible limb, and which is the late sign?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Paraesthesia (early nerve ischaemia — threatened limb) and paralysis (LATE sign of irreversible ischaemia, needs urgent surgery).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does an embolic acute limb ischaemia differ from thrombosis in situ — onset and source?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Embolus: sudden onset (<24h), no prior claudication; source = AF, mural thrombus post-MI, AAA, prosthetic valve. Thrombosis in situ: prior claudication with acute deterioration; source = atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does the contralateral leg help distinguish embolus from thrombosis in acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Embolus → normal pulses in the other leg (localised disease). Thrombosis → reduced pulses (widespread atherosclerosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: How does treatment differ between embolic and thrombotic acute limb ischaemia?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Embolus → embolectomy / intra-arterial thrombolysis. Thrombosis → thrombolysis / angioplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Outline the immediate management of acute limb ischaemia.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: A–E; IV opioids (pain); IV heparin (prevent propagation); ECG (AF?), handheld Doppler, serum lactate, CT arteriogram; urgent vascular referral → embolectomy/thrombolysis/angioplasty.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Which medication is given in acute limb ischaemia to prevent clot propagation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: IV heparin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What findings in acute limb ischaemia indicate an irreversible limb requiring amputation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Mottled non-blanching skin + woody hard muscles → amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is reperfusion injury after revascularisation, and what does it cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Compartment syndrome (→ fasciotomy); hyperkalaemia; metabolic acidosis; myoglobinuria → AKI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the cause and site of arterial, venous, and neuropathic leg ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Arterial: PAD/ischaemia; distal — toes, heel, pressure points. Venous: venous insufficiency (80% of ulcers); gaiter area (medial malleolus). Neuropathic: neuropathy (diabetes, B12 deficiency); pressure points — sole, metatarsal heads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the appearance of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Arterial: deep, 'punched-out', well-defined, necrotic base. Venous: shallow, irregular, granulating base. Neuropathic: punched-out, surrounded by callus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the pain and surrounding skin of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Pain: arterial = painful (worse on elevation); venous = aching (better on elevation); neuropathic = painless. Surrounding skin: arterial = cold, hairless, reduced pulses; venous = haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, warm; neuropathic = warm, good pulses, sensory loss.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Compare the key management of arterial, venous, and neuropathic ulcers.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Arterial: revascularise (treat as PAD). Venous: compression bandaging (check ABPI ≥0.8 first). Neuropathic: offload, glycaemic control, foot care, check for osteomyelitis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is safety rule 1 regarding compression bandaging in leg ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Always check ABPI before compression bandaging — apply full compression only if ABPI ≥0.8; never compress an ischaemic leg (<0.5), and 0.5–0.8 only under specialist guidance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is safety rule 2 regarding deep neuropathic ulcers?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: X-ray any deep neuropathic ulcer for osteomyelitis (if bone is visible, osteomyelitis is confirmed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is gangrene, and what are its three types by cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Gangrene = irreversible tissue death — the endpoint of the ischaemia pathway (Fontaine IV / CLI's worst). Dry and wet gangrene arise from ischaemia; gas gangrene from infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe dry gangrene and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Ischaemic, aseptic; dehydrated, mummified, black; well-defined demarcation line; the classic PAD endpoint; typically affects digits. Mx: revascularise where possible; allow auto-amputation or surgical amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe wet gangrene and its management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Ischaemia + infection; moist, swollen, foul-smelling; no clear demarcation; a surgical emergency with rapid spread; common in diabetics. Mx: urgent debridement + IV antibiotics + revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: Describe gas gangrene — organism, trigger, signs, and management.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Clostridium perfringens; post-trauma/contaminated wound; crepitus on palpation + gas on X-ray; extremely rapid spread; life-threatening. Mx: emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin/clindamycin + fasciotomies + hyperbaric O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What are the primary indications for amputation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Extensive weight-bearing necrosis; uncontrolled sepsis from an infected limb; paresis/irreversible ischaemia; limited life expectancy (palliation); failed/impossible revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What conservative measures apply in general PAD management?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Smoking cessation (single biggest modifiable risk factor); exercise (supervised programme for claudication); diet, weight loss; optimise diabetes and hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What medical management applies in general PAD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg (all established CVD); clopidogrel 75 mg (first-line antiplatelet; aspirin if intolerant); naftidrofuryl (for claudication if exercise fails); ACEi/ARB for BP control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: In the surgical options table, what is angioplasty ± stent best for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Short stenosis (<10 cm); aortoiliac segment preferred; less invasive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is a bypass graft/endarterectomy best for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Long or multifocal disease (>10 cm); femoropopliteal; more durable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.front: What is intra-arterial thrombolysis best for, and when is amputation indicated?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.back: Intra-arterial thrombolysis: acute thrombotic occlusion, <14 days onset. Amputation: last resort — unreconstructable disease, extensive necrosis, sepsis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a thoracic aortic aneurysm, and why does location matter?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Dilatation of the thoracic aorta. Location matters — it drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are at the ascending aorta/root, what causes them, and what is the repair threshold?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 60%. Most common causes — Marfan's, bicuspid AV, syphilis. Repair threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower in CT disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs involve the aortic arch, and what features and threshold apply?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 10%. Neck pain; high cerebral ischaemia risk during repair. Threshold ≥5.5 cm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are in the descending aorta, what causes them, and what is the threshold and preferred repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 40%. Posterior thoracic pain; atherosclerosis/dissection. Higher threshold ≥6 cm; prefer TEVAR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of TAAs are thoracoabdominal, and what is notable about repair?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: 10%. Extends into the abdomen — complex repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How does TAA compare with AAA in terms of definition, physics, aetiology, and screening?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Shared definition (localised dilatation) and Laplace physics; different aetiology (CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis vs atherosclerosis) and different screening policy (no national TAA screening programme).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a true aneurysm, and which layers are involved?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: All 3 layers (intima, media, adventitia) are intact but dilated. This describes most TAAs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm), and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Intima + media rupture → blood contained only by adventitia. Caused by trauma, surgery, infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is a dissecting aneurysm?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Blood enters between the intima and media layers (see separate Aortic Dissection note).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the mechanism of TAA formation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: List the main TAA-specific causes.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Connective tissue disease (Marfan's [FBN1], Ehlers-Danlos); bicuspid aortic valve (50–70% of ascending TAA); tertiary syphilis (classic ascending aneurysm — exam favourite); trauma; aortic dissection; Takayasu's arteritis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What proportion of ascending TAA is associated with a bicuspid aortic valve?
Which TAA cause is the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Tertiary syphilis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the shared risk factors for TAA (with AAA)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Hypertension (key modifiable RF), smoking, atherosclerosis, male sex, advanced age, family history, high BMI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is 'the discriminator' between TAA and AAA aetiology?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: TAA → think Marfan's / EDS / bicuspid AV / syphilis. AAA → think atherosclerosis. This contrast is frequently tested.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How do most TAAs present?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Most are asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging. There is no national screening programme.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What pain location corresponds to each TAA segment?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Ascending aorta → anterior chest pain; aortic arch → neck pain; descending aorta → posterior thoracic/back pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What compression syndrome arises from trachea/left bronchus involvement?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Cough, SOB, stridor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does recurrent laryngeal nerve compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Hoarse voice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does oesophageal compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Dysphagia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does SVC compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Distended neck veins, facial oedema, SVC obstruction syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does aortic valve involvement cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Aortic regurgitation → heart failure signs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does spinal compression cause in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Back pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the key differentials for TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: PE, ACS, pneumothorax, aortic dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What routine bloods are taken in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: FBC, U&Es, clotting.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the role of ECG in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Exclude ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What CXR findings are seen in TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation — often the incidental finding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Which is the preferred/definitive imaging modality in TAA, and what does it provide?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: CT angiogram — gives anatomy, size, extent, and TEVAR suitability. It is the definitive investigation for size, extent and surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does TOE assess in TAA, and in which patients is it always done?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Assesses valve involvement, AR, and dissection. Done in all Marfan's patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What medical management applies to all TAA patients?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: BP control (key modifiable factor); statin + antiplatelet; smoking cessation; optimise diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, weight.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an ascending/root TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower, ~4.5–5 cm, in Marfan's/bicuspid/CT disease). Dacron graft replacement; Bentall procedure if the root is involved (graft + prosthetic aortic valve).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an aortic arch TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold ≥5.5 cm. Multi-limbed graft (allows great vessel branching); high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the surgical threshold and preferred procedure for a descending TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold ≥6 cm. Open or TEVAR (endovascular — preferred).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: Why is the repair threshold lower in Marfan's/Ehlers-Danlos/bicuspid AV?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Threshold is lower (~4.5–5 cm) — operate earlier because the wall is structurally weaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the Bentall procedure?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Aortic root replacement + prosthetic valve — a key eponym to know.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: How is TEVAR performed?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: A stent graft is delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What happens when a TAA ruptures, and what determines the clinical picture?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Rupture causes bleeding into the mediastinum, with high mortality. The site of bleeding determines the clinical picture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What does a ruptured TAA bleeding into the oesophagus, airway/lungs, or pericardial cavity each cause?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Oesophagus → haematemesis; airway/lungs → haemoptysis; pericardial cavity → cardiac tamponade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the symptoms of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Severe acute-onset chest or back pain; collapse/syncope; haematemesis/haemoptysis (site-dependent).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What are the signs of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Haemodynamic instability — tachycardia + hypotension; signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.front: What is the management of a ruptured TAA?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.back: Emergency open surgical repair with synthetic graft replacement of the affected segment. High mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Every valve lesion in this reference follows the same revision template. What are the six steps in order?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aetiology → Pathophysiology → Symptoms → Signs → Investigations → Management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A murmur is ejection systolic, crescendo-decrescendo, heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space and radiates to the carotids. Name the lesion.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic stenosis (AS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which valve lesion produces a pansystolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral regurgitation (MR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap is heard at the apex, loudest with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position on expiration. What is the lesion?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral stenosis (MS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: An early-diastolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur is heard at the left sternal edge, best with the patient sitting forward in expiration. Name it.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic regurgitation (AR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that gets louder on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: List the key added peripheral features that point to aortic stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft S2, and an S4.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Beyond the murmur, what three findings flag mitral regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Soft S1, an S3, and a displaced apex beat.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which auscultatory and clinical extras accompany mitral stenosis?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Loud S1, an opening snap, malar flush, and atrial fibrillation (AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What peripheral signs go with aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Wide pulse pressure, a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, and a displaced apex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which added features signal tricuspid regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Giant V waves in the JVP, a pulsatile liver, and a raised JVP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: The mnemonic ASSES groups which class of murmurs, and which lesions does it cover?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Systolic murmurs — AS, SS (innocent), ES, ES…

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which mnemonic covers diastolic murmurs, and what does it stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: 'My Slaves Might Die' — Mitral Stenosis, Aortic Regurgitation, etc. (diastolic murmurs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Rheumatic fever affects valves in a characteristic order captured by 'MAPT'. What is the sequence?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral (most common) → Aortic → Pulmonary → Tricuspid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: On a murmur-timing diagram, which lesion shows a crescendo-decrescendo 'diamond' shape filling systole?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic stenosis (ejection systolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion appears as a uniform band of sound occupying the whole of systole between S1 and S2?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mitral regurgitation (pansystolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: On the timing diagram, what shape and position identifies aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Early-diastolic, decrescendo murmur beginning immediately after S2.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Mitral stenosis sits where in the cardiac cycle on a timing diagram?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Mid-diastolic — a rumble after the opening snap.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A patent ductus arteriosus produces a murmur with a distinctive timing. Describe it.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A continuous 'machinery' murmur spanning both systole and diastole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: The mnemonic RILE summarises manoeuvre effects. What does it stand for?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Right-sided murmurs louder on Inspiration; Left-sided murmurs louder on Expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Mechanistically, why does inspiration make right-sided murmurs louder?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, raising right-sided flow and therefore murmur intensity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which murmurs get louder on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Right-sided murmurs — tricuspid regurgitation, tricuspid stenosis, and pulmonary murmurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does expiration accentuate left-sided murmurs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Expiration increases pulmonary venous return to the left heart, raising left-sided flow.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which murmurs are loudest in expiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS, MR, MS, and AR (all left-sided).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Beyond expiration, what extra manoeuvre maximises the mitral stenosis murmur, and why?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Left lateral decubitus position — it brings the apex closer to the chest wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is the optimal positioning to hear aortic regurgitation?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Patient sitting forward with breath held in expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: How do Valsalva and squatting differ in their effect on HOCM and MVP murmurs?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Valsalva decreases preload and makes HOCM & MVP murmurs louder; squatting increases preload and makes them quieter.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Two murmurs have signature radiation patterns you should always check. Name them.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: AS radiates to the carotids; MR radiates to the axilla.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What causes the first heart sound (S1), and which lesion makes it louder versus softer?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S1 = mitral and tricuspid valve closure (start of systole). Louder in MS (rigid but still mobile valves snap shut); softer in MR (valve doesn't close properly).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What produces S2, and what makes it split on inspiration?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S2 = aortic and pulmonary valve closure. It splits on inspiration because the pulmonary valve closes slightly later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: In which valve lesion is S2 soft or absent, and which condition gives a wide fixed split of S2?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S2 is soft/absent in severe AS; a wide fixed split occurs in ASD. S2 is loud in pulmonary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What does S3 represent, when is it physiological, and when is it pathological?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S3 = rapid ventricular filling. Physiological in the young, athletic, and in pregnancy. Pathological in heart failure (LV dilatation) and severe MR — gives a 'gallop' rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why is S4 always pathological, and what generates it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: S4 is atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle — this never occurs normally. Heard in AS (pressure overload), HCM, hypertension, and ischaemic disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: An opening snap follows S2 in mitral stenosis. What does a shorter S2–snap interval indicate?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: The earlier the snap occurs after S2, the higher the left atrial pressure and the more severe the stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: A pericardial knock can be mistaken for an S3. How does it differ, and what causes it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: It sounds like S3 but occurs earlier and is louder; it is caused by abrupt halting of ventricular filling in constrictive pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: What is a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse, and which lesion produces it?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: A slow, low-amplitude aortic upstroke caused by obstruction to LV outflow — characteristic of aortic stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Explain the mechanism of the narrow pulse pressure in aortic stenosis.
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Reduced stroke volume lowers systolic BP, while raised LV end-diastolic pressure raises the diastolic — narrowing the gap between them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Which lesion gives a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, and what is the underlying mechanism?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.back: Aortic regurgitation — regurgitation lowers diastolic pressure while compensatory increased stroke volume raises systolic, producing a wide pulse pressure and bounding, collapsing pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.front: Why does aortic regurgitation cause a wide pulse pressure?
