conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient is given atropine and the heart rate rises. Why does blocking the vagus speed the heart?
options: Because sympathetic tone dominates at rest, so blocking the vagus simply unmasks the already-high adrenergic drive that then accelerates the node
Because atropine increases myocardial contractility, and the stronger stroke volume reflexively drives the sinoatrial node to a faster rate
Because atropine directly steepens the phase 4 slope of pacemaker cells, acting on the SA node itself rather than through any autonomic tone
Because atropine blocks the funny (If) current, and losing that brake on phase 4 depolarisation lets the SA node discharge more rapidly
Because the vagus dominates at rest (intrinsic SA rate ~100, held ~70 by vagal tone), so removing vagal tone allows the rate to rise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: At rest the vagus dominates (intrinsic SA rate ~100; vagal tone holds it ~70), which is why atropine (blocking the vagus) speeds the heart.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does digoxin help with rate control in AF, per this note?
options: It blocks the funny current in the SA node
It increases vagal tone, slowing AV conduction
It steepens the phase 4 slope
It blocks fast Na⁺ channels
It hyperpolarises ventricular myocytes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Digoxin increases vagal tone, which slows AV conduction — useful in AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why can't cardiac muscle be tetanised?
options: Because it has no refractory period, so successive stimuli summate freely and the muscle can be driven into a sustained tetanic contraction like skeletal muscle
Because the fast Na⁺ channels never inactivate, keeping the cell continuously depolarised so that no further excitatory stimulus can ever take effect
Because the cardiac action potential is very short, ending well before the twitch peaks, so there is no window in which a second stimulus could summate
Because specialised pacemaker cells actively suppress any incoming stimuli, overriding external drive and thereby preventing the summation of contractions
The long plateau gives a long absolute refractory period, so the cell can't be re-excited until repolarised — preventing tetany and summation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The long plateau produces a long absolute refractory period during which the cell cannot be re-excited until repolarised, preventing tetany and summation and limiting how fast the ventricles can be driven.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: The AV nodal delay corresponds to which part of the ECG?
options: The PR interval
The P wave
The QRS complex
The T wave
The ST segment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In the conduction-to-ECG mapping, the AV nodal delay corresponds to the PR interval (SA firing/atrial depolarisation → P wave; ventricular depolarisation → QRS; ventricular repolarisation → T wave).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does progressive AV nodal/His disease manifest as heart block worsens?
options: It has no effect on the ECG, since AV nodal and His conduction are electrically silent and never alter the tracing
PR prolongation (1st degree) → dropped beats (2nd degree) → AV dissociation + escape rhythm (3rd/complete)
It only causes a tall peaked T wave, reflecting delayed repolarisation through the diseased conducting tissue
It shortens the PR interval progressively as conduction speeds up, producing a delta wave and pre-excitation
It abolishes the QRS entirely from the outset, leaving only P waves as the ventricles fail to depolarise at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Heart block from AV nodal/His disease progresses from PR prolongation (1st degree) to dropped beats (2nd degree) to AV dissociation with an escape rhythm (3rd/complete), explained by the conduction sequence and pacemaker hierarchy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: In the Vaughan-Williams classification, which action-potential target corresponds to each class?
options: I = K⁺ channel (phase 0); II = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal); III = Na⁺ channel (phase 3); IV = β-blocker acting on sympathetic phase 4 depolarisation
I = Na⁺ channel (phase 0); II = β-blockers (phase 4/sympathetic); III = K⁺ channel (phase 3, prolong AP); IV = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal phase 0)
I = β-blocker (phase 4); II = Na⁺ channel (phase 0); III = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal); IV = K⁺ channel prolonging phase 3 repolarisation of the AP
I = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal phase 0); II = K⁺ channel (phase 3); III = β-blocker (phase 4); IV = Na⁺ channel blocker acting on the phase 0 upstroke
All four classes act on phase 2 of the plateau, differing only in how strongly they prolong the calcium-dependent portion of the action potential
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The Vaughan-Williams classes map onto the AP: I = Na⁺ channel (phase 0), II = β-blockers (phase 4/sympathetic), III = K⁺ channel (phase 3, prolong AP), IV = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal phase 0).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the mechanism of ivabradine and its key advantage?
options: A β-blocker that reduces contractility and BP while slowing the SA node, giving rate control at the cost of lowering blood pressure and output
A Na⁺ channel blocker acting on phase 0 of the ventricular AP, slowing conduction velocity and widening the QRS while it controls the rate
A funny-current (If) blocker that slows the SA node specifically (phase 4), giving rate control without affecting BP/contractility
A K⁺ channel blocker that prolongs phase 3 repolarisation, lengthening the QT interval to achieve rate control acting at the SA node
A Ca²⁺ channel blocker acting on the nodal phase 0 upstroke, slowing SA and AV conduction while also relaxing vascular smooth muscle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Ivabradine is a funny-current (If) blocker that slows the SA node specifically (phase 4), giving rate control without affecting BP or contractility.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why does hyperkalaemia alter the action potential (tall T, broad QRS)?
options: Because K⁺ governs phase 0 depolarisation
Because it blocks fast Na⁺ channels only
Because K⁺ governs phases 2-3 of the action potential
Because it steepens the phase 4 slope
Because it increases the funny current
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Hyperkalaemia alters the AP (tall T, broad QRS) because K⁺ governs phases 2-3 of the action potential.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What does the ECG record?
options: The mechanical contraction of the ventricles, mapping the pressure-driven squeeze of the chambers as it spreads across the myocardial wall
The pressure changes within the chambers, tracing the rise and fall of intracardiac pressure as blood is ejected through the valves each cycle
The summed electrical activity of the heart from the body surface — the conduction sequence + action potentials viewed from outside
The coronary blood flow, recording the perfusion of the myocardium through the coronary arteries as it varies across the cardiac cycle
The oxygen saturation of cardiac muscle, reflecting the moment-to-moment metabolic demand of the myocardium as it contracts and relaxes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The ECG records the summed electrical activity of the heart from the body surface — the conduction sequence and action potentials viewed from outside.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the single organising principle from which every ECG feature follows?
options: Depolarisation moving towards a recording electrode gives a downward (negative) deflection, while a wave moving away produces an upward positive one
A wave of depolarisation moving towards a recording electrode gives an upward (positive) deflection; moving away gives a downward deflection
Repolarisation always gives an upward deflection regardless of its direction, so every recovery wave registers as positive no matter which electrode faces it
The size of a deflection depends only on the heart rate, growing taller as the rhythm speeds up and shrinking again as the sinus rate slows down
Deflection direction is entirely random and unrelated to the direction in which the wave of depolarisation happens to travel across the myocardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The single organising principle is that depolarisation moving towards a recording electrode gives an upward (positive) deflection and moving away gives a downward one; every ECG feature follows from this plus the fixed conduction sequence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: According to the towards/away rule, what deflection results when depolarisation moves perpendicular to a lead?
options: A large positive deflection
No trace at all
A deep negative deflection
A biphasic or flat deflection
A tall tented T wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Depolarisation towards an electrode gives a positive deflection, away gives negative, and perpendicular gives a biphasic/flat deflection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why are the QRS and T wave both usually upright, despite representing opposite electrical processes?
options: Because both depolarisation and repolarisation spread in the same endocardium-to-epicardium direction, so their identical charge and identical path produce two matching upright deflections on the tracing
Because repolarisation generates far too small a voltage to register meaningfully on its own, so the upright T wave is really just a passive electrical echo of the large preceding QRS complex

Because the T wave is actually a second depolarisation event rather than recovery, spreading in the same direction as the QRS and therefore inscribing an upright deflection identical in polarity to it
Because depolarisation spreads endocardium→epicardium while repolarisation goes epicardium→endocardium — opposite direction and opposite charge cancel into same-direction deflections
Because the recording leads automatically invert the repolarisation wave before display, flipping what would otherwise be a downward T deflection into the upright shape that is conventionally seen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Depolarisation spreads endocardium→epicardium but repolarisation goes epicardium→endocardium (opposite direction and opposite charge), so the two cancel into same-direction deflections — which is why the QRS and T wave are both usually upright.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which plane do the limb leads and chest leads view the heart in?
options: Limb leads = vertical/coronal plane; chest leads = horizontal plane
Limb leads = horizontal plane; chest leads = vertical plane
Both view only the sagittal plane
Limb leads = sagittal; chest leads = coronal
Neither views the heart from a fixed plane
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The leads view the heart from different angles: limb leads in the vertical/coronal plane and chest leads in the horizontal plane, each seeing the same events from its own direction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: The P wave corresponds to which electrical event and conduction step?
options: Atrial depolarisation; SA node fires → atria
Ventricular depolarisation; His-Purkinje spread
Ventricular repolarisation; phase 3
The AV nodal delay
Ventricles fully depolarised (plateau)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation as the SA node fires and the signal spreads to the atria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: The PR interval spans which events, and what key delay does it include?
options: Start of atrial depolarisation to start of ventricular depolarisation; includes the AV nodal delay
Ventricular depolarisation to repolarisation; it includes the plateau of the ventricular action potential
The whole ventricular action potential from phase 0 to phase 3; it includes the repolarising phase 3 limb
Atrial repolarisation only, the small hidden wave that follows the P wave beneath the QRS complex
The T wave to the next P wave, spanning the electrical diastole between two successive cardiac cycles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The PR interval spans the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular depolarisation and includes the AV nodal delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: The QT interval represents which of the following?
options: Atrial depolarisation only, corresponding to the surface P wave of the ECG
The plateau phase only, the phase 2 portion of the ventricular action potential
The AV nodal conduction delay between atrial and ventricular activation
Total ventricular depolarisation + repolarisation — the whole ventricular AP
Ventricular repolarisation only, the recovery limb that inscribes the T wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The QT interval represents total ventricular depolarisation plus repolarisation — the whole ventricular action potential.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Where is atrial repolarisation on the ECG, and why is it not seen?
options: It forms the T wave and is always clearly visible, appearing as a distinct positive deflection after every single P wave
It is hidden within the QRS, being too small to see and masked by the much larger ventricular depolarisation
It forms the P wave itself, the atrial recovery process being what inscribes that initial rounded upward deflection
It appears as the ST segment, the flat portion representing atrial recovery between the QRS and the T wave
It is seen as a distinct U wave, the small deflection following the T wave that reflects atrial repolarisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Atrial repolarisation is hidden within the QRS — too small to see and masked by the much larger ventricular depolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why does AV block manifest as PR changes on the ECG?
options: Because the PR interval reflects ventricular repolarisation
Because the P wave represents ventricular depolarisation
Because the PR interval is the AV nodal delay made visible
Because AV block widens the QRS
Because AV block abolishes the T wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The PR interval is the AV nodal delay made visible, which is why AV block shows as PR changes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: At standard settings, what time does one small square represent?
options: 1 s
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: At standard speed (25 mm/s), a small square = 0.04 s (1 mm), a large square = 0.2 s (5 mm), and 5 large squares = 1 s.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is heart rate estimated from a regular rhythm on the ECG?
options: Count the P waves in 10 seconds
60 ÷ (small squares between R waves)
Multiply the QRS width by 6
300 ÷ (large squares between R waves)
Count large squares across the whole strip
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: For a regular rhythm, rate = 300 ÷ (large squares between R waves); for an irregular rhythm, count the QRS complexes on the rhythm strip and multiply by 6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the normal PR interval?
options: 0.04-0.08 s (1-2 small squares)
<0.12 s (under 3 small squares)
0.20-0.40 s (5-10 small squares)
0.12-0.20 s (3-5 small squares)
~0.44 s (about 11 small squares)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The normal PR interval is 0.12-0.20 s (3-5 small squares); a normal QRS is <0.12 s and the QTc is ~<0.44 s.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the normal cardiac axis, and why does it point down-and-left?
options: +90° to +180°, because the thicker right ventricle dominates the mean vector
Exactly 0° and horizontal, because the two ventricles are electrically equal
−90° to −180° (up-and-left), because the combined atrial mass dominates
~−30° to +90° (down-and-left), because the large left ventricle dominates
It has no normal range, varying unpredictably from beat to beat in everyone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The cardiac axis is the overall direction of the ventricular depolarisation wave, normally down-and-left (~−30° to +90°) because the large left ventricle dominates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which conditions are associated with right axis deviation?
options: LVH and conduction blocks
Atrial fibrillation and hypokalaemia
RVH and PE
Hypercalcaemia and torsades
Complete heart block and BBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Right axis deviation is associated with RVH and PE, whereas left axis deviation is associated with LVH and conduction blocks; axis is detected by which leads are positive/negative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient's ECG shows a broad QRS. What is the physiological basis?
options: AV nodal delay slowing atrio-ventricular conduction before the ventricles depolarise
Injury current from acute ischaemia shifting the baseline across the myocardial wall
Prolonged ventricular repolarisation stretching out phase 3 of the action potential
No organised atrial depolarisation reaching the ventricular conducting system at all
Slow/abnormal ventricular spread (bundle branch block, ventricular origin, hyperkalaemia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: A broad QRS reflects slow or abnormal ventricular spread — as in bundle branch block, a ventricular origin, or hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the physiological basis of ST elevation or depression?
options: AV nodal and His-bundle conduction block interrupting the path between atria and ventricles
Prolonged repolarisation causing torsades, as phase 3 lengthens and the QT interval stretches out
Injury current from ischaemia/infarction, because depolarised and injured myocardium differ in charge
No organised atrial depolarisation, so the fibrillating atria continuously distort the ST baseline
Slow abnormal ventricular spread through diseased tissue, broadening and displacing the ST segment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: ST elevation/depression arises from an injury current in ischaemia/infarction, because depolarised versus injured myocardium differ in charge.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: An ECG shows absent P waves with an irregular rhythm. What does this indicate?
options: Complete heart block with AV dissociation and an escape rhythm
Atrial fibrillation (no organised atrial depolarisation)
First-degree AV block with a uniformly prolonged PR interval
Long QT syndrome predisposing to torsades de pointes
Bundle branch block producing a broad abnormal QRS complex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Absent P waves with an irregular rhythm indicate atrial fibrillation, in which there is no organised atrial depolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: An ECG shows no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete (3rd degree) heart block — AV dissociation
First-degree heart block — a fixed prolonged PR interval
Atrial fibrillation — no organised atrial depolarisation
Second-degree heart block — intermittently dropped beats
Sinus tachycardia — a fast rhythm with a normal P-QRS link
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: No P-QRS relationship indicates complete (3rd degree) heart block with AV dissociation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient with renal failure has hyperkalaemia. What is the expected sequence of ECG changes?
options: U waves → short QT → normalisation
Tall tented T → broad QRS → sinusoidal
Long QT → torsades → U waves
Absent P waves → irregular rhythm only
Short QT → tall tented T → normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Hyperkalaemia progresses on the ECG as tall tented T waves → broad QRS → sinusoidal; hypokalaemia causes U waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How do calcium disturbances affect the QT interval, and why?
options: Hypocalcaemia → long QT; hypercalcaemia → short QT, because Ca²⁺ governs the plateau
Hypocalcaemia → short QT; hypercalcaemia → long QT, since Ca²⁺ chiefly sets the phase-0 upstroke
Both hypo- and hypercalcaemia lengthen the QT by prolonging repolarisation and the plateau phase
Both hypo- and hypercalcaemia produce prominent U waves rather than any change in the QT interval
Calcium has no effect on QT; only potassium fluxes govern ventricular repolarisation timing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT and hypercalcaemia shortens it, because Ca²⁺ governs the plateau of the action potential.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the unifying idea for interpreting any abnormal ECG?
options: Every abnormality on an ECG ultimately reflects myocardial ischaemia, since reduced coronary perfusion is the single common pathway that alters every waveform, interval, and rhythm you will encounter
Every abnormality on an ECG is simply a benign normal variant, so tracings never need pathological interpretation and any deviation from textbook morphology can be safely dismissed as physiological
Every abnormality on an ECG stems from an electrolyte disturbance, because shifts in potassium, calcium, sodium and magnesium are what generate every change in rhythm, conduction and waveform shape

Every abnormality on an ECG reflects an underlying valve lesion, since stenosis or regurgitation drives the chamber enlargement and the axis or waveform changes seen across all the tracings you interpret
Every abnormal ECG is either an abnormal rhythm (where the impulse starts), abnormal conduction (how it spreads), or an abnormal myocardium (ischaemia/electrolyte/structural changing the AP)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The unifying idea is that every abnormal ECG is either an abnormal rhythm (where the impulse starts), an abnormal conduction (how it spreads), or an abnormal myocardium (ischaemia/electrolyte/structural changing the AP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What does Starling's law (the Frank-Starling mechanism) state?
options: The more the ventricle is filled in diastole, the less forcefully it contracts, so stroke volume falls as end-diastolic volume rises because the fibres lose contractile power
Stroke volume falls progressively as end-diastolic volume rises, because greater diastolic filling overstretches the sarcomeres and weakens each systolic contraction
Stroke volume is entirely independent of end-diastolic volume, being fixed instead by the intrinsic contractile state of the myocardium whatever the diastolic stretch
Contraction force depends only on heart rate, so stroke volume is set purely by how fast the SA node fires and bears no relationship to the degree of ventricular filling
The more the ventricle is filled (stretched) in diastole, the more forcefully it contracts, so stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume rises, within limits
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Starling's law states that the more the ventricle is filled (stretched) in diastole, the more forcefully it contracts, so stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume rises, within limits.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which of the three determinants of stroke volume is Starling's law specifically about?
options: Afterload
Ejection fraction
Contractility
Heart rate
Preload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Stroke volume is governed by preload, afterload and contractility; Starling's law is specifically about preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
options: Increased heart rate raises the force of contraction, because faster SA node firing loads the myocytes with more calcium per beat and directly strengthens each contraction
Sympathetic nerves physically stretch the sarcomere to its optimal length, and this direct neural pull on the filaments increases actin-myosin overlap and force
Stretching the sarcomere to its optimal length increases actin-myosin overlap and calcium sensitivity → stronger contraction (length-tension relationship)
Reduced afterload increases actin-myosin filament overlap, and this greater overlap from easier ejection is the cellular event underlying the stronger contraction
Calcium is actively expelled from the cell during stretch, and this fall in cytosolic calcium is paradoxically what strengthens contraction as the sarcomere lengthens
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The cellular basis is that stretching the sarcomere to its optimal length increases the overlap and calcium sensitivity of actin-myosin filaments, giving a stronger contraction — the length-tension relationship.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the functional purpose of the Frank-Starling mechanism?
options: To demand nervous control for every heartbeat, so each contraction depends on autonomic input to match output to venous return
To match output to input automatically (more blood in → more pumped out) and to balance the two ventricles
To keep stroke volume constant regardless of venous return, so the ventricle ejects a fixed volume no matter how much arrives
To raise the heart rate whenever preload falls, using stretch of the SA node to speed firing and defend cardiac output
To reduce ventricular output whenever venous return rises, ejecting less blood precisely when more arrives in diastole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The Frank-Starling mechanism matches output to input automatically beat-to-beat without nervous control, and balances the two ventricles (if the right pumps more, the left receives more and matches it).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What does the plateau/descending portion of the Starling curve represent?
options: The normal operating range where more diastolic filling always gives proportionally more output as the ventricle climbs the ascending limb
The effect of increased contractility, showing how a positive inotropic state lifts the whole curve so more force is generated at any filling
The zone beyond optimal stretch where fibres are overstretched and contraction weakens — the decompensated heart failure zone
The effect of reduced afterload, showing how easier ejection against a lower resistance raises stroke volume for any end-diastolic volume
The single point of maximum ejection fraction, marking where the ventricle empties most completely and the SV-to-EDV ratio peaks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The plateau/descending portion is where, beyond optimal stretch, the fibres are overstretched and contraction weakens — the decompensated heart failure zone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient is given an inotrope. In which direction does the Starling curve shift, and what does this mean?
options: Down + right; less SV for the same preload
The curve does not move with inotropes
Down + left; no change in SV
Up + right; less filling needed but lower SV
Up + left; more SV for the same preload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Increased contractility (sympathetic, inotropes) shifts the curve up + left, giving more stroke volume for the same preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: In heart failure, ischaemia, or with β-blockers, how does the Starling curve shift and what does this imply?
options: Up and to the left; the curve rises so more stroke volume is produced for the same preload
No shift occurs at all; stroke volume stays unchanged for any given preload under these conditions
Down + right; less SV for the same preload, needing higher filling pressures for any given output
Up and to the right; less filling pressure is needed to achieve any given stroke volume
Down and to the left; a higher stroke volume is generated at low preload with these conditions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Reduced contractility (heart failure, ischaemia, β-blockers) shifts the curve down + right, giving less SV for the same preload and needing higher filling pressures for any given output.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why is the failing heart 'preload-dependent' and prone to congestion?
options: It operates on an elevated, upward-shifted curve that needs only very little filling to generate a normal stroke volume
It has excessive intrinsic contractility that drives the ventricle to eject too forcefully, emptying so completely that congestion develops
It operates on a depressed curve, needing high filling pressures, which back up into the lungs (pulmonary oedema)
It is completely insensitive to afterload, so changes in the resistance it pumps against do not affect stroke volume or congestion
It has a permanently reduced resting heart rate, and this fixed bradycardia forces it to rely heavily on preload for output
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The failing heart operates on a depressed curve, needing high filling pressures that back up into the lungs, causing pulmonary oedema — hence it is preload-dependent and prone to congestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is preload defined, and what is its effect on stroke volume?
options: The resistance the ventricle pumps against during ejection; raising it reduces stroke volume (↓SV)
The heart rate set by the SA node's pacemaker firing; changing it has little effect on stroke volume
The intrinsic force of myocardial contraction, independent of filling; raising it increases stroke volume (↑SV)
The stretch/filling at end-diastole (EDV) — the Starling factor; ↑SV (up the curve)
The cross-sectional area of the aortic valve orifice; narrowing it lowers stroke volume (↓SV)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Preload is the stretch/filling at end-diastole (EDV) — the Starling factor — increased by venous return, fluids, lying down, exercise and bradycardia, raising SV (up the curve).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Hypertension, aortic stenosis and vasoconstriction increase which determinant, and what is the effect on stroke volume?
options: Preload; ↑SV
Contractility; ↑SV
Afterload; ↓SV (harder to eject)
Heart rate; ↑SV
Preload; ↓SV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Afterload — the resistance the ventricle pumps against — is increased by hypertension, aortic stenosis and vasoconstriction, reducing SV because it is harder to eject.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is contractility (inotropy), and what increases it?
options: The degree of stretch on the fibres at end-diastole; it is increased chiefly by giving intravenous fluids that expand blood volume and raise venous return to the heart
The intrinsic force of contraction, independent of preload/afterload; increased by sympathetic/adrenaline, inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine) and Ca²⁺
The resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood; it is increased by systemic hypertension, aortic stenosis and any rise in vascular resistance
The rate at which the SA node fires each minute; it is increased by exercise, fever and sympathetic drive that steepens the phase-4 pacemaker depolarisation slope
The fraction of end-diastolic volume ejected per beat; it is increased by loop diuretics that offload the ventricle and reduce the volume it must handle in diastole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Contractility (inotropy) is the intrinsic force of contraction independent of preload/afterload, increased by sympathetic/adrenaline, inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine) and Ca²⁺, raising SV (curve up-left).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How can preload be estimated clinically?
options: By arterial BP alone
By heart rate only
By CVP / JVP / EDV
By ejection fraction only
By the QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Preload determinants include venous return, blood volume, atrial kick, venous tone and posture, and preload is estimated by CVP / JVP / EDV.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why does a chronically increased afterload lead to LVH, and why does afterload reduction help heart failure?
options: ↑afterload → harder ejection → the ventricle compensates with hypertrophy (LVH); a failing ventricle is very afterload-sensitive, so vasodilators/afterload reduction help
↑afterload actually makes ejection easier, so with less work the muscle gradually atrophies and thins; afterload reduction therefore removes a helpful stimulus in failure
Afterload bears no relationship to hypertrophy, which arises purely from genetic and hormonal signals; lowering afterload with vasodilators is irrelevant to the failing ventricle
Afterload reduction actively worsens ejection in heart failure, because the ventricle relies on high outflow resistance to build the pressure that opens the aortic valve
Left ventricular hypertrophy develops only from chronically increased preload, as excessive diastolic filling thickens the wall; the resistance ejected against plays no part
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Increased afterload makes ejection harder, so the ventricle compensates with hypertrophy (LVH); the failing ventricle is very afterload-sensitive, which is why vasodilators/afterload reduction help heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What do the formulae for stroke volume and cardiac output state?
options: SV = EDV + ESV; CO = SV ÷ heart rate
SV = EDV − ESV; CO = SV × heart rate
SV = ESV − EDV; CO = SV + heart rate
SV = EDV × ESV; CO = SV − heart rate
SV = heart rate ÷ EDV; CO = SV × ESV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: SV = EDV − ESV and CO = SV × heart rate, so cardiac output is governed by the three SV determinants plus heart rate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is ejection fraction, its normal range, and what does a reduced EF indicate?
options: EDV − ESV; ~30-40%; reduced EF = diastolic failure
EDV / SV; ~40-50%; reduced EF = valve disease
ESV / EDV; ~80-90%; reduced EF = normal
SV × EDV; ~55-70%; reduced EF = hypertension
SV / EDV; ~55-70%; reduced EF = systolic heart failure (HFrEF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: EF = SV / EDV (normally ~55-70%), the clinical marker of contractility; reduced EF = systolic heart failure (HFrEF), while preserved EF with poor filling = HFpEF (diastolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient has a preserved ejection fraction but symptoms of heart failure due to poor filling. What is this called?
options: HFrEF (systolic heart failure)
HFpEF (diastolic heart failure)
High-output failure
Aortic stenosis
Cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Preserved EF with poor filling is HFpEF (diastolic heart failure), in contrast to reduced EF which is HFrEF (systolic).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is heart failure treated in Starling/SV terms?
options: ↑preload with fluids and ↑afterload with vasopressors
↑afterload and ↓contractility
↓preload (diuretics), ↓afterload (ACEi/vasodilators), ± inotropes
↑preload and ↓heart rate only
No pharmacological intervention is useful
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The failing heart operates on a depressed/shifted-right curve needing high filling pressure and causing congestion, so it is treated by reducing preload (diuretics), reducing afterload (ACEi/vasodilators) and, where needed, inotropes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient in shock is given a fluid bolus. In Starling terms, when will this raise stroke volume?
options: Always, wherever they sit on the Starling curve, since any added fluid must raise preload and stroke volume
Only if they are on the rising part of the curve ('fluid-responsive') — the bolus ↑preload → ↑SV
Only if they are already on the flat plateau, where extra filling finally raises the stroke volume
Never, because a fluid bolus cannot raise stroke volume; only inotropes acting on contractility can
Only if their contractility is already maximal, so the activated myocardium converts preload into stroke volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: A fluid bolus increases preload and raises SV by climbing the Starling curve — but only if the patient is on the rising part ('fluid-responsive').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does aortic stenosis fit the Starling/SV framework?
options: It reduces afterload and increases SV
It raises contractility
It increases preload directly
Fixed ↑afterload → LVH → eventually failure
It has no effect on the ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Aortic stenosis imposes a fixed increased afterload, leading to LVH and eventually failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How do ACEi/vasodilators improve stroke volume in the failing heart?
options: ↑afterload → harder ejection against greater resistance → ↑SV in the failing heart
↑preload from fluid retention stretches the ventricle further → ↑SV in failure
↓afterload → easier ejection → ↑SV in the afterload-sensitive failing heart
↑contractility directly, as ACEi act as positive inotropes on the myocardium → ↑SV
↓heart rate lengthens diastolic filling time → ↑SV in the failing ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: ACEi/vasodilators reduce afterload, making ejection easier and increasing SV in the afterload-sensitive failing heart.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How can atrial fibrillation reduce cardiac output, particularly in a stiff ventricle?
options: Loss of the atrial kick → ↓preload → can drop CO in a stiff ventricle
By increasing the atrial kick and overfilling the ventricle
By raising contractility excessively
By reducing afterload too much
By increasing ejection fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In AF, loss of the atrial kick reduces preload, which can drop cardiac output particularly in a stiff ventricle that depends on the atrial contribution.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does Starling's ventricle-balancing role explain right-sided strain developing after left-sided failure?
options: Right-sided failure almost always precedes left-sided failure, the right ventricle failing first and straining the left
Left-sided failure → blood backs up → right-sided strain (Starling balances the ventricles)
The two ventricles operate completely independently, so the state of one has no effect on the other's workload
Left-sided failure actually reduces the right ventricle's workload, easing its strain by delivering less blood to the lungs
Right-sided strain works to reduce left atrial pressure, decompressing the pulmonary circulation and protecting the left heart
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Because Starling balances the ventricles, left-sided failure causes blood to back up, producing right-sided strain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is cardiac output?
options: The volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of diastole, just before systole, which sets the degree of fibre stretch
The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute — the central measure of how well the heart meets the body's demands
The total resistance the ventricle must pump against during ejection, largely set by the tone of the systemic arterioles
The volume of blood ejected by the ventricle in a single beat, set by preload, afterload and the contractile state of the muscle
The peak pressure generated in the ventricle during systole, reflecting how forcefully the chamber drives blood into the aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute — the central measure of how well the heart meets the body's demands.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the master equation for cardiac output?
options: CO = EDV − ESV
CO = BP × SVR
CO = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate
CO = SV / EDV
CO = Heart Rate ÷ Stroke Volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The master equation is CO = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate; everything that changes CO works through one of these two terms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Using typical resting values, what is the approximate cardiac output?
options: SV ≈ 120 mL, HR ≈ 100 bpm → CO ≈ 12 L/min
SV ≈ 70 mL, HR ≈ 70 bpm → CO ≈ 20 L/min
SV ≈ 30 mL, HR ≈ 40 bpm → CO ≈ 1 L/min
SV ≈ 70 mL, HR ≈ 70 bpm → CO ≈ 5 L/min
SV ≈ 50 mL, HR ≈ 50 bpm → CO ≈ 2.5 L/min
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Typical resting values are SV ≈ 70 mL and HR ≈ 70 bpm, giving CO ≈ 5 L/min — roughly the whole blood volume per minute.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the cardiac index, and why is it used?
options: Cardiac output multiplied by heart rate; used to estimate arterial blood pressure
Cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance; used to find afterload
Stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume; used to measure contractility
CO / body surface area; it normalises for body size (the clinical measure)
Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate; used as a bedside measure of preload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Cardiac index = CO / body surface area, which normalises for body size and is the clinical measure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which factors govern each of the two levers of cardiac output?
options: SV is set by autonomic tone; HR is governed by preload, afterload and contractility
SV is set by systemic vascular resistance; HR is governed chiefly by blood volume
Both stroke volume and heart rate are governed solely by how fast the SA node fires
SV = preload/afterload/contractility; HR = autonomic tone (SA node phase-4 slope)
SV is set by whole-body O₂ consumption; HR by the arteriovenous oxygen difference
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Stroke volume is governed by preload, afterload and contractility, while heart rate is governed by autonomic tone (the SA node phase-4 slope).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A patient develops a very fast SVT and their cardiac output falls, causing presyncope. Why does CO fall despite the high heart rate?
options: At very high rates diastole shortens → less filling time → ↓EDV → ↓SV, so beyond an optimal rate the lost filling time outweighs the rate increase and CO falls
Because a higher heart rate always lowers cardiac output, since every rise in rate reduces the volume ejected per minute whatever happens to filling
Because myocardial contractility is completely abolished at high rates, so the ventricle loses all intrinsic force and can no longer generate stroke volume
Because afterload effectively disappears during the tachycardia, removing the resistance needed to build ejection pressure so forward stroke volume collapses
Because venous return increases far too much in the tachycardia, overfilling and overstretching the ventricle so it can no longer generate an adequate stroke volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: HR and CO are not simply linear: at very high rates (fast AF, SVT) diastole shortens, reducing filling time, EDV and SV, so beyond the optimal rate the lost filling time outweighs the rate increase and CO can fall — causing syncope/shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does the sympathetic nervous system raise cardiac output?
options: ↑HR + ↑contractility + venoconstriction (↑venous return) → ↑CO
↓HR + ↓contractility + arteriolar vasodilation, lowering cardiac output
↓HR alone, slowing the SA node so that fewer beats occur each minute
↑afterload alone, raising the resistance the ventricle ejects against
It has no effect at all on cardiac output under any circumstances
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Sympathetic activation increases HR and contractility and causes venoconstriction (increasing venous return), raising CO; parasympathetic activity lowers HR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why is venous return described as the often-forgotten driver of cardiac output?
options: Because CO cannot exceed what returns to the heart — venous return and CO are interdependent, and the heart only pumps out what it receives
Because the ventricles can eject far more blood than the veins deliver, so cardiac output routinely and greatly exceeds venous return during each beat
Because venous return is an entirely separate process with no bearing on cardiac output, as the heart independently sets its own output regardless of inflow
Because venous return becomes relevant only during strenuous exercise via the muscle pump; at rest it has no influence on determining cardiac output
Because venous return is the main determinant of afterload, setting the aortic pressure the left ventricle must overcome to eject blood on each beat
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Venous return is the often-forgotten driver: CO cannot exceed what returns to the heart, so venous return and CO are interdependent — the heart only pumps out what it receives, and Starling ensures it matches.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: By roughly how much can cardiac output increase in exercise, and by what mechanisms?
options: By only ~10%, driven purely by ↑afterload as the aorta stiffens, with heart rate and stroke volume adding almost nothing
By 4-6× (~20-25 L/min), driven purely by a large rise in systemic vascular resistance, with heart rate and stroke volume unchanged
It paradoxically falls in exercise as rising sympathetic tone cuts stroke volume and venous pooling drops preload below resting levels
By 4-6× (~20-25 L/min in athletes), via ↑HR + ↑SV (↑contractility + ↑venous return via the muscle pump), with SVR falling
By only ~30-50%, generated solely by an acute expansion of circulating blood volume, with no help from heart rate or contractility
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In exercise CO rises 4-6× (~20-25 L/min in athletes) via increased HR and SV (from increased contractility and venous return via the muscle pump), with SVR falling from muscle vasodilation so BP rises only modestly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does cardiac output change in pregnancy?
options: It falls by ~30-50%, driven by ↓SV and ↓blood volume, with SVR rising
It rises modestly, driven only by ↑SVR from placental vasoconstriction
It stays unchanged, as ↑blood volume is exactly offset by a fall in HR
It rises ~30-50%, via ↑SV + ↑HR + ↑blood volume, with SVR falling
It falls transiently each trimester, then returns to baseline levels
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In pregnancy CO rises by ~30-50% via increased SV, HR and blood volume, with SVR falling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why is early sepsis a high-output state ('warm shock')?
options: ↓SVR (vasodilation) → reflex ↑HR/CO
↑SVR causes a reflex fall in CO
The heart fails as a pump, lowering CO
Blood volume falls, raising CO
Contractility is abolished
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In early sepsis, vasodilation lowers SVR, producing a reflex increase in HR and CO — a high-output state ('warm shock').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why does cardiac output transiently fall on standing?
options: Gravity boosts venous return → ↑preload → ↑CO transiently on standing
Standing permanently raises SVR → ↑afterload → sustained fall in CO
Gravity → ↓venous return → ↓preload → baroreflex compensates
Standing abolishes ventricular contractility → SV collapses → ↓CO
Standing rapidly increases circulating blood volume → ↓CO reflexly
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: On standing, gravity reduces venous return and hence preload, causing a transient fall in CO until the baroreflex compensates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the Fick principle for measuring cardiac output?
options: CO = SV × HR
CO = O₂ consumption / arteriovenous O₂ difference
CO = BP × SVR
CO = thermodilution temperature change
CO = SV from LV outflow on echo
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The Fick principle is the classic method: CO = O₂ consumption / arteriovenous O₂ difference.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which method uses a pulmonary artery catheter to measure cardiac output?
options: Fick principle
Echocardiography
Thermodilution
Non-invasive monitors
Cardiac index calculation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Thermodilution measures CO via a pulmonary artery catheter; other methods include the Fick principle, echocardiography (SV from LV outflow) and non-invasive monitors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does cardiac output explain the features of heart failure?
options: Excessive cardiac output overwhelms the venous system, forcing fluid into the lungs and periphery → the congestion and oedema seen in heart failure
Cardiac output stays completely normal in every form of heart failure; symptoms arise solely from electrical conduction defects
A persistently high cardiac output directly signals the kidneys to retain salt and water, driving the fluid overload characteristic of heart failure
Heart failure is defined purely by a raised systemic vascular resistance, with cardiac output and ventricular filling remaining normal
The heart can't generate adequate CO for demand → fatigue, poor perfusion + congestion; low CO → RAAS activation → fluid retention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In heart failure the heart cannot generate adequate CO for demand, causing fatigue, poor perfusion and congestion; the low CO activates RAAS, leading to fluid retention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is shock characterised in cardiac-output terms?
options: Shock is always characterised by a high cardiac output combined with a high systemic vascular resistance, regardless of the underlying cause or type
Shock is defined solely by a low heart rate reducing cardiac output; blood pressure, perfusion and vascular resistance are irrelevant to the diagnosis
Shock arises only ever from a failing myocardial pump; reduced preload and loss of vascular tone can never by themselves produce a true shock state
Shock is only ever due to inadequate preload from volume loss; pump failure and vasodilatory maldistribution play no part in its development
Inadequate CO and/or perfusion: ↓CO (cardiogenic — pump; hypovolaemic — ↓preload) or ↓SVR with maldistribution (septic/distributive)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Shock is inadequate CO and/or perfusion: reduced CO (cardiogenic from pump failure, hypovolaemic from reduced preload) or reduced SVR with maldistribution (septic/distributive).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why can a very slow bradyarrhythmia cause syncope despite increased stroke volume?
options: Because a compensatory ↑SV always fully overrides the slow HR, keeping CO normal
Because a very low HR reduces CO despite ↑SV compensation (CO = SV × HR)
Because severe bradycardia raises systemic vascular resistance → ↓CO → syncope
Because profound bradycardia abolishes venous return → ↓preload → syncope
Because bradycardia markedly raises ventricular afterload → ↓CO → syncope
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In bradyarrhythmias, a very low heart rate reduces CO despite compensatory increased SV, leading to syncope — since CO = SV × HR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How do inotropes such as dobutamine raise cardiac output in cardiogenic shock?
options: ↓contractility → ↓SV → ↑CO
↑HR only, with no change in SV
↑afterload → ↑CO
↑contractility → ↑SV → ↑CO
↓preload → ↑CO
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Inotropes such as dobutamine increase contractility, raising SV and thus CO in cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What limits exercise tolerance in relation to cardiac output?
options: The peak systolic blood pressure the arteries can achieve
The systemic vascular resistance measured purely at rest
The resting heart rate alone, set before any exertion
The heart's ability to increase CO (cardiac reserve)
The resting ejection fraction measured only while at rest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Exercise tolerance is limited by the heart's ability to increase CO — its cardiac reserve.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does cardiac output feed into blood pressure, and what do low CO/perfusion and inadequate CO for demand signify?
options: BP = CO ÷ SVR; low CO = hypertension; inadequate CO = normal
BP = CO × SVR; low CO/perfusion = shock; inadequate CO for demand = heart failure
BP = SV × HR; low CO = sepsis only; inadequate CO = pregnancy
BP = CO − SVR; low CO = exercise; inadequate CO = standing
BP is independent of CO
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: BP = CO × SVR; low CO/perfusion indicates shock, while inadequate CO for the body's demand indicates heart failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the master equation for blood pressure, and what does it imply?
options: BP = SV × HR; because output is fixed by rate and stroke volume, only heart rate can ever be targeted by antihypertensive drugs
BP = blood volume alone; pressure is set entirely by the amount of circulating fluid, independent of cardiac output or systemic vascular resistance
BP = Cardiac Output ÷ Systemic Vascular Resistance; because pressure falls as resistance rises, every drug works purely by adjusting circulating volume
BP = Systemic Vascular Resistance − Cardiac Output; regulation is therefore purely neural, with no hormonal or renal contribution to arterial control
BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance; every regulatory mechanism and antihypertensive drug works by adjusting one or both
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance; every regulatory mechanism and every antihypertensive drug works by adjusting one or both.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: In the expanded master equation, what mainly sets systemic vascular resistance?
options: Venous capacitance in the large veins
Arteriolar tone (the 'resistance vessels')
Cardiac contractility of the ventricles
The total circulating blood volume
Resting heart rate set by the SA node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: BP = CO × SVR, where CO = SV × HR and SVR is set mainly by arteriolar tone — the resistance vessels.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which drug class targets the blood-volume lever of blood pressure?
options: β-blockers
α-blockers only
CCBs only
Diuretics (and ACEi/ARB)
Nitrates
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Blood volume (→ preload → CO) is raised by Na⁺/water retention (RAAS, aldosterone) and is targeted by diuretics and ACEi/ARB; β-blockers target HR/contractility and CCBs/α-blockers/ACEi/ARB target SVR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Where are the baroreceptors located, and to where do they report?
options: In the renal juxtaglomerular apparatus, reporting directly to the adrenal cortex
In the ventricular myocardium, reporting to the thoracic spinal cord segments
In the walls of the cardiac atria, reporting directly to the SA node pacemaker
In the pulmonary vasculature, reporting upward to the hypothalamic centres
In the carotid sinus and aortic arch, reporting to the medulla (vasomotor centre)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that detect arterial stretch (pressure) and report to the medulla (vasomotor centre).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: A rise in blood pressure triggers the baroreceptor reflex. What is the response?
options: ↓baroreceptor firing → ↑sympathetic outflow → ↑HR, ↑contractility and vasoconstriction → BP rises further
No change in autonomic tone occurs, as the baroreflex ignores rising pressure and leaves HR and vascular tone unchanged
↑baroreceptor firing → ↑sympathetic drive → ↑HR and vasoconstriction → BP is driven even higher
↑baroreceptor firing → ↑parasympathetic + ↓sympathetic → ↓HR, ↓contractility, vasodilation → BP falls back
↓parasympathetic outflow → ↑HR and ↑contractility → cardiac output climbs → BP rises even higher
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: A rise in BP increases baroreceptor firing, increasing parasympathetic and decreasing sympathetic activity, so HR, contractility fall and vasodilation occurs, bringing BP back down.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: On standing, the baroreceptor reflex responds to the fall in BP. How?
options: ↓baroreceptor firing → ↑sympathetic + ↓parasympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility, vasoconstriction → BP restored
↑baroreceptor firing → ↑parasympathetic outflow → ↓HR, ↓contractility and vasodilation → BP falls further
No autonomic response occurs until BP has fallen to a critically low level, at which point reflex correction finally begins
↑parasympathetic outflow → widespread vasodilation and ↓HR → cardiac output falls → standing BP drops further
↓sympathetic outflow → ↓HR, ↓contractility and vasodilation → cardiac output falls and standing BP declines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: A fall in BP (standing, haemorrhage) reduces baroreceptor firing, increasing sympathetic and decreasing parasympathetic activity, raising HR, contractility and causing vasoconstriction to restore BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Failure of which reflex leads to orthostatic hypotension, and what are its key features?
options: The RAAS; it acts slowly over hours to days and is the reflex responsible for buffering the sudden BP drop on standing
The baroreceptor reflex; it is fast (seconds) and buffers moment-to-moment changes, most importantly on standing
The chemoreceptor reflex; it senses circulating volume and provides the rapid second-to-second correction of BP on standing
Autoregulation; acting only at the level of individual organ beds, it provides the fast whole-body buffering lost on standing
The ANP/BNP response; by dumping salt within seconds it provides the moment-to-moment BP buffering needed on standing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The baroreceptor reflex is fast (seconds) and buffers moment-to-moment BP changes, most importantly on standing where it prevents the gravity BP drop; its failure leads to orthostatic hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which system is the long-term controller of blood pressure, and over what timescale does it act?
options: The baroreceptor reflex, acting over seconds — with the carotid sinus as the long-term controller of arterial pressure
The peripheral chemoreceptors, acting over minutes — with the carotid body serving as the long-term controller of pressure
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), over hours-days — with the kidney as the long-term controller
Organ-level autoregulation, acting essentially instantaneously — with each vascular bed serving as the long-term controller
The ANP/BNP natriuretic system, acting over seconds — with the cardiac atria as the long-term controller of arterial pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: The RAAS controls BP over hours-days by adjusting blood volume and vascular tone, with the kidney as the long-term BP controller.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What triggers renin release from juxtaglomerular cells?
options: ↑renal perfusion pressure, ↑Na⁺ delivery and ↑BP
↓renal perfusion / ↓BP / ↓Na⁺ / ↑sympathetic
↑circulating blood volume and ↑atrial stretch
↑parasympathetic vagal tone to the kidney
↑circulating ANP and natriuretic peptides
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to reduced renal perfusion, reduced BP, reduced Na⁺, or increased sympathetic activity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: In the RAAS cascade, what does ACE (in the lungs) do?
options: Converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I
Releases aldosterone
Converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II
Blocks the AT-II receptor
Converts angiotensin II → renin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Renin converts angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I, and ACE (lungs) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What does aldosterone do in the RAAS?
options: Causes systemic vasodilation and natriuresis → ↓Na⁺ reabsorption → ↓blood volume
Reduces blood volume by promoting renal Na⁺ and water excretion
Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II within the pulmonary capillary bed
Blocks ADH release from the posterior pituitary → free water diuresis
Increases Na⁺ and water reabsorption in the distal nephron → ↑blood volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Aldosterone (from the adrenal cortex) increases Na⁺ and water reabsorption in the distal nephron, raising blood volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which of the following is one of the four ways angiotensin II raises BP?
options: Natriuresis and vasodilation
Reducing ADH and thirst
Vasoconstriction (↑SVR)
Blocking aldosterone
Dilating the efferent arteriole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Angiotensin II raises BP four ways: vasoconstriction (↑SVR), ↑aldosterone (Na⁺/water retention → ↑volume), ↑ADH + thirst, and direct renal Na⁺ reabsorption + efferent arteriolar constriction (maintaining GFR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How do ARBs act within the RAAS?
options: They block the conversion of AT-I to AT-II
They increase ANP
They block aldosterone directly
They inhibit renin release
They block the AT-II receptor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Among RAAS drugs, ACE inhibitors block AT-I→AT-II conversion, ARBs block the AT-II receptor, and spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What are the effects of ANP/BNP, and when are they released?
options: Released from the atria in dehydration → systemic vasoconstriction and Na⁺ retention → ↑blood volume and ↑BP
Released when atria/ventricles are stretched (volume overload) → natriuresis + vasodilation → ↓BP
Released by the kidney in hypovolaemia → enhanced Na⁺ and water retention → ↑blood volume → ↑BP
Released alongside renin during ↓perfusion → Na⁺ and water retention → ↑circulating volume and ↑BP
Released in tissue hypoxia → reflex sympathetic activation and vasoconstriction → ↑HR and ↑BP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: ANP/BNP are released when the atria/ventricles are stretched (volume overload), causing natriuresis and vasodilation to lower BP — the counter-regulator, with BNP a heart-failure marker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why does BNP form the basis of a blood test in heart failure?
options: Because BNP rises in heart failure due to the stretched ventricle
Because BNP falls in heart failure as a failing ventricle stops making it
Because BNP is released only by the kidney in a low sodium state
Because BNP rises and falls exactly in step with plasma renin levels
Because BNP causes vasoconstriction that raises vascular resistance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: ANP/BNP are the natural opposite of RAAS, dumping salt and water and vasodilating; BNP rises in heart failure (stretched ventricle), forming the basis of the BNP blood test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is organ-level autoregulation, and when is it overwhelmed?
options: Individual organs maintaining constant blood flow despite changing BP by adjusting their own arteriolar tone; overwhelmed at extremes (hypertensive emergency, severe hypotension)
The systemic baroreflex arc that sets whole-body arterial pressure through vagal and sympathetic outflow to the heart and vessels; overwhelmed even by mild, stable essential hypertension
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system acting on the kidney alone to fix each organ's flow via aldosterone-driven sodium handling; overwhelmed by any dose of loop or thiazide diuretic
The carotid-sinus baroreflex acting solely on the heart to hold each organ's perfusion steady by varying heart rate alone; overwhelmed the very moment a person stands upright
A purely hormonal natriuretic system dumping salt from every organ bed to keep local flow steady; overwhelmed whenever mild dehydration lowers the circulating blood volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Autoregulation is individual organs (brain, kidney, heart) maintaining constant blood flow despite changing BP by adjusting their own arteriolar tone (myogenic + metabolic); it is overwhelmed at extremes such as hypertensive emergency or severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: In BP-regulation terms, what characterises most 'essential' hypertension?
options: Chronically ↓CO and ↓SVR, with most essential HTN driven by a low-output state
Chronically ↑CO and/or ↑SVR, with most essential HTN involving ↑SVR ± RAAS
Purely a chronic low blood volume state from persistent renal salt and water loss
Failure of organ autoregulation only, with normal CO and SVR throughout the body
Excess ANP/BNP secretion driving sustained sodium retention and a raised SVR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Hypertension is chronically increased CO and/or SVR; most essential HTN involves increased SVR ± RAAS, and drugs target each lever.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does antihypertensive choice map onto BP = CO × SVR?
options: All antihypertensive drug classes act only on heart rate to bring the CO term down
Diuretics act on SVR by relaxing arterioles; CCBs act on volume via renal sodium loss
ACEi/ARB (RAAS/volume + SVR), CCB (SVR), diuretic (volume), β-blocker (CO)
β-blockers act on volume via diuresis; ACEi act on heart rate only through vagal tone
All classes act solely on organ autoregulation, resetting each arteriolar bed's tone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Antihypertensives map onto BP = CO × SVR: ACEi/ARB (RAAS/volume + SVR), CCB (SVR), diuretic (volume) and β-blocker (CO).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: An elderly patient on antihypertensives feels dizzy on standing. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Excessive RAAS activation on standing, driving angiotensin II vasoconstriction and a surge in BP
Overactive carotid-body chemoreceptors on standing, triggering hyperventilation and reflex vasodilation
Inappropriate ANP release on standing, causing natriuresis and a sudden fall in circulating volume
Failed baroreceptor reflex on standing (elderly, autonomic neuropathy, drugs) — orthostatic hypotension
Renal artery stenosis lowering kidney perfusion and driving a fixed, posture-independent rise in BP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is caused by a failed baroreceptor reflex on standing, seen in the elderly, autonomic neuropathy and with certain drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is shock explained in BP-regulation terms?
options: ↑BP from a sustained ↑CO with no baroreflex or RAAS compensation → reflex bradycardia and brisk diuresis
Failure of organ autoregulation only, with normal CO and SVR but lost arteriolar tone → warm, well-perfused tissues
↓BP purely from excess ANP-driven natriuresis, with compensatory parasympathetic drive → bradycardia + polyuria
↑SVR from intense arteriolar constriction with reflex bradycardia and preserved renal perfusion sustaining urine flow
↓BP from ↓CO (cardiogenic/hypovolaemic) or ↓SVR (distributive/septic), with compensatory sympathetic + RAAS → tachycardia + oliguria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Shock is reduced BP from reduced CO (cardiogenic/hypovolaemic) or reduced SVR (distributive/septic), with compensatory sympathetic and RAAS activation causing tachycardia and oliguria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the physiological response to acute haemorrhage?
options: ↑BP → pure parasympathetic activation with reflex bradycardia and splanchnic vasodilation
↑ANP secretion → systemic vasodilation and a further drop in venous return and cardiac preload
↓BP → atrial ANP release → natriuresis and diuresis, further lowering the circulating volume
No haemodynamic response until about 24 hours, when delayed marrow erythropoiesis begins
↓BP → baroreceptor reflex (immediate tachycardia/vasoconstriction) + RAAS (volume retention)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In haemorrhage, the fall in BP triggers the baroreceptor reflex (immediate tachycardia/vasoconstriction) and RAAS (volume retention).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How does renal artery stenosis cause secondary hypertension?
options: ↑renal perfusion → RAAS suppression → secondary hypertension from salt retention
Direct arteriolar dilation of the renal bed → reflex ↑SVR → secondary hypertension
Excess ANP release from atrial stretch → sodium retention → secondary hypertension
Carotid baroreflex failure → unopposed sympathetic drive → secondary hypertension
↓renal perfusion → inappropriate RAAS activation → secondary hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Renal artery stenosis reduces renal perfusion, causing inappropriate RAAS activation and secondary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why are ACEi and diuretics core treatment in heart failure, in BP-regulation terms?
options: Because a persistently high CO drives renal fluid retention and congestion, which ACEi + diuretics reverse
Because ACEi + diuretics block ANP-driven natriuresis, easing the failing ventricle's pumping workload
Because ACEi + diuretics raise SVR and afterload, shifting blood away from the congested pulmonary vessels
Because low CO → RAAS activation → fluid retention (worsens congestion), which ACEi + diuretics counteract
Because ACEi + diuretics increase circulating blood volume, restoring the failing heart's lost preload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: In heart failure, low CO activates RAAS, causing fluid retention that worsens congestion — which is why ACEi and diuretics are core treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the organising principle governing blood flow, and the specialised job of each vessel type?
options: Flow = pressure × resistance (haemodynamic Ohm's law); every vessel type shares the single role of moving blood forward
Flow = resistance ÷ pressure gradient; capillaries set resistance, arterioles exchange solutes, veins carry the pulse
Flow = pressure gradient ÷ resistance (haemodynamic Ohm's law); arterioles set resistance, capillaries exchange, veins store volume
Flow = pressure gradient × resistance; veins set resistance, capillaries store volume, arterioles handle exchange
Flow is independent of resistance and set by vessel length alone; arterioles exchange, capillaries store the volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Blood flow is governed by flow = pressure gradient ÷ resistance (the haemodynamic Ohm's law), and each vessel has a specialised job — arterioles set resistance, capillaries exchange, veins store volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which vessels are the 'resistance vessels' that set SVR, and what is their key structural feature?
options: Elastic arteries; thin-walled
Venules; low pressure
Capillaries; one cell thick
Veins; valved and distensible
Arterioles; heavily smooth-muscle-walled
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Arterioles are the resistance vessels — they adjust radius to control flow and BP, set SVR, and are heavily smooth-muscle-walled.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which vessels are the capacitance vessels, and roughly what fraction of blood volume do they hold?
options: Arteries; ~10%
Capillaries; ~30%
Arterioles; ~50%
Elastic arteries; ~65-70%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Veins are the capacitance vessels, holding ~65-70% of blood volume at low pressure; venoconstriction shifts blood back to increase preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the Windkessel effect of the elastic arteries?
options: Arterioles constricting to raise BP
Capillary exchange of gases
Aortic elastic recoil sustaining diastolic flow
Venous valves preventing backflow
The steepest pressure drop across arterioles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Elastic arteries conduct blood at high pressure, and aortic elastic recoil sustains diastolic flow — the Windkessel effect.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: According to Poiseuille's law, how does resistance depend on vessel radius?
options: R ∝ r⁴ (directly)
R is independent of radius
R ∝ 1 / r² — so halving the radius doubles resistance
R ∝ r² (directly)
R ∝ 1 / r⁴ — so halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Poiseuille's law states resistance depends overwhelmingly on radius: R ∝ 1 / r⁴, so halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold — tiny changes in arteriolar calibre produce huge changes in flow/BP.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Why are arterioles — not capillaries — the control point for flow and BP?
options: Because capillaries carry the thickest ring of smooth muscle in the circulation, so their constriction sets total resistance and is the physical basis of every vasoconstrictor and vasodilator effect
Because arterioles act as the main capacitance vessels holding most of the blood volume, so shifting that reservoir sets resistance and drives all vasoconstrictor and vasodilator responses
Because capillaries carry the highest hydrostatic pressure in the circuit, so tiny changes in their calibre dominate resistance and underlie every vasoconstrictor and vasodilator drug effect
Because the r⁴ relationship means a small amount of arteriolar smooth-muscle constriction dramatically raises resistance — the physical basis of all vasoconstrictor/vasodilator effects
Because capillaries generate and set the arterial pulse pressure, so their rhythmic constriction governs total resistance and forms the basis of every vasoconstrictor and vasodilator effect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Because R ∝ 1/r⁴, a small amount of arteriolar smooth-muscle constriction dramatically raises resistance — the physical basis of all vasoconstrictor/vasodilator effects, making arterioles (not capillaries) the control point.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Besides radius, which factor increases vascular resistance, for example in polycythaemia?
options: Decreased blood viscosity
Increased blood viscosity
Shorter vessel length
Increased capillary permeability
Reduced venous tone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Resistance also rises with blood viscosity (e.g. polycythaemia) and vessel length (fixed), though radius dominates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Where is the steepest pressure drop across the circulation, and what does it achieve?
options: Across the capillaries; it raises pulsatility
Across the arterioles (highest resistance); it dampens the pulsatility
Across the veins; it stores volume
Across the elastic arteries; it sustains diastolic flow
There is no significant pressure drop anywhere
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Pressure is high and pulsatile in arteries, and the steepest drop is across the arterioles (highest resistance), which dampens the pulsatility so pressure is low and steady in capillaries and veins.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: How is mean arterial pressure (MAP) estimated and expressed?
options: MAP ≈ systolic − diastolic; MAP = CO ÷ SVR
MAP ≈ ⅓(systolic); MAP = CO − SVR
MAP ≈ systolic + ⅓(diastolic); MAP = SV × HR
MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓(pulse pressure); MAP = CO × SVR
MAP is the same as pulse pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: MAP is the average arterial pressure driving organ perfusion: MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓(pulse pressure), or MAP = CO × SVR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is pulse pressure, and what tends to widen it?
options: Systolic + diastolic pressure summed; widened in early shock as the stroke volume climbs sharply
Systolic − diastolic; widened in stiff arteries (age, atherosclerosis, aortic regurgitation)
Diastolic − systolic pressure; widened in aortic stenosis as the stiff valve raises stroke volume
MAP minus diastolic pressure; narrowed by atherosclerosis as arterial walls grow more compliant
CO × SVR product; widened by a chronically low stroke volume and a slow resting heart rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic; it is widened in stiff arteries (age, atherosclerosis, aortic regurgitation) and narrowed in low-SV states (shock, aortic stenosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which Starling force pushes fluid OUT of the capillary, and where does it dominate?
options: Plasma oncotic pressure; filtration dominant at the arteriolar end of the capillary
Plasma oncotic pressure; filtration dominant at the slow venular end
Interstitial oncotic pressure; filtration dominant at the venular end
Capillary hydrostatic pressure; filtration dominant at the arteriolar end
Lymphatic drainage pressure; filtration dominant throughout the capillary
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, causing filtration that is dominant at the arteriolar end.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: Which Starling force pulls fluid IN, and what is it due to?
options: Capillary hydrostatic pressure; due to blood flow, causing reabsorption dominant at the arteriolar end
Lymphatic pressure; due to lymph flow, drawing fluid back into the capillary at the venular end
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure; due to tissue fluid, driving reabsorption at the venular end
Plasma oncotic pressure; due to albumin, causing reabsorption (dominant at the venular end)
Raised capillary permeability; due to inflammation, pulling fluid inward mainly at the venular end
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.explanation: Plasma oncotic pressure (from albumin) pulls fluid in, causing reabsorption that is dominant at the venular end.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations.question: What is the net result of the capillary Starling forces, and how is it handled?
options: Slight net filtration out → returned by the lymphatics
Net reabsorption in; removed by the arteries
No net movement; forces are exactly balanced
Massive filtration out; returned by the veins directly
Net reabsorption; returned by the lymphatics
