conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What are the criteria for cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) in heart failure?
options: EF ≤35% plus a previous VT or VF cardiac arrest only
Preserved EF ≥50% with a narrow QRS below 120 ms
Any patient in atrial fibrillation regardless of QRS
EF ≤35% + QRS ≥130 ms (especially LBBB) + NYHA II–IV
Narrow QRS <120 ms with NYHA class I symptoms
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: EF ≤35% + QRS ≥130 ms (especially LBBB) + NYHA II–IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: CRT requires EF ≤35%, QRS ≥130 ms (especially LBBB) and NYHA II–IV. The biventricular pacemaker resynchronises ventricular contraction to increase cardiac output; CRT-D adds ICD function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: Which vaccinations are recommended for patients with chronic heart failure?
options: Annual influenza + one-off pneumococcal
BCG + hepatitis B
Annual pneumococcal only
One-off influenza only
No vaccinations are indicated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: Patients are offered an annual influenza vaccine plus a one-off pneumococcal vaccine; surgical correction of underlying valvular disease is offered where indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is the classic auscultation triad of heart failure?
options: S4 + ejection systolic murmur + raised JVP
Pericardial rub + S4 + oedema
Pansystolic murmur + S3 + ascites
S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles
Mid-diastolic murmur + displaced apex + clubbing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: S3 gallop + displaced apex + bibasal crackles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: The classic auscultation triad of heart failure is an S3 gallop, a displaced apex beat, and bibasal crackles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is the mortality benefit drug class in HFrEF that acts on the renin-angiotensin system?
options: Digoxin, a cardiac glycoside used for rate control
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine
Loop diuretics such as intravenous furosemide and bumetanide
ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) — reduce mortality by ~25%
Amiodarone, a potassium-channel antiarrhythmic agent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) — reduce mortality by ~25%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: ACE inhibitors are first-line in all HFrEF (EF <40%) regardless of symptoms. They reduce mortality ~25% (CONSENSUS, SOLVD trials). ARBs (e.g. candesartan) if ACE inhibitor intolerant. ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) is superior to ACE inhibitor if tolerated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What class of drug should be avoided in HFrEF despite being used in diastolic heart failure?
options: Diuretics, especially loop diuretics like furosemide, as they reduce preload and cardiac output
Rate-limiting calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) — negative inotropes in HFrEF
Beta-blockers such as bisoprolol, because their negative inotropy is harmful in HFrEF
ACE inhibitors such as ramipril, owing to their vasodilator effect and hypotension risk
SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin, due to the risk of volume depletion and hypotension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Rate-limiting calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) — negative inotropes in HFrEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: Rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) are contraindicated in HFrEF — they reduce contractility and worsen outcomes. Amlodipine/felodipine (dihydropyridines) are safe if needed for angina/hypertension. CCBs can be used in HFpEF for rate control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is ARNI (angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor) and its role in HFrEF?
options: Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) — superior to ACE inhibitor, reduces mortality and hospitalisation in HFrEF
An ACE inhibitor equivalent that offers no additional benefit over ramipril in terms of mortality or hospitalisation
A second-line agent used only if an ACE inhibitor fails to control symptoms adequately in HFrEF
A drug used only during episodes of acute decompensation to relieve congestion and pulmonary oedema
An aldosterone antagonist that blocks mineralocorticoid receptors and reduces sodium retention in HFrEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) — superior to ACE inhibitor, reduces mortality and hospitalisation in HFrEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) is now preferred over ACE inhibitors in HFrEF — PARADIGM-HF trial showed 20% relative risk reduction in CV death/hospitalisation vs enalapril. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (natriuretic peptide degradation) + valsartan (ARB). Monitor for hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is the role of SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) in chronic heart failure?
options: Only an add-on therapy reserved for when the other three drug pillars have already failed
Used only in diabetic patients with heart failure to improve glycaemic control and outcomes
They exert a diuretic effect only, offering symptom relief but no mortality benefit in HF
Contraindicated once the eGFR falls below 45, as they lose all benefit at this level
Reduce hospitalisation and CV death in both HFrEF and HFpEF, regardless of diabetes status
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Reduce hospitalisation and CV death in both HFrEF and HFpEF, regardless of diabetes status
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin — DAPA-HF; empagliflozin — EMPEROR-Reduced/Preserved) reduce CV death and HF hospitalisation in both HFrEF and HFpEF regardless of diabetes. Now standard of care in HF alongside ACEI/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is the 'fantastic four' of HFrEF disease-modifying therapy?
options: Digoxin + diuretic + ACE-I + aspirin
ACE-I/ARB/ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor
Beta-blocker + diuretic + statin + ACE-I
ACE-I + CCB + MRA + diuretic
Diuretic + nitrate + hydralazine + digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: Current HFrEF 'fantastic four' (quadruple therapy): ARNI (or ACE-I/ARB) + beta-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol) + mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone) + SGLT2 inhibitor. All four have independent mortality/morbidity benefit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: What is cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) used for in HFrEF?
options: Used as an outright alternative to guideline drug therapy rather than alongside it in HFrEF
Indicated in all heart failure patients regardless of QRS duration or morphology on the ECG
Used only to treat arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia, not to improve synchrony
Wide QRS (>130 ms, LBBB morphology) with EF <35% — improves synchrony, symptoms, and mortality
Reserved for HFpEF only, where a preserved ejection fraction responds best to resynchronisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: Wide QRS (>130 ms, LBBB morphology) with EF <35% — improves synchrony, symptoms, and mortality
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: CRT (biventricular pacing) resynchronises RV and LV contraction in patients with bundle branch block (QRS >130 ms, LBBB). NICE criteria: EF ≤35%, QRS >130 ms on optimal medical therapy. Reduces mortality ~36%, improves exercise tolerance and symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: A 72-year-old man with HFrEF has EF 28% on optimal medical therapy. He had a VT arrest 3 months ago. What device therapy is indicated?
options: A wearable cardioverter defibrillator only, worn temporarily until medical therapy is optimised
CRT-P only, providing biventricular pacing without defibrillator backup for this patient
CRT-D combining CRT and an ICD, but only if LBBB with a QRS above 130 ms is present
ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) — secondary prevention post-VT/VF arrest
No device therapy is needed; simply optimise medications first and reassess the EF later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) — secondary prevention post-VT/VF arrest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: ICD is indicated for secondary prevention (prior VT/VF arrest) in patients with EF ≤35% and life expectancy >1 year with good functional status. Primary prevention ICD: EF ≤35% on optimal therapy for ≥3 months. If also wide QRS+LBBB: CRT-D.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the significance of an elevated NT-proBNP in a patient with dyspnoea?
options: NT-proBNP is only useful in acute heart failure and has no role in the diagnosis or monitoring of chronic HF
A normal NT-proBNP value is above 500 ng/L, and levels below this effectively exclude any possibility of heart failure
An NT-proBNP above 50 ng/L is diagnostic of heart failure and warrants immediate initiation of drug treatment
NT-proBNP >125 ng/L supports HF diagnosis; >2000 ng/L suggests decompensated HF — use to guide diagnosis and monitor treatment
NT-proBNP elevation is entirely non-specific and adds nothing useful to the assessment of suspected heart failure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.answer: NT-proBNP >125 ng/L supports HF diagnosis; >2000 ng/L suggests decompensated HF — use to guide diagnosis and monitor treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Chronic Hear.explanation: NT-proBNP (or BNP) is the biomarker for heart failure. NT-proBNP >125 ng/L (BNP >35 ng/L) supports HF diagnosis. >2000 ng/L indicates high acuity. Values fall with treatment. NICE: use to rule out HF in new dyspnoea — very high sensitivity means low values reliably exclude HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the central mechanism producing pulmonary oedema in acute heart failure?
options: Right ventricular failure backing up into the systemic veins, raising jugular venous pressure
Increased capillary permeability from inflammatory cytokine-mediated endothelial damage
LV unable to pump forward → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs
Lymphatic obstruction in the thorax impairing drainage of interstitial fluid from the lungs
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia allowing fluid to leak into the alveoli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: LV unable to pump forward → backlog into the left atrium, pulmonary veins and lungs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: In AHF the LV cannot pump blood forward efficiently, so blood backs up into the LA, pulmonary veins and lungs, filling the alveoli with interstitial fluid (pulmonary oedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient with no prior cardiac history presents with acute heart failure following a new MI. How is this best classified?
options: De novo acute heart failure
Decompensated chronic HF
High-output failure
Right heart failure
Chronic HFpEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: De novo acute heart failure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: De novo AHF is a first-ever presentation with no prior HF diagnosis, often caused by a new MI, hypertensive emergency or acute valve rupture, and requires a full diagnostic workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which is the more common form of acute heart failure, and what is the key management priority?
options: De novo AHF; complete a full diagnostic workup before initiating any empirical treatment
Decompensated chronic HF; abruptly stop all chronic heart failure medications to reduce load
High-output failure; correct the underlying cause such as anaemia, sepsis or thyrotoxicosis
De novo AHF; arrange immediate cardiac transplant referral without further medical management
Decompensated chronic HF; identify and treat the trigger while optimising chronic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Decompensated chronic HF; identify and treat the trigger while optimising chronic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Decompensated chronic HF is the more common form; management focuses on identifying and treating the precipitating trigger while optimising chronic therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which of the following is a recognised trigger for decompensation of chronic heart failure?
options: Dehydration
New AF or arrhythmia
Hypothyroidism
Hypoglycaemia
Excessive diuresis alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: New AF or arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Triggers include MI/ACS, new AF/arrhythmia, hypertensive emergency, sepsis/infection, iatrogenic IV fluids, medication non-compliance, anaemia/PE and valvular rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which symptom is characteristic of acute heart failure?
options: Sharp central chest pain relieved by sitting forward and worsened by lying flat
Localised chest wall pain that is reproduced by palpation over costochondral joints
Gradual painless ankle and leg swelling developing slowly over several months
Acute shortness of breath that is worse lying flat and improves sitting up
Productive green sputum with fever, malaise and pleuritic pain but no breathlessness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Acute shortness of breath that is worse lying flat and improves sitting up
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Acute SOB worse when flat and relieved by sitting up is characteristic, often with cough productive of frothy white/pink sputum, raised RR, low sats and extreme anxiety.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Hypotension in a patient with acute heart failure most concerningly indicates what?
options: A normal compensatory response
Septic shock by definition
Over-diuresis only
Cardiogenic shock
Improving cardiac function
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Hypotension occurs in severe AHF and signals cardiogenic shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the main purpose of performing an arterial blood gas in acute heart failure?
options: To measure serum troponin and confirm an acute myocardial infarction
To exclude a pulmonary embolism by assessing oxygenation and alveolar gradient
To diagnose anaemia and correct the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
To assess hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV/intubation
To classify the ejection fraction and grade the severity of systolic dysfunction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: To assess hypoxia and hypercapnia, guiding the need for NIV/intubation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The ABG assesses the degree of hypoxia and hypercapnia, which guides whether NIV or intubation is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the primary role of a 12-lead ECG in the acute heart failure workup?
options: To measure the ejection fraction and quantify the degree of ventricular impairment
To quantify the severity of pulmonary oedema seen on the chest radiograph
To identify the trigger — arrhythmia (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI), LBBB
To assess renal function and detect any electrolyte abnormalities present
To measure the BNP level and confirm myocardial wall stretch and volume overload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: To identify the trigger — arrhythmia (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI), LBBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The ECG looks for arrhythmias, ischaemia and LBBB, helping to identify the precipitating trigger of AHF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which level of care is warranted for a patient with severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock?
options: HDU or ITU
Routine ward admission only
Discharge with oral diuretics
Outpatient cardiology clinic
Observation in the waiting area
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: HDU or ITU
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: AHF requires hospital admission; severe pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock warrants HDU or ITU level care.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What does the SODIUM mnemonic for first-line acute heart failure management stand for?
options: Sit up, Oxygen, Diuretic IV, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause, Monitor
Statin, Oxygen, Digoxin, IV fluids, Ultrasound, Morphine
Sit up, Oxygen, Dobutamine, Inotrope, Underlying cause, Morphine
Sodium restrict, Oxygen, Diuretic, IV fluids, Underlying cause, MRA
Sit up, Opioids, Diuretic, Inotrope, Ultrasound, Monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Sit up, Oxygen, Diuretic IV, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause, Monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: SODIUM = Sit up, Oxygen, IV Diuretic, IV fluids stop, Underlying cause (treat trigger), Monitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Why is sitting the patient upright beneficial in acute heart failure?
options: It increases venous return to the heart, boosting preload and stroke volume output
It prevents aspiration of gastric contents only, protecting the airway during treatment
It raises systemic blood pressure by increasing peripheral vascular resistance and afterload
It reduces the heart's cardiac output demand to almost zero by resting the myocardium
It reduces venous return (preload) and improves diaphragmatic mechanics, easing the work of breathing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Gravity moves fluid to the lung bases, clearing the upper/mid zones for gas exchange
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Sitting up reduces venous return (preload) and lets the diaphragm move more freely, improving respiratory mechanics and gas exchange.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the oxygen saturation target in acute heart failure, and what is added if it is not met on oxygen alone?
options: SpO₂ ≥88%; add a beta-blocker
SpO₂ ≥90%; add IV morphine
SpO₂ ≥94%; add CPAP/NIV
SpO₂ 100%; add inotropes
SpO₂ ≥92%; add IV fluids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: SpO₂ ≥94%; add CPAP/NIV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Target SpO₂ is ≥94%; CPAP/NIV is added if this is not achieved on oxygen alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What IV diuretic regimen is used first-line in acute heart failure, and what is its effect?
options: IV bumetanide 1 mg — a loop diuretic that increases venous preload and filling pressure
IV furosemide 40–80 mg — increases urine output and reduces circulating volume
IV spironolactone 50 mg — a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks aldosterone receptors
IV mannitol — an osmotic diuretic that draws fluid into the tubules for rapid diuresis
Oral furosemide 20 mg — a slower enteral route to gently offload fluid over hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV furosemide 40–80 mg — increases urine output and reduces circulating volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: First-line is IV furosemide 40–80 mg, which increases urine output and reduces circulating volume.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A fluid-overloaded patient in acute heart failure is on maintenance IV fluids. What should be done?
options: Increase the infusion rate
Stop all IV fluid infusions
Switch to colloid
Add a fluid bolus
Continue unchanged
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Stop all IV fluid infusions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: The 'I' in SODIUM is IV fluids stop — all IV fluid infusions should be stopped in the fluid-overloaded AHF patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In the BP-stratified approach, a patient with AHF and SBP >100 mmHg should be managed with which strategy?
options: Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support
Beta-blockade
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation
Vasodilator (IV GTN, with close BP monitoring)
Watchful waiting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Vasodilator-led (IV GTN/nitroprusside/BNP)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: With SBP >100 mmHg a vasodilator (IV GTN) may be added to reduce afterload — only with close BP monitoring and not routinely (reserve for hypertension/ischaemia/severe oedema) — plus CPAP/NIV for respiratory failure; the cornerstone remains the IV loop diuretic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient with AHF has an SBP of 90 mmHg. According to the BP-stratified approach, what is the appropriate strategy?
options: High-dose IV vasodilator alone to aggressively reduce afterload despite the low pressure
Vasodilator ± inotrope (lower-dose GTN + dobutamine, or PDEI if poor response)
Noradrenaline plus intra-aortic balloon pump as immediate first-line mechanical support
A rapid IV crystalloid fluid bolus to raise the filling pressure and cardiac output
Stop all pharmacological therapy and simply observe the patient on cardiac monitoring
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Vasodilator ± inotrope (lower-dose GTN + dobutamine, or PDEI if poor response)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: For SBP 85–100 mmHg the strategy is vasodilator ± inotrope: lower-dose GTN plus dobutamine, or a PDEI if the response is poor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A patient in cardiogenic shock has an SBP of 78 mmHg. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Vasodilator-led strategy with high-dose IV GTN to reduce afterload and relieve congestion
Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support (dobutamine, noradrenaline, consider IABP/LVAD)
Repeated large IV crystalloid fluid boluses to restore preload and improve the low pressure
IV beta-blocker to slow the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand in shock
Oral furosemide with early discharge home and outpatient cardiology follow-up arranged
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support (dobutamine, noradrenaline, consider IABP/LVAD)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: For SBP <85 mmHg (cardiogenic shock): inotrope/vasopressor ± mechanical support — dobutamine (↑contractility/CO), noradrenaline (↑SVR), and IABP/LVAD if no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Why is IV morphine no longer routinely recommended in acute heart failure?
options: Evidence shows harm — increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries
It is too expensive and not cost-effective compared with standard diuretic therapy
It causes dangerous hyperkalaemia by impairing renal potassium and acid excretion
It raises the systemic blood pressure dangerously and worsens myocardial oxygen demand
It interferes with furosemide absorption and blunts the diuretic response to treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Evidence shows harm — increased ventilation rates and mortality in registries
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Although historically used for anxiolysis and preload reduction, morphine is associated with increased ventilation rates and mortality, so it is avoided unless in a palliative context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In which situations is IV GTN specifically indicated in acute heart failure?
options: Cardiogenic shock with a low SBP below 85 mmHg
Isolated right heart failure only, with raised JVP
All AHF cases regardless of the blood pressure
Septic AHF only, driven by systemic vasodilation
Hypertensive AHF (SBP >100) and ACS-triggered AHF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Hypertensive AHF (SBP >100) and ACS-triggered AHF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: IV GTN is specifically indicated in hypertensive AHF (SBP >100) and ACS-triggered AHF, where afterload reduction is beneficial.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: How does fluid management in cardiogenic shock differ from that in septic shock?
options: Both require aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloid boluses to restore preload and cardiac output
Cardiogenic shock is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics first to cover the infective trigger
Cardiogenic shock needs far more fluids than septic shock to raise its low filling pressures
Neither is given any treatment acutely; both are simply observed until they settle on their own
In cardiogenic shock do NOT give fluids — give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: In cardiogenic shock do NOT give fluids — give inotropes and arrange urgent revascularisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Unlike septic shock, cardiogenic shock should not be fluid-loaded; management is inotropes plus urgent revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the role of NIV/CPAP in acute heart failure?
options: It replaces diuretics entirely, so no IV furosemide is needed once CPAP is started to clear the pulmonary oedema
It is only used in cardiogenic shock, once systolic BP has fallen and inotropes such as dobutamine have been started
Used early if oxygen alone is insufficient — reduces work of breathing, decreases preload, improves oxygenation
It increases preload to support the circulation, raising venous return and left ventricular filling to boost output
It is reserved for palliative cases, offered only for comfort once active treatment of the heart failure is stopped
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Used early if oxygen alone is insufficient — reduces work of breathing, decreases preload, improves oxygenation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: NIV/CPAP is used early when oxygen alone is insufficient; it reduces work of breathing, decreases preload and improves oxygenation. Invasive ventilation is for refractory cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In cardiogenic shock, what are the respective roles of dobutamine and noradrenaline?
options: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility/CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR)
Both are pure vasopressors that raise vascular resistance without affecting contractility
Dobutamine raises SVR by vasoconstriction; noradrenaline raises contractility and stroke volume
Both are vasodilators reducing systemic vascular resistance and afterload to improve flow
Dobutamine is a loop diuretic promoting fluid loss; noradrenaline is an inotrope agent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Dobutamine is an inotrope (↑contractility/CO); noradrenaline is a vasopressor (↑SVR)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Dobutamine increases contractility and cardiac output (inotrope); noradrenaline increases systemic vascular resistance (vasopressor). IABP/LVAD is considered if there is no response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A 72-year-old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy presents with acute breathlessness, SpO₂ 84% on air, widespread crepitations, and pink frothy sputum. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 120 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Sublingual GTN spray plus oral bisoprolol then reassess
Oral furosemide with early discharge home and GP follow-up
IV furosemide alone and observe on the ward overnight
IV fluids 500 mL bolus to support blood pressure and perfusion
IV furosemide + IV dobutamine + non-invasive ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV furosemide + IV dobutamine + non-invasive ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema requires IV diuresis, inotropic support (dobutamine), and NIV for respiratory failure. Oral furosemide is insufficient in this emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the CXR finding most specific for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (as opposed to ARDS)?
options: Bilateral diffuse infiltrates with normal heart size
Cardiomegaly + upper lobe blood diversion + Kerley B lines
Unilateral opacification
Hyperinflated lung fields
Pleural effusion alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Cardiomegaly + upper lobe blood diversion + Kerley B lines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, and Kerley B lines (interstitial oedema) point to elevated PCWP from cardiac cause. ARDS has bilateral infiltrates with normal heart size.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What NT-proBNP cut-off helps rule out AHF in a patient presenting with acute dyspnoea?
options: <100 pg/mL
<300 pg/mL
<1000 pg/mL
<500 pg/mL
<50 pg/mL
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: <300 pg/mL
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL has high NPV for excluding AHF. Age-stratified cut-offs also exist for confirming diagnosis (>450 for <50y, >900 for 50–75y, >1800 for >75y).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In AHF with hypertensive crisis (SBP >180 mmHg) and pulmonary oedema, what treatment should be added to diuretics?
options: IV adrenaline
IV metoprolol
IV/SL glyceryl trinitrate (GTN)
IV calcium channel blocker
Oral ACE inhibitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: IV/SL glyceryl trinitrate (GTN)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Nitrates reduce preload and afterload rapidly in hypertensive AHF — combined with diuretics to offload fluid. Beta-blockers are contraindicated acutely in decompensated HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A 65-year-old woman is admitted with acute decompensated HF. Her home medications include bisoprolol, ramipril, and spironolactone. She is now in cardiogenic shock. Which drug should be withheld?
options: All three should be continued
Ramipril (ACE inhibitor)
Spironolactone
Bisoprolol (beta-blocker)
Only diuretics should be added
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Bisoprolol (beta-blocker)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Beta-blockers are negative inotropes — withhold in cardiogenic shock as they worsen low output. ACE inhibitors and spironolactone can usually be continued unless hypotension is severe.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the Killip classification IV?
options: Pulmonary oedema
Cardiogenic shock
Mild heart failure with S3
No signs of heart failure
Bilateral crepitations only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Killip I = no HF; II = S3/mild; III = pulmonary oedema; IV = cardiogenic shock (SBP <90, hypoperfusion). Higher Killip class = worse post-MI mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP) in acute pulmonary oedema acts primarily by:
options: Improving cardiac output through a direct positive inotropic effect
Increasing alveolar recruitment and reducing work of breathing
Reducing heart rate by dampening sympathetic drive to the heart
Diuresing excess fluid directly from the congested alveoli
Dilating systemic arteries to lower afterload and resistance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Increasing alveolar recruitment and reducing work of breathing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: CPAP splints alveoli open, improving oxygenation, and the positive intrathoracic pressure also reduces LV afterload — reducing need for intubation in pulmonary oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the most common precipitant of acute decompensation in a patient with stable chronic HF?
options: Non-compliance with medications or dietary sodium
New-onset coronary artery disease or acute ischaemia
Acute pulmonary embolism obstructing the circulation
Undiagnosed thyroid disease altering metabolic demand
Progressive anaemia reducing oxygen delivery to tissues
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Non-compliance with medications or dietary sodium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Medication non-compliance and high sodium/fluid intake are the commonest precipitants. Always ask about this on history — FAILURE mnemonic covers other causes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A 55-year-old presents with AHF. Echo shows EF 20%, dilated LV, mitral regurgitation. What haemodynamic intervention bridges patients to transplant in refractory cardiogenic shock?
options: Oral hydralazine as a peripheral vasodilator
IV furosemide infusion titrated to output
High-flow humidified oxygen therapy alone
IV digoxin for rate and contractility
Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or LVAD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or LVAD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: IABP reduces afterload and improves coronary perfusion; LVAD (left ventricular assist device) provides mechanical circulatory support — both bridge patients to transplant or recovery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which finding on echocardiography distinguishes HFrEF from HFpEF?
options: EF <50% = HFrEF; EF ≥50% with normal filling = HFpEF
EF <40% = HFrEF; EF ≥50% with diastolic dysfunction = HFpEF
Regional wall motion abnormality seen in HFpEF only
Left ventricular cavity dilatation present in HFpEF only
Significant valvular heart disease seen in HFrEF only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: EF <40% = HFrEF; EF ≥50% with diastolic dysfunction = HFpEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: HFrEF = reduced EF (<40%); HFpEF = preserved EF (≥50%) with signs of diastolic dysfunction on echo/Doppler. HFmrEF = mid-range 40–49%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: In acute pulmonary oedema, what is the primary mechanism of benefit from IV furosemide within the first 15–30 minutes (before diuresis begins)?
options: Direct inotropic effect
Venodilation reducing preload
Bronchodilation
Reducing heart rate
Systemic vasoconstriction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Venodilation reducing preload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: IV furosemide has an early venodilatory effect (before diuresis begins) reducing preload and pulmonary congestion — the diuretic effect follows over 1–2 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: A 70-year-old with AHF has been given IV furosemide but remains hypoxic with SpO₂ 88%. BP is 150/95. What is the next best step?
options: CPAP/NIV
Increase furosemide dose
Intubate immediately
IV adrenaline
Oral bisoprolol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: CPAP/NIV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: CPAP is the appropriate escalation for respiratory failure from pulmonary oedema not responding to diuretics and oxygen — reduces intubation rates and improves oxygenation quickly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: Which diuretic combination is used in diuretic-resistant AHF?
options: Two loop diuretics given simultaneously for added effect
Loop diuretic + thiazide (sequential nephron blockade)
Loop diuretic combined with an ACE inhibitor for synergy
Loop diuretic combined with a beta-blocker for control
Only up-titrating the loop diuretic dose progressively
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Loop diuretic + thiazide (sequential nephron blockade)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Adding metolazone (thiazide-like) to a loop diuretic causes sequential nephron blockade — powerful combination for diuretic resistance in AHF. Monitor electrolytes closely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the target urine output after IV furosemide in acute pulmonary oedema?
options: 100 mL/hour regardless of weight
50 mL/hour
>2 mL/kg/hour
No specific target needed
200–400 mL of urine in the first hour
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour or 200–400 mL in first hour
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: Adequate diuretic response is 200–400 mL in the first hour of IV furosemide. Insufficient response suggests resistant fluid overload — dose escalation or combination diuresis needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What is the correct action if a patient in cardiogenic shock is also found to have a STEMI?
options: Thrombolysis first then PCI
Emergency PCI (primary percutaneous coronary intervention)
Medical management only
IABP insertion then PCI 48 hours later
Coronary artery bypass grafting immediately
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: Emergency PCI (primary percutaneous coronary intervention)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: STEMI + cardiogenic shock = emergency primary PCI — reperfusing the culprit vessel is the only intervention that reduces mortality. Door-to-balloon time is critical.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: What ECG finding in AHF points to a reversible ischaemic cause requiring urgent treatment?
options: Right bundle branch block conduction pattern
Sinus tachycardia with a rapid regular rate
Prolonged QTc interval seen on the ECG trace
Tall peaked T waves across the chest leads
New LBBB or STEMI (acute coronary syndrome)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: New LBBB or STEMI (acute coronary syndrome)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: New LBBB or STEMI indicates ACS as the precipitant of AHF — requires emergency PCI. This distinguishes it from other causes of AHF where the management differs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the first-line investigation combination to confirm AHF in a breathless patient in ED?
options: Pulmonary function tests
CXR alone
Troponin alone
CXR + BNP/NT-proBNP + ECG + echo
CT chest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.answer: CXR + BNP/NT-proBNP + ECG + echo
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart.explanation: CXR shows pulmonary oedema/cardiomegaly; BNP confirms cardiac origin; ECG identifies arrhythmia/ischaemia; echo assesses function. This combination confirms diagnosis and guides treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 72-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 30%) develops worsening symptoms despite maximum tolerated ACEi and bisoprolol. His HR is 82bpm in sinus rhythm. What is the next most appropriate addition?
options: Digoxin
Ivabradine
Spironolactone
Sacubitril/valsartan
Amlodipine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: After an ACEi (or ARB) plus a beta-blocker, the next step in still-symptomatic HFrEF is to ADD a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) — spironolactone (or eplerenone). Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) is introduced later and REPLACES the ACEi rather than being added; ivabradine is also later (sinus rhythm, HR ≥75, EF ≤35%). Together these form the 'four pillars' of HFrEF therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 65-year-old woman with HFrEF has NT-proBNP of 3500 ng/L. How quickly should she receive an echocardiogram?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 6 weeks
Within 2 weeks
Within 3 months
Within 48 hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: NT-proBNP >2000 ng/L = urgent specialist assessment and echocardiogram within 2 weeks. 400–2000 ng/L = within 6 weeks. <400 ng/L makes HF unlikely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which beta-blocker is licensed for use in HFrEF in the UK?
options: Atenolol
Bisoprolol
Metoprolol
Propranolol
Labetalol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol are the beta-blockers licensed for HFrEF in the UK. Atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol and labetalol are NOT licensed for heart failure. They must be started at low dose and titrated up slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the mechanism of benefit of ACE inhibitors in HFrEF?
options: Positive inotropic effect that raises intracellular calcium and directly increases the force of myocardial contraction
Prevent myocardial fibrosis by directly blocking cardiac aldosterone receptors and reducing collagen deposition
Direct heart-rate reduction by slowing sinoatrial node depolarisation and prolonging atrioventricular nodal conduction
Block angiotensin II vasoconstriction + increase bradykinin vasodilation + reduce Na/water retention
Reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis in the collecting duct, promoting sodium excretion and lowering plasma volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: ACEi inhibit conversion of Ang I → Ang II (preventing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release) AND prevent bradykinin breakdown (bradykinin causes vasodilation). Result: reduce afterload, preload, and neurohormonal activation in HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with chronic HF presents with acute severe breathlessness. CXR shows bat-wing pulmonary oedema. What is the immediate priority?
options: Oral bisoprolol
IV furosemide 50mg
12-lead ECG
Start sacubitril/valsartan
Oral furosemide 40mg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: IV furosemide 50mg is first-line in acute LVF — rapidly reduces circulating volume, relieving pulmonary oedema. The mnemonic SODIUM: Sit up, Oxygen, Diuretics (IV furosemide), IV fluids stopped, Underlying cause, Monitor. Bisoprolol can worsen acute decompensation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What does upper lobe diversion on CXR indicate?
options: Raised pulmonary venous pressure from left heart failure
Pulmonary arterial hypertension enlarging the central vessels
Aortic dissection widening the mediastinal contour on film
Tension pneumothorax shifting the trachea to the opposite side
Bilateral pleural effusions blunting both costophrenic angles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Normally, lower lobe vessels are larger. In raised pulmonary venous pressure (LHF), upper lobe vessels engorge and become more prominent than lower lobe vessels on erect CXR — upper lobe diversion (cephalisation of blood flow).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: An 80-year-old man with HFrEF develops a potassium of 6.2 mmol/L after starting spironolactone alongside ramipril. What should be done?
options: Continue both — hyperkalaemia expected and safe
Stop both, consider alternative
Stop spironolactone only and recheck U&E
Stop ramipril only
Add calcium resonium to chelate potassium and continue both drugs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: K⁺ >6.0 mmol/L is dangerously high. Both ACEi and aldosterone antagonists raise K⁺ — the combination is high-risk. Stop both, manage hyperkalaemia (ECG, calcium gluconate if ECG changes, consider Patiromer), recheck U&E, then restart at lower doses with close monitoring if indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Digoxin is most strongly indicated in HF in which additional clinical context?
options: Sinus tachycardia >100bpm
Concurrent atrial fibrillation
LVEF <25%
Renal impairment
NYHA Class II symptoms despite optimal therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Digoxin is 3rd line in HFrEF and is most strongly indicated when concurrent AF is present (rate control + inotrope). In sinus rhythm, its benefit is modest and there is risk of toxicity. It is actually contraindicated in Wolff-Parkinson-White with AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the mechanism of action of ivabradine in HFrEF?
options: Beta-1 receptor blockade
Calcium channel blockade in SA node
Inhibition of Na/K-ATPase in myocardial cells
Alpha-2 agonist reducing sympathetic outflow
Inhibition of the If 'funny channel' in SA node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Ivabradine inhibits the If funny channel in the SA node → reduces HR without affecting contractility or blood pressure. Criteria: sinus rhythm, HR >75bpm, LVEF ≤35%. It cannot be used in AF (no SA node activity).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which of the following is a cause of HIGH-OUTPUT heart failure?
options: Ischaemic cardiomyopathy
Thyrotoxicosis
Aortic stenosis
Hypertensive heart disease
Dilated cardiomyopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: High-output HF = normal or increased cardiac output that cannot meet metabolic demands. Causes: thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, pregnancy, Paget's disease, beriberi (thiamine deficiency), AV fistula. The others are causes of low-output HF from reduced cardiac contractility.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with HF is started on carvedilol. After one week they develop worsening breathlessness and ankle swelling. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop carvedilol permanently
Increase the carvedilol dose
Add spironolactone to counteract fluid retention
Switch to bisoprolol
Continue carvedilol and add higher dose loop diuretic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Carvedilol (and all BB in HF) can cause initial fluid retention when first started. Do NOT stop — add or increase loop diuretic (furosemide) to manage fluid, then continue titrating the beta-blocker. Starting doses should be very low and titrated slowly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy) is indicated in HF with which combination of findings?
options: LVEF ≤35%, LBBB with QRS ≥130ms, NYHA Class II–IV
LVEF ≤35%, QRS <120ms, NYHA Class IV
LVEF 40–50%, AF, NYHA Class III
Any HF with AF and HR >90bpm
LVEF ≤35%, QRS ≥130ms RBBB, NYHA Class I
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: CRT indications: LVEF ≤35% + widened QRS especially LBBB ≥130ms + NYHA Class II–IV on optimal medical therapy. The LBBB causes dyssynchrony between LV and RV — biventricular pacing resynchronises contractions to improve CO.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is orthopnoea and what does it indicate?
options: Breathlessness on exertion — indicates pulmonary hypertension
Sudden nocturnal breathlessness — indicates pulmonary oedema
Breathlessness when lying flat — indicates left heart failure
Breathlessness at rest — indicates severe COPD
Breathlessness waking patient from sleep — indicates cardiac asthma
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Orthopnoea = breathlessness when lying flat, relieved by sitting up. Lying flat increases venous return to the already-failing left heart → pulmonary oedema. Patients use extra pillows to sleep — ask how many pillows they need.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What are the clinical signs of acute LVF on auscultation?
options: Wheeze and prolonged expiration
Loud P2 and split S2
Bilateral basal crackles and S3 gallop
Pan-systolic murmur throughout
Fixed split S2 and right ventricular heave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Acute LVF: bibasal crackles (pulmonary oedema fluid in airways) + S3 gallop rhythm (ventricular filling sound indicating poor LV compliance/dilation). S3 in adults >40 is always pathological. Wheeze suggests bronchospasm; loud P2 suggests pulmonary hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 55-year-old with HFrEF is admitted with decompensation. Their usual medications include furosemide, ramipril, and bisoprolol. Which drug should NOT be started during acute decompensation?
options: IV furosemide
Spironolactone
Oxygen
Sacubitril/valsartan
IV furosemide at higher dose than usual
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Sacubitril/valsartan should NOT be initiated during acute decompensation — evidence only supports use in stable, optimised HFrEF patients. Starting it acutely can cause dangerous hypotension. Also avoid: starting ACEi/BB for the first time in acute decompensation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: BNP is released by which cardiac structure and what triggers its release?
options: Atria in response to atrial stretch
Renal tubular cells in response to hypoxia
SA node in response to tachycardia
Coronary endothelium in response to ischaemia
Ventricles in response to ventricular wall stress
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide, also called Brain natriuretic peptide) is released from ventricular myocardium in response to increased wall stress (volume/pressure overload). It acts to reduce preload/afterload via vasodilation and natriuresis. NT-proBNP is the inactive cleavage product measured in blood.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which of these is NOT a recognised cause of raised BNP/NT-proBNP?
options: Pulmonary embolism
Sepsis
Hypothyroidism
Chronic kidney disease
Atrial fibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: BNP/NT-proBNP is raised in many conditions beyond HF: PE, sepsis, CKD, COPD, tachycardia, AF, acute coronary syndrome. Hypothyroidism is actually associated with LOW BNP (reduced myocardial metabolism and wall stress). This is why BNP is sensitive but not specific for HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: In acute LVF, why does sitting the patient upright help?
options: Reduces systemic vascular resistance
Reduces sympathetic drive
Increases venous return to improve cardiac output
Gravity redistributes fluid from upper lung zones to the bases
Improves diaphragmatic excursion by lowering abdominal contents
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Sitting upright uses gravity to redistribute pulmonary oedema fluid to the lung bases, leaving the upper/middle zones clearer for gas exchange. Also reduces venous return (reduces preload on the failing LV). This is why S in SODIUM mnemonic comes first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 68-year-old Afro-Caribbean man with HFrEF develops an intractable cough on ramipril. He is switched to losartan but remains symptomatic on bisoprolol and losartan. What is the most appropriate third agent?
options: Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) in place of losartan
Hydralazine + isosorbide mononitrate
Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist
Ivabradine to slow the sinoatrial node rate
Eplerenone, a selective aldosterone blocker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Hydralazine + nitrate combination has specific evidence in Afro-Caribbean patients with HFrEF who cannot tolerate ACEi or ARB (A-HeFT trial). It is a recommended alternative to the renin-angiotensin system drugs in this population. Sacubitril/valsartan cannot be combined with ARB (risk of angioedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the NYHA classification for a patient who can walk on flat ground but develops breathlessness climbing stairs?
options: Class I
Class III
Class II
Class IV
Class IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: NYHA Class II = mild symptoms with slight limitation — comfortable at rest, symptoms with moderate exertion (e.g. climbing stairs). Class I = no limitation. Class III = symptoms with less than ordinary activity. Class IV = symptoms at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which of the following is the correct FIRST-LINE treatment for symptomatic fluid overload in heart failure?
options: Spironolactone, an aldosterone-blocking diuretic
Thiazide diuretic acting on the distal convoluted tubule
IV furosemide (acute) or oral furosemide (chronic)
Sacubitril/valsartan combination ARNI therapy started
ACE inhibitor to reduce cardiac preload and afterload
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are first-line for symptomatic fluid relief in HF — acute IV furosemide for acute decompensation, oral furosemide for chronic management. Spironolactone is 2nd line for improving prognosis. Thiazides are weak in HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 78-year-old woman has HFpEF (EF 58%). Which medication has proven benefit (reduced heart failure hospitalisation) in HFpEF?
options: Bisoprolol, a cardioselective beta-blocker
Ramipril, an ACE inhibitor agent
Spironolactone, an aldosterone blocker
Empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor)
Ivabradine, a funny-current blocker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: HFpEF is difficult to treat — ACEi, beta-blockers and MRAs have not shown a clear mortality benefit. SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are the first class shown to reduce heart failure hospitalisation in HFpEF (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER); the proven benefit is on hospitalisation rather than mortality. Now guideline-recommended.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the target heart rate for rate control in AF complicating HFrEF?
options: <60bpm
<80bpm at rest
<100bpm at rest
<120bpm regardless of activity
<70bpm at rest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Rate control target in AF: HR <80bpm at rest (lenient control) or <110bpm (lenient rate control — acceptable in stable patients per RACE II trial). In HFrEF with AF, bisoprolol is preferred for rate control. Avoid diltiazem/verapamil (negative inotropic effect worsens HFrEF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with HFrEF is on ACEi + bisoprolol + spironolactone. Potassium is 5.2 mmol/L. Which drug change is most appropriate?
options: Stop ACEi and spironolactone both
Continue all drugs — K⁺ 5.2 is acceptable
Reduce spironolactone dose and recheck U&E in 5 days
Add patiromer (potassium binder) and continue all drugs
Switch spironolactone to eplerenone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: K⁺ 5.2 mmol/L is borderline high. Reduce spironolactone dose first (most likely contributor), recheck U&E in 5 days. Stop if K⁺ >5.5. Adding potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) can allow continuation of RAA-blocking drugs in HF patients prone to hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in heart failure?
options: Any patient with HFrEF
EF <35% with NYHA Class I symptoms on optimal medical therapy for >1 month
EF <50% with LBBB
Any patient with ICD-eligible arrhythmia regardless of EF
EF <35% with history of sustained VT or VF, or primary prevention after optimised medical therapy for >3 months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: ICD indications in HF: secondary prevention (previous sustained VT/VF/cardiac arrest) OR primary prevention (EF <35% on optimal medical therapy for ≥3 months with NYHA II–III). ICD shocks VF/VT back to sinus rhythm. Different from CRT (biventricular pacing for dyssynchrony).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the mechanism by which furosemide relieves pulmonary oedema in acute LVF?
options: Positive inotropic effect that increases myocardial contractility and cardiac output, thereby driving accumulated fluid out of the congested lungs
Coronary artery vasodilation that improves left ventricular perfusion and contractile function, reducing back-pressure within the pulmonary circulation
Inhibits Na/K/2Cl in loop of Henle → natriuresis/diuresis → reduces circulating volume → reduces pulmonary venous pressure
Direct bronchodilation of airway smooth muscle that improves alveolar gas exchange and rapidly relieves the sensation of breathlessness in the patient
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule, causing a bicarbonate-rich diuresis that offloads circulating volume and lung water
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Furosemide: inhibits Na/K/2Cl cotransporter in thick ascending limb of Loop of Henle → rapid natriuresis and diuresis → reduces circulating volume → reduces pulmonary venous pressure → reduces pulmonary oedema. Also has rapid venodilatory effect (even before diuresis) reducing preload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the NYHA classification for a patient with severe HF who becomes breathless walking 20 metres on the flat?
options: Class I
Class III
Class II
Class IV
Class II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: NYHA Class III: marked limitation — symptoms with less than ordinary activity. Walking 20 metres (less than ordinary) causing breathlessness = Class III. Class II = symptoms with ordinary activity (walking on flat comfortable). Class IV = symptoms at rest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with acute LVF has BP of 200/120. Which additional drug can be used alongside diuretics?
options: IV metoprolol
Oral ACEi immediately
IV adrenaline
IV nitrates (glyceryl trinitrate)
IV labetalol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: IV nitrates (GTN) in acute LVF with hypertension: vasodilation → reduces preload AND afterload → reduces pulmonary venous pressure and LV wall stress → relieves pulmonary oedema. Most beneficial when ACS or hypertension is the trigger. Avoid if SBP <90.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which of the following is the correct first-line treatment for symptomatic HFrEF according to NICE?
options: ACE inhibitor AND beta-blocker simultaneously, both titrated up
Loop diuretic alone, titrated upward to relieve congestive symptoms
Digoxin first for rate control and inotropy, then add an ACE inhibitor
Spironolactone as the sole first agent, before any ACE inhibitor
Aldosterone antagonist first, with an ACE inhibitor added later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: NICE recommends starting BOTH ACEi (or ARB) AND beta-blocker simultaneously at low doses in HFrEF, then titrating both up together. This dual neurohormonal blockade (RAAS + sympathetic) is the cornerstone of HFrEF treatment. Loop diuretics for symptoms only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which investigation is used to guide diuretic therapy in acute heart failure?
options: Serial BNP/NT-proBNP
Serial troponin
Serial echocardiography
Renal ultrasound
Daily weights and fluid balance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Daily weights and strict fluid balance (input vs output) are the primary tools for monitoring diuretic response in acute HF. Target: negative fluid balance of 0.5–1 L/day. BNP/NT-proBNP also used to assess response and guide discharge. The patient should be weighed daily at the same time.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A 65-year-old with HFrEF (EF 28%) is on optimal medical therapy but remains NYHA III. QRS is 160ms LBBB. What additional device therapy should be considered?
options: CRT-D (cardiac resynchronisation therapy with defibrillator)
ICD alone
AV node ablation and pacemaker
Permanent pacemaker only
CRT-P (cardiac resynchronisation therapy with pacemaker only)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: CRT-D is indicated: EF ≤35% + LBBB with QRS ≥130ms + NYHA II–III on optimal medical therapy. This patient meets all criteria. CRT-D combines biventricular pacing (resynchronisation → improved CO) with ICD function (treat VF/VT). Preferred over CRT alone in patients with ICD indication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the mechanism of benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors in HFrEF?
options: Direct positive inotropic effect that raises intracellular calcium in cardiomyocytes and directly augments the force of ventricular contraction with each beat
Coronary arterial vasodilation that increases myocardial oxygen delivery, relieves ischaemia and thereby restores contractile function of the failing ventricle
Blockade of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation, reducing angiotensin II vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium and water retention in the kidney
Multiple mechanisms: reduced cardiac preload/afterload, anti-inflammatory, metabolic effects, reduced cardiac fibrosis, diuretic effect
Inhibition of neprilysin that slows breakdown of natriuretic peptides such as BNP, enhancing natriuresis, vasodilation and reducing cardiac filling pressures
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) in HF: osmotic diuresis (reduce preload), reduced arterial stiffness, anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory, improved mitochondrial function, reduced sympathetic activation. Exact mechanism in HF not fully elucidated but major trials (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced) showed significant mortality/hospitalisation reduction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What are Kerley B lines on CXR and where are they seen?
options: Rounded hilar shadows caused by enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, seen centrally on both sides of the trachea in sarcoidosis or lymphoma
Calcified pleural plaques from previous asbestos exposure, seen along the parietal pleura and over the diaphragm on the chest radiograph
Short horizontal lines at lung periphery/bases — represent interlobular septal oedema in pulmonary venous hypertension
Air bronchograms formed by air-filled bronchi outlined against surrounding alveolar consolidation, seen within the affected lobe on the film
Linear opacities radiating outward from the hilum that represent thickening of the inflamed bronchial walls in chronic airway disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Kerley B lines: short horizontal lines at lung periphery, perpendicular to pleural surface, most visible at bases on PA CXR. Represent thickened interlobular septa filled with lymphatic fluid in pulmonary venous hypertension. Classic sign of HF/pulmonary oedema.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: In cardiogenic shock from acute LVF, inotropes are needed. Which inotrope is first-line?
options: Adrenaline
Noradrenaline
Dobutamine
Dopamine
Milrinone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Dobutamine (beta-1 agonist) is the inotrope of choice in cardiogenic shock from HF — positive inotrope increasing CO without excessive vasoconstriction. Noradrenaline is a vasopressor (raises SVR) used if hypotension persists despite inotropes. Adrenaline has combined effects but more side effects.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: Which HF drug is SPECIFICALLY beneficial in Afro-Caribbean patients who cannot tolerate ACEi/ARB?
options: Ivabradine to slow the sinoatrial node
Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) therapy
Digoxin for rate control and inotropy
Hydralazine + isosorbide mononitrate
Eplerenone, a selective aldosterone blocker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Hydralazine + isosorbide mononitrate (H-ISDN) combination has proven mortality benefit specifically in Afro-Caribbean/Black patients with HFrEF (A-HeFT trial). Also used when ACEi/ARB are not tolerated. Cannot be combined with sacubitril/valsartan (risk of angioedema).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with HFrEF is started on sacubitril/valsartan. Which drug must be stopped first and why?
options: Beta-blocker — risk of bradycardia
Aldosterone antagonist — hyperkalaemia risk
ACE inhibitor — 36-hour washout required to prevent angioedema
Diuretic — risk of volume depletion
Spironolactone — aldosterone antagonism competes with valsartan
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Before starting sacubitril/valsartan, stop ACEi and wait 36 HOURS (washout). If ACEi and neprilysin inhibitor (sacubitril) are combined → bradykinin accumulates severely → angioedema. ARB can be switched directly to sacubitril/valsartan without washout (ARBs don't affect bradykinin).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What vaccine should ALL patients with heart failure receive annually?
options: Influenza vaccine annually + pneumococcal vaccine (one-off)
Hepatitis B only
Pneumococcal only
No routine vaccines recommended in HF
COVID-19 vaccine only — no other vaccines routinely indicated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: All HF patients: annual influenza vaccine + one-off pneumococcal vaccine. Respiratory infections (influenza, pneumonia) are major precipitants of acute decompensation in HF and carry high mortality. Vaccination significantly reduces hospitalisation risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: What is the most common precipitant of acute decompensation in chronic heart failure?
options: Starting a new medication such as an inhaled corticosteroid
Non-compliance with medication or dietary sodium restriction
Excessive physical exertion overwhelming cardiac reserve
Exposure to cold weather causing peripheral vasoconstriction
Initiation of a new beta-blocker at an excessively high dose
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: Non-compliance with medications (especially diuretics) and excessive dietary sodium/fluid intake are the most common precipitants of acute decompensation. Other major triggers: infection, arrhythmias (AF), MI, uncontrolled hypertension, anaemia. Always identify the precipitant and treat it alongside the acute decompensation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: A patient with acute LVF has SpO₂ 84% on high-flow oxygen. What is the next escalation step?
options: IV furosemide 200mg
Non-invasive ventilation (NIV/CPAP)
IV amiodarone
Increase diuretic to 3 doses per day
IV morphine 2.5–5mg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: If SpO₂ remains low despite high-flow O₂ in acute LVF → Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP). CPAP: positive pressure keeps alveoli open, reduces work of breathing, improves oxygenation, reduces LV afterload. If still deteriorating → intubation and invasive ventilation (ITU/HDU).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.question: NT-proBNP of 150 ng/L in a patient with breathlessness. What does this suggest?
options: Makes heart failure unlikely — consider other causes of breathlessness
Confirms heart failure
Intermediate probability — proceed to echo immediately
Requires urgent ITU admission
Requires repeat testing in 2 weeks to establish a trend
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Failur.explanation: NT-proBNP <400 ng/L makes HF unlikely (high negative predictive value). 400–2000 ng/L = possible HF (echo within 6 weeks). >2000 ng/L = probable HF (echo within 2 weeks). A normal BNP/NT-proBNP in a breathless patient should prompt investigation for other causes: COPD, PE, pneumonia, anaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 68-year-old woman with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 3. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No treatment needed
Aspirin 75mg OD
Warfarin only
Apixaban (DOAC)
Clopidogrel 75mg OD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women = oral anticoagulation required. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are first-line over warfarin for non-valvular AF due to better safety profile, fixed dosing, and no routine INR monitoring.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 55-year-old presents with new-onset AF for 30 hours. He is haemodynamically stable with HR 135bpm. What is the appropriate management?
options: Rate control only, because atrial fibrillation lasting beyond 24 hours can no longer be cardioverted safely
Immediate DC cardioversion with no anticoagulation cover, as the embolic stroke risk here is negligible
Rhythm control is appropriate — anticoagulate with heparin and cardiovert
Rate control for three weeks first, then arrange a purely elective outpatient cardioversion later
Digoxin alone for rapid rate control, then cardiovert once the ventricular response has settled
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF <48h in a haemodynamically stable patient → rhythm control is appropriate. Anticoagulate with heparin immediately before cardioversion (no need for 3 weeks prior anticoagulation if <48h), then continue anticoagulation for minimum 4 weeks after cardioversion. DC cardioversion or flecainide.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF and structural heart disease needs pharmacological cardioversion. Which drug is most appropriate?
options: Flecainide
Amiodarone
Digoxin
Adenosine
Sotalol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone is the drug of choice for pharmacological cardioversion or rhythm control in AF with structural heart disease (IHD, HF, LV dysfunction). Flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease (proarrhythmic risk). Digoxin is for rate control only. Adenosine treats SVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the ventricular rate in typical 2:1 atrial flutter?
options: 300bpm
200bpm
75bpm
150bpm
250bpm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Atrial rate in flutter = ~300bpm. With 2:1 AV block, every other atrial impulse conducts → ventricular rate = 300/2 = 150bpm. 3:1 block → 100bpm. Sawtooth flutter waves (F waves) are diagnostic on ECG.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient's warfarin INR is 4.8. They are asymptomatic with no bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Emergency FFP
Temporarily withhold warfarin, recheck INR in 1–2 days
Vitamin K 5mg IV
Continue warfarin at same dose, recheck in 1 week
Give oral vitamin K 1mg immediately
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: INR 4.8 with no bleeding → temporarily withhold 1–2 doses of warfarin and recheck INR in 1–2 days. Target INR 2–3. Vitamin K is used if INR >5 or bleeding present. Emergency FFP/PCC for major bleeding with supratherapeutic INR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is NOT an indication for immediate DC cardioversion in AF?
options: New-onset AF for 72 hours in a stable patient
Acute LVF
Haemodynamic compromise
Rapid AF in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Acute chest pain with rapid AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Immediate DC cardioversion is for haemodynamically unstable AF (shock, acute LVF, severe chest pain) or WPW+AF (risk of VF via accessory pathway). Stable AF of 72h duration does not need emergency cardioversion — rate control and elective cardioversion after 3 weeks anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the main risk of using flecainide in atrial flutter?
options: Marked QT prolongation precipitating torsades de pointes
1:1 AV conduction causing rapid ventricular response
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis driving the deterioration
Profound sinus bradycardia with a junctional escape rhythm
Acute renal failure with dangerous accumulation of the drug
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide slows the atrial rate in flutter from ~300 to ~200bpm. This can paradoxically make it easier for the AV node to conduct every impulse (1:1), causing a dangerous ventricular rate of 200bpm. Avoid flecainide in flutter — use DC cardioversion or amiodarone instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 42-year-old athlete with no structural heart disease has paroxysmal AF and wants to self-manage episodes. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Daily flecainide prophylaxis
Pill-in-the-pocket with flecainide
Catheter ablation immediately
Long-term amiodarone
Rate control with verapamil
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Pill-in-the-pocket with flecainide is appropriate for young patients with infrequent, well-tolerated paroxysmal AF and no structural heart disease. They take flecainide at onset of symptoms. Catheter ablation is considered if pharmacological rhythm control fails. Long-term amiodarone has significant side effects and is not first-line.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Amiodarone causes thyroid dysfunction. What monitoring is required?
options: TFTs once before starting
TFTs only if symptoms of thyroid disease develop
Annual TFTs only
No monitoring needed unless symptoms develop
TFTs before treatment, then every 6 months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause BOTH hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism. TFTs must be checked before starting, then every 6 months during treatment. Also monitor: LFTs, CXR (pulmonary fibrosis), eye exam (corneal deposits), peripheral nerve exam.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 78-year-old woman with AF and CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 2 starts warfarin. Her target INR should be:
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Target INR for AF anticoagulation with warfarin is 2–3 (not higher — increased bleeding risk). INR 2.5–3.5 is for mechanical heart valves. An INR <2 is subtherapeutic for AF stroke prevention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is a direct thrombin inhibitor DOAC used in AF?
options: Rivaroxaban
Apixaban
Fondaparinux
Edoxaban
Dabigatran
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Dabigatran is the only direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI) used in AF. Rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban are all direct factor Xa inhibitors. Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors by andexanet alfa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the preferred pharmacological treatment for rate control in AF with concurrent heart failure?
options: Bisoprolol (beta-blocker)
Diltiazem (a rate-limiting CCB)
Verapamil (a calcium-channel blocker)
Digoxin (a cardiac glycoside agent)
Amiodarone (a class III agent)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol) are first-line for rate control in AF with HF. Rate-limiting CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) are contraindicated in HFrEF — negative inotropic effect worsens heart failure. Digoxin can be added as adjunct but is not first-line alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 60-year-old with AF and a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 0 (male, no risk factors). What is the recommended anticoagulation?
options: Aspirin 75mg daily
Low-dose warfarin (target INR 1.5)
No antithrombotic therapy
Apixaban
Clopidogrel plus aspirin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0 in a male → no antithrombotic therapy recommended. The annual stroke risk is very low (<1%) and the bleeding risk from anticoagulation outweighs the benefit. Aspirin is no longer recommended for AF stroke prevention (ineffective and still causes bleeding).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What distinguishes AF from atrial flutter on a rhythm strip?
options: AF produces the sawtooth flutter waves, whereas atrial flutter shows chaotic fibrillatory f waves
AF gives a perfectly regular ventricular rate, whereas atrial flutter is the irregularly irregular rhythm
AF is irregularly irregular; flutter has regular F waves and typically a regular ventricular rate
Both lack P waves, but AF is distinguished by a characteristically broad QRS complex on the ECG
AF has a much slower atrial rate than flutter, usually well under 200 beats per minute
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF: irregularly irregular rhythm, fine fibrillation (f) waves, no true P waves. Atrial flutter: regular sawtooth F waves at ~300bpm, regular ventricular rate (e.g. 150bpm in 2:1 block). Both can have narrow QRS unless aberrant conduction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient who had electrical cardioversion 6 weeks ago for AF now develops palpitations. ECG shows AF again. What is the appropriate rhythm control drug given they have no structural heart disease?
options: Amiodarone
Verapamil
Digoxin
Flecainide
Bisoprolol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide is first-line for rhythm control (prevention of AF recurrence) in patients WITHOUT structural heart disease. Amiodarone is used if structural heart disease is present. Digoxin and verapamil are for rate control, not rhythm control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: In AF with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, which drug is absolutely contraindicated?
options: Flecainide
Procainamide
Synchronised DC cardioversion
Amiodarone
Verapamil
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: In WPW with AF, all AV-nodal blocking drugs are absolutely contraindicated — verapamil (and diltiazem), beta-blockers, digoxin and adenosine. Blocking the AV node forces conduction down the accessory pathway at the full atrial rate, risking VF. Treatment is synchronised DC cardioversion (if unstable) or a class Ia/Ic agent such as procainamide or flecainide (amiodarone with caution).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: How long should anticoagulation be continued AFTER successful cardioversion of AF?
options: No anticoagulation needed if sinus rhythm restored
2 weeks
Minimum 4 weeks
Lifelong only if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2
Minimum 3 months regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Anticoagulation must continue for a MINIMUM of 4 weeks after cardioversion regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score — atrial stunning occurs after cardioversion and thromboembolism risk persists for 4 weeks even if sinus rhythm is maintained. Thereafter, anticoagulation continues based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the AV node ablation ('ablate and pace') strategy used for?
options: Young patients with paroxysmal AF
Patients with HF and AF awaiting catheter ablation
All patients with permanent AF
Elderly patients with poor rate control despite optimal medical therapy
Patients with paroxysmal AF refractory to one antiarrhythmic drug
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Ablate and pace = AV node ablation to create complete heart block + permanent pacemaker implantation. Used for elderly patients with permanent AF and poor ventricular rate control despite optimal drug therapy. Provides definitive rate control but makes patient pacemaker-dependent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 75-year-old woman with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 5. She has a history of falls. What is the most appropriate approach to anticoagulation?
options: Withhold anticoagulation due to fall risk
Start anticoagulation — fall risk does not outweigh stroke risk
Give aspirin instead as safer option
Refer for catheter ablation before deciding
Refer for left atrial appendage occlusion device instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Falls alone are not a contraindication to anticoagulation in AF. The stroke risk at CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5 (~6.7%/year) far outweighs the annual bleeding risk from falls (very high number of falls needed to equal the harm from a major stroke). Assess ORBIT score for bleeding risk; optimise fall prevention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following correctly describes how to calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc?
options: Stroke/TIA scores 1 point; age ≥75 scores 1 point
All factors score 1 point each except female sex which scores 0
Age ≥75 scores 2 points; Stroke/TIA scores 2 points; female sex scores 1 point
Heart failure and diabetes each score 2 points
Vascular disease scores 2 points
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc: C(1), H(1), A₂ age≥75(2), D(1), S₂ stroke/TIA(2), V vascular disease(1), A age 65-74(1), Sc female sex(1). Stroke/TIA and age ≥75 are the highest-weighted factors at 2 points each. Maximum score is 9.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF is on digoxin for rate control. Which finding would suggest digoxin toxicity?
options: A resting heart rate of around 90 beats per minute
A supratherapeutic INR of approximately 3.5
Nausea, vomiting, and visual halos (yellow-green)
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema up to the knees
Peripheral oedema with several kilograms of weight gain
