conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Digoxin toxicity: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, visual disturbances (yellow-green halos, blurred vision — classic), bradycardia, heart block, arrhythmias. Hypokalaemia increases toxicity risk. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index — monitor drug levels and renal function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: After starting amiodarone for AF, a patient develops exertional breathlessness and a dry cough 6 months later. What is the most likely cause?
options: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis
ACEi-related cough from concurrent ramipril
New-onset heart failure
Amiodarone-induced pulmonary fibrosis/toxicity
Amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis/fibrosis) presents with dyspnoea, dry cough, reduced transfer factor, and bilateral infiltrates on CXR/CT. It can occur months to years after starting. Diagnosis: CXR, CT chest, PFTs. Treat: stop amiodarone, consider steroids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 65-year-old man with paroxysmal AF has CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 1 (hypertension only). What is the recommended management?
options: No antithrombotic therapy
Consider oral anticoagulation — discuss risks and benefits
Aspirin 75mg daily
Mandatory anticoagulation — score ≥1 in male
Anticoagulation only if additional risk factor develops
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 1 in a male: anticoagulation may be considered (1-2% annual stroke risk). Discuss with patient. Score 0 in male = no treatment. Score ≥2 in male = anticoagulate. Female sex adds 1 point but is not independently sufficient to mandate treatment (need ≥2 in females for definite indication).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 4. ORBIT score is 5 (high bleeding risk). What is the correct approach?
options: Withhold anticoagulation entirely because the bleeding risk outweighs any stroke benefit
Use aspirin monotherapy instead, as it protects against stroke with much less bleeding risk
Start anticoagulation — high stroke risk outweighs even high bleeding risk
Refer for AF ablation first and postpone the anticoagulation decision until afterwards
Switch to warfarin, which is inherently safer than DOACs at high bleeding risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Even with high ORBIT score, the annual stroke risk at CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4 (~4%/year) usually outweighs the bleeding risk. Anticoagulate and MODIFY bleeding risk factors (optimise BP, review interacting drugs, manage anaemia). Bleeding risk scores guide risk modification — they are NOT contraindications to anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which DOAC is taken TWICE daily for AF stroke prevention?
options: Rivaroxaban
Edoxaban
Dabigatran
Edoxaban
Apixaban
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Apixaban (Eliquis): 5mg TWICE DAILY (or 2.5mg BD in patients meeting ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60kg, creatinine ≥133 μmol/L). Rivaroxaban: once daily with evening meal. Dabigatran: twice daily. Edoxaban: once daily.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with permanent AF develops an ischaemic stroke. She was not anticoagulated as her GP felt her fall risk was too high. Was this correct?
options: Yes — a significant falls risk is a firm, well-established contraindication that should always preclude anticoagulation
It depends entirely on the severity; only recurrent major injurious falls should ever preclude anticoagulation
No — a patient would need to fall approximately 300 times per year to offset the benefit of anticoagulation in preventing strokes
Yes, provided the CHA2DS2-VASc score is only 2, in which case the fall risk tips the balance against treatment
Yes, particularly once the patient is over 80, when advancing age makes falls an absolute contraindication
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: IMPORTANT: a patient needs to fall approximately 295 times per year for the fall risk to outweigh the stroke prevention benefit of anticoagulation. Fall risk alone is NOT a contraindication to anticoagulation in AF. Address fall risk (physio, medication review, home hazard assessment) rather than withholding anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What distinguishes permanent AF from persistent AF from paroxysmal AF?
options: Permanent AF is simply defined as any episode continuing unbroken for at least twelve months
Paroxysmal: self-terminates <48h; persistent: >7 days not self-terminating; permanent: cardioversion not pursued/failed
Paroxysmal AF cannot be cardioverted, persistent AF can, and permanent AF is cardioverted routinely
Duration is completely irrelevant; the categories are distinguished purely by how symptomatic the patient feels
Long-standing persistent AF means over 6 months, at which point cardioversion becomes technically impossible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF classification: Paroxysmal = self-terminates <48h (usually). Persistent = lasts >7 days, not self-terminating, can be cardioverted. Long-standing persistent = >12 months, cardioversion still considered. Permanent = cardioversion not pursued (patient and doctor decision) — rate control only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 50-year-old with paroxysmal AF wants pharmacological cardioversion. She has no structural heart disease. What drug is used?
options: Amiodarone
Sotalol
Digoxin
Flecainide
Adenosine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Flecainide is first-line for pharmacological cardioversion and rhythm control in paroxysmal AF WITHOUT structural heart disease. Dose: 200-300mg oral (pill-in-pocket) or IV. Contraindicated in structural heart disease (IHD, HF, LVH) due to proarrhythmic risk. Amiodarone used if structural disease present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the mechanism of atrial flutter and what defines its ECG?
options: Organised re-entry circuit (usually around tricuspid valve) — regular sawtooth F waves at 300bpm
Random re-entry throughout atria — fine fibrillatory baseline
Multiple ectopic foci — irregular tachycardia with P waves
AV nodal re-entry — regular narrow complex tachycardia with P behind QRS
Triggered activity from pulmonary veins — irregular sawtooth baseline
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Atrial flutter: single organised re-entry circuit (most commonly around the tricuspid annulus — cavotricuspid isthmus flutter). Atrial rate ~300bpm → regular sawtooth F waves on ECG (best in II, III, aVF, V1). AV node usually blocks 2:1 → ventricular rate ~150bpm. Radiofrequency ablation is curative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Rate control with digoxin in AF is MOST appropriate in which patient?
options: Active young patient with lone AF
Patient with AF and acute myocardial infarction
Patient with AF and hyperthyroidism
Patient with AF and COPD
Elderly sedentary patient with AF and low activity level
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Digoxin for rate control in AF: most appropriate in elderly sedentary/inactive patients. It is ineffective during exertion (primarily vagotonic — reduces resting rate but inadequate rate control during exercise). Not first-line. Better options for active patients: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB. Also useful in AF + HF (where CCBs are contraindicated).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with AF undergoes successful DC cardioversion to sinus rhythm. What is the minimum post-cardioversion anticoagulation duration?
options: 4 weeks minimum, then CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided
1 week
48 hours
Until INR normalises
2 weeks if sinus rhythm confirmed on ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: MINIMUM 4 weeks anticoagulation after ALL cardioversions (electrical or pharmacological). 'Atrial stunning' post-cardioversion → high clot formation risk in left atrial appendage for 4 weeks even in sinus rhythm. After 4 weeks → continue based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc. If patient is at high stroke risk, anticoagulate indefinitely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the key distinction between AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and AF on ECG?
options: AVNRT has no P waves at all, whereas AF shows clearly visible, normal upright P waves before each QRS
AVNRT always needs DC cardioversion to terminate, whereas AF can simply be rate-controlled
AVNRT always runs at a substantially faster ventricular rate than atrial fibrillation does
AVNRT is regular, narrow complex; AF is irregularly irregular with no true P waves
AVNRT produces a broad-complex QRS, whereas atrial fibrillation is always narrow-complex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AVNRT: rapid, REGULAR narrow QRS tachycardia (HR typically 150–250bpm), P waves buried in or just after QRS. AF: IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR, no true P waves (only fibrillation f waves). Regularity is the key distinction — regular narrow complex = SVT (AVNRT, AT, flutter); irregular = AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which anticoagulant is preferred when a patient with AF also has significant renal impairment (CrCl 20 mL/min)?
options: Dabigatran — renally cleared
Rivaroxaban — once daily dosing
Apixaban — least renally excreted, preferred in CKD
Warfarin — unaffected by renal function
Edoxaban — once daily and safest in CKD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Apixaban has the LEAST renal excretion (~27%) among DOACs — preferred when eGFR is significantly reduced. Dabigatran is predominantly renally excreted (~80%) — contraindicated in severe CKD. Rivaroxaban ~33% renal. Warfarin: metabolised hepatically, but monitoring is complex. DOACs generally preferred over warfarin in CKD if CrCl >15-25.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: How does idarucizumab reverse dabigatran?
options: It works by directly inhibiting factor Xa, thereby reducing thrombin generation and stopping the bleed
It reverses the anticoagulant by strongly activating antithrombin III within the coagulation cascade
Monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity, reversing its anticoagulant effect
It simply provides concentrated clotting factors that directly override the drug's anticoagulant effect
It competitively displaces dabigatran from the thrombin active site, thereby restoring normal clotting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Idarucizumab (Praxbind): humanised monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with 350x greater affinity than thrombin → completely neutralises dabigatran within minutes. Used for life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery in patients on dabigatran. Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with new-onset AF (duration unknown) needs rate control while awaiting elective cardioversion. What must be started simultaneously with rate control?
options: Nothing additional — rate control alone is sufficient
Beta-blocker AND CCB together for faster rate control
Antiarrhythmic drug (flecainide) immediately
Anticoagulation for minimum 3 weeks before cardioversion
TOE to exclude LAA thrombus — mandatory before any cardioversion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: If AF duration >48h or unknown → risk of left atrial appendage thrombus. Must anticoagulate for MINIMUM 3 WEEKS before elective cardioversion (to allow any existing thrombus to organise/dissolve). Alternative: TOE to exclude LAA thrombus → early cardioversion with pre-procedure anticoagulation. Then 4 weeks post-cardioversion regardless.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is the role of pulmonary vein isolation in AF?
options: It surgically removes the sinoatrial node itself, which permanently prevents any future atrial fibrillation arising
It creates an extensive surgical maze of atrial scars that channels every impulse along fixed protected corridors
Ablates the pulmonary vein ostia — site of ectopic triggers for paroxysmal AF — electrically isolating them from the left atrium
It implants an intracardiac device that continuously monitors for and automatically shocks any AF episode developing
It deliberately occludes the coronary sinus to interrupt the re-entrant circuits that sustain atrial fibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI): catheter ablation targeting the pulmonary vein ostia (PVs) where ectopic atrial beats triggering AF originate. Radiofrequency or cryoenergy creates encircling lesions isolating PVs from LA. Success rates: ~50-80% for paroxysmal AF at 1 year. Indicated: symptomatic AF failed antiarrhythmic drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Which of the following is a side effect UNIQUE to amiodarone due to its iodine content?
options: Both hypo- and hyperthyroidism
Dry cough
Bradycardia
QT prolongation
Corneal microdeposits
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Amiodarone contains ~37% iodine by weight → can cause BOTH hypothyroidism (iodine load inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis — Wolff-Chaikoff effect) AND hyperthyroidism (iodine provides substrate for autonomous thyroid production). Check TFTs before starting and every 6 months during treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient's CHA₂DS₂-VASc score components are: age 72 (1pt), hypertension (1pt), previous TIA (2pts), female (1pt). Total score?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: C=0 (no HF), H=1 (HTN), A₂=1 (age 65-74, NOT ≥75 so 1pt), D=0, S₂=2 (TIA), V=0, A=1 (age 65-74), Sc=1 (female). Total = 0+1+1+0+2+0+1+1 = 6. Wait — age 72 = A₂ component (65-74) = 1 point. Score = 1+2+1+1 = 5. Requires anticoagulation (score ≥3 in female).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is meant by 'rate versus rhythm control' — and what does AFFIRM trial evidence show?
options: Rhythm control is always superior — reduces mortality
Rate control is superior — lower mortality and fewer adverse effects
Both strategies have similar mortality — choose based on patient symptoms and preference
Rhythm control is superior only in patients <65 years
Rhythm control is superior only in patients with HFrEF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AFFIRM trial: rate control (HR <80bpm, remain in AF) vs rhythm control (cardioversion to maintain sinus rhythm) in AF. RESULT: similar mortality between strategies, but rhythm control patients had MORE hospitalisations and drug side effects. Rate control preferred in older, less symptomatic patients. Rhythm control for younger, symptomatic, or HF patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 55-year-old man with recent-onset AF <24h is haemodynamically stable but very symptomatic (severe palpitations). What is the most appropriate rhythm management?
options: Rhythm control — can cardiovert with anticoagulation cover — amiodarone or flecainide (if no SHD)
Urgent DC cardioversion without anticoagulation is safe and appropriate
Rate control with diltiazem only
Anticoagulate for 3 weeks then elective cardioversion
Rate control with bisoprolol plus anticoagulation for 3 weeks before considering rhythm control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AF <48h in a STABLE patient: rhythm control is appropriate. Can cardiovert (pharmacological or DC) with anticoagulant cover (heparin pre-procedure), then continue anticoagulation for 4 weeks. Urgent DC cardioversion without anticoagulation is reserved for HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE patients only.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of sudden-onset rapid regular palpitations terminating abruptly. ECG during episode: HR 185bpm, regular, narrow QRS, P waves not visible. No delta wave in sinus rhythm. What is the diagnosis and first-line acute treatment?
options: Atrial fibrillation — immediate rate control with oral bisoprolol
AVNRT — vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva) then adenosine 6mg IV
Ventricular tachycardia — a 300mg IV amiodarone loading dose
AVRT with pre-excitation — urgent synchronised DC cardioversion
Atrial flutter — first-line rate control using intravenous digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: AVNRT: most common SVT. Regular narrow complex tachycardia, abrupt onset/termination, P waves hidden in QRS. No delta wave (not WPW). First-line: vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva). If fails → adenosine 6mg IV (12mg, 18mg). Monitor ECG continuously. If haemodynamically unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A 22-year-old presents with SVT. ECG in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval of 90ms and a slurred upstroke of the QRS. He is now in AF with a rapid irregular broad complex tachycardia. What should NOT be given?
options: DC cardioversion
Procainamide
Amiodarone (with caution)
Adenosine
Flecainide
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: WPW + AF: NEVER give adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, or diltiazem. These block the AV node → all conduction forced through the accessory pathway at the full rapid atrial rate → extremely fast ventricular response → VF → cardiac arrest. Treatment: DC cardioversion (if unstable) or procainamide/flecainide (if stable). Amiodarone has been used but may worsen in some cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Adenosine 6mg is given rapidly IV for SVT. The patient has a brief period of chest tightness and asystole, then sinus rhythm returns. Was the response appropriate?
options: No — the adenosine has caused a genuine cardiac arrest, so start CPR and give adrenaline immediately
No — adenosine should never produce any asystole, so this indicates a serious dosing or delivery error
Yes — transient asystole and chest tightness are expected effects. Sinus rhythm returned = successful.
No — this appearance means the patient urgently needs full anticoagulation before anything else is done
No — the chest tightness signals an acute adenosine allergy, so treat with antihistamine and steroids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Adenosine causes transient AV block → brief asystole (seconds) before sinus rhythm restores. Patients commonly experience: chest tightness, facial flushing, breathlessness, and a sense of impending doom (lasting 10–30 seconds). This is expected and transient due to adenosine's very short half-life (<10 seconds). Warn patients before administration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Carotid sinus massage is being considered for SVT. What must be checked first?
options: Listen for carotid bruits / history of TIA or stroke — contraindicated if carotid stenosis present
Simply check the blood pressure, as this is the only safety step needed before the manoeuvre
Check the serum potassium level first, since this is the key safety check before proceeding
Perform a 12-lead ECG first purely to exclude atrial fibrillation before attempting the manoeuvre
Check the INR beforehand, as a deranged clotting result is the main contraindication here
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Carotid sinus massage contraindicated in patients with carotid artery stenosis (risk of dislodging atherosclerotic plaque → stroke) or recent TIA/stroke. Always auscultate for carotid bruits before performing carotid sinus massage. If bruits present → avoid bilateral massage. Perform on one side only for 5–10 seconds. Can be repeated on the other side if needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: What is synchronised DC cardioversion and why is synchronisation important?
options: Shock delivered on the P wave to reset atrial activity
Shock synchronised with the R wave to avoid shocking during the T wave (which would cause VF)
Shock given continuously throughout the cardiac cycle
Shock given at a random point to maximise energy delivery
Shock delivered asynchronously at maximum energy to terminate arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion: the defibrillator detects QRS complexes and delivers the shock at the peak of the R wave. This is critical because shocking during the T wave (vulnerable period of ventricular repolarisation) can trigger VF. This is why synchronisation is used for PULSED arrhythmias. Pulseless VT/VF: no synchronisation (unsynchronised defibrillation) as there are no organised QRS complexes to sync to.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: Long-term management of recurrent AVNRT is required for a 35-year-old professional musician. He has had 5 hospital admissions in 2 years. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
options: Commit the patient to lifelong daily flecainide as the definitive long-term solution
Prescribe a beta-blocker indefinitely, which is regarded here as the curative treatment
Radiofrequency catheter ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway — curative in >95% of cases
Arrange routine annual DC cardioversion sessions to keep the arrhythmia suppressed
Implant a permanent pacemaker, which definitively cures the underlying re-entry circuit
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Radiofrequency ablation is the definitive curative treatment for AVNRT (slow AV nodal pathway ablation). Success rate >95%. Preferred for patients with frequent recurrences, drug intolerance, or who prefer a cure over lifelong medication. Performed under sedation/GA via femoral vein in the catheter lab. Risk of AV block ~1%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.question: A patient with regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150bpm has sawtooth baseline activity visible in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the diagnosis?
options: AVNRT — terminate it acutely with a rapid IV adenosine bolus
Ventricular tachycardia — give adenosine then IV amiodarone
Atrial fibrillation — simple long-term ventricular rate control
Sinus tachycardia driven by pain — treat the underlying cause
Atrial flutter — rate control and consider cardioversion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Supraventric.explanation: Regular sawtooth F waves at 300bpm + ventricular rate 150bpm (2:1 conduction) = atrial flutter. The sawtooth pattern is most visible in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and V1. Management: rate control (beta-blocker, diltiazem) and rhythm control (DC cardioversion or pharmacological). Radiofrequency ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is curative (>95% success for typical flutter).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is hypertension described as the 'silent killer'?
options: It always presents with a severe pounding morning headache
It causes sudden painless bilateral loss of vision
It only affects elderly patients over eighty years of age
It is rapidly fatal within a few days without treatment
It is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: It is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Hypertension is a sustained elevation of BP that is usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs — hence the 'silent killer'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why must a raised clinic BP be confirmed with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing hypertension?
options: To assess renal function
To measure cholesterol
To exclude the white-coat effect
To detect arrhythmias
To grade retinopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: To exclude the white-coat effect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Clinic measurement is confirmed with ABPM or HBPM to exclude the white-coat effect; white-coat hypertension is common and ABPM prevents over-treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What are the Stage 1 hypertension thresholds for clinic and ABPM/HBPM?
options: Clinic ≥160/100, ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95
Clinic ≥180/120, ABPM/HBPM ≥170/110
Clinic ≥140/90, ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85
Clinic ≥130/80, ABPM/HBPM ≥125/75
Clinic ≥150/95, ABPM/HBPM ≥140/90
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Clinic ≥140/90, ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 1 is clinic BP ≥140/90 and ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: When should Stage 1 hypertension be treated?
options: Always, regardless of other factors
If <80 yrs with end-organ damage, CV risk >10%, or T2DM/CKD
Only if >80 yrs
Only in pregnancy
Never — it is observed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: If <80 yrs with end-organ damage, CV risk >10%, or T2DM/CKD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 1 is treated if the patient is <80 yrs with end-organ damage, CV risk >10%, or T2DM/CKD; Stage 2 is treated regardless of other factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient has a clinic BP of ≥180/120. What is the appropriate action?
options: Routine review in 4 weeks, with no urgent bloods or examination needed today
Offer antihypertensive treatment immediately regardless of any other risk factor
Same-day assessment for end-organ damage; if present → hypertensive emergency
Repeat ABPM at home and review the averaged readings again in 3 months
No action needed, as this reading sits within acceptable clinic limits
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Same-day assessment for end-organ damage; if present → hypertensive emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Stage 3/Severe (≥180/120) warrants same-day assessment for end-organ damage; if present, it is a hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Approximately what proportion of hypertension is primary/essential, and what characterises it?
options: ~50% — single-gene disorder
~10% — always has an identifiable cause
~70% — always drug-induced
~30% — purely environmental
~90% — no identifiable cause, polygenic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: ~90% — no identifiable cause, polygenic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Primary/essential hypertension accounts for ~90%, has no identifiable cause and is polygenic (multiple genes plus lifestyle).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the commonest category of secondary hypertension?
options: Endocrine
Renal (~80% of secondary)
Drug-induced
Coarctation
Obstructive sleep apnoea
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Renal (~80% of secondary)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Renal causes are the commonest category of secondary hypertension (~80%), including CKD, renovascular disease and polycystic kidney disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which of the following is listed as an endocrine cause of secondary hypertension?
options: Polycystic kidney disease (an inherited cause)
Coarctation of the aorta (a vascular cause)
Obstructive sleep apnoea (a sleep-related cause)
Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
Chronic NSAID use retaining salt and water
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Endocrine causes include Conn's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, acromegaly and hypothyroidism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which of these drugs is listed as a cause of secondary hypertension?
options: Paracetamol
Liquorice
Metformin
Amoxicillin
Omeprazole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Liquorice
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Listed drug causes are NSAIDs, oestrogen (OCP), alcohol, liquorice, cocaine and ciclosporin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: When should you 'think secondary' hypertension?
options: Young, resistant (≥3 drugs), or sudden onset
Older patients with well-controlled BP
Any patient over 60
Only if the patient is pregnant
Only if BP is below target
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Young, resistant (≥3 drugs), or sudden onset
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Think secondary if Young, Resistant (≥3 drugs) or Sudden onset — especially under 40, refractory HTN, or with a clinical clue (e.g. hypokalaemia → Conn's).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient with hypertension has muscle weakness, polyuria and cramps, with hypokalaemia. Which secondary cause does this suggest, and what is the clue?
options: Phaeochromocytoma — paroxysmal BP spikes with sweating, palpitations and episodic headache
Cushing's — moon face with central obesity, striae and proximal muscle weakness
Conn's syndrome — hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise
Coarctation — radiofemoral delay with weaker, delayed pulses felt in both legs
Renal/RAS — an audible renal bruit heard on auscultation of the flank or abdomen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Conn's syndrome — hypokalaemia + HTN → primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Muscle weakness, polyuria, cramps with hypokalaemia point to Conn's; hypokalaemia + HTN means primary hyperaldosteronism until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor with paroxysmal BP spikes suggest which secondary cause, and what is the investigation clue?
options: Conn's — a raised aldosterone:renin ratio on screening bloods
Phaeochromocytoma — 24h urinary catecholamines / metanephrines
Cushing's — failure of overnight dexamethasone suppression
Pre-eclampsia — screen for HELLP with proteinuria after 20 weeks
Coarctation — inferior rib notching seen on the chest X-ray
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Phaeochromocytoma — 24h urinary catecholamines / metanephrines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor with paroxysmal BP spikes suggest phaeochromocytoma; clue is 24h urinary catecholamines/metanephrines.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A young patient has radiofemoral delay and weak femoral pulses. Which secondary cause is this, and what confirms it?
options: Renal/RAS — asymmetric kidney sizes seen on ultrasound scanning
Cushing's — central obesity with moon face and purple striae
Conn's — hypokalaemia with a raised aldosterone:renin ratio
Coarctation — BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching
Pre-eclampsia — new proteinuria and oedema after 20 weeks gestation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Coarctation — BP differential arms vs legs; chest X-ray rib notching
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Radiofemoral delay and weak femoral pulses in a young patient suggest coarctation; clue is a BP differential between arms and legs, with rib notching on chest X-ray.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which fundoscopy finding confirms severely raised ICP from a hypertensive emergency (grade IV Keith-Wagener)?
options: A sharp disc margin
Arteriovenous nipping only
Normal optic disc
Microaneurysms only
Papilloedema — a blurred disc margin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Papilloedema — a blurred disc margin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Papilloedema (blurred disc margin) indicates severely raised ICP from a hypertensive emergency — grade IV Keith-Wagener retinopathy; a normal disc has a sharp margin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: On fundoscopy, cotton-wool spots (soft exudates) represent what, and which retinopathy grade do they mark?
options: Retinal micro-infarcts from arteriolar occlusion — hallmark of grade III–IV
Lipid deposits — hard yellow exudates marking grade I retinopathy
Normal healthy vessels — grade 0 with no hypertensive changes seen
Drusen deposits beneath the retina — marking grade II retinopathy
Retinal pigment changes — an early feature marking grade I disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Retinal micro-infarcts from arteriolar occlusion — hallmark of grade III–IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Cotton-wool spots (soft exudates) are retinal micro-infarcts due to arteriolar occlusion and are a hallmark of grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy in a hypertensive emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is the clinic measurement performed in Step 1 of diagnosis?
options: A single clinic reading is taken and needs no device validation or repeat
Average of 5 readings taken over 1 week and reviewed before any diagnosis
Validated device, average of 2 readings, confirm on a second visit unless ≥180/120
Home readings only, taken twice daily over a week, with no clinic reading
Confirm the diagnosis on a second visit only if the reading is ≥140/90
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Validated device, average of 2 readings, confirm on a second visit unless ≥180/120
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Step 1: clinic ≥140/90 using a validated device, average of 2 readings, confirmed on a second visit unless ≥180/120.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which ECG finding is assessed as part of end-organ damage in hypertension, and by which criteria?
options: RVH — Sokolow-Lyon
Long QT
Delta wave — WPW
P mitrale — LA enlargement
LVH — Sokolow-Lyon criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: LVH — Sokolow-Lyon criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: The ECG is checked for LVH (Sokolow-Lyon criteria) and AF as part of assessing end-organ damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which test screens for Conn's syndrome when there is low K+ or resistant hypertension?
options: 24h urinary catecholamines
TFTs
Overnight dexamethasone suppression
Renal USS Doppler
Aldosterone:renin ratio
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Aldosterone:renin ratio
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: The aldosterone:renin ratio screens for Conn's if there is low K+ or resistant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is QRISK3 used in hypertension management?
options: Calculate 10-year CV risk; if >10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg; statin regardless if established CVD
Confirm the diagnosis of secondary hypertension and identify the underlying cause of raised BP
Grade the severity of hypertensive retinopathy from the fundoscopic examination findings
Set the individual patient's target blood pressure according to their calculated risk score
Decide between an ACE inhibitor and a calcium-channel blocker as first-line therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Calculate 10-year CV risk; if >10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg; statin regardless if established CVD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: QRISK3 calculates 10-year CV risk; if >10% offer atorvastatin 20 mg (primary prevention), and give a statin regardless of score if CVD is established.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is antihypertensive drug choice driven by age and ethnicity?
options: Because a patient's age and ethnicity together reliably determine their ideal body weight
Because age and ethnicity directly determine the measured creatinine clearance and renal dose
Because they predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best
Because age and ethnicity reliably predict a patient's long-term adherence to daily therapy
Because a patient's age and ethnicity together set the individual target blood pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Because they predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Age and ethnicity predict renin status, which determines which drug class works best (the basis of the ACD algorithm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: According to the renin logic, which patient group is high-renin and responds best to ACEi/ARB?
options: Older/Black African/Caribbean
Pregnant patients
All patients over 55
Younger/Caucasian
Patients with gout
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Younger/Caucasian
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Younger/Caucasian patients are high-renin (RAAS-dependent), so ACEi/ARB works best; older/Black African/Caribbean are low-renin, favouring CCB or diuretic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A 48-year-old Caucasian (not Black African/Caribbean) needs monotherapy. What is first-line?
options: C — calcium channel blocker
A — ACEi or ARB
D — thiazide-like diuretic
Spironolactone
Beta-blocker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A — ACEi or ARB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For patients <55 yrs and not Black African/Caribbean, step 1 is A (ACEi or ARB) — a high-renin state where RAAS blockade is most effective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: A patient with T2DM of any age/ethnicity needs first-line monotherapy. What is chosen?
options: C — CCB
A — ACEi or ARB (renoprotective)
D — thiazide-like diuretic
Alpha-blocker
Spironolactone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A — ACEi or ARB (renoprotective)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: T2DM at any age/ethnicity → A (ACEi or ARB), which is renoprotective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the preferred Step 2 two-drug combination in hypertension?
options: A + D in every patient, as a diuretic is always the best second agent
C + D only, combining a calcium-channel blocker with a thiazide diuretic
A + C (preferred), or A + D if CCB not tolerated / fluid overloaded
A + spironolactone, adding an aldosterone antagonist as the second drug
C + beta-blocker, combining a calcium-channel blocker with bisoprolol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: A + C (preferred), or A + D if CCB not tolerated / fluid overloaded
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Step 2 is A + C (preferred), or A + D if a CCB is not tolerated or there is fluid overload.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In Step 4 resistant hypertension with K+ ≤4.5 mmol/L, what is added and what must be monitored?
options: Add an alpha-blocker such as doxazosin; monitor fasting blood glucose regularly
Spironolactone 25 mg; check U&E before and 1 month after (hyperkalaemia risk)
Add a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol; monitor the resting heart rate closely
Add a second calcium-channel blocker; monitor for worsening ankle oedema
Add a thiazide-like diuretic; monitor serum urate for a rising gout risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Spironolactone 25 mg; check U&E before and 1 month after (hyperkalaemia risk)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: If K+ ≤4.5, add spironolactone 25 mg (aldosterone antagonist); check U&E before and 1 month after because of hyperkalaemia risk — especially effective if a Conn's component is suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In Step 4 resistant hypertension with K+ >4.5 mmol/L, what is added?
options: Add spironolactone 25 mg, since a low potassium always favours an aldosterone antagonist
Add a second ACE inhibitor to intensify blockade of the renin-angiotensin system further
An alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers less preferred
Add a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide to enhance sodium and water excretion
Nothing further — stop escalation as maximal medical therapy has already been reached
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: An alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers less preferred
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: If K+ >4.5, add an alpha-blocker (doxazosin) or beta-blocker (bisoprolol); beta-blockers are less preferred due to metabolic side effects, and specialist advice is sought.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which is a recognised non-pharmacological measure for hypertension at all stages?
options: A high-salt diet with liberal added table salt to maintain circulating volume
Increase alcohol intake modestly each day to promote peripheral vasodilation
Salt restriction <6g/day, DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week
Strict bed rest with avoidance of exertion until the blood pressure settles
Daily high-protein supplements to support the endothelium and lower the BP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Salt restriction <6g/day, DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Non-pharmacological measures at all stages: salt restriction (<6g/day), DASH diet, aerobic exercise ≥150 min/week, weight loss, limit alcohol, stop smoking.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which side effect is characteristic of ACEi but not ARBs, and what is the explanation?
options: Ankle oedema — from peripheral arteriolar vasodilation, as also seen with CCBs
Gynaecomastia — an anti-androgen effect on breast tissue, as with spironolactone
Gout flares — driven by a rise in serum urate from reduced renal excretion
Dry cough (10–15%) — bradykinin accumulation; switch to ARB which has no cough
Reflex tachycardia — a baroreceptor response to rapid arteriolar vasodilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Dry cough (10–15%) — bradykinin accumulation; switch to ARB which has no cough
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: ACEi cause a dry cough in 10–15% from bradykinin accumulation; switching to an ARB (same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation) avoids the cough.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why are ACEi (and ARBs) contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
options: They raise the serum potassium far too much, causing dangerous life-threatening hyperkalaemia
They precipitate acute gout attacks by markedly raising the serum urate concentration
They cause a persistent dry irritating cough through accumulation of bradykinin in the lungs
They are strongly teratogenic, causing fetal renal and skull defects in early pregnancy
They reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: They reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: In bilateral RAS, ACEi reduce GFR by removing the efferent arteriolar tone that maintains filtration pressure, so they are contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which is the most common side effect of dihydropyridine CCBs such as amlodipine?
options: Dry cough
Hypokalaemia
Hyperkalaemia
Gynaecomastia
Ankle oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Ankle oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Ankle oedema is the most common side effect of dihydropyridine CCBs, along with flushing, headache and reflex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which antihypertensive class is a relative contraindication in gout, and why?
options: ACEi — causes hyperkalaemia by reducing aldosterone
Thiazide-like diuretic — raises urate (gout attacks)
CCB — causes dose-dependent ankle oedema and flushing
Beta-blocker — masks the warning signs of hypoglycaemia
ARB — raises serum creatinine and reduces filtration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Thiazide-like diuretic — raises urate (gout attacks)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Thiazide-like diuretics raise urate and can precipitate gout attacks, making gout a relative contraindication; caution also applies in T2DM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which side effects are associated with spironolactone, the Step 4 aldosterone antagonist?
options: Dry cough and angioedema
Hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity
Ankle oedema and flushing
Postural hypotension and urinary incontinence
Hypokalaemia and raised glucose
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia (men), menstrual irregularity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Spironolactone causes hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia in men and menstrual irregularity; check K+ before starting and use caution if eGFR <45.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which antihypertensives are recommended in pregnancy, and which classes are absolutely contraindicated?
options: Use an ACE inhibitor throughout pregnancy; avoid labetalol because of the risk of fetal bradycardia
Use spironolactone to control the pressure; avoid calcium-channel blockers as they are unsafe
Use labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa; ACEi and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated (teratogenic)
Use thiazide diuretics as first-line control; avoid methyldopa because of its sedating effects
Use ARBs safely in all trimesters; avoid beta-blockers as they reliably restrict fetal growth
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Use labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa; ACEi and ARBs are absolutely contraindicated (teratogenic)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: In pregnancy use labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa; ACEi and ARBs are teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the clinic BP target for a patient under 80 years?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For patients <80 years the clinic target is <140/90 (ABPM/HBPM <135/85).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: What is the clinic BP target for a patient with CKD, diabetes or CVD?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For CKD / Diabetes / CVD the clinic target is <130/80.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why is the BP target less aggressive in patients over 80 years?
options: Their kidneys are always structurally and functionally normal
Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion
They cannot tolerate any antihypertensive medication at all
Their blood pressure is never genuinely high at this age
They have no established end-organ damage to protect against
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: In the elderly (>80), aggressive lowering risks falls, syncope and hypoperfusion, so the clinic target is 150/90 unless significant CVD/CKD warrants tighter control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: How is a malignant / accelerated hypertensive emergency defined?
options: BP ≥180/120 plus evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone
A clinic reading of ≥140/90 alone, which on its own is sufficient to define the emergency
Any raised blood pressure accompanied by a headache, regardless of any organ involvement seen
A BP of ≥160/100 in a young patient, as youth alone makes the reading an emergency by definition
A BP of >130/80 in a patient with diabetes, as this threshold on its own defines the emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: BP ≥180/120 plus evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Malignant/accelerated HTN is BP ≥180/120 with evidence of end-organ damage; severity is defined by the damage, not the number alone.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In a hypertensive emergency with chest pain, what is done if aortic dissection is identified?
options: Oral amlodipine
IV labetalol urgently
Observe and repeat BP
Oral ramipril
Sublingual GTN only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: IV labetalol urgently
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: For the ACS/aortic dissection presentation, work-up is ECG, troponin and CXR; if dissection is present, give IV labetalol urgently.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Why must BP be lowered slowly in a hypertensive emergency, and what is the target rate?
options: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion; reduce MAP by ≤25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 hours
To save on medication costs; the BP should simply be dropped by 50% immediately with a single large IV bolus
To allow an early switch to oral dosing; the BP should be brought fully down to a normal level within 30 minutes
Because the automated BP machine reads inaccurately at high pressures, so it must be rechecked before acting on it
There is no real need to lower it slowly; rapid normalisation is perfectly safe and the pressure can be dropped fast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion; reduce MAP by ≤25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion, so reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then cautiously to 160/100 over 2–6 hours.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which IV agent is first-line for most hypertensive emergencies including dissection and pregnancy?
options: Sodium nitroprusside
Nicardipine IV
Labetalol IV
GTN infusion
Oral amlodipine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Labetalol IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: IV labetalol (an α and β blocker) is first-line for most emergencies including dissection and pregnancy; other agents include GTN infusion, sodium nitroprusside and IV nicardipine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which IV agent carries a thiocyanate toxicity risk but is highly titratable in a hypertensive emergency?
options: Labetalol IV
Sodium nitroprusside
GTN infusion
Nicardipine IV
Bisoprolol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Sodium nitroprusside
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Sodium nitroprusside is highly titratable but carries a thiocyanate toxicity risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Which set of complications represents the cardiac end-organ damage of untreated hypertension?
options: Stroke, TIA and vascular dementia from small-vessel disease
Hypertensive retinopathy graded from 1 to 4 on fundoscopy
CKD with nephrosclerosis and proteinuria from chronic renal damage
PAD, aortic aneurysm and dissection from large-vessel disease
LVH → heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF, sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: LVH → heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF, sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Cardiac complications are LVH leading to heart failure (HFpEF), IHD, AF and sudden cardiac death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Hypertension is the second commonest cause of which end-stage condition?
options: End-stage renal disease (ESRD)
End-stage liver disease
End-stage heart failure
Blindness
Dementia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: End-stage renal disease (ESRD)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Among renal complications (CKD, nephrosclerosis, proteinuria), HTN is the 2nd commonest cause of ESRD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: In the retinal complications of hypertension, which retinopathy grade signifies malignant HTN?
options: Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3/4
Grade 0
Any grade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Grade 3/4
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: Hypertensive retinopathy is graded 1–4; grade 3/4 signifies malignant HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.question: Exam pearl: a patient on an ACEi develops a persistent dry cough. What is the appropriate switch, and why does it work?
options: Switch to an ARB — same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough
Switch to a CCB — a different mechanism with no direct effect on renal function
Switch to a thiazide — a diuretic acting on an entirely different drug target
Switch to spironolactone — a potassium-sparing diuretic that avoids the cough
Stop all antihypertensive drugs and simply monitor the BP off treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.answer: Switch to an ARB — same mechanism, no bradykinin accumulation → no cough
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension.explanation: ACEi dry cough occurs in 10–15%; switch to an ARB, which has the same mechanism but no bradykinin accumulation, so no cough.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the pathological hallmark of infective endocarditis?
options: A fibrinous pericardial exudate coating the epicardium, a sign of acute pericarditis
The vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells
A myocardial abscess of necrotic muscle, the defining lesion of acute viral myocarditis
Concentric ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload, as in aortic stenosis
A dilated aortic root with cystic medial degeneration, the hallmark of Marfan aortopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: The vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The vegetation — platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells on the endocardium/valves — is the pathological hallmark of IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: How do acute IE and subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) classically differ?
options: Acute: fulminant (hours–days), normal/damaged valves, Staph aureus; subacute: insidious (weeks–months), damaged valves, Strep viridans
Acute: indolent over weeks-months caused by Strep viridans on damaged valves; subacute: fulminant over hours-days caused by Staph aureus on normal valves
Both forms run a fulminant hours-to-days course driven by Staph aureus on previously normal valves, with no insidious subacute variant existing at all
Acute: affects only prosthetic valves early after surgery; subacute: affects only native valves, differing solely by valve type and not by clinical tempo
They are identical in tempo and organism, both progressing over weeks with Strep viridans and showing no clinical or microbiological distinction of note
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Acute: fulminant (hours–days), normal/damaged valves, Staph aureus; subacute: insidious (weeks–months), damaged valves, Strep viridans
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Acute IE is fulminant (hours–days), often Staph aureus on normal or damaged valves; subacute SBE is insidious (weeks–months), classically Strep viridans on damaged valves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the single strongest risk factor for infective endocarditis?
options: IV drug use
Previous infective endocarditis
Rheumatic heart disease
A prosthetic valve
Poor dental hygiene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Previous infective endocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Previous IE is the strongest risk factor for developing IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the approximate in-hospital mortality of IE, and how often is surgery needed?
options: 5–10% mortality; surgery in ~10%
1–2% mortality; surgery rarely
50–60% mortality; surgery in ~90%
20–30% mortality; surgery in ~50%
20–30% mortality; surgery in ~5%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 20–30% mortality; surgery in ~50%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: IE has an in-hospital mortality of 20–30%, with surgery required in roughly half of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient who injects drugs develops IE. Which organism and valve are most likely?
options: Strep viridans; mitral valve
Staph aureus; tricuspid (right-sided)
Staph epidermidis; aortic valve
Strep bovis; pulmonary valve
Enterococcus; mitral valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staph aureus; tricuspid (right-sided)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Staph aureus is the most common organism overall and the classic cause in IVDU, where right-sided (tricuspid) IE predominates.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: IE following poor dental hygiene or a dental procedure is classically caused by which organism?
options: Staph aureus
Enterococcus
Staph epidermidis
Coxiella burnetii
Strep viridans
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Strep viridans
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Strep viridans, an oral commensal, classically causes IE after poor dental hygiene or dental procedures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Prosthetic valve IE occurring within 2 months of surgery is most likely due to which organism?
options: Strep viridans seeded from oral flora
Enterococcus from the urinary tract
Strep bovis from a colonic source
Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative)
Candida from fungal contamination
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Early prosthetic valve IE (<2 months, perioperative contamination) is classically caused by coagulase-negative Staph epidermidis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Strep bovis is isolated from blood cultures in a patient with IE. What does this mandate?
options: An urgent dental review to find an oral source of infection
Colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma ('bovis = bowel')
A bronchoscopy to look for an occult bronchial carcinoma
An immediate valve replacement before any further imaging
A skin biopsy to identify a cutaneous portal of entry
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Colonoscopy to exclude colorectal carcinoma ('bovis = bowel')
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Strep bovis IE is linked to colorectal cancer ('bovis = bowel'), so colonoscopy is mandated to exclude colorectal carcinoma.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which set of organisms/causes is associated with culture-negative IE?
options: Staph aureus and Strep viridans, the usual readily culturable causes
HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, and prior antibiotics
Enterococcus and Staph epidermidis, both growing easily on standard media
Candida and Aspergillus only, as the sole fungal culture-negative causes
Strep bovis and Strep pneumoniae, both routinely recovered on blood agar
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, and prior antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Culture-negative IE is caused by fastidious organisms (HACEK, Coxiella/Q fever, Bartonella, Brucella) or by prior antibiotic administration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which conditions cause non-infective (sterile) vegetations?
options: Staph aureus bacteraemia and IVDU
Rheumatic fever and dental procedures
SLE (Libman-Sacks) and malignancy (marantic endocarditis)
Q fever and brucellosis
Prosthetic valves and congenital heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: SLE (Libman-Sacks) and malignancy (marantic endocarditis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Sterile vegetations occur in SLE (Libman-Sacks endocarditis) and malignancy (marantic endocarditis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the correct sequence of events in vegetation formation?
options: Bacteraemia seeds a normal valve, then dystrophic calcification and a mature vegetation form
Systemic embolisation, then valve infarction, then a vegetation growing at the infarcted site
Immune complex deposition on the valve leaflet, then progressive fibrosis, then a vegetation
Endothelial damage → platelet-fibrin thrombus → pathogen seeding during bacteraemia → vegetation
The vegetation forms first on intact endothelium, then causes secondary endothelial damage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Endothelial damage → platelet-fibrin thrombus → pathogen seeding during bacteraemia → vegetation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Endothelial damage allows a platelet-fibrin thrombus to form, which is then seeded by pathogens during bacteraemia to create a vegetation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: The three consequence streams of IE explain almost every sign. What are they?
options: Inflammation, progressive fibrosis and dystrophic calcification
Local destruction, embolisation, immune complex deposition
Bacteraemia, systemic sepsis and circulatory shock
Tissue ischaemia, infarction and myocardial scarring
Valve stenosis, regurgitation and leaflet prolapse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Local destruction, embolisation, immune complex deposition
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The three streams — local destruction, embolisation, and immune complex deposition — account for almost all the signs of IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient with aortic-valve IE develops a new AV block on ECG. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A septic pulmonary embolus reaching the conduction system from the right heart
Drug-induced bradycardia from beta-blockers given to control the fever
Immune complex glomerulonephritis causing uraemic slowing of AV conduction
A Janeway lesion embolising to the atrioventricular node and blocking it
An aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: An aortic root / annulus abscess from local destruction — a surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A new AV block reflects an aortic root/annulus abscess (local destruction extending into the conduction system) and is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which finding belongs to the EMBOLISATION stream of IE?
options: Osler's nodes, the painful immune-complex vasculitic lesions of the finger pulps
Roth spots, the immune-mediated retinal haemorrhages with pale centres seen
Glomerulonephritis, an immune-complex deposition phenomenon within the kidney
Janeway lesions (painless infarcts) and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided)
Splinter haemorrhages, the immune-complex microvascular lesions under the nails
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Janeway lesions (painless infarcts) and septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Embolic phenomena include Janeway lesions (painless infarcts), left-sided emboli (brain, spleen, kidneys, coronary), and right-sided septic pulmonary emboli.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which findings belong to the IMMUNE COMPLEX stream of IE?
options: Janeway lesions and embolic stroke, both from vegetation embolisation
Septic pulmonary emboli seeding the lungs from right-sided vegetations
Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages and glomerulonephritis
Valve regurgitation and heart failure from local leaflet destruction
Aortic root abscess extending from direct local valvular invasion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages and glomerulonephritis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Immune complex deposition produces small-vessel vasculitis: Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, and glomerulonephritis (with raised RF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the most consistent clinical sign of infective endocarditis?
options: A new murmur
Splenomegaly
Fever
Clubbing
Roth spots
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Fever
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Fever is the most consistent sign of IE, alongside malaise, night sweats and weight loss.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Approximately what proportion of IE patients have a new or changing murmur?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A new or changing murmur is present in roughly 85% of IE cases, reflecting valve involvement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the classic exam discrimination between Janeway lesions and Osler's nodes?
options: Both are painful immune-complex phenomena affecting the finger and toe pulps with identical pathophysiology
Both are painless embolic infarcts scattered over the palms and soles with no immune component at all
Janeway = painful vasculitic nodules; Osler's = painless embolic macules on the soles, with features swapped
Janeway = painless embolic infarcts (palms/soles); Osler's = painful immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps)
Janeway = retinal haemorrhages; Osler's = subungual splinter haemorrhages of the nail beds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Janeway = painless embolic infarcts (palms/soles); Osler's = painful immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Janeway lesions are painless embolic infarcts on the palms/soles; Osler's nodes ('Ouch') are painful immune-vasculitic nodules on the finger/toe pulps.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: How should blood cultures be taken in suspected IE?
options: A single set after starting antibiotics
1 set from a central line only
2 sets from the same site after antibiotics
3 sets from different sites before antibiotics
Cultures are not needed if echo is positive
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 3 sets from different sites before antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Three sets from different sites are taken before antibiotics; ≥2 positive with a typical organism is a major Duke criterion, and persistent bacteraemia is characteristic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient has a normal transthoracic echo but strong clinical suspicion of IE. What is the correct next step?
options: IE is excluded by the normal echo, so the diagnostic workup can be stopped
Repeat the transthoracic echo in 6 weeks rather than escalating imaging now
Proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) — a normal echo does not exclude IE
Start empirical antibiotics and discharge the patient for outpatient review
Perform a CT coronary angiogram to seek the source of the emboli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) — a normal echo does not exclude IE
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: A normal echo does not exclude IE; with strong clinical suspicion, TOE (more sensitive) is indicated, especially for prosthetic valves, poor windows, or complications.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the characteristic echocardiographic finding in IE?
options: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet
A pericardial effusion with diastolic right-atrial collapse
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a small cavity
A dilated aortic root measured well above four centimetres
A septal bounce indicating constrictive pericardial physiology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: A vegetation — a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The characteristic echo finding is a vegetation: a mobile echogenic mass attached to a valve leaflet.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Under the Modified Duke criteria, which combination establishes 'definite IE'?
options: 1 major criterion alone is sufficient to confirm definite IE
3 minor criteria on their own establish definite disease
2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof
1 minor criterion combined with any positive echo finding
Any fever above 38°C accompanied by any audible cardiac murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor, OR pathological proof
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor, or pathological proof.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which of the following is a MAJOR Duke criterion?
options: Fever above 38°C, which is only one of the recognised minor supporting criteria rather than a major one
Janeway lesions, a vascular embolic phenomenon that is classified only among the minor Duke criteria
A predisposing cardiac risk factor such as a prosthetic valve or intravenous drug use, counted as a minor criterion
Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation)
A raised rheumatoid factor, an immunological phenomenon counted merely as a minor Duke criterion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, or prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The two major criteria are positive blood cultures with a typical organism and endocardial involvement on echo (or new valvular regurgitation). Fever, risk factors, Janeway lesions and raised RF are minor criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Why does IE require prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics?
options: Oral antibiotics are unavailable for these organisms, so the intravenous route must be used over many weeks
Because essentially all endocarditis organisms are inherently resistant to short oral antibiotic courses
To eradicate the dental focus that seeded the valve and prevent recurrent oral bacteraemia over time
The avascular vegetation has poor vascular penetration, requiring high drug concentrations for weeks
To directly suppress the circulating immune complexes that drive the systemic manifestations of disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: The avascular vegetation has poor vascular penetration, requiring high drug concentrations for weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: The vegetation is avascular with poor drug penetration, so prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics at high concentrations are needed to sterilise it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the first-line regimen for native-valve MSSA Staph aureus IE?
options: Vancomycin × 6 weeks
Benzylpenicillin × 4 weeks
Amoxicillin + gentamicin × 2 weeks
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours × 4–6 weeks
Daptomycin × 4 weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours × 4–6 weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Native-valve MSSA IE is treated with flucloxacillin 2 g IV q4h for 4–6 weeks; vancomycin + rifampicin is the penicillin-allergic/MRSA alternative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the empirical (blind) regimen for native-valve IE, and the penicillin-allergy/MRSA alternative?
options: Amoxicillin (± gentamicin); vancomycin + gentamicin
Flucloxacillin alone; daptomycin monotherapy
Benzylpenicillin; oral amoxicillin substitution
Vancomycin monotherapy; flucloxacillin instead
Gentamicin monotherapy; rifampicin substitution
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Amoxicillin (± gentamicin); vancomycin + gentamicin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Empirical native-valve therapy is amoxicillin ± gentamicin; if penicillin-allergic or MRSA, vancomycin + gentamicin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the regimen for MRSA infective endocarditis?
options: Vancomycin × 6 weeks (daptomycin as an alternative)
Flucloxacillin given for a full 4 to 6 weeks
Amoxicillin combined with gentamicin for 4 weeks
High-dose benzylpenicillin given for 4 weeks
Rifampicin used as monotherapy across 6 weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Vancomycin × 6 weeks (daptomycin as an alternative)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: MRSA IE is treated with vancomycin for 6 weeks, with daptomycin as an alternative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgery in IE?
options: A single positive blood culture growing from just one venepuncture site
An isolated Roth spot seen on fundoscopy without any other systemic feature
Fever settling promptly within 48 hours of starting appropriate antibiotics
Severe heart failure from acute valve regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise
A small vegetation under 5 mm that is shrinking on antibiotic therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Severe heart failure from acute valve regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Surgical indications include severe HF from acute regurgitation, valve destruction, root abscess (especially with AV block), recurrent emboli despite antibiotics, resistant organisms, prosthetic dehiscence/persistent bacteraemia, and worsening renal failure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: An IVDU presents with right-sided IE. Which imaging finding would you expect?
options: Cavitating lung lesions on CXR from septic pulmonary emboli
A globular, flask-shaped cardiac silhouette on the chest film
Bilateral pleural effusions blunting both costophrenic angles
A widened mediastinum suggesting proximal aortic involvement
Pericardial calcification encircling the cardiac border
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Cavitating lung lesions on CXR from septic pulmonary emboli
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Right-sided (tricuspid) IE in IVDU sends septic emboli to the lungs, producing cavitating lung lesions on CXR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Resistance to which type of organism is itself an indication for surgery in IE?
options: Fungi and highly resistant bacteria
Strep viridans, an oral streptococcus
Enterococcus of a colonic source
Staph epidermidis on prosthetics
The fastidious HACEK organism group
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Fungi and highly resistant bacteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Fungal IE and infection with highly resistant bacteria are difficult to clear with antibiotics alone and are indications for surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A 35-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever, night sweats, and a new pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which valve is most commonly affected in IVDU-related endocarditis?
options: Mitral valve
Tricuspid valve (right-sided)
Aortic valve
Pulmonary valve
Multiple valves equally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Tricuspid valve (right-sided)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: IVDU endocarditis classically affects the tricuspid valve — bacteria injected directly into venous circulation seed the right heart. Right-sided IE causes septic pulmonary emboli (cavitating lung lesions on CXR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What are the Duke criteria used for in infective endocarditis?
options: Severity scoring for surgical referral
Diagnosis of IE using major and minor criteria
Antibiotic selection
Risk stratification for embolic events
Echocardiographic assessment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Diagnosis of IE using major and minor criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Duke criteria: definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major: positive blood cultures + echocardiographic evidence (vegetation/abscess/dehiscence). Widely used in clinical practice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting IE vegetations and perivalvular complications?
options: PET-CT
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)
CT chest
Cardiac MRI
Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: TOE is more sensitive than TTE for vegetations (<5 mm), perivalvular abscesses, prosthetic valve IE. TTE is the first-line investigation; TOE is done if TTE is inconclusive or prosthetic valve is present.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which organism is the most common cause of native valve infective endocarditis?
options: Streptococcus viridans (oral streptococci)
Staphylococcus aureus, a skin commensal
Enterococcus faecalis, a gut organism
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a Gram-negative rod
Candida albicans, an opportunistic yeast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Staphylococcus aureus, a skin commensal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: In the developed world, Staphylococcus aureus is now the most common cause of infective endocarditis overall, including native-valve IE (acute, often on normal or damaged valves). Streptococcus viridans — from the oral flora, seeded during dental procedures — is the classic cause of SUBACUTE IE and was historically the commonest. Staph aureus also predominates in IVDU (right-sided/tricuspid).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A 55-year-old with aortic stenosis develops fever, new aortic regurgitation, and embolic stroke. Which complication of IE is most likely responsible?
options: Renal infarction
Aortic root abscess
Mitral valve prolapse
Vegetation embolising to the brain
Janeway lesions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Vegetation embolising to the brain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Embolic complications of IE occur in ~30% — cerebral emboli cause ischaemic stroke. Left-sided IE (aortic/mitral) causes systemic emboli; right-sided causes pulmonary emboli. Embolic stroke = IE until proven otherwise in appropriate context.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What are Osler's nodes and Janeway lesions?
options: Osler's nodes = painless macules; Janeway lesions = painful nodules, with the pain and morphology of the two lesions swapped around from the truth
Osler's nodes = painful nodules on fingertips (immune complex); Janeway lesions = painless haemorrhagic macules on palms/soles (embolic)
Both are embolic phenomena, seeding septic material from the valve vegetation into the skin of the palms, soles and finger pulps alike
Both are immune-complex phenomena, arising from deposition of antibody complexes in the small vessels of the fingers, toes, palms and soles
Both occur on the very same site, appearing together on the palms and soles with an identical painful, embolic character and shared timing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Osler's nodes = painful nodules on fingertips (immune complex); Janeway lesions = painless haemorrhagic macules on palms/soles (embolic)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Classic IE peripheral stigmata: Osler = painful fingers/toes (immune-mediated); Janeway = painless haemorrhagic macules on palms/soles (embolic). Roth spots = retinal haemorrhages. Splinter haemorrhages = subungual.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: What empirical antibiotic regimen is used for native valve IE?
options: Ciprofloxacin monotherapy, chosen for its broad Gram-negative activity
Metronidazole alone, targeting the anaerobic organisms presumed to cause it
Oral co-amoxiclav alone, relying on its broad Gram-positive and negative cover
Amoxicillin + gentamicin (or flucloxacillin + gentamicin if Staph suspected)
