Vancomycin alone, as a single agent covering resistant staphylococci
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Amoxicillin + gentamicin (or flucloxacillin + gentamicin if Staph suspected)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Native valve IE empirical therapy: amoxicillin + gentamicin (covers streptococci and enterococci); add flucloxacillin if Staphylococcus aureus suspected. Vancomycin if penicillin allergy or MRSA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgery in IE?
options: Elevated ESR
Low-grade fever
Positive blood cultures alone
Splinter haemorrhages
Heart failure from valvular destruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: Heart failure from valvular destruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Surgical indications in IE: heart failure from valve regurgitation/destruction; uncontrolled infection (perivalvular abscess, fistula, persistent bacteraemia); embolic events with large vegetation >10 mm; prosthetic valve IE.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: A patient with a mechanical aortic valve develops fever and bacteraemia with Staph epidermidis. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: CT chest
TTE (transthoracic echocardiography)
TOE (transoesophageal echocardiography)
PET-CT
Coronary angiogram
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: TOE (transoesophageal echocardiography)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires TOE — TTE has poor sensitivity for prosthetic valves due to acoustic shadowing. TOE can visualise perivalvular abscesses and dehiscence which are critical for management decisions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.question: EXAM PEARL: How many sets of blood cultures should be taken in IE and why?
options: 3 sets from different sites before antibiotics — maximises sensitivity (~98%)
A single set is sufficient, since one sample reliably captures the bacteraemia
Culture only when the patient is febrile at the exact moment of sampling
Take the cultures after 24 hours of antibiotics once levels are steady
Two sets drawn from the same site moments apart are adequate for diagnosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.answer: 3 sets from different sites before antibiotics — maximises sensitivity (~98%)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective En.explanation: Three sets of blood cultures (aerobic + anaerobic) from separate sites at different times = optimal sensitivity before starting antibiotics. Cultures positive in >90% of IE cases if taken correctly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What diameter defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and where are most located?
options: >2 cm; mostly suprarenal
>5 cm; mostly thoracic
>4 cm; mostly juxtarenal
>3 cm; mostly infrarenal
>2.5 cm; mostly at the bifurcation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: >3 cm; mostly infrarenal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An AAA is a permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta >3 cm (normal ~2 cm); most are infrarenal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How do the vast majority of AAAs present?
options: With acute severe back pain radiating to the flank
With acute lower limb ischaemia and absent pulses
Asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally
With a large upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage
With sudden syncopal collapse and hypotension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The vast majority of AAAs are asymptomatic and found on screening or incidentally — which is why a screening programme exists.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA?
options: Smoking
Hyperlipidaemia
Hypertension
Obesity
Atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Smoking
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the pathological mechanism of AAA formation?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque directly erodes and dilates the aortic wall through progressive luminal narrowing
Acute in-situ thrombosis of the aortic wall occludes flow, causing ischaemic dilatation of the vessel
Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → degradation of elastin and collagen → wall weakening → dilatation
Progressive calcium deposition stiffens the medial layer, which then balloons outward under arterial pressure
Immune complex deposition within the aortic media triggers vasculitic necrosis and aneurysmal outpouching
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Chronic inflammation → MMP activation → degradation of elastin and collagen → wall weakening → dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Chronic inflammation activates MMPs, which degrade elastin and collagen in the aortic wall, causing progressive weakening and dilatation; atherosclerosis is associated, not directly causative.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which major cardiovascular risk factor is protective against AAA?
options: Hypertension
Smoking
Diabetes
Hyperlipidaemia
Male sex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Diabetes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Diabetes is protective — the only major cardiovascular risk factor that reduces AAA risk; this counterintuitive fact is frequently examined.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An older man presents with back pain and collapse. What must be assumed until proven otherwise?
options: Renal colic
Appendicitis
Diverticulitis
Ruptured AAA
Ovarian torsion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Ruptured AAA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Back pain + collapse in an older man = ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; renal colic is the key mimic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is found on examination of a symptomatic unruptured AAA?
options: A non-pulsatile mass below the umbilicus
A fixed epigastric mass that does not move
Hepatomegaly
A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
Splenomegaly
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: A pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Examination reveals a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus; rarely there are signs of retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: The National AAA Screening Programme offers screening to which group?
options: All women at age 60 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
All men at age 65 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
All adults at age 50 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
Men and women at age 70 with a screening ultrasound
Only those with a first-degree family history of AAA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: All men at age 65 — a one-off abdominal ultrasound
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The programme offers a one-off abdominal ultrasound for all men at age 65; women are not routinely screened (lower risk), with USS considered if >70 with risk factors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An AAA measuring 3.0–4.4 cm on screening is classified and managed how?
options: Normal — no further action
Medium AAA — 3-monthly USS surveillance
Small AAA — yearly USS surveillance
Large AAA — refer for repair
Small AAA — immediate repair
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Small AAA — yearly USS surveillance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A 3.0–4.4 cm aorta is a small AAA, managed with yearly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An AAA measuring 4.5–5.4 cm warrants what surveillance interval?
options: No further action
3-monthly USS
Yearly USS
Immediate referral for repair
6-monthly CT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: 3-monthly USS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A 4.5–5.4 cm aorta is a medium AAA, requiring 3-monthly USS surveillance.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: An aorta measuring ≥5.5 cm on screening prompts what action?
options: Refer vascular surgery — consider repair
Switch to 3-monthly ultrasound surveillance
Continue routine yearly ultrasound scans
No further action — reassure and discharge
Repeat a surveillance ultrasound in 5 years
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Refer vascular surgery — consider repair
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An aorta ≥5.5 cm is a large AAA, prompting referral to vascular surgery to consider repair.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What are the driving rules for AAA?
options: >6 cm → inform DVLA; >6.5 cm → disqualified from driving
>5 cm → inform DVLA; >6 cm → disqualified
>4 cm → inform DVLA; >5 cm → disqualified
>5.5 cm → inform DVLA; >7 cm → disqualified
No driving restrictions apply
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: >6 cm → inform DVLA; >6.5 cm → disqualified from driving
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: AAA >6 cm → inform DVLA; AAA >6.5 cm → disqualified from driving.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the first-line investigation for AAA, and why?
options: CT angiogram — gives EVAR anatomy
MRI aorta — best soft tissue detail
Abdominal USS — cheap, no radiation, repeatable
Plain abdominal X-ray — quick
Angiography — gold standard
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Abdominal USS — cheap, no radiation, repeatable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Abdominal USS is first-line for diagnosis and surveillance — it is cheap, involves no radiation and is repeatable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: When is CT angiogram used in AAA?
options: For initial screening of all men aged 65 in place of the standard abdominal ultrasound
Only after open surgical repair to confirm graft position and check for anastomotic leak
Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) — gives anatomy for EVAR planning; also used in stable rupture
For routine yearly surveillance of small sub-threshold AAAs measuring under 5.5 cm
Never — abdominal ultrasound alone is sufficient for both surveillance and planning
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) — gives anatomy for EVAR planning; also used in stable rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: CT angiogram is used once at threshold (≥5.5 cm) to provide anatomy for EVAR suitability planning, and in stable rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: On ultrasound, how is the AAA distinguished from the IVC?
options: AAA is round, pulsatile, thick-walled; IVC is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled
AAA is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled; IVC is round, pulsatile, thick-walled
Both are round and pulsatile
AAA lies behind the vertebral body; IVC lies in front
They cannot be distinguished on USS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: AAA is round, pulsatile, thick-walled; IVC is ovoid, collapsible, thin-walled
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: On USS the AAA is round, pulsatile and thick-walled, while the IVC is ovoid, collapsible and thin-walled, with the vertebral body shadow below.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which conservative measure is the biggest modifiable factor in slowing AAA progression?
options: Statin + aspirin
Exercise
BP control
Weight loss
Smoking cessation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Smoking cessation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Among the conservative measures (smoking cessation, BP control <140/90, statin + aspirin, weight loss + exercise), smoking cessation is the biggest modifiable factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgical repair of an AAA?
options: Diameter of 4.0 cm on surveillance ultrasound
Slow growth of only 0.3 cm per year on scans
An asymptomatic 3.5 cm AAA found on screening
Growth >1 cm/year regardless of absolute size
Any AAA detected in a patient older than 65
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Growth >1 cm/year regardless of absolute size
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Surgical repair indications (any one of): diameter ≥5.5 cm, growth >1 cm/year (regardless of absolute size), or symptomatic (pain/tenderness in an otherwise fit patient).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Why might repair be delayed to 6 cm in some patients despite a diameter ≥5.5 cm?
options: In unfit patients, due to elective surgical mortality risk
Because aneurysms smaller than 6 cm essentially never rupture
Because EVAR is unavailable at the local vascular centre
To allow further cross-sectional imaging and surgical planning
Because co-existing diabetes is protective against rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: In unfit patients, due to elective surgical mortality risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Repair may be delayed to 6 cm in unfit patients because of the elective surgical mortality risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the examinable trade-off between EVAR and open AAA repair?
options: EVAR is more durable long-term; open has lower peri-op mortality
Open repair has a higher reintervention rate
Both have identical outcomes
EVAR = better short-term (lower peri-op mortality); open = better long-term durability
EVAR is only used for ruptures
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: EVAR = better short-term (lower peri-op mortality); open = better long-term durability
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR offers better short-term outcomes (lower peri-op mortality, shorter stay) while open repair offers better long-term durability; both are valid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which is a disadvantage of EVAR compared with open repair?
options: Higher 30-day post-operative mortality than open repair
Longer hospital stay and a slower initial recovery
A longer overall recovery period after the procedure
A much larger midline laparotomy incision is required
Higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Higher reintervention rate + endoleak risk + late rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR has lower 30-day mortality and a shorter stay, but a higher reintervention rate, endoleak risk and late rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the overall mortality of a ruptured AAA, and which rupture site is more common?
options: 80% mortality; 80% retroperitoneal (posterior — may be temporarily contained)
50% mortality; rupture is mostly anterior into the free peritoneal cavity
30% mortality; rupture is usually posterior into the inferior vena cava
95% mortality; virtually all ruptures are anterior and intraperitoneal
20% mortality; rupture is mostly retroperitoneal and often contained
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: 80% mortality; 80% retroperitoneal (posterior — may be temporarily contained)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Ruptured AAA carries 80% overall mortality; 80% of ruptures are retroperitoneal (posterior, may be temporarily contained), 20% into the peritoneal cavity (anterior, very poor prognosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the classic triad of a ruptured AAA, present in 50% of cases?
options: Central chest pain + acute dyspnoea + a raised JVP
Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass
High fever + generalised abdominal pain + watery diarrhoea
Severe headache + sudden visual loss + generalised seizures
Frank haematuria + severe loin pain + burning dysuria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: The classic ruptured AAA triad is flank/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile abdominal mass, present in 50% of cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Why might SpO₂ appear falsely normal in a ruptured AAA, and what is done?
options: The pulse oximeter probe is faulty; replace it and re-measure the saturation
SpO₂ always reads low in rupture, so any normal value reliably excludes it
Hypotension paradoxically raises the measured oxygen saturation reading
The patient is hyperventilating and over-saturated; withhold supplemental O₂
Remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: SpO₂ may be falsely normal because the remaining Hb is fully saturated despite blood loss — still give high-flow O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: In a ruptured AAA, what is the permissive hypotension target and its rationale?
options: Aim SBP >120 mmHg to keep vital organs adequately perfused during resuscitation
Aim SBP <100 mmHg — raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot → torrential haemorrhage
Aim MAP >90 mmHg to guarantee full cerebral and renal perfusion until repair
Aim for an SBP of 140 mmHg to maintain flow through the narrowed aortic segment
No blood pressure target is needed; simply transfuse back to normal values
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Aim SBP <100 mmHg — raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot → torrential haemorrhage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Permissive hypotension aims for SBP <100 mmHg and avoids over-resuscitation, because raising BP dislodges the tamponading clot and causes torrential haemorrhage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How is an unstable patient with a ruptured AAA managed?
options: CT angiogram first to define the anatomy, then proceed to EVAR only if suitable
Arrange yearly ultrasound surveillance and routine outpatient vascular review
Conservative care with permissive hypotension and close observation on the ward only
Immediate transfer to theatre for open repair — no time for imaging, do NOT delay with CT
Discharge home with early outpatient vascular clinic follow-up and analgesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Immediate transfer to theatre for open repair — no time for imaging, do NOT delay with CT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An unstable ruptured AAA goes immediately to theatre for open repair with no time for imaging — do not delay with CT; a stable patient gets CT angiogram first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How is a stable patient with a ruptured AAA managed?
options: Immediate open surgical repair in theatre without any pre-operative imaging
Permissive hypotension with analgesia, then discharge home once the pain settles
CT angiogram first, assess anatomy + EVAR suitability, EVAR if suitable / open if not
Routine ultrasound surveillance with interval outpatient vascular follow-up
Crossmatch blood only and observe on the ward without any active intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: CT angiogram first, assess anatomy + EVAR suitability, EVAR if suitable / open if not
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: A stable ruptured AAA gets CT angiogram first to assess anatomy and EVAR suitability — EVAR if suitable, open if not.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is an endoleak following EVAR?
options: Incomplete seal → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → sac re-expands → risk of rupture
Bacterial infection of the endovascular graft causing systemic sepsis and graft breakdown
Migration of the deployed graft down into the iliac arteries, obstructing distal limb flow
Acute thrombosis of the endovascular stent, occluding the graft and causing limb ischaemia
Rupture of the femoral arterial access site, producing a large expanding groin haematoma
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Incomplete seal → blood leaks into the aneurysm sac around the graft → sac re-expands → risk of rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: An endoleak is an incomplete seal around the graft allowing blood into the aneurysm sac, causing the sac to re-expand with a risk of rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Which endoleak type is the most common in AAA?
options: Type 1 — leak at graft ends
Type 4 — porosity
Type 3 — graft fabric defect
Type 2 — back-fill from branch vessels
Type 5 — endotension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Type 2 — back-fill from branch vessels
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Type 2 endoleak (back-fill from branch vessels) is the most common in AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What should prompt investigation for an endoleak after EVAR?
options: A stable sac size
A normal follow-up scan
Resolution of symptoms
Any post-EVAR sac expansion
Reduced graft diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Any post-EVAR sac expansion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Endoleaks are usually asymptomatic, so any post-EVAR sac expansion should prompt investigation for an endoleak.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: How does the aetiology of AAA differ from thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)?
options: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection)
AAA is mostly caused by Marfan's syndrome and a bicuspid aortic valve, the same connective-tissue processes seen in TAA
Both AAA and TAA share an identical degenerative aetiology driven by atherosclerosis and connective-tissue disease
TAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas AAA is congenital, arising from Marfan's and a bicuspid valve
AAA is almost always infective (mycotic), seeding the aortic wall from a distant bacterial focus elsewhere
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory, whereas TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: AAA is predominantly degenerative/inflammatory; TAA has a different aetiology (Marfan's, bicuspid AV, dissection) and is kept separate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: A 68-year-old man is found to have a 5.8 cm AAA on USS. He is asymptomatic. What is the recommended management?
options: Watchful waiting until 8 cm
Annual surveillance USS
Medical management only with beta-blockers
Emergency surgery
Urgent elective repair (EVAR or open) — threshold 5.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Urgent elective repair (EVAR or open) — threshold 5.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: NICE guidelines: elective AAA repair is recommended when diameter ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women). 5.8 cm exceeds threshold — offer EVAR (if anatomy suitable) or open repair. Risk of rupture outweighs operative mortality at this size.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is EVAR and when is it preferred over open repair?
options: EVAR can only be performed under general anaesthesia with full laparotomy exposure of the aorta
EVAR is always the first-line option regardless of aortic neck anatomy or iliac access suitability
EVAR has lower long-term durability than open repair across every patient group and anatomy
Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair — preferred in older/high operative risk patients if anatomy suitable
EVAR cannot be used in a ruptured AAA and is strictly reserved for stable elective cases only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair — preferred in older/high operative risk patients if anatomy suitable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: EVAR = stent-graft deployed via femoral arteries. Lower 30-day mortality than open repair (1% vs 5%). Preferred for older/comorbid patients. However, requires suitable neck anatomy (≥15 mm infrarenal neck, no extreme angulation). Long-term requires annual CT surveillance for endoleaks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the risk of AAA rupture per year for a 5.5 cm aneurysm?
options: Less than 1% per year, even as the diameter increases
~10% per year — increases exponentially above 5.5 cm
Around 50% per year once it reaches 5 cm diameter
It only ruptures once it has grown beyond 7 cm diameter
Rupture risk rises in a linear fashion with diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: ~10% per year — increases exponentially above 5.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Rupture risk: <4 cm ~0.5%/yr; 4–5 cm ~5%/yr; 5–6 cm ~10%/yr; >6 cm ~25%/yr. Risk doubles approximately every 0.5 cm increase. At 5.5 cm, elective repair mortality (~2–5%) is lower than rupture risk, justifying surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What investigation is used to plan EVAR in an elective AAA patient?
options: Duplex ultrasound of the aorta and both iliac vessels to assess anatomy
CT angiography (CTA) of aorta — assesses anatomy, neck length, iliac access
Conventional invasive catheter angiography of the aorta and iliacs
MRI of the aorta with gadolinium contrast for detailed luminal anatomy
A plain supine abdominal X-ray demonstrating aortic wall calcification
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: CT angiography (CTA) of aorta — assesses anatomy, neck length, iliac access
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: CTA is mandatory for EVAR planning: measures aneurysm dimensions, neck length (≥15 mm required), neck angulation, iliac artery diameter and tortuosity. It determines EVAR suitability and guides stent-graft sizing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: Why is diabetes actually protective against AAA formation?
options: Diabetics have consistently higher HDL cholesterol, which protects the aortic wall
Diabetics reliably run lower systemic blood pressures, reducing aortic wall stress
Circulating insulin acts directly on elastin to strengthen the aortic wall matrix
Metformin exerts a direct vasoprotective effect that prevents medial degeneration
Diabetes promotes collagen crosslinking → stiffer aortic wall resistant to dilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Diabetes promotes collagen crosslinking → stiffer aortic wall resistant to dilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Counter-intuitively, diabetes reduces AAA risk. Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) cause collagen crosslinking → stiffer, less compliant aortic wall that resists aneurysmal dilation. This is despite diabetes increasing atherosclerosis risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.question: What is the 5-year survival following AAA rupture compared with elective repair?
options: Elective open surgical repair carries a very high 30-day operative mortality of around 20 to 25%
Ruptured: around 80% survive to discharge; elective repair: only 50% survive the first month
Both ruptured and elective repair carry a broadly similar overall 5-year survival rate of about 60%
Ruptured AAA carries markedly better long-term survival outcomes than planned elective repair
Ruptured: ~50% die before reaching hospital; overall survival <25%. Elective repair: 30-day mortality ~2–5%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.answer: Ruptured: ~50% die before reaching hospital; overall survival <25%. Elective repair: 30-day mortality ~2–5%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Abdominal Ao.explanation: Ruptured AAA: ~50% die before reaching hospital; of those who reach hospital and have surgery, mortality is ~40%; overall survival <25%. This catastrophic prognosis justifies elective repair when diameter reaches 5.5 cm with 2–5% operative mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the defining pathology of aortic dissection?
options: Symmetrical dilatation of all three intact aortic wall layers, forming a true aneurysmal sac
Occlusive thrombosis filling the true aortic lumen, arising on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque
Rupture of an atheromatous plaque within a coronary artery, causing acute thrombotic occlusion
Progressive calcific degeneration of the aortic valve cusps, restricting leaflet opening in systole
A tear in the aortic intima → blood between intima and media → a propagating false lumen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: A tear in the aortic intima → blood between intima and media → a propagating false lumen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Aortic dissection is a tear in the intima allowing blood between intima and media, creating a false lumen that propagates along the aortic wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why is a Type A dissection so time-critical?
options: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery
Mortality is fixed regardless of timing
It always resolves spontaneously
It is managed medically
It only affects the descending aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type A dissection mortality rises ~1–2% per hour without surgery, making it a time-critical emergency; management hinges on Stanford A vs B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Retrograde propagation of a dissection toward the aortic root can cause which complications?
options: Lower limb ischaemia and renal malperfusion from distal spread
Acute iliac artery occlusion causing sudden painful leg ischaemia
Isolated mesenteric ischaemia from superior mesenteric involvement
Paraplegia caused by occlusion of a spinal segmental artery
Aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Retrograde propagation to the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement and cardiac tamponade; anterograde propagation causes limb ischaemia and renal/mesenteric malperfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How are acute and chronic aortic dissection defined?
options: Acute <7 days; chronic >7 days
Acute <14 days; chronic >14 days
Acute <30 days; chronic >30 days
Acute <48 hours; chronic >48 hours
Acute <90 days; chronic >90 days
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Acute <14 days; chronic >14 days
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Acute dissection is <14 days; chronic is >14 days.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which classification matters clinically because it determines surgical vs medical management?
options: DeBakey
Keith-Wagener
Crawford
Stanford
Simon Broome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Stanford
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: The Stanford classification is the clinically important one — it directly determines surgical vs medical management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: A Stanford Type A dissection is defined how, and how is it managed?
options: Distal to left subclavian — medical
Involves the ascending aorta — surgical emergency
Descending only — TEVAR
Arch only — observation
Abdominal aorta — open repair
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Involves the ascending aorta — surgical emergency
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta (± arch/descending) and is a surgical emergency; Type B is distal to the left subclavian and managed medically if uncomplicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which DeBakey types correspond to Stanford A?
options: DeBakey I and II
DeBakey III only
DeBakey II and III
DeBakey IIIa and IIIb
DeBakey I only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: DeBakey I and II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: DeBakey I (ascending + arch + beyond) and II (ascending only) = Stanford A; DeBakey III (descending only) = Stanford B.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the most important modifiable risk factor for aortic dissection, and which surges are especially dangerous?
options: Hypertension — transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting
Hyperlipidaemia — post-prandial triglyceride surges after heavy fatty meals
Diabetes — autonomic catecholamine surges triggered by severe hypoglycaemia
Smoking — transient catecholamine and nicotine spikes with each cigarette
Obesity — repeated pressure surges provoked by episodes of heavy overeating
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Hypertension — transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor; transient surges from cocaine use and heavy weightlifting are especially dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How does a bicuspid aortic valve predispose to dissection?
options: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics
Through turbulent transvalvular flow alone, mechanically eroding the ascending aortic wall
By directly causing systemic hypertension that raises wall stress on the ascending aorta
Through showering of valvular thrombus emboli into the coronary and aortic wall vessels
By accelerating atherosclerosis of the aortic wall only, without any medial weakness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Associated aortopathy — intrinsic media weakness independent of valve haemodynamics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve carries an associated aortopathy with intrinsic media weakness, independent of valve haemodynamics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the cardinal symptom of aortic dissection, and how does it differ from MI?
options: Gradual crushing central chest pain that builds over minutes with exertion, exactly like myocardial infarction
Sharp pleuritic chest pain, worse on inspiration and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward
Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain, maximal at onset (unlike MI which builds)
Burning epigastric pain radiating upward after meals, eased somewhat by antacids and belching
Positional interscapular ache that worsens with movement and eases with rest and simple analgesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Sudden-onset, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest pain, maximal at onset (unlike MI which builds)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: The cardinal symptom is sudden-onset, severe tearing/ripping chest pain that is maximal at onset, unlike MI pain which builds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Where is the pain typically felt in Type A versus Type B dissection?
options: Type A → back; Type B → anterior chest
Type A → anterior chest; Type B → interscapular/back
Both → epigastrium
Type A → neck; Type B → abdomen
Both → left arm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A → anterior chest; Type B → interscapular/back
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type A causes anterior chest pain (ascending aorta); Type B causes interscapular/back pain (descending aorta).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What causes a pulse deficit in aortic dissection?
options: The false lumen occluding a branch — absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse
Chronic atherosclerosis of the peripheral arteries causing gradual narrowing and weak pulses
Cardiac tamponade reducing stroke volume, producing weak and thready peripheral pulses
Aortic regurgitation causing a collapsing pulse from rapid diastolic runoff into the ventricle
Coronary ostium occlusion reducing cardiac output and thereby weakening all peripheral pulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: The false lumen occluding a branch — absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A pulse deficit results from the false lumen occluding a branch, giving an absent or weak carotid/brachial/femoral pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: A >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference in a chest pain patient is the classic discriminating sign of what, and what should be done?
options: MI — give thrombolysis without delay to restore coronary perfusion
Pericarditis — give high-dose NSAIDs with colchicine for symptom relief
PE — start therapeutic anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin
Dissection with subclavian involvement — check both arms in every chest pain
Musculoskeletal chest wall pain — reassure the patient and discharge home
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Dissection with subclavian involvement — check both arms in every chest pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: A >20 mmHg inter-arm BP difference indicates subclavian involvement in dissection — the classic discriminating sign; check both arms in every chest pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why might a new aortic regurgitation murmur appear in aortic dissection?
options: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation
Anterograde dissection extending down toward the iliac arteries
Coronary ostium occlusion by the dissection flap → acute ischaemia
Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery causing cord ischaemia
Renal artery involvement producing malperfusion and hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root → aortic regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Retrograde dissection to the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation, producing a new early diastolic murmur.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Hypotension and tachycardia in a dissection patient should be assumed to be which type until proven otherwise?
options: Type B
Uncomplicated dissection
DeBakey III
Type A
Chronic dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Type A
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Hypotension/tachycardia (from blood loss, cardiac tamponade or severe AR) indicates haemodynamic instability = Type A until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which end-organ effect results from coronary ostium involvement in dissection?
options: Stroke
Paraplegia
Mesenteric ischaemia
AKI
MI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: MI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Coronary ostium involvement causes MI; other malperfusion effects include stroke (carotid), paraplegia (spinal artery), limb ischaemia (iliac/femoral), AKI (renal) and mesenteric ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why must a suspected aortic dissection never be thrombolysed or anticoagulated?
options: Because a dissection almost always seals and resolves spontaneously, so intervention only adds needless bleeding risk
Because it has no haemodynamic effect at all, so anticoagulation is merely wasted rather than being harmful
Because thrombolysis dangerously raises the blood pressure and thereby accelerates propagation of the false lumen
Because it produces sharp pleuritic pain that anticoagulation and thrombolysis characteristically make far worse
Because dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics it — anticoagulation/thrombolysis is fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Because dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics it — anticoagulation/thrombolysis is fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Dissection can cause MI via coronary involvement and mimics ACS, but the key danger is that thrombolysis/anticoagulation causes catastrophic haemorrhage into the false lumen (rupture, tamponade, exsanguination) — rapidly fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How does pericarditis differ from aortic dissection in its pain character?
options: Sudden tearing chest pain maximal at the very onset, radiating through to the interscapular region
Sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, no tearing quality
Chest pain with a measurable inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference of more than 20 mmHg
Chest pain accompanied by an obvious pulse deficit in one carotid, brachial or femoral artery
Severe chest pain radiating downward to the groin as the process extends toward the iliac vessels
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Sharp positional chest pain, pleuritic, relieved by leaning forward, no tearing quality
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Pericarditis gives sharp positional, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward with no tearing quality, unlike dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the safety rule regarding dissection and anticoagulation for suspected MI/PE?
options: Always anticoagulate immediately with heparin, since prompt clot prevention outweighs any small dissection risk in chest pain
Give aspirin and discharge the patient home, arranging routine outpatient follow-up imaging over the next several weeks
Thrombolyse straight away and simply observe, as reperfusion is the priority and dissection features can be reviewed later
Exclude dissection first — CT angiogram if any dissection features (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit)
Anticoagulate unless the resting ECG is entirely normal, treating a clean tracing as enough to exclude a dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Exclude dissection first — CT angiogram if any dissection features (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Exclude dissection before anticoagulating for suspected MI/PE — get a CT angiogram first if any dissection features are present (tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the role of ECG in aortic dissection?
options: It is diagnostic of dissection, showing a characteristic pattern of diffuse ST depression across all precordial leads
Often normal or non-specific — used to exclude/identify MI; a normal ECG in severe chest pain raises dissection
It directly quantifies the size of the false lumen and the length of intimal flap propagation along the aorta
It measures the inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference by comparing voltages recorded from each limb lead
It reliably confirms the Stanford type by localising the entry tear to the ascending or descending aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Often normal or non-specific — used to exclude/identify MI; a normal ECG in severe chest pain raises dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: The ECG is often normal or non-specific and is used to exclude/identify MI; a normal ECG in severe chest pain actually raises suspicion of dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the gold-standard/first-line definitive investigation for aortic dissection?
options: CXR
ECG
CT angiogram
Transthoracic echo
Troponin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: CT angiogram
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: CT angiogram is the gold-standard first-line definitive investigation — it shows the intimal flap, true/false lumen, extent and branch vessel involvement, used for classification and surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: When is TOE preferred in aortic dissection?
options: For routine outpatient surveillance of a stable chronic dissection, replacing repeat CT to spare radiation exposure
To exclude a pulmonary embolism by directly visualising thrombus within the main and lobar pulmonary artery branches
To measure renal function and quantify the degree of kidney malperfusion caused by extension into the renal arteries
If the patient is too unstable for CT, or to assess aortic valve/root involvement — sensitive for proximal dissection
For long-term follow-up imaging only, since it is far too slow and invasive to be of any value in the acute setting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: If the patient is too unstable for CT, or to assess aortic valve/root involvement — sensitive for proximal dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: TOE is used if the patient is too unstable for CT or to assess aortic valve/root involvement; it is sensitive for proximal dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the key caveat about CXR findings in aortic dissection?
options: A completely normal chest X-ray reliably excludes dissection and removes the need for CT angiography
The chest X-ray is diagnostic of dissection, directly showing the intimal flap and the false lumen
Widened mediastinum is classic, but the CXR may be normal — it does not exclude dissection
The chest X-ray always demonstrates a left-sided pleural effusion from leakage of blood into the pleura
The chest X-ray reliably replaces CT angiography as the definitive confirmatory test for dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Widened mediastinum is classic, but the CXR may be normal — it does not exclude dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: CXR may show a widened mediastinum, double/irregular aortic contour and pleural effusion, but it may be normal and does not exclude dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the target SBP in aortic dissection, and what is the rationale?
options: 140–160 mmHg — kept high deliberately to maintain vital organ perfusion pressure
No specific target is needed, as blood pressure barely affects propagation
<90 mmHg — permissive hypotension to minimise any flow across the intimal tear
160–180 mmHg — kept elevated to prevent branch-vessel malperfusion downstream
100–120 mmHg — reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) and limit propagation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: 100–120 mmHg — reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) and limit propagation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Target SBP 100–120 mmHg to reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) and limit propagation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the first-line agent for BP and HR control in dissection, and why?
options: IV nitroprusside — a pure arterial vasodilator that rapidly drops afterload
Oral ramipril — an ACE inhibitor giving sustained afterload reduction
Oral amlodipine — a long-acting calcium channel blocker for gradual control
IV furosemide — a loop diuretic reducing preload through brisk diuresis
IV labetalol (beta-blocker) — lowers both BP and HR simultaneously
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: IV labetalol (beta-blocker) — lowers both BP and HR simultaneously
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: IV labetalol is first-line because it lowers both BP and HR simultaneously; an IV calcium channel blocker (diltiazem/verapamil) is used if a beta-blocker is contraindicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Why must vasodilators not be used alone in aortic dissection?
options: They lower the blood pressure far too slowly to control an acute dissection safely
They increase HR → worsen shear stress — always cover with a beta-blocker first
They cause dangerous hyperkalaemia by shifting potassium out of the vascular cells
They precipitate cardiac tamponade by rupturing the already weakened aortic root
They have essentially no effect on blood pressure once the false lumen is expanding
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: They increase HR → worsen shear stress — always cover with a beta-blocker first
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Vasodilators alone (e.g. nitroprusside) increase HR and worsen shear stress, so always cover with a beta-blocker first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the surgical management of a Stanford A dissection?
options: TEVAR stent-graft deployed across the descending thoracic aorta to seal the entry tear and exclude the false lumen
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty of the aortic valve to relieve the associated regurgitation and root dilatation
Bed rest with an IV beta-blocker and strict blood pressure control, reserving any surgery for later complications
Emergency sternotomy + excision of ascending aorta, Dacron graft ± arch reconstruction; Bentall if root involved
Conservative management with tight BP control and serial surveillance imaging at one, three and twelve months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Emergency sternotomy + excision of ascending aorta, Dacron graft ± arch reconstruction; Bentall if root involved
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Stanford A is treated with emergency sternotomy and excision of the ascending aorta, synthetic Dacron graft ± arch reconstruction, and a Bentall procedure if the root is involved; untreated mortality is ~1–2%/hour.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: How is an uncomplicated Stanford B dissection managed?
options: Emergency median sternotomy with excision of the affected aorta and interposition of a Dacron graft as the immediate first step
Systemic thrombolysis to dissolve the false-lumen thrombus, followed by therapeutic anticoagulation to keep the true lumen patent
Immediate TEVAR stent-grafting for every case, deploying an endovascular stent to cover the entry tear and exclude the false lumen
Bed rest + strict BP control, IV beta-blocker first-line, then oral antihypertensives, surveillance imaging at 1, 3, 12 months
A Bentall procedure combining composite aortic root and valve replacement with reimplantation of both coronary artery ostia together
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Bed rest + strict BP control, IV beta-blocker first-line, then oral antihypertensives, surveillance imaging at 1, 3, 12 months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Uncomplicated Type B is managed medically: bed rest, strict BP control, IV beta-blocker first-line, transition to oral antihypertensives, and surveillance imaging at 1, 3, 12 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the commonest long-term complication of a Type B dissection?
options: Cardiac tamponade
Stroke
Acute aortic regurgitation
MI
Aneurysm formation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Aneurysm formation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Aneurysm formation is the commonest long-term complication of a Type B (anterograde + distal) dissection; Type A complications include tamponade, acute AR, MI, stroke and death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: A 55-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. His BP is 170/100 in the right arm and 135/85 in the left. CXR shows widened mediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
options: Aortic aneurysm rupture
STEMI
Pulmonary embolism
Aortic dissection (Type A)
Oesophageal rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Aortic dissection (type A)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Classic aortic dissection: sudden tearing/ripping chest pain, hypertension, blood pressure differential between arms (>20 mmHg — subclavian involvement), widened mediastinum on CXR. Type A (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is the initial medical management target for Type B aortic dissection?
options: Immediate systemic anticoagulation with a therapeutic intravenous heparin infusion
Systolic BP below 180 mmHg alone, with no specific heart rate target required
Systolic BP below 100 mmHg alone, accepting permissive hypotension without rate control
Heart rate <60 bpm and systolic BP 100–120 mmHg — IV labetalol (beta-blocker first)
Immediate TEVAR stent-grafting of the descending aorta as the initial intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Heart rate <60 bpm and systolic BP <120 mmHg — IV labetalol (beta-blocker first)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type B dissection: medical management targets HR <60 (reduces aortic wall stress) and SBP 100–120 mmHg. IV labetalol (alpha+beta blocker) is first-line. Add sodium nitroprusside if needed. Avoid pure vasodilators without beta-blockade (reflex tachycardia worsens shear stress).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What neurological complication can occur with Type A aortic dissection?
options: Only a cauda equina syndrome causing saddle anaesthesia and acute urinary retention
Only a symmetrical peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy affecting the distal limbs
Only an isolated Horner syndrome from compression of the cervical sympathetic chain
An isolated cerebellar haemorrhage producing acute ataxia, vertigo and nystagmus
Stroke (carotid artery involvement) or spinal cord ischaemia (intercostal artery occlusion)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Stroke (carotid artery involvement) or spinal cord ischaemia (intercostal artery occlusion)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Type A dissection extending to the arch can occlude carotid arteries → stroke (15%). Paraplegia occurs from intercostal artery occlusion (spinal cord ischaemia) — more common in extensive Type B/DeBakey I dissection or TEVAR procedures. Coronary involvement causes MI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: Which imaging finding on CXR is most suggestive of aortic dissection?
options: Pulmonary oedema
Widened mediastinum (>8 cm on PA CXR)
Elevated left hemi-diaphragm
Hilar lymphadenopathy
Pleural effusion alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Widened mediastinum (>8 cm on PA CXR)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: Widened mediastinum (>8 cm on PA CXR at T4 level) is the classic CXR finding in aortic dissection. Also: deviation of trachea/oesophagus, aortic knuckle blurring, left pleural effusion (haemothorax). CXR is often normal — CT is mandatory if clinical suspicion exists.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What is TEVAR and when is it used for aortic dissection?
options: A less invasive endovascular alternative to open sternotomy for a Stanford Type A ascending dissection
The first-line definitive treatment for every aortic dissection, whether Stanford Type A or Type B
Thoracic EVAR — stent-graft for complicated Type B dissection (malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion)
A technique reserved solely for infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and never for any dissection
A procedure reserved only for stable chronic dissections, never used in the acute presenting phase
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Thoracic EVAR — stent-graft for complicated Type B dissection (malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: TEVAR (thoracic EVAR) is used for complicated Type B dissection: malperfusion syndrome (visceral/limb ischaemia), rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain, or uncontrolled hypertension. Covers the primary tear to redirect flow into the true lumen and promote false lumen thrombosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.question: What predisposing conditions increase risk of aortic dissection in young patients?
options: Premature atherosclerosis of the aortic wall driven by hyperlipidaemia and smoking
Poorly controlled essential hypertension acting as the sole risk factor in the young
Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve
Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with progressive left ventricular systolic impairment
Infective endocarditis of the aortic valve seeding septic emboli into the aortic wall
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.answer: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Disse.explanation: In young patients, aortic dissection is associated with connective tissue diseases: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation, aortic root dilation), Ehlers-Danlos (type IV, vascular subtype), bicuspid aortic valve, and Turner syndrome. These cause medial degeneration independent of atherosclerosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How is bradycardia defined, and what is the most clinically important distinction?
options: HR <50 bpm; acute vs chronic
HR <40 bpm; nodal vs infranodal
HR <60 bpm; symptomatic vs incidental
HR <60 bpm; narrow vs broad QRS
HR <100 bpm; sinus vs junctional
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: HR <60 bpm; symptomatic vs incidental
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Bradycardia is HR <60 bpm. The key clinical distinction is symptomatic (haemodynamic compromise → needs treatment) vs incidental (e.g. athlete or sleep → physiologically normal).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the central organising principle for understanding bradycardias and heart block?
options: The heart rate determines everything
The QRS axis determines management
The patient's age determines the prognosis
The anatomical level of the block determines everything
The P-wave morphology determines the cause
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The anatomical level of the block determines everything
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The anatomical level of the block determines the escape rate, QRS width, escape reliability, response to atropine, and whether pacing is needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What are the typical features of a block at the SA node level?
options: Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective
Escape ~60 bpm, narrow QRS, atropine works
Junctional escape 40–60 bpm, broad QRS, pacing mandatory
No escape rhythm, atropine ineffective
Escape ~30 bpm, narrow QRS, atropine works
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Escape ~60 bpm, narrow QRS, atropine works
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: SA node-level problems (sinus bradycardia, sick sinus) have an escape ~60 bpm, narrow QRS, and respond to atropine.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: An infranodal (His-Purkinje) block produces which set of features?
options: Escape ~60 bpm, narrow QRS, atropine works
Junctional escape 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, usually benign
Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective — must pace
Escape ~50 bpm, narrow QRS, responds to atropine
No bradycardia, just a delay
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, atropine ineffective — must pace
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Infranodal blocks (Mobitz II, CHB with broad escape) give a ventricular escape <40 bpm, broad QRS, and atropine is ineffective — the patient must be paced.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which statement captures the key principle linking the level of block to the escape rhythm?
options: The lower the block, the faster and narrower the escape — and the more stable and reliable it is
The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape — and the less reliable it is
The level of block has no effect at all on the escape rate, width, or its reliability
Higher blocks always need immediate permanent pacing regardless of the escape rhythm present
The escape rate is always fixed at exactly 60 bpm regardless of the level of block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape — and the less reliable it is
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The lower the block, the slower, broader and less reliable the escape rhythm becomes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why is atropine ineffective in an infranodal block?
options: The block sits too high in the conduction system for atropine to physically reach and reverse it
Atropine reliably increases the block ratio in all patients by slowing AV nodal conduction
Atropine only works when the patient is in normal sinus rhythm and never during any block
Infranodal blocks are vagally mediated only at night, so atropine helps during daytime hours
Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it; an infranodal block is below the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Atropine acts on the AV node, not below it; an infranodal block is below the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic acting on the vagally-innervated AV node. An infranodal block is below the AV node, so atropine cannot improve conduction there — pacing is required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What defines sinus bradycardia on the ECG?
options: Absent P waves with an irregular baseline
A broad QRS escape rhythm
P waves dissociated from the QRS
Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat
HR <60 bpm with normal-morphology P waves preceding every QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: HR <60 bpm with normal-morphology P waves preceding every QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: In sinus bradycardia the SA node fires (just slowly): HR <60 bpm with normal P waves preceding every QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which of the following is a DRUG cause of sinus bradycardia?
options: Salbutamol, a beta-2 agonist raising the rate
Dobutamine, a beta-1 agonist raising the rate
Adrenaline, a catecholamine speeding the heart
Atropine, an antimuscarinic speeding the heart
Rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Drug causes include beta-blockers, digoxin, rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem), and amiodarone/lithium.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient with raised intracranial pressure has bradycardia, hypertension and irregular respirations. What is this triad called?
options: Beck's triad
Charcot's triad
Virchow's triad
Cushing's reflex
Brady-tachy syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Cushing's reflex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Cushing's reflex is the response to raised ICP, producing bradycardia, hypertension and irregular respirations.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which systemic condition is a recognised cause of sinus bradycardia?
options: Hyperthyroidism
Sepsis
Hypercalcaemia
Anaemia
Hypothyroidism (myxoedema)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Hypothyroidism (myxoedema)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Systemic causes of sinus bradycardia include hypothyroidism (myxoedema), hypothermia, raised ICP (Cushing's reflex) and cholestasis (bile salts are vagotonic on the SA node).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why does an inferior MI commonly cause sinus bradycardia?
options: The RCA supplies the SA node in ~60% and inferior MI is vagally mediated
The LAD supplies the SA node in most people, so inferior MI directly infarcts it
Inferior MI always damages the His-Purkinje system, giving a broad escape
It causes acute hyperkalaemia which suppresses the sinus node and slows the rate
The circumflex supplies the AV node exclusively, so any inferior MI blocks it
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: The RCA supplies the SA node in ~60% and inferior MI is vagally mediated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The right coronary artery supplies the SA node in ~60% of people, and inferior MI is also vagally mediated, so RCA-territory infarction frequently causes bradycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the most common cause of sick sinus syndrome?
options: Acute viral myocarditis inflaming the sinus node tissue
Digoxin toxicity chronically poisoning the sinus node
Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node (elderly)
Hyperthyroidism driving degeneration of the sinus node
Congenital heart disease disrupting sinus node development
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node (elderly)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome is most commonly due to idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node, typically in elderly patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What characterises brady-tachy syndrome?
options: Fixed complete heart block with a stable junctional escape
AV dissociation with a slow broad ventricular escape rhythm
Persistent inappropriate sinus tachycardia without any pauses
Progressive PR lengthening with intermittently dropped beats
Alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Brady-tachy syndrome (a form of sick sinus syndrome) features alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF/flutter; treating the tachy can worsen the brady.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the therapeutic dilemma in brady-tachy syndrome, and how is it resolved?
options: Atropine worsens the tachycardic episodes, so give a beta-blocker first and the bradycardia settles
There is no safe treatment because every option worsens one arm of the syndrome, so only observe closely
Anticoagulation for the AF is what causes the bradycardia, so stop the warfarin first and it is safe
Pacing worsens the paroxysmal AF, so ablate the atrial focus first and a pacemaker becomes unnecessary
Antiarrhythmics for the AF worsen the bradycardia; pace first, then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Antiarrhythmics for the AF worsen the bradycardia; pace first, then it is safe to use antiarrhythmics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Antiarrhythmics used to control the AF worsen the bradycardia, so the approach is to pace first, after which antiarrhythmics can be used safely. Anticoagulation is given for the AF component.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How is symptomatic sick sinus syndrome managed when the cause is not reversible?
options: Lifelong atropine
Observation only
Beta-blockade
Catheter ablation of the SA node
A permanent pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: A permanent pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Management is to treat any reversible cause (stop offending drugs, replace thyroid hormone) and give atropine for acute episodes; a permanent pacemaker is implanted if symptomatic and the cause is not reversible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which ECG morphology is characteristic of RBBB?
options: A deep S (dominant downward deflection) in V1
ST elevation in V1–V3
A delta wave with short PR
Sawtooth waves in II/III/aVF
An RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: An RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: RBBB shows an RSR' ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in V6. LBBB, by contrast, shows a deep S in V1 and a broad/notched R in V6.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: An incidental finding of sinus bradycardia at 52 bpm in a well-trained marathon runner with no symptoms should be managed how?
options: No treatment — it is physiologically normal (enhanced vagal tone)
Atropine immediately to restore a normal resting heart rate
Urgent permanent pacemaker insertion to prevent sudden collapse
Start an isoprenaline infusion to chronotropically drive the rate
Admit for urgent temporary transvenous pacing wire insertion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: No treatment — it is physiologically normal (enhanced vagal tone)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Resting bradycardia is expected in athletes (enhanced vagal tone) and during sleep; incidental, asymptomatic bradycardia needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Beyond the degree of block, what is the key discriminator for classifying AV blocks?
options: The patient's absolute resting heart rate measured on the ECG
Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal
The P-wave axis and its morphology seen across the six limb leads
The presence or absence of associated ischaemic chest pain
The corrected QT interval measured on the surface ECG tracing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The nodal-vs-infranodal location determines the escape rhythm, atropine response and need for pacing — not just the degree of block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What defines first-degree AV block, and how is it managed?
options: Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat; pacemaker
Complete P–QRS dissociation; pacemaker
Fixed PR with sudden dropped beats; pacemaker
PR >200 ms, fixed, every P conducts; benign, no treatment
Shortened PR with a delta wave; ablation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: PR >200 ms, fixed, every P conducts; benign, no treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-degree AV block is a fixed PR >200 ms with every P wave conducting. It is at the AV node level, benign, and needs no treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which ECG pattern describes Mobitz I (Wenckebach)?
options: Fixed unchanging PR interval with an abrupt, unheralded dropped QRS
Complete dissociation of P waves from the QRS with an escape rhythm
Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets
A prolonged PR over 200 ms but with every single beat still conducting
A short PR interval with a slurred delta-wave upstroke on the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle resets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR lengthening until a beat is dropped, then resets. It is AV nodal, narrow QRS, and usually benign.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient has a fixed PR interval with sudden, unheralded dropped QRS complexes and a broad QRS. What is the diagnosis and key concern?
options: Mobitz I Wenckebach — a benign nodal block; simply monitor with no pacemaker needed at all
Sinus bradycardia — simply identify and treat the underlying reversible cause, no pacing needed
First-degree AV block — entirely benign, needs no treatment and never progresses further
Mobitz II — infranodal, high risk of progression to complete heart block; needs a pacemaker
Complete third-degree heart block — already maximal, so no further progression is possible now
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II — infranodal, high risk of progression to complete heart block; needs a pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden dropped QRS, broad QRS) is infranodal, carries a high risk of progression to CHB, and requires a pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the defining ECG feature of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: P waves and QRS complexes fully dissociated, ventricles driven by an escape rhythm
Progressive PR lengthening beat by beat until a single QRS complex is finally dropped
A fixed unchanging PR interval with occasional sudden non-conducted dropped beats
A prolonged PR over 200 ms in which every P wave still conducts through to a QRS
A slurred delta wave with an abnormally short PR interval and a wide QRS complex
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: P waves and QRS complexes fully dissociated, ventricles driven by an escape rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: In CHB the atria and ventricles are fully dissociated; ventricular output depends on an escape rhythm. A broad QRS escape indicates an unreliable infranodal origin, and a pacemaker is mandatory.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which AV block carries NO asystole risk and needs no treatment?
options: Mobitz II
First-degree block
Complete heart block
Mobitz I with a broad escape
Bifascicular block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: First-degree block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-degree block has no dropped beats, no asystole risk, and needs no treatment. Mobitz II and CHB (broad escape) carry high asystole risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In which AV block is atropine clearly useful?
options: Mobitz II
Complete heart block with a broad escape
Trifascicular block
Infranodal block of any type
Mobitz I
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz I
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine works at the AV node, so it is useful in Mobitz I (AV nodal). It is ineffective in Mobitz II and CHB with a broad (infranodal) escape; in CHB it helps only with a narrow escape acutely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why may atropine paradoxically worsen the block ratio in an infranodal (e.g. Mobitz II) block?
options: It directly damages and inflames the His-Purkinje fibres, so conduction through the diseased infranodal tissue deteriorates further
It paradoxically slows the sinus node rather than speeding it, so fewer atrial impulses arrive and the block ratio appears worse
It causes an acute rise in serum potassium, and the resulting hyperkalaemia depresses infranodal conduction so more impulses block
It increases the atrial rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so more are blocked
It triggers short runs of ventricular fibrillation in the diseased His-Purkinje tissue, disrupting the escape and worsening the block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It increases the atrial rate, but the diseased infranodal tissue cannot conduct the extra impulses, so more are blocked
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine raises the atrial (sinus) rate, but infranodal tissue cannot conduct the additional impulses, so a greater proportion are blocked, worsening the block ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In complete heart block, a NARROW escape (His bundle) has which features?
options: Rate under 40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, atropine ineffective, and it demands urgent permanent pacing
Rate around 100 bpm, narrow QRS, entirely stable and reliable, so pacing is never needed under any circumstances
No escape rhythm arises at all, so the ventricles stay in asystole and the patient cannot survive without pacing
Rate 50–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, often inferior MI/reversible, may respond to atropine acutely
Rate under 30 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, but it responds well to atropine given acutely at the bedside
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate 50–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, often inferior MI/reversible, may respond to atropine acutely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A His-bundle (narrow) escape is 50–60 bpm with a narrow QRS, more reliable, often from inferior MI/a reversible cause, and may respond to IV atropine acutely — though it usually still needs permanent pacing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A BROAD escape (His-Purkinje) in complete heart block is characterised by what, and what does it mandate?
options: Rate <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, causes Stokes-Adams attacks; permanent pacemaker mandatory
Rate 50–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable and stable, so simple observation on a monitored ward suffices
Rate around 70 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable, and it responds fully to atropine alone with no pacing needed
No significant bradycardia develops, the escape keeps pace, so simple reassurance and discharge suffice
Rate under 40 bpm but with a narrow QRS, which responds promptly to atropine so no pacemaker is needed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rate <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable, causes Stokes-Adams attacks; permanent pacemaker mandatory
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A His-Purkinje (broad) escape is <40 bpm, broad QRS, unreliable (may fail without warning), causes Stokes-Adams attacks, is atropine-ineffective, and mandates a permanent pacemaker.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is a Stokes-Adams attack?
options: A prolonged epileptic seizure with tonic-clonic movements followed by a long period of post-ictal drowsiness and confusion
A vasovagal faint triggered by prolonged standing, with slow onset, sweating and nausea, and a gradual recovery after
Central crushing ischaemic chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest
A sudden LOC from CHB due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion
A transient ischaemic attack causing focal neurological deficit and limb weakness that fully resolves within a day
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: A sudden LOC from CHB due to transient asystole or VT, with rapid complete recovery and no post-ictal confusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: A Stokes-Adams attack is sudden loss of consciousness from CHB (transient asystole or VT) with rapid complete recovery; the patient goes pale then flushes as circulation restores.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which features help distinguish a Stokes-Adams attack from an epileptic seizure?
options: Prolonged post-ictal drowsiness and confusion for many minutes, with lateral tongue-biting and aching limb muscles
Urinary incontinence during the episode and a slow, prolonged recovery over minutes with lingering drowsiness
An aura of a rising epigastric sensation or déjà vu preceding the collapse, as seen in temporal lobe seizures
Rapid complete recovery, no post-ictal confusion, no tongue-biting, no incontinence, with pallor then flushing
Lateral tongue-biting with rhythmic tonic-clonic limb-jerking and cyanosis during the episode rather than pallor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Rapid complete recovery, no post-ictal confusion, no tongue-biting, no incontinence, with pallor then flushing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Stokes-Adams attacks recover rapidly and completely without post-ictal confusion, tongue-biting or incontinence, with characteristic pallor then flushing — distinguishing them from seizures.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Is bundle branch block a bradycardia, and what produces its wide QRS?
options: Yes; the SA node discharges too slowly, producing a sinus bradycardia that widens the QRS as conduction lags
Yes; a slow infranodal ventricular escape rhythm takes over, giving both the bradycardia and the broad QRS
No — it is a conduction delay; the AV node and His bundle conduct normally but the delay is in one bundle branch
No — it results from AV dissociation, with atria and ventricles beating independently and widening the QRS
