Yes; it invariably coexists with complete heart block, so the ventricular rate is slow and the QRS is broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: No — it is a conduction delay; the AV node and His bundle conduct normally but the delay is in one bundle branch
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: BBB is a conduction delay, not a bradycardia. The AV node and His bundle conduct normally; the delay in one bundle branch produces a wide QRS (>120 ms) with characteristic morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Using the WiLLiAM mnemonic, which morphology indicates LBBB?
options: M in V1, W in V6
W in V1 (deep QS/rS), M in V5/V6
RSR' in V1, slurred S in V6
Delta wave in V1
Sawtooth waves in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: W in V1 (deep QS/rS), M in V5/V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: LBBB = WiLLiAM: a W in V1 (deep QS or rS) and an M in V5/V6 (broad notched R), with QRS >120 ms and left axis deviation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which statement about LBBB is correct?
options: It is always pathological (causes include AS, HTN, IHD, cardiomyopathy); new LBBB with chest pain is a STEMI equivalent
It is usually a benign normal variant seen in fit young athletes and needs no further cardiac investigation
It is best treated with an urgent permanent pacemaker in all cases to prevent progression to complete heart block
It produces a short PR interval and a slurred delta wave from accessory-pathway pre-excitation of the ventricle
It can be a normal variant in healthy young people and, unlike RBBB, carries no link with structural heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It is always pathological (causes include AS, HTN, IHD, cardiomyopathy); new LBBB with chest pain is a STEMI equivalent
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: LBBB is always pathological. New LBBB with chest pain is treated as a STEMI equivalent (primary PCI). RBBB, by contrast, can be a normal variant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Using the MoRRoW mnemonic, which morphology indicates RBBB, and what is its significance?
options: W in V1 and M in V6 (the opposite pattern); always pathological and requiring a pacemaker
Sawtooth flutter waves in V1 indicating underlying atrial flutter with the block
Deep S in V1 with a broad slurred R in V6; always pathological and never a normal variant
A delta wave in V1 indicating ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway
M in V1 (RSR' 'rabbit ears'), W in V5/V6; can be a normal variant in young people
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: M in V1 (RSR' 'rabbit ears'), W in V5/V6; can be a normal variant in young people
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: RBBB = MoRRoW: an M in V1 (RSR') and a W in V5/V6 (broad slurred S). It can be a normal variant in young people; other causes include PE (acute RV strain), RVH and congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient presents with chest pain and a new left bundle branch block. How should this be managed?
options: Reassure the patient and discharge home with routine GP follow-up
Insert a permanent pacemaker urgently to restore conduction
Treat as a STEMI equivalent — activate the primary PCI pathway
Give IV atropine 500 mcg to reverse the conduction block
Treat as Mobitz II block and arrange transcutaneous pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Treat as a STEMI equivalent — activate the primary PCI pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: New LBBB with chest pain is a STEMI equivalent and warrants the primary PCI (PPCI) pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which of the following is one of the four adverse features signifying haemodynamic instability in bradycardia?
options: Palpitations with an intermittent fluttering sensation in the chest
Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion)
Mild dizziness only on standing quickly, resolving within seconds
A resting heart rate of 58 bpm noted incidentally on the monitor
An incidental ECG finding in an otherwise well, asymptomatic patient
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Shock (hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, cold extremities, confusion)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The four adverse features are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and heart failure — any of these means the patient is unstable and needs immediate treatment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which is one of the four high-risk-of-asystole situations warranting aggressive treatment even if the patient is currently stable?
options: First-degree AV block
An isolated RBBB
Sinus bradycardia at 55 bpm
Mobitz I
Mobitz II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: The four high-risk situations are recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete heart block with a broad QRS, and ventricular pauses >3 seconds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What does Step 1 (stabilise) of the peri-arrest bradycardia algorithm involve?
options: Immediate insertion of a permanent transvenous pacemaker before any other assessment or investigation
ABCDE assessment, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, monitoring, and identifying/treating reversible causes
Give atropine 3 mg IV as a single large bolus dose first, before any assessment or monitoring
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J to restore a normal sinus rhythm and rate
Empirical IV glucagon for all patients regardless of the underlying cause of the bradycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: ABCDE assessment, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, monitoring, and identifying/treating reversible causes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Step 1 is to stabilise: ABCDE, oxygen, IV access, 12-lead ECG, continuous monitoring, and treating reversible causes (electrolytes, hypoxia, hypothermia, drugs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: If adverse features are present in bradycardia, what is the first-line drug, dose and maximum?
options: Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus repeated as needed, with no maximum dose
Atropine 3 mg IV given once as a single large one-off bolus dose
Isoprenaline 5 mcg/min IV infusion, titrated to rate with no maximum
Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg
Glucagon 10 mg slow IV bolus followed by a maintenance infusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 min to a maximum of 3 mg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: First-line is atropine 500 mcg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes up to a maximum total of 3 mg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In which scenarios is atropine ineffective in bradycardia?
options: Sinus bradycardia and Mobitz I, where the block is infranodal and unresponsive to vagal blockade
All bradycardias respond reliably to atropine because it blocks the vagus at the AV node
First-degree AV block, an infranodal delay that atropine cannot overcome once established
Drug-induced bradycardia alone, such as beta-blocker toxicity, which never responds to atropine
Mobitz II, CHB, and a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II, CHB, and a broad escape (all infranodal — below the vagally-innervated AV node)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic acting on the AV node, so it is ineffective for infranodal problems (Mobitz II, CHB, broad escape), which sit below the vagally-innervated AV node.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: A patient with refractory bradycardia from a beta-blocker overdose is not responding to atropine and pacing. What is the specific antidote?
options: Glucagon
Calcium gluconate
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Sodium bicarbonate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Glucagon
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Glucagon is the specific antidote for beta-blocker and CCB overdose causing bradycardia when atropine and pacing are insufficient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: If atropine gives an inadequate response, which is a recognised interim escalation measure?
options: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J under sedation
Rapid IV adenosine 6 mg bolus to restore the rate
Immediate surgical implantation of a permanent ICD device
High-dose intravenous beta-blocker infusion therapy
Transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Interim measures include isoprenaline, adrenaline, aminophylline, transcutaneous pacing (a painful bridge needing sedation), and glucagon for BB/CCB overdose.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How does transvenous pacing compare with transcutaneous pacing?
options: Transcutaneous pacing is more reliable and definitive, giving consistent capture without needing venous access
Transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV) is more reliable; both are bridges to a permanent device
They are equally reliable, so either can be chosen as the definitive long-term pacing method for the patient
Transvenous pacing is reserved only for cardiac arrest and has no role in peri-arrest bradycardia management
Transcutaneous pacing is painless, well tolerated, and the preferred option for long-term definitive pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Transvenous (pacing wire via subclavian/femoral to the RV) is more reliable; both are bridges to a permanent device
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Transvenous pacing (a wire via the subclavian/femoral/IJV to the RV) is more reliable than transcutaneous pacing; both are temporary bridges to a permanent device.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: In a bradycardic patient with NO adverse features, how is management decided?
options: Always insert a permanent pacemaker urgently, since any bradycardia without adverse features still progresses to arrest
Give IV atropine 500 mcg regardless of the rhythm, as it reliably restores conduction in every type of bradycardia
Assess asystole risk: high (Mobitz II, CHB+broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable; low → observe and monitor
Discharge the patient immediately once symptoms settle, as the absence of adverse features excludes any asystole risk
Start an IV glucagon infusion empirically in all such patients to protect against progression to complete heart block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Assess asystole risk: high (Mobitz II, CHB+broad QRS, pauses >3s, recent asystole) → treat as unstable; low → observe and monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Without adverse features, asystole risk is assessed: high-risk patients are treated as unstable, while low-risk patients are observed and monitored with regular review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Which is a recognised indication for a permanent pacemaker?
options: First-degree AV block
Sinus bradycardia in an athlete
Asymptomatic RBBB
Mobitz II AV block
Mobitz I in a young patient
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Mobitz II AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Indications include symptomatic sinus bradycardia (reversible causes excluded), sick sinus syndrome, Mobitz II, complete (3rd-degree) HB, symptomatic bifascicular/trifascicular block, and recurrent Stokes-Adams attacks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: What is the difference between a VVI and a DDD pacemaker?
options: VVI paces both the atrium and ventricle, whereas DDD is a single-lead device that paces only the ventricle
They are functionally identical devices, differing only in the manufacturer's naming convention for the leads
VVI paces/senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (atrial kick)
DDD is a temporary external device only, used as a short-term bridge until a VVI system can be implanted
VVI is a dual-chamber system maintaining AV synchrony, whereas DDD paces only the single ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: VVI paces/senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, maintaining AV synchrony (atrial kick)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: VVI paces and senses the ventricle only; DDD paces both atrium and ventricle, preserving AV synchrony (the atrial kick) — important in impaired LV function.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why is a permanent pacemaker indicated in Mobitz II regardless of symptoms?
options: It carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block
It always precipitates immediate cardiac arrest within minutes
Atropine permanently cures the underlying conduction defect
It is a benign normal variant needing only routine monitoring
It occurs only in young endurance athletes and is benign
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Mobitz II (fixed PR then sudden dropped beat) has a high risk of progressing to CHB, so a permanent pacemaker is indicated even when asymptomatic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: How does complete heart block from an ANTERIOR MI compare with that from an INFERIOR MI?
options: Anterior MI = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing, worse prognosis; inferior = AV nodal, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine
Anterior MI produces a narrow, reliable junctional escape near 50 bpm that responds well to atropine, whereas inferior MI causes a broad, unreliable ventricular escape needing urgent pacing
Both produce identical narrow-complex escape rhythms near 50 bpm, are always transient, and reliably respond to atropine without ever requiring temporary or permanent pacing
Inferior MI causes a His-Purkinje block with a broad unreliable escape always needing urgent pacing, whereas anterior MI causes a benign AV nodal block that resolves spontaneously

Neither an anterior nor an inferior MI ever causes heart block, since the coronary arteries supplying both the AV node and the His-Purkinje conduction system remain unaffected by an acute myocardial infarction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: Anterior MI = His-Purkinje level, broad QRS, unreliable escape 30–40 bpm → urgent pacing, worse prognosis; inferior = AV nodal, narrow QRS, usually transient, often responds to atropine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Anterior MI damages the His-Purkinje system (broad, unreliable escape → urgent pacing, worse prognosis), while inferior MI affects the AV node (narrow, usually transient block that often responds to atropine and resolves with reperfusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.question: Why is transcutaneous pacing used only as a bridge rather than a definitive treatment?
options: It is unreliable and ineffective, rarely achieving electrical capture even at maximum output settings
It frequently triggers ventricular fibrillation, so it is abandoned in favour of transvenous pacing
It is fast but painful and needs sedation, so it is used only until a more definitive measure is available
It is a permanent implanted system that cannot easily be removed once the pads are attached
It only captures in narrow-complex escape rhythms and always fails whenever the QRS complex is broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.answer: It is fast but painful and needs sedation, so it is used only until a more definitive measure is available
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias.explanation: Transcutaneous pacing (defibrillator pads on the chest) is fast but painful and requires sedation, so it serves as a bridge until transvenous or permanent pacing is established.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why is rhythm classification the critical first step in cardiac arrest management?
options: It determines the entire management pathway — shocking a non-shockable rhythm wastes time, and delaying adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm loses the only effective treatment
It determines the patient's prognosis only — it predicts likely survival and neurological outcome but has no bearing on the choice of drugs, shocks, or interventions given during resuscitation
It is required purely for documentation purposes — the rhythm strip must be recorded in the notes for medico-legal and audit reasons but does not influence any treatment decision at the bedside
It identifies the underlying cause directly — the rhythm alone reveals the exact reversible aetiology such as hypoxia or hyperkalaemia, so no further 4Hs and 4Ts assessment is then needed
It has no effect on management — the identical sequence of compressions, shocks, and adrenaline is delivered whatever the rhythm, so classification is an academic exercise with no bedside value
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: It determines the entire management pathway — shocking a non-shockable rhythm wastes time, and delaying adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm loses the only effective treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Rhythm classification drives the whole pathway: defibrillation only helps shockable rhythms, while non-shockable rhythms depend on early adrenaline and fixing the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which pair of rhythms is SHOCKABLE?
options: PEA and asystole
PEA and pulseless VT
Asystole and VF
Sinus bradycardia and PEA
VF and pulseless VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: VF and pulseless VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless VT (pVT). PEA and asystole are non-shockable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which pair of rhythms is NON-SHOCKABLE?
options: VF and pulseless VT
PEA and asystole
VF and asystole
Pulseless VT and PEA
VF and PEA
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: PEA and asystole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The non-shockable rhythms are pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the ECG appearance of ventricular fibrillation?
options: Organised wide-complex tachycardia with regular monomorphic QRS complexes
A flat isoelectric line with no electrical activity or baseline
Sawtooth flutter waves at a regular atrial rate of around 300 per minute
Erratic fibrillatory waveforms with no discernible QRS complexes
Normal narrow QRS complexes occurring at a slow regular rate near 40/min
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Erratic fibrillatory waveforms with no discernible QRS complexes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: VF is chaotic, disorganised activity — the ventricles quiver with no coordinated contraction, giving erratic fibrillatory waveforms and no discernible QRS complexes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What defines pulseless VT (pVT)?
options: Organised ventricular tachycardia (wide QRS, rate >100) but with no palpable pulse
A flat line with no electrical activity
An irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm
Organised activity that looks like any rhythm but with no pulse
Progressive PR lengthening with dropped beats
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Organised ventricular tachycardia (wide QRS, rate >100) but with no palpable pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: pVT is organised wide-complex VT, rate >100, that is too fast for effective cardiac output, so there is no palpable pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why does defibrillation work in VF/pVT?
options: It speeds up the heart rate by driving the sinoatrial node, raising ventricular output enough to restore a palpable pulse and adequate perfusion
It corrects the underlying electrolyte abnormality by driving potassium back into cells, so the arrhythmia resolves once the membrane gradient is restored
It directly contracts the ventricle by mechanically stimulating the myocardium, forcing a single coordinated squeeze that ejects blood and makes a pulse
A single high-energy shock simultaneously depolarises the whole myocardium → brief asystole → intrinsic pacemakers can restart a coordinated rhythm
It blocks the AV node, interrupting the re-entrant circuit conducting through it so the ventricles slow and an organised sinus rhythm can take over control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: A single high-energy shock simultaneously depolarises the whole myocardium → brief asystole → intrinsic pacemakers can restart a coordinated rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The shock depolarises the entire myocardium at once, producing brief asystole so the heart's intrinsic pacemakers can re-establish a coordinated rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the defining feature of pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
options: A chaotic fibrillatory baseline with no organised complexes but a weak, thready palpable pulse
Sawtooth flutter waves on the monitor at a regular atrial rate with no palpable pulse felt at all
A completely flat isoelectric line on the monitor with no electrical activity and no palpable pulse
A wide-complex tachycardia on the monitor accompanied by a weak but definitely palpable central pulse
Organised electrical activity on the monitor (looks like a rhythm) but no palpable pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Organised electrical activity on the monitor (looks like a rhythm) but no palpable pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: PEA shows organised electrical activity (it can look like any rhythm) but mechanical function has failed, so there is no palpable pulse. It is almost always caused by a reversible 4H/4T.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is asystole, and what determines its outcome?
options: Organised electrical activity with no palpable pulse; readily reversed by a single unsynchronised defibrillation shock
A shockable rhythm that responds well to defibrillation; a prompt single shock usually restores an organised output
A wide-complex tachycardia with a chaotic baseline; invariably fatal and unresponsive to any drug or shock
A flat line with no electrical activity; terminal unless an underlying cause is identified and reversed rapidly
Sinus rhythm at an abnormally slow rate; an entirely benign finding needing only observation and no treatment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: A flat line with no electrical activity; terminal unless an underlying cause is identified and reversed rapidly
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. It is terminal unless a reversible underlying cause is rapidly identified and corrected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why is defibrillation ineffective in PEA and asystole?
options: The patient is already in an organised sinus rhythm with a pulse, so a shock is unnecessary and potentially harmful
The heart is too cold from hypothermia to respond electrically, so active rewarming must precede any defibrillation
The defibrillator energy is set too low to capture the myocardium; a higher biphasic setting would make the shock work
The pads cannot be positioned correctly on the chest wall, so the delivered current fails to reach the arrested heart
There is no disorganised electrical activity to 'reset', so a shock does not help and wastes critical time
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: There is no disorganised electrical activity to 'reset', so a shock does not help and wastes critical time
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Defibrillation works by resetting disorganised activity; in PEA/asystole there is nothing to reset, so shocking is futile and wastes time better spent on CPR and treating the cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the first intervention for a shockable rhythm versus a non-shockable rhythm?
options: Both: CPR 2 min then adrenaline
Both: immediate defibrillation
Shockable: adrenaline first; non-shockable: shock first
Shockable: 1 shock → CPR 2 min; non-shockable: CPR 2 min + adrenaline ASAP
Shockable: amiodarone first; non-shockable: shock first
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Shockable: 1 shock → CPR 2 min; non-shockable: CPR 2 min + adrenaline ASAP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A shockable rhythm gets one shock then 2 minutes of CPR; a non-shockable rhythm gets immediate CPR with adrenaline as soon as possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In which arrest arm is amiodarone used, and what is the regimen?
options: Non-shockable arm: amiodarone 300 mg IV as a bolus given after the 3rd loop of CPR
Both arms: amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus given immediately once IV or IO access is secured
Shockable: 300 mg after the 3rd shock and 150 mg after the 5th shock; never in non-shockable
Shockable arm: amiodarone 150 mg IV bolus given immediately with the very first shock
Non-shockable arm only: amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd cycle, never in the shockable arm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Shockable: 300 mg after the 3rd shock and 150 mg after the 5th shock; never in non-shockable
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Amiodarone is for the shockable arm only: 300 mg after the 3rd shock and 150 mg after the 5th shock. It is never given in PEA or asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the main outcome driver in a non-shockable arrest?
options: Early defibrillation
Finding and fixing the reversible cause
High-dose adrenaline
Amiodarone administration
Rapid intubation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Finding and fixing the reversible cause
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Non-shockable arrests are won by finding and fixing the reversible cause (4Hs/4Ts); for shockable arrests the outcome driver is early defibrillation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A patient has a witnessed, monitored cardiac arrest in the cath lab with a defibrillator immediately to hand. What is the recommended initial approach?
options: Begin the standard ALS cycle straight away with one unsynchronised shock
Withhold all shocks and give amiodarone 300 mg IV as the first intervention
Give adrenaline 1 mg IV immediately, before any defibrillation shock
Give 3 quick stacked shocks first, then begin the standard ALS cycle
Perform a full 2 minutes of chest compressions before the first shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Give 3 quick stacked shocks first, then begin the standard ALS cycle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The monitored arrest exception: if witnessed in a monitored environment (CCU, cath lab, ICU) with a defibrillator immediately available, give 3 quick stacked shocks first, then begin the standard ALS cycle.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: PEA is described as 'almost always caused by' what?
options: A primary arrhythmia
An electrolyte derangement only
Coronary thrombosis exclusively
A reversible 4H/4T cause
Hypothermia exclusively
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: A reversible 4H/4T cause
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: PEA reflects intact electrical activity with failed mechanical function and is almost always caused by a reversible 4H/4T — which is why finding and fixing the cause is key.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the correct sequence of initial steps in the ALS algorithm before assessing the rhythm?
options: Confirm unresponsive + not breathing → call resus team → CPR 30:2 and attach defibrillator → assess rhythm
Assess the rhythm on the monitor first → then start CPR at 30:2 → then call the resuscitation team once help is needed
Give adrenaline 1 mg immediately → then start CPR at 30:2 → then deliver a single unsynchronised shock to the heart
Attach the monitor first → give amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus → then begin chest compressions at a 30:2 ratio
Check the carotid pulse for a full 60 seconds → deliver a shock → then commence CPR at a ratio of 30:2
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Confirm unresponsive + not breathing → call resus team → CPR 30:2 and attach defibrillator → assess rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The algorithm runs: unresponsive + not breathing normally → call the resuscitation team → CPR 30:2 and attach the defibrillator/monitor → assess the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in CPR before the airway is secured?
options: Continuous compressions with no ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Before a definitive airway is secured, CPR uses a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What shock energy is used in the shockable arm, and why must it be unsynchronised?
options: 120–150 J biphasic; unsynchronised because there is no R wave to lock onto in VF/pVT
50–100 J biphasic, synchronised to the R wave to avoid triggering an R-on-T phenomenon
200 J biphasic, synchronised to the QRS complex to prevent an R-on-T induced arrhythmia
70–120 J biphasic, unsynchronised, escalating with each subsequent shock delivered
360 J monophasic, synchronised to the R wave on every shock in the shockable arm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 120–150 J biphasic; unsynchronised because there is no R wave to lock onto in VF/pVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The first shock is 120–150 J biphasic, delivered unsynchronised because VF/pVT has no organised R wave to synchronise to.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Immediately after delivering a shock for VF/pVT, what should be done?
options: Check the carotid pulse carefully for a full 10 seconds
Immediately deliver a second unsynchronised shock at once
Resume CPR for 2 minutes without pausing to check the pulse
Give adrenaline 1 mg IV before resuming any compressions
Reassess the monitor rhythm immediately without any CPR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Resume CPR for 2 minutes without pausing to check the pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: After a shock, CPR is resumed immediately for 2 minutes without pausing to check the pulse — pulse/rhythm are reassessed at the next 2-minute check.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In the shockable arm, when are adrenaline and amiodarone first given, and at what doses?
options: After the 1st shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus, both given without any delay
Never in the shockable arm: neither adrenaline nor amiodarone is given for VF or pulseless VT
Immediately on arrest: adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 150 mg IV bolus given before the first shock
After the 5th shock only: adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus given together as one
After the 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV (once compressions restarted) and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: After the 3rd shock: adrenaline 1 mg IV (once compressions restarted) and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: In the shockable arm, after the 3rd shock give adrenaline 1 mg IV (once compressions are restarted) and amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When is the second dose of amiodarone given in the shockable arm, and at what dose?
options: After the 3rd shock, 300 mg
Every 3–5 minutes, 150 mg
After the 4th shock, 300 mg
After the 5th shock, 150 mg
It is never repeated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: After the 5th shock, 150 mg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The second amiodarone dose is 150 mg IV after the 5th shock (the first was 300 mg after the 3rd shock).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In the non-shockable arm, when is the first dose of adrenaline given?
options: After the 3rd cycle of CPR, once chest compressions have restarted
Immediately, as soon as IV/IO access is obtained — do not delay
Only if the rhythm subsequently changes and becomes shockable
After a full 10 minutes of uninterrupted chest compressions
Never at all — adrenaline is withheld entirely in this arm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Immediately, as soon as IV/IO access is obtained — do not delay
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: In PEA/asystole, adrenaline 1 mg IV is given immediately as soon as IV/IO access is obtained, with no delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: How often is adrenaline repeated once started, in both arms of the ALS algorithm?
options: Every 3–5 minutes (every other cycle)
Every minute
Every 10 minutes
Only once
Continuously by infusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Every 3–5 minutes (every other cycle)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Once started, adrenaline 1 mg is repeated every 3–5 minutes (every alternate cycle) in both arms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In the non-shockable arm, which two interventions are NOT performed, and what becomes the priority?
options: No defibrillation, no amiodarone; prioritise identifying and treating reversible causes (4Hs/4Ts)
No CPR and no adrenaline are given; the priority instead becomes early endotracheal intubation
No adrenaline and no IV fluids are given; the priority instead becomes delivering a prompt shock
No oxygen and no IV access are needed; the priority instead becomes transcutaneous cardiac pacing
No chest compressions and no drugs are used; the priority instead becomes rapid transport to theatre
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: No defibrillation, no amiodarone; prioritise identifying and treating reversible causes (4Hs/4Ts)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: In PEA/asystole there is no defibrillation and no amiodarone; the priority is to identify and treat the reversible causes (4Hs and 4Ts).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: How often is the rhythm reassessed during an ALS cycle, regardless of arm?
options: Every 30 seconds
Every 5 minutes
Every 2 minutes
After every shock
Only when the team leader requests it
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Every 2 minutes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Both arms loop back to a rhythm check every 2 minutes until ROSC or a decision to stop.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A thrombolytic is given during cardiac arrest for suspected PE. How does this change CPR duration?
options: Stop CPR immediately after administration
Continue CPR for a further 10 minutes
Continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after administration
Continue CPR for 24 hours
CPR duration is unchanged
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after administration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: If a thrombolytic is given for suspected PE, CPR should continue for 60–90 minutes afterwards to allow the drug time to work.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What are the target depth and rate for high-quality chest compressions?
options: 3–4 cm at 80/min
4–5 cm at 60–80/min
As deep and fast as possible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Compressions should be 5–6 cm deep (deeper risks injury) at 100–120/min (faster reduces perfusion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why is allowing full chest recoil between compressions important?
options: It reduces the risk of rib fractures only, but has no effect on cardiac filling or output
It allows the heart to refill — incomplete recoil reduces venous return and perfusion
It speeds up the achievable compression rate, letting you push well above 120 per minute
It is only relevant once the airway has been secured and the patient has been intubated
It prevents the defibrillator pads from dislodging during vigorous chest compressions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: It allows the heart to refill — incomplete recoil reduces venous return and perfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Complete chest recoil lets the heart refill; incomplete recoil impairs venous return and therefore perfusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why should the person performing compressions be rotated every 2 minutes?
options: To allow a brief pause for careful rhythm analysis on the monitor
Because fatigue rapidly degrades compression quality (depth and rate)
To re-site and re-check the defibrillator pad positions regularly
To create a natural moment to give the next dose of adrenaline
It is unnecessary if the current compressor still feels physically well
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Because fatigue rapidly degrades compression quality (depth and rate)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Compressor fatigue quickly reduces the quality of compressions, so rotating every 2 minutes maintains effective depth and rate.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the maximum acceptable duration of any pause in chest compressions?
options: No more than 10 seconds
No more than 20 seconds
No more than 5 seconds
No more than 30 seconds
Pauses do not matter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: No more than 5 seconds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Interruptions should be minimised, with no pause longer than 5 seconds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Once an endotracheal tube is secured, how should compressions and ventilation be delivered?
options: Continue with the same 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio exactly as before
Ventilate at a rate of 30 breaths per minute with continuous compressions
Stop compressions during each delivered breath to avoid gastric inflation
Switch to continuous compressions and ventilate at 10 breaths/min (no ratio)
Pause compressions briefly every 30 seconds to deliver two rescue breaths
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Switch to continuous compressions and ventilate at 10 breaths/min (no ratio)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: After ETT placement, switch to continuous compressions with ventilation at 10 breaths/min (no ratio), and confirm tube placement immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the gold-standard method for confirming endotracheal tube placement?
options: 5-point auscultation
Chest X-ray
Oxygen saturation rise
Misting of the tube
Waveform capnography
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Waveform capnography
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Waveform capnography is the gold standard for confirming ETT placement (a CO₂ waveform means the tube is in the trachea); 5-point auscultation and CXR (when stable) are adjuncts.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When a supraglottic airway (e.g. iGel) is inserted during CPR, what is the recommended approach?
options: Stop CPR for 30 seconds to insert it
Only insert after intubation fails twice
Insert it without stopping CPR, then attempt ventilation
Insert and then revert to 30:2 mouth-to-mouth
Insert only once ROSC is achieved
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Insert it without stopping CPR, then attempt ventilation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A supraglottic airway is inserted without interrupting CPR, after which ventilation is attempted.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the first-line vascular access in cardiac arrest, and a key practical point?
options: Large-bore peripheral IV (antecubital fossa preferred), flushing drugs with a 20 mL bolus
Central venous line as first choice; drugs need no saline flush after administration
Intraosseous access first-line in every arrest patient, before any attempt at an IV
Femoral arterial line for drug delivery, flushed with a 20 mL saline bolus each time
Subcutaneous injection of arrest drugs into the abdominal wall for slow absorption
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Large-bore peripheral IV (antecubital fossa preferred), flushing drugs with a 20 mL bolus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: IV is first-line: a large-bore peripheral cannula, antecubital fossa preferred, with each drug flushed with a 20 mL bolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When is intraosseous (IO) access used, and how does it compare to IV?
options: IO is genuinely first-line and pharmacologically superior to IV for all arrest drugs
IO requires every ALS drug dose to be halved because of the marrow route used
IO can only be used to deliver fluids and blood, never drugs such as adrenaline
IO is strictly contraindicated during active CPR because of the marrow pressures
IO is used if IV fails; it is equally effective for all ALS drugs and rapid to insert
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: IO is used if IV fails; it is equally effective for all ALS drugs and rapid to insert
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: IO (tibial, sternal, or humeral) is used if IV access fails; it is equally effective for all ALS drugs and rapid to insert under CPR conditions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: An ETCO₂ value above which threshold indicates adequate chest compressions?
options: >0.5 kPa
>2.0 kPa
>5.0 kPa
>1.0 kPa
>10 kPa
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: >2.0 kPa
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: An ETCO₂ >2.0 kPa indicates adequate chest compressions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: During CPR, a sudden rise in ETCO₂ on the capnograph most likely indicates what?
options: Tube displacement into the oesophagus — reintubate the trachea now
Development of a tension pneumothorax — perform needle decompression
Worsening compression quality — push harder and faster right now
Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) — stop and check the pulse
Onset of asystole — a flat line has replaced the organised rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) — stop and check the pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A sudden rise in ETCO₂ during CPR suggests ROSC; the team should stop and check the pulse at the next opportunity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which capnography finding is a poor prognostic marker in cardiac arrest?
options: Persistently very low ETCO₂ (<1.0 kPa after 20 minutes of ALS)
ETCO₂ held persistently above 5 kPa throughout the resuscitation
A steadily and consistently rising ETCO₂ trend over the arrest
An ETCO₂ reading holding steady at approximately 2.5 kPa
A widely fluctuating ETCO₂ that varies with each breath given
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Persistently very low ETCO₂ (<1.0 kPa after 20 minutes of ALS)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A persistently very low ETCO₂ (<1.0 kPa after 20 minutes of ALS) is a marker of poor prognosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which of the following is one of the 4 Ts?
options: Hypothermia
Hyperkalaemia
Hypovolaemia
Hypoxia
Tamponade (cardiac)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Tamponade (cardiac)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The 4 Ts are thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, and toxins. Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypothermia are the 4 Hs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A cardiac arrest patient is known to have renal failure, and the ECG shows peaked T waves and a broad QRS. What is the immediate treatment for the likely cause?
options: Sodium bicarbonate alone
Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV
50% dextrose
Magnesium sulfate
Insulin only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Peaked T waves/broad QRS in a renal-failure patient suggests hyperkalaemia — treat with calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV (sodium bicarbonate is added for severe acidosis or TCA overdose).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A drowning victim is in cardiac arrest with a core temperature of 28°C and J-waves on the ECG. Which rule guides resuscitation?
options: Follow the standard rule and stop resuscitation after 20 minutes of asystole
Give amiodarone 300 mg IV first, since antiarrhythmic drugs act normally at a core of 28°C
Defibrillate at once and repeat shocks normally, as hypothermia does not alter the response
'Not dead until warm and dead' — do not stop CPR until core temperature is >35°C
Delay all active rewarming until after ROSC has been achieved on the monitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 'Not dead until warm and dead' — do not stop CPR until core temperature is >35°C
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Hypothermia (J/Osborn waves, core <30°C) is protective; the rule is 'not dead until warm and dead' — continue CPR until the core temperature is >35°C.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: How is hypovolaemia recognised and treated as a cause of arrest?
options: Peaked T waves, a widened QRS and a flattened P wave; give calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV with insulin-dextrose to shift potassium
A cold, peripherally shut-down patient with J-waves (Osborn waves); give warmed IV fluids and rewarm actively while continuing prolonged CPR
Visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, AAA; rapid IV/IO fluids, early blood products, control the haemorrhage source
Muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins and hypotension (Beck's triad); perform urgent pericardiocentesis or resuscitative thoracotomy
Unequal breath sounds with tracheal deviation and hyperresonance; perform immediate needle decompression followed by a definitive chest drain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, AAA; rapid IV/IO fluids, early blood products, control the haemorrhage source
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Hypovolaemia is recognised by visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, haematemesis or AAA, and treated with rapid IV/IO fluids, early blood products, and source control (surgery/IR).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A patient arrests with preceding chest pain, a STEMI on the ECG, and known CAD. What is the appropriate management of this reversible cause?
options: Give immediate IV thrombolysis with alteplase, as restoring coronary flow takes priority over transfer for PCI
Perform immediate needle decompression of the chest to release trapped air compressing the heart and the great vessels
Perform urgent pericardiocentesis to drain the pericardial sac, relieving tamponade as the cause of the arrest
CPR whilst arranging PCI (primary PPCI) post-ROSC; thrombolysis if PCI unavailable and PE also suspected
Give calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV to stabilise the myocardium and reverse the electrical cause of the arrest
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: CPR whilst arranging PCI (primary PPCI) post-ROSC; thrombolysis if PCI unavailable and PE also suspected
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Coronary thrombosis is managed with CPR whilst arranging PCI (primary PPCI) post-ROSC; thrombolysis is reserved for when PCI is unavailable and PE is also suspected.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A sudden arrest with PE risk factors, an RBBB pattern, and no other cause found. What is the treatment, and how does it affect CPR?
options: Thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV) — continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after; surgical embolectomy if available
Give calcium chloride 10% IV and stop CPR after 10 minutes, as prolonged resuscitation offers no further benefit here
Perform pericardiocentesis to drain the pericardial effusion and continue CPR only for the usual standard duration
Perform needle decompression of the tension pneumothorax, then stop CPR immediately once the chest is decompressed
Give magnesium 2 g IV and continue CPR for a further 5 minutes only before considering stopping efforts
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV) — continue CPR for 60–90 minutes after; surgical embolectomy if available
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Pulmonary thrombosis (PE) is treated with thrombolysis (alteplase 50 mg IV) and CPR continued for 60–90 minutes afterwards; surgical embolectomy is used if available.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: A ventilated, traumatic-arrest patient has unequal breath sounds and late tracheal deviation. What is the first treatment step?
options: Perform immediate pericardiocentesis to drain blood from the pericardial sac, relieving the tamponade compressing the heart
Give IV thrombolysis with alteplase 50 mg to dissolve a suspected pulmonary embolus, then continue prolonged CPR afterwards
Immediate needle decompression at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line → confirm with finger thoracostomy → chest drain
Give calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV to stabilise the myocardium against a presumed electrolyte-driven cause of the arrest
Deliver immediate unsynchronised defibrillation at 150 J, treating the rhythm as shockable regardless of the breath sounds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Immediate needle decompression at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line → confirm with finger thoracostomy → chest drain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is treated with immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS midclavicular line), confirmed with finger thoracostomy, then a chest drain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is Beck's triad, and which reversible cause does it point to?
options: Unequal breath sounds, tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance — tension pneumothorax
Hypotension, tachycardia, fever — sepsis
Chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis — PE
Bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing — raised ICP
Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Beck's triad (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds) points to cardiac tamponade, treated with US-guided pericardiocentesis (or emergency thoracotomy in traumatic arrest).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which antidote is correctly matched to its toxin in cardiac arrest?
options: Opioid overdose → atropine as the specific antidote
Organophosphate poisoning → naloxone as the antidote
Local anaesthetic toxicity → 20% lipid emulsion
Digoxin toxicity → flumazenil to reverse it
Beta-blocker overdose → DigiFab antibody fragments
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Local anaesthetic toxicity → 20% lipid emulsion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Local anaesthetic toxicity is treated with 20% lipid emulsion. Other pairings: organophosphates → atropine; opioids → naloxone; digoxin → digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When should activated charcoal be considered in a toxin-related arrest?
options: In all poisoned patients regardless of timing
Never during cardiac arrest
Only after 6 hours
Only if the toxin is unknown
Only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Activated charcoal is appropriate only if the patient is alert and within 1 hour of ingestion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What can POCUS distinguish during the arrest pulse-check window, and what is the time constraint?
options: The coronary artery anatomy and site of the occlusion; the operator has under 60 seconds during the pulse check to obtain the views needed
The exact left-ventricular ejection fraction as a precise percentage, which can be carefully measured with no time limit during the arrest
The serum potassium and other electrolyte abnormalities driving the arrest; this must be assessed within 30 seconds at the pulse check
Cardiac motion (fine VF vs true asystole), pericardial effusion, flat IVC, and pleural fluid; requires <10 seconds at the pulse check
Only the underlying heart rate, counted directly off the screen; up to 5 minutes may be taken to complete this during compressions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Cardiac motion (fine VF vs true asystole), pericardial effusion, flat IVC, and pleural fluid; requires <10 seconds at the pulse check
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: POCUS can distinguish fine VF from true asystole, and identify a pericardial effusion, a flat IVC (hypovolaemia), and pleural fluid — all within a <10-second pulse-check window.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When is UNSYNCHRONISED defibrillation used, and why is synchronisation not possible?
options: For an organised tachycardia that still has a pulse; the R waves are too small for the defibrillator to detect and time the shock to
For supraventricular tachycardia, because the ventricular rate is simply too fast for the defibrillator to synchronise a shock to it
For atrial fibrillation only, because the rhythm is far too irregular for the machine to lock onto and synchronise a timed shock to
For asystole, because there is a completely flat trace and no organised electrical rhythm for the device to time the shock delivery to
For VF / pulseless VT; there are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the shock is delivered immediately on the button press
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: For VF / pulseless VT; there are no organised R waves to synchronise to, so the shock is delivered immediately on the button press
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Unsynchronised defibrillation is used for VF/pVT; with no organised R waves to synchronise to, the device delivers the shock immediately when the button is pressed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the first-shock energy for unsynchronised defibrillation, and how are subsequent shocks managed?
options: A fixed 50 J delivered for the first and all subsequent shocks, with no escalation at any stage
A 200 J first shock, then the energy halved with each successive shock delivered
A fixed 360 J monophasic shock delivered at full energy for the first and every later shock
A fixed 70–120 J biphasic shock repeated at the same energy for every subsequent shock
120–150 J biphasic first shock, escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 120–150 J biphasic first shock, escalating for subsequent shocks up to the device maximum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The first shock is 120–150 J biphasic, with subsequent shocks escalated up to the device maximum.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Why does synchronised cardioversion wait for the R wave before delivering the shock?
options: To concentrate and increase the total energy that is delivered to the myocardium during the cardioversion
To avoid delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could induce VF
To give the operator a few extra seconds to confirm the leads and position the paddles safely
To reduce skin burns by spreading the delivered current away from the vulnerable T-wave period
To confirm the underlying rhythm diagnosis on the monitor before finally committing to the shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: To avoid delivering the shock during the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could induce VF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronisation times the shock to the R wave, avoiding the vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T), which could otherwise precipitate VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Synchronised cardioversion is used for which type of rhythm?
options: VF and pulseless VT without any output
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension
Asystole with no electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)
An organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: An organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion is for an organised tachyarrhythmia with a pulse; pulseless VF/VT requires unsynchronised defibrillation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What are the cardioversion energies for AF versus atrial flutter/SVT?
options: AF 120–150 J biphasic; flutter/SVT 70–120 J
AF at 50 J; atrial flutter and SVT at 70 J
AF at 200 J; atrial flutter and SVT at 150 J
Both AF and flutter/SVT at 120–150 J biphasic
AF at 30 J; flutter and SVT at 360 J
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: AF 70–120 J biphasic; flutter/SVT 50–100 J
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion (RCUK) uses 120–150 J biphasic for AF and 70–120 J for atrial flutter/SVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the correct defibrillation safety drill?
options: 'Charge · Shock · Check pulse' — press charge, deliver the shock and then immediately assess for a central pulse before resuming
'Oxygen on · All clear · Shock' — keep oxygen flowing over the chest, confirm the team is clear, then deliver the shock safely
'Clear · Shock · Resume' — simply call clear once, deliver the shock and immediately resume chest compressions without any pause
'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m from patient) · All clear · Shock' — visually confirm all personnel clear before each shock
'Pulse check · Charge · Clear' — check for a pulse first, then charge the defibrillator and call clear before delivering the shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: 'Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m from patient) · All clear · Shock' — visually confirm all personnel clear before each shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The safety drill is: stand clear, oxygen away (≥1 m from patient), all clear, shock — with a visual confirmation that all personnel are clear before each shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the target oxygen saturation in immediate post-ROSC care, and why?
options: SpO₂ of 100%, using maximal FiO₂ to maximise tissue oxygen delivery
No specific oxygen saturation target is required after ROSC
SpO₂ 88–92% in all post-arrest patients, matching the COPD target
SpO₂ 85–90% deliberately, to limit ongoing reperfusion injury
SpO₂ 94–98%, avoiding hyperoxia (which causes oxidative injury)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: SpO₂ 94–98%, avoiding hyperoxia (which causes oxidative injury)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Post-ROSC, titrate to SpO₂ 94–98% and avoid hyperoxia, which is harmful through oxidative injury.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the target PaCO₂ in post-ROSC care?
options: Normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa)
Hypocapnia (PaCO₂ <4.0 kPa)
Hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >7.0 kPa)
PaCO₂ 2.0–3.0 kPa
PaCO₂ is not monitored post-ROSC
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Post-ROSC ventilation aims for normocapnia, a PaCO₂ of 4.5–6.0 kPa.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What does targeted temperature management involve post-ROSC?
options: Actively warm the patient to a core temperature of 38°C to support the metabolism
Cool every patient to a core temperature of 28°C for full neuroprotection
Prevent fever (target 36°C), and consider cooling to 33°C for comatose survivors
Apply no temperature control at all until 72 hours have elapsed after ROSC
Maintain a core temperature of 40°C to drive and support cerebral metabolism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Prevent fever (target 36°C), and consider cooling to 33°C for comatose survivors
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Targeted temperature management prevents fever (target 36°C) and considers cooling to 33°C in comatose survivors.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: When should neurological prognostication be performed after ROSC, and why the delay?
options: Within the first hour after ROSC, before sedation and cooling can confound it
Only after 2 full weeks have passed, once all sedation has completely worn off
At 12 hours post-ROSC, once initial stabilisation on the ICU is complete
Immediately on ICU admission, while the patient is still sedated and cooled
Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Not before 72 hours — hypothermia (and sedation) delays neurological assessment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Prognostication should not occur before 72 hours, as hypothermia and sedation delay reliable neurological assessment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: In which situation should CPR NOT be started?
options: A valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present
A witnessed arrest with a shockable rhythm on the monitor, where defibrillation is likely to succeed
Any cardiac arrest occurring in an elderly patient, where resuscitation is considered futile by age
Any arrest where the underlying cause is unknown, so no reversible factor can be targeted early
A hypothermic cardiac arrest, where the cold core temperature makes any resuscitation pointless
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: A valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or rigor mortis / dependent lividity present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: CPR should not be started if there is a valid DNACPR order, injuries incompatible with life, or signs of death such as rigor mortis or dependent lividity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which set of criteria supports stopping CPR?
options: After exactly 10 minutes of ALS in every case, regardless of rhythm, reversible causes or response to treatment
ROSC achieved, all reversible causes excluded, prolonged ALS without ROSC (>20–30 min in most cases), and team-leader consensus
As soon as the very first defibrillation shock fails to restore a perfusing rhythm on the subsequent pulse check
Only when the family present at the bedside specifically requests that all resuscitation efforts now be stopped
When the supply of adrenaline finally runs out, since further ALS cannot continue without the drug being available anymore
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: ROSC achieved, all reversible causes excluded, prolonged ALS without ROSC (>20–30 min in most cases), and team-leader consensus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: CPR is stopped when ROSC is achieved, or when reversible causes are excluded after prolonged ALS without ROSC (>20–30 min in most cases) with team-leader consensus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is described as the most-tested ALS fact regarding adrenaline timing (the 'adrenaline timing trap')?
options: Adrenaline 1 mg IV is given immediately in both the shockable and non-shockable arms as the very first drug
Shockable → adrenaline immediately with the first shock; non-shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock
Non-shockable → adrenaline immediately; shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st)
Adrenaline is withheld until after the 5th shock in both the shockable and non-shockable arms
Adrenaline is never used in modern ALS and has been removed from both arms of the algorithm entirely
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Non-shockable → adrenaline immediately; shockable → adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: The classic trap: adrenaline is immediate in non-shockable arrest but only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st) in shockable arrest.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: Which statement about amiodarone in cardiac arrest is correct?
options: It is given in both the shockable and non-shockable arms, alongside adrenaline, as a standard part of every arrest
It is ONLY for the shockable arm; never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there
It is the first-line antiarrhythmic drug in asystole, given as a 300 mg IV bolus before the first adrenaline
It replaces adrenaline entirely in the non-shockable arm and is given after the first cycle of compressions
It is given immediately at the start of all cardiac arrests, before any rhythm assessment has been made
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: It is ONLY for the shockable arm; never give it in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence there
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Amiodarone is for the shockable arm only; it has no role and no evidence in PEA or asystole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is magnesium 2 g IV specifically indicated for in cardiac arrest, and is it routine?
options: It is indicated in all cardiac arrests routinely, given as a standard 2 g IV bolus early in the algorithm
Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT) specifically — it is NOT routine in all arrests
It is indicated routinely in asystole, given as a 2 g IV bolus alongside the first dose of adrenaline
It is the first-line treatment for hyperkalaemic arrest, given ahead of calcium to stabilise the heart
It is indicated routinely in pulseless electrical activity, given as a 2 g IV bolus with each cycle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT) specifically — it is NOT routine in all arrests
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: Magnesium 2 g IV is the specific treatment for torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT); it is not routine in all cardiac arrests.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.question: What is the most time-critical post-arrest intervention if the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG shows a STEMI?
options: Targeted temperature management
Thrombolysis at 24 hours
Emergency PCI
Prognostication
Repeat defibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.answer: Emergency PCI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arre.explanation: A STEMI on the post-ROSC 12-lead ECG mandates emergency PCI — the most time-critical post-arrest intervention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What are the three main consequences of myocardial inflammation in myocarditis?
options: Valve stenosis, regurgitation, and prolapse
Pericardial effusion, tamponade, and constriction
Myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia
Coronary thrombosis, infarction, and scarring
Endocardial vegetation, embolisation, and abscess
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium leading to myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the typical clinical course of myocarditis?
options: A viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia) → days to weeks later → cardiac symptoms
Sudden severe chest pain with no viral prodrome, peaking within minutes of onset
Chronic exertional angina developing gradually over many years of stable effort
A sudden tearing chest pain radiating through to the interscapular back region
Painless progressive breathlessness alone, without any preceding febrile illness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: A viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia) → days to weeks later → cardiac symptoms
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis classically follows a viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia), with cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, HF) appearing days to weeks later.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: A 24-year-old presents with chest pain, a raised troponin, and a recent viral illness. Coronary angiography is normal. What is the key clinical flag?
options: Young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → think myocarditis before ACS (troponin raised, coronaries normal)
This confirms a STEMI needing immediate primary PCI, as the raised troponin and pain prove acute coronary occlusion
This is definitely acute pericarditis given the young age, recent viral history and pleuritic pain, so treat with NSAIDs
The raised troponin reliably excludes myocarditis, because myocardial inflammation never causes any cardiac enzyme leak
Normal coronary arteries exclude any cardiac pathology, so the chest pain must be musculoskeletal or wholly non-cardiac
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → think myocarditis before ACS (troponin raised, coronaries normal)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: A young patient with chest pain and a recent viral illness, a raised troponin, and normal coronaries should prompt thinking of myocarditis before ACS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the commonest cause of myocarditis overall (and in the UK)?
options: Chagas' disease
Giant cell myocarditis
Diphtheria
Doxorubicin
Coxsackie B virus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Coxsackie B virus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Viral infection is the commonest cause in the UK, and Coxsackie B is the most common overall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: A patient from South America develops a dilated cardiomyopathy from myocarditis. Which organism is the likely cause?
options: Borrelia (Lyme)
Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas' disease)
Coxsackie B
Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Toxoplasma
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas' disease)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is a protozoal cause of myocarditis common in South America.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which drug class is a high-yield emerging cause of fulminant myocarditis?
options: ACE inhibitors, via a dose-dependent direct myocyte toxicity
Beta-blockers, through a negative inotropic myocyte injury
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab)
Statins, via an immune-mediated necrotising myocyte damage
Loop diuretics, through electrolyte-driven inflammatory injury
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) are a high-yield emerging cause of fulminant myocarditis; management is to stop the drug and give high-dose steroids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which chemotherapy agent causes dose-dependent cardiotoxic myocarditis?
options: Cisplatin
Doxorubicin
Methotrexate
Vincristine
5-fluorouracil
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Doxorubicin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Doxorubicin causes dose-dependent cardiotoxicity and myocarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which rare but aggressive form of myocarditis carries a high mortality and is a poor prognostic factor?
options: Eosinophilic myocarditis
Lyme myocarditis
Viral myocarditis
Giant cell myocarditis
Toxoplasma myocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Giant cell myocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Giant cell myocarditis is rare but aggressive with high mortality, and is a recognised poor prognostic factor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: The clinical features of myocarditis arise from which two overlapping processes?
options: Ischaemia from coronary occlusion and subsequent reperfusion injury to myocytes
The inflammatory process itself and secondary myocardial dysfunction (HF)
Coronary embolisation and immune complex deposition within the myocardial wall
Progressive valve leaflet destruction and resulting severe regurgitant flow
Diffuse myocardial fibrosis and dystrophic calcification of the ventricle wall
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: The inflammatory process itself and secondary myocardial dysfunction (HF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Symptoms arise from the inflammatory process itself and from secondary myocardial dysfunction (heart failure).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is myopericarditis?
options: Myocarditis inevitably progressing to tamponade from a large haemorrhagic pericardial effusion needing urgent drainage
A purely autoimmune pericardial disease with no viral trigger, driven solely by circulating anti-pericardial antibodies
Pericarditis without any myocardial involvement, so troponin stays normal and only the pericardium is inflamed on imaging
A myocardial infarct that has extended to involve the overlying pericardium, producing a Dressler-type inflammation
Myocarditis overlapping with pericarditis (e.g. pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes) — treat both components
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Myocarditis overlapping with pericarditis (e.g. pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes) — treat both components
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myopericarditis is myocarditis overlapping with pericarditis, with features of both (pericardial rub, troponin rise, ST changes); both components are treated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which examination finding reflects ventricular dysfunction in myocarditis?
options: An S3 gallop with soft/muffled heart sounds
A loud S1 and opening snap
A collapsing pulse
A mid-systolic click
An ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: An S3 gallop with soft/muffled heart sounds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Signs of ventricular dysfunction include an S3 gallop, soft/muffled heart sounds, disproportionate tachycardia, and bibasal crackles (LHF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which two blood markers respectively indicate myocyte damage and ventricular dysfunction in myocarditis?
options: CRP and ESR, which quantify myocyte necrosis and ventricular systolic function
Troponin/CK-MB (myocyte damage) and BNP/NT-proBNP (ventricular dysfunction)
D-dimer (myocyte damage) and fibrinogen (ventricular wall dysfunction) levels
WCC (myocyte injury) and procalcitonin (ventricular dysfunction) measurements
Serum lactate for myocyte damage and arterial pH for ventricular dysfunction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Troponin/CK-MB (myocyte damage) and BNP/NT-proBNP (ventricular dysfunction)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Raised troponin/CK-MB reflects myocyte damage (mimicking ACS), and raised BNP/NT-proBNP reflects ventricular dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: How do the ECG changes of myocarditis classically differ from those of STEMI?
options: Myocarditis: territory-based; STEMI: diffuse
Myocarditis: no ECG changes; STEMI: ST elevation
Both are identical
Myocarditis: diffuse non-specific ST/T changes; STEMI: territory-based
Myocarditis: pathological Q waves; STEMI: PR depression
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Myocarditis: diffuse non-specific ST/T changes; STEMI: territory-based
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis causes diffuse (widespread) non-specific ST/T changes, the key difference from the territory-based changes of STEMI — though it can mimic STEMI with widespread ST elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What does echocardiography typically show in myocarditis?
options: A globular water-bottle silhouette with a smooth enlarged outline typical of a large pericardial effusion
A mobile vegetation on a valve leaflet with associated destruction and a new regurgitant jet on Doppler
Completely normal chamber size, wall motion and ejection fraction in every case, reliably excluding it
Ventricular dilatation, reduced EF, wall motion abnormalities (and excludes structural/valve pathology)
Dense pericardial calcification with a thickened rigid pericardium causing a constrictive filling pattern
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Ventricular dilatation, reduced EF, wall motion abnormalities (and excludes structural/valve pathology)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Echo shows ventricular dilatation, reduced EF and wall motion abnormalities, a pericardial effusion if myopericarditis, and excludes structural/valve pathology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Why is cardiac MRI the key modern non-invasive test for myocarditis?
options: It is the pathological gold standard, directly sampling myocardial tissue to confirm inflammation without any biopsy
Late gadolinium enhancement shows myocardial inflammation/fibrosis; it uses the Lake Louise criteria and guides prognosis
It directly cultures the causative virus from myocardial tissue, giving a definitive microbiological aetiology non-invasively
It replaces serial troponin measurement entirely, quantifying myocyte necrosis more accurately than any blood biomarker
It is the only reliable way to exclude acute coronary syndrome, showing coronary stenoses better than invasive angiography
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Late gadolinium enhancement shows myocardial inflammation/fibrosis; it uses the Lake Louise criteria and guides prognosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Cardiac MRI is the non-invasive gold standard: late gadolinium enhancement reveals inflammation/fibrosis, the Lake Louise criteria are applied, and it guides prognosis and risk stratification.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the pathological gold-standard investigation for myocarditis, and which criteria does it use?
options: Cardiac MRI; Lake Louise criteria
Echo; Simpson's criteria
Endomyocardial biopsy; Dallas criteria
Blood cultures; Duke criteria
CT; Agatston score
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Endomyocardial biopsy; Dallas criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Endomyocardial biopsy is the pathological gold standard, using the Dallas criteria (inflammatory infiltrate + myocyte necrosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Why is endomyocardial biopsy rarely performed in myocarditis?
