options: It is far too cheap and quick to justify, so clinicians instead reserve costlier non-invasive imaging such as cardiac MRI for the great majority of straightforward suspected cases
It cannot identify the underlying aetiology at all, since the histology looks identical whether the cause is viral, autoimmune, giant cell or eosinophilic myocardial disease
It is almost always inconclusive because patchy myocardial involvement means the sampling needle frequently misses inflamed areas, yielding false-negative histology in nearly every case
Because of the risk vs benefit — it is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, suspected giant cell/eosinophilic disease, or an unclear diagnosis after non-invasive workup
It has been replaced entirely by a panel of blood tests including troponin, BNP and viral serology, which now match its diagnostic accuracy in essentially every setting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Because of the risk vs benefit — it is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, suspected giant cell/eosinophilic disease, or an unclear diagnosis after non-invasive workup
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Biopsy is rarely done due to risk vs benefit; it is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, suspected giant cell/eosinophilic myocarditis, or diagnostic uncertainty after non-invasive workup.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the mainstay of management for myocarditis?
options: Immediate cardiac transplantation for most patients, as the inflamed myocardium seldom recovers function
Lifelong immunosuppression for every patient using high-dose steroids and azathioprine indefinitely
Supportive care (most cases self-limiting) and treating the underlying cause where possible
Urgent primary PCI to reperfuse the culprit coronary artery causing the myocardial injury
Routine endomyocardial biopsy in every case to guide targeted first-line drug therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Supportive care (most cases self-limiting) and treating the underlying cause where possible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Supportive care is the mainstay, as most cases are self-limiting; the underlying cause is treated where possible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Why are myocarditis patients admitted for cardiac monitoring?
options: To monitor blood pressure only
Because they always need surgery
To repeat the troponin hourly
Because of the arrhythmia risk (VT/VF)
To administer prophylactic antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Because of the arrhythmia risk (VT/VF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Hospital admission with cardiac monitoring is used because of the arrhythmia risk (VT/VF), with anti-arrhythmics and a defibrillator on standby if needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: How is myocarditis caused by an immune checkpoint inhibitor managed?
options: Continue the drug unchanged and simply observe the patient
Benznidazole to clear the underlying parasitic infection
High-dose steroids and hold the checkpoint inhibitor
Doxycycline to treat the responsible bacterial pathogen
Immediate cardiac transplantation as first-line therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: High-dose steroids and hold the checkpoint inhibitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: ICI-associated myocarditis is managed with high-dose steroids and holding the checkpoint inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the treatment for Chagas' myocarditis?
options: Doxycycline
Benzylpenicillin
Ceftriaxone
High-dose steroids
Benznidazole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Benznidazole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Chagas' disease myocarditis is treated with benznidazole (Lyme myocarditis, by contrast, with doxycycline or ceftriaxone).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What exercise advice is given after myocarditis, and why?
options: Abstain from competitive sport for a minimum of 3–6 months (or until MRI/echo confirms resolution), as it risks arrhythmia and is a cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes
Resume competitive sport immediately, as vigorous exercise during active myocardial inflammation actually speeds healing and poses no arrhythmic or sudden-death risk in fit young athletes
Light everyday exercise is dangerous and must be avoided, but full competitive sport is safe, since only low-level exertion aggravates the inflamed myocardium and provokes dangerous arrhythmia
Avoid all movement permanently on strict lifelong bed rest, because any physical activity whatsoever reactivates the myocardial inflammation and inevitably triggers a fatal ventricular arrhythmia
Exercise has no effect on outcome, so no restriction is ever needed, because the myocardial inflammation resolves on its own regardless of activity and never predisposes to any arrhythmia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Abstain from competitive sport for a minimum of 3–6 months (or until MRI/echo confirms resolution), as it risks arrhythmia and is a cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Strenuous exercise risks haemodynamic deterioration and life-threatening arrhythmia, so competitive sport is avoided for ≥3–6 months; myocarditis is a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the prognosis of myocarditis in the majority of cases?
options: Uniformly fatal within weeks despite maximal supportive therapy in almost all affected patients
A chronic relapsing course in every patient with repeated flares of myocardial inflammation
Always progresses to end-stage heart failure requiring cardiac transplantation within a year
Good — most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously with full recovery over weeks–months
Immediate cardiogenic shock in most patients, requiring urgent mechanical circulatory support
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Good — most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously with full recovery over weeks–months
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously with full recovery of cardiac function over weeks–months; a viral cause with mild dysfunction has an excellent outlook.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which of the following is a poor prognostic factor in myocarditis?
options: A viral cause with mild dysfunction
Absence of arrhythmia
Full recovery within weeks
A normal echo
Fulminant presentation / cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Fulminant presentation / cardiogenic shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Poor prognostic factors include fulminant presentation/cardiogenic shock, giant cell myocarditis, progression to dilated cardiomyopathy, sudden cardiac death, and persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What does persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months in myocarditis prompt?
options: Discharge with no follow-up
Consideration of cardiac transplantation
Repeat viral serology only
Immediate endomyocardial biopsy
Cessation of all medication
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Consideration of cardiac transplantation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months is a poor prognostic factor that prompts consideration of cardiac transplantation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Myocarditis is an important cause of which two outcomes in young people?
options: Aortic stenosis and syncope
Pulmonary embolism and DVT
Hypertension and stroke
Atrial fibrillation and heart block
Dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis is an important cause of dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death in young people, hence the advice to avoid exercise for ≥3–6 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: A 22-year-old marathon runner develops chest pain and shortness of breath 3 days after a flu-like illness. ECG shows widespread ST elevation with saddle-shaped morphology and troponin is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Aortic dissection
STEMI
Pericarditis
Myocarditis
Pulmonary embolism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Myocarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Young patient + recent viral illness + chest pain + raised troponin = myocarditis. Widespread ST changes (not localised as in STEMI) and saddle-shape suggest pericardial involvement (myopericarditis). Echo may show wall motion abnormalities.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the most common cause of myocarditis in young adults?
options: Viral infection (Coxsackievirus B, parvovirus B19, adenovirus)
Bacterial endocarditis spreading from an infected heart valve
Autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Cardiac sarcoidosis with granulomatous myocardial infiltration
Drug toxicity, classically from recreational cocaine use
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Viral infection (Coxsackievirus B, parvovirus B19, adenovirus)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Coxsackievirus B is the classic cause of viral myocarditis — enterovirus causing direct myocyte injury and immune-mediated damage. Parvovirus B19 is increasingly recognised. Rare causes include SLE, sarcoid, and drugs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the non-invasive gold standard for diagnosing myocarditis?
options: ECG
Echocardiography
Cardiac MRI with gadolinium (CMR)
Endomyocardial biopsy
Troponin level
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Cardiac MRI with gadolinium (CMR)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: CMR with gadolinium is the gold standard non-invasive test — shows myocardial oedema, hyperaemia, and fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement). Endomyocardial biopsy is definitive but rarely performed due to risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Why is exercise restriction advised in myocarditis?
options: Exercise directly worsens the troponin elevation by mechanically leaking more myocyte enzyme
Risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death during myocardial inflammation
Physical exertion causes the myocardial inflammation to spread into adjacent healthy tissue
Rest prevents the myocardial inflammation from progressing into an overlying acute pericarditis
There is no specific reason; it is merely routine general convalescent advice after illness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death during myocardial inflammation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Inflamed myocardium is electrically unstable — exercise dramatically increases arrhythmia risk. Young athletes have died from SCD in myocarditis. Exercise restriction for 3–6 months until inflammation resolves is standard.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which complication of myocarditis requires long-term follow-up?
options: Acute pericarditis with a persistent pericardial effusion
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) — develops in ~10% of cases
Pulmonary hypertension from chronic left-sided filling pressures
Accelerated coronary artery disease with premature atheroma
Progressive valvular stenosis from chronic leaflet inflammation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) — develops in ~10% of cases
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: ~10% of myocarditis progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy with persistent LV dysfunction. Long-term echocardiographic follow-up is recommended. DCM is the third most common cause of heart failure after IHD and hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with myocarditis. Her echo shows EF 30%. What medical therapy is indicated?
options: Empirical antiviral therapy with intravenous aciclovir
Prednisolone (high-dose corticosteroid immunosuppression)
NSAIDs such as high-dose ibuprofen for symptom control
Colchicine to suppress the ongoing myocardial inflammation
Standard HFrEF therapy (ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + MRA)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Standard HFrEF therapy (ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + MRA)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis causing LV dysfunction/HFrEF is treated with standard HF therapy (ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA). Steroids are not routinely used (no survival benefit in viral myocarditis). Colchicine is for pericarditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Giant cell myocarditis — what should be suspected and how does it differ from viral myocarditis?
options: A form that responds reliably to NSAIDs and colchicine, the same anti-inflammatory regimen used in pericarditis
A mild self-limiting viral infection that settles spontaneously within days and needs only supportive care
A common and easily treated condition that responds fully to a short outpatient course of oral therapy
A diagnosis made by troponin elevation alone, without any need for biopsy or histological confirmation
Rapidly progressive, refractory HF + arrhythmias + young adults — biopsy shows giant cells; requires immunosuppression
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Rapidly progressive, refractory HF + arrhythmias + young adults — biopsy shows giant cells; requires immunosuppression
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Giant cell myocarditis is rare but fulminant — rapidly progressive HF, ventricular arrhythmias, high mortality. Biopsy shows multinucleate giant cells. Requires immunosuppression (steroids + ciclosporin) and often cardiac transplantation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which arrhythmia is most dangerous in acute myocarditis?
options: Ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation (VT/VF)
Sinus tachycardia from fever and heightened sympathetic drive
First-degree AV block with a prolonged PR interval only
Atrial flutter with a regular sawtooth flutter pattern
Bundle branch block widening the QRS complex duration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation (VT/VF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: VT/VF is the most dangerous arrhythmia in myocarditis — cause of SCD in young athletes. Complete heart block can also occur. ECG monitoring is essential in acute myocarditis with troponin elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What finding on CMR (cardiac MRI) with gadolinium is characteristic of myocarditis?
options: Late gadolinium enhancement in the mid-wall/epicardium (non-ischaemic pattern)
Subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement (ischaemic pattern)
Pericardial effusion only
Normal in all cases
RV dilatation only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Late gadolinium enhancement in the mid-wall/epicardium (non-ischaemic pattern)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Myocarditis = mid-wall or epicardial LGE (non-ischaemic pattern). IHD causes subendocardial or transmural LGE following coronary territory. This distinction helps differentiate myocarditis from infarction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: Which of the following should be urgently excluded in a young patient with troponin rise and chest pain?
options: Pericarditis
Myocarditis
STEMI (acute coronary syndrome)
Pulmonary embolism
Aortic stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: STEMI (acute coronary syndrome)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Troponin rise + chest pain = rule out STEMI urgently (ECG, coronary angiogram if indicated). Myocarditis can mimic ACS — 'myocarditis-STEMI mimic'. Young patients with troponin rise after viral illness may proceed to CMR after ACS excluded.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: A 19-year-old develops myocarditis after receiving an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. What is the management?
options: Empirical antiviral therapy targeting the vaccine mRNA antigen
Immediate cardiac transplantation as definitive first-line therapy
High-dose corticosteroid immunosuppression continued for six months
Rest, monitoring, NSAIDs/colchicine — usually self-limiting
No treatment and no monitoring at all, as it always resolves
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Rest, monitoring, NSAIDs/colchicine — usually self-limiting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: mRNA vaccine-associated myocarditis (mainly in young males after 2nd dose) is usually mild and self-limiting — treated with rest, NSAIDs/colchicine. Serious cases managed as per standard myocarditis guidelines.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: How long should athletes abstain from competitive sport after myocarditis?
options: Permanently, with a lifelong ban from all competitive sport
Just 2 weeks of rest, then an unrestricted return to full play
A fixed 1 full year of abstinence regardless of imaging recovery
3–6 months minimum, until full recovery on imaging (CMR/echo)
Only until the serum troponin level has completely normalised
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: 3–6 months minimum, until full recovery on imaging (CMR/echo)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Current guidelines recommend 3–6 months abstinence from sport after myocarditis diagnosis. Return is allowed only when CMR/echo shows normal function and arrhythmia monitoring is reassuring.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: What is the treatment for eosinophilic myocarditis?
options: No treatment at all, since eosinophilic myocardial infiltration resolves spontaneously without any therapy
Empirical antiviral therapy directed at the presumed viral trigger of the eosinophilic infiltration
Standard heart failure therapy alone, without immunosuppression, letting the eosinophilia settle by itself
NSAIDs such as high-dose ibuprofen alone to suppress the eosinophil-driven myocardial inflammation
Steroids (corticosteroids) + treat the underlying cause (drug reaction, parasite, hypereosinophilic syndrome)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Steroids (corticosteroids) + treat the underlying cause (drug reaction, parasite, hypereosinophilic syndrome)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Eosinophilic myocarditis responds to steroids — causes include hypersensitivity drug reactions, parasites, hypereosinophilic syndrome. Identifying and removing the trigger (e.g. drug) is critical alongside steroid therapy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic presentation of acute myocarditis in a young patient?
options: New valvular regurgitation with a loud pansystolic murmur and no accompanying rise in cardiac troponin
A silent myocardial infarction presenting with painless ischaemic ECG changes and a large troponin rise
Isolated arrhythmias only, such as palpitations from ventricular ectopy, with no chest pain or troponin rise
Chest pain + raised troponin + new LV dysfunction after recent viral illness in a young person
An isolated pericardial effusion alone, causing muffled heart sounds without any true myocardial injury
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.answer: Chest pain + raised troponin + new LV dysfunction after recent viral illness in a young person
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis.explanation: Classic myocarditis: young patient, antecedent viral illness (1–4 weeks prior), chest pain, troponin elevation, new LV dysfunction. Must exclude ACS first. CMR confirms. Rest + HF therapy if EF reduced.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which sequence correctly describes the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis?
options: Acute plaque rupture first → lipid deposition into the arterial wall → secondary inflammation of the intima → progressive luminal stenosis
Rapid endothelial healing → spontaneous regression of existing plaque → remodelling back to a structurally normal, healthy vessel wall
Luminal stenosis → myocardial infarction → subsequent lipid deposition within the vessel wall → late inflammatory response and fibrosis
Lipid deposition in the media → outward arterial dilatation → aneurysm formation → eventual wall rupture with haemorrhage
Chronic arterial wall inflammation → lipid deposition → fibrous plaque formation → stiffening, stenosis, and plaque rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Chronic arterial wall inflammation → lipid deposition → fibrous plaque formation → stiffening, stenosis, and plaque rupture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Atherosclerosis is chronic arterial wall inflammation → lipid deposition → fibrous plaque formation → arterial stiffening, stenosis and plaque rupture, leading to MI, stroke and PAD.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: In atherosclerosis, what do monocytes become after adhering to the intima and engulfing LDL?
options: T cells
Smooth muscle cells
Endothelial cells
Macrophage foam cells
Mast cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Macrophage foam cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Monocytes adhere via adhesion molecules, differentiate into macrophages, engulf LDL and form macrophage foam cells, driving chronic inflammation and plaque development.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the goal and tool of primary prevention in atherosclerosis?
options: Prevent recurrence after an established CVD event using high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg
Treat an episode of acute pancreatitis triggered by severely elevated fasting serum triglyceride levels
Screen first-degree relatives for inherited disease using the Simon Broome diagnostic criteria
Lower serum triglycerides using a fibrate such as fenofibrate to reduce pancreatitis risk
Calculate risk and intervene before disease manifests, using QRISK3 (≥10% → atorvastatin 20 mg)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Calculate risk and intervene before disease manifests, using QRISK3 (≥10% → atorvastatin 20 mg)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Primary prevention has no prior CVD event; the goal is to calculate risk and intervene early, using QRISK3 with a ≥10% threshold for atorvastatin 20 mg.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the secondary prevention regimen after a CVD event, and what is notable about cholesterol level?
options: Atorvastatin 20 mg started only if baseline total cholesterol is elevated
Ezetimibe monotherapy alone, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption
Lifestyle and dietary measures alone, without lipid-lowering drug therapy
A fibrate combined with high-dose omega-3, given regardless of cholesterol
Atorvastatin 80 mg + the 4 A's, regardless of baseline cholesterol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Atorvastatin 80 mg + the 4 A's, regardless of baseline cholesterol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Secondary prevention (post-MI, stroke, PVD) is atorvastatin 80 mg plus the 4 A's, given regardless of baseline cholesterol, to prevent recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which of the following is a non-modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis?
options: Smoking
Poor diet
Obesity
Family history of premature CVD
Physical inactivity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Family history of premature CVD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Non-modifiable risk factors are age, male sex and family history of premature CVD; smoking, obesity, poor diet and inactivity are modifiable.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which comorbidity is listed as increasing atherosclerosis risk through raised metabolic risk?
options: Asthma
Migraine
Osteoarthritis
Atypical antipsychotics
GORD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Atypical antipsychotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Listed comorbidities include diabetes, hypertension, CKD, inflammatory disease (RA, SLE) and atypical antipsychotics (increased metabolic risk).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which clinical sign is pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia?
options: Xanthelasma
Corneal arcus
Tendon xanthomata
Acute pancreatitis
Palmar crease pigmentation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Tendon xanthomata
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Tendon xanthomata (hard cholesterol nodules over extensor tendons/Achilles) are pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: A grey-white ring at the corneal periphery in a 35-year-old suggests what?
options: A normal age-related finding requiring no further action
Acute pancreatitis from severe hypertriglyceridaemia
An underlying lipid disorder (premature <45 years)
Chronic open-angle glaucoma with raised eye pressure
An early cataract causing painless blurring of vision
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: An underlying lipid disorder (premature <45 years)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Corneal arcus is normal in the elderly, but premature arcus (<45 years) suggests an underlying dyslipidaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which lipid abnormality can precipitate acute pancreatitis, and at what level?
options: Raised LDL >5 mmol/L
Low HDL <1 mmol/L
Severe hypertriglyceridaemia >10 mmol/L
Raised total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L
Raised ApoB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia >10 mmol/L
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis, a serious complication.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which single lifestyle change is described as the most effective CVD intervention?
options: Reducing salt intake
Smoking cessation
Increasing oily fish
Strength training
Limiting alcohol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Smoking cessation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Smoking cessation is described as the single most effective CVD intervention.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: In the primary prevention pathway, what is rechecked at 3 months and what is the target?
options: LFTs only — aim for transaminases within the normal range
Creatine kinase — aim for a level below five times the ULN
Fasting lipids — aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol
HbA1c — aim for a value below 48 mmol/mol off treatment
Blood pressure — aim for a reading below 130/80 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Fasting lipids — aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: After starting atorvastatin 20 mg in primary prevention, recheck lipids at 3 months aiming for a ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which patient qualifies for an automatic statin without a QRISK calculation?
options: A 30-year-old with normal lipids and no comorbidities
Any patient over 40
A patient with isolated hypertension
A patient with a family history only
A patient with CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: A patient with CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3) warrants atorvastatin 20 mg regardless of QRISK, as CKD independently multiplies CVD risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which Type 1 diabetes criterion triggers an automatic statin (no QRISK needed)?
options: Any T1DM patient regardless of age or duration
Only if cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L
>40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy
Only if QRISK ≥20%
Only after a CVD event
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: >40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: In T1DM, atorvastatin 20 mg is given automatically if >40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy — no QRISK calculation needed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: In the secondary prevention 4 A's, what is the antiplatelet regimen post-MI?
options: Aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely as the sole antiplatelet, with no dual therapy at any stage
No antiplatelet therapy is required once the patient is discharged following the infarct
Clopidogrel 75 mg monotherapy continued lifelong, without any aspirin or ticagrelor cover
Ticagrelor 90 mg taken for one month only, then stopped with no ongoing antiplatelet therapy
Aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely; DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor) for 12 months post-MI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely; DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor) for 12 months post-MI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: The antiplatelet 'A' is aspirin 75 mg OD indefinitely, with post-MI DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor) for 12 months.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Why is a beta-blocker (e.g. bisoprolol/atenolol) included in the secondary prevention 4 A's?
options: To block intestinal absorption of dietary cholesterol at the brush border
Rate control, reduce cardiac remodelling post-MI, reduce sudden death risk
To upregulate hepatic LDL receptors and accelerate LDL particle clearance
To prevent acute pancreatitis caused by very high serum triglycerides
To lower fasting triglyceride levels by activating lipoprotein lipase
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Rate control, reduce cardiac remodelling post-MI, reduce sudden death risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: The beta-blocker 'A' provides rate control, reduces cardiac remodelling post-MI and reduces sudden death risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: State the key contrast between primary and secondary prevention regimens.
options: Primary = atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); Secondary = atorvastatin 80 mg + antiplatelet + beta-blocker + ACEi
Primary = high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg for everyone; Secondary = low-dose atorvastatin 20 mg used on its own
Both regimens use atorvastatin 80 mg combined with the full 4 A's of antiplatelet, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and aspirin
Primary prevention relies on fibrates first-line; Secondary prevention relies on ezetimibe monotherapy for lipid lowering
Primary uses PCSK9 inhibitors from the outset; Secondary uses a standard statin once atherosclerotic disease is established
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Primary = atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); Secondary = atorvastatin 80 mg + antiplatelet + beta-blocker + ACEi
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Primary prevention is atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); secondary is atorvastatin 80 mg plus antiplatelet, beta-blocker and ACEi.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the mechanism of statins?
options: Block intestinal cholesterol absorption via the NPC1L1 transporter → reduced chylomicron cholesterol delivery to liver
Activate endothelial lipoprotein lipase → enhanced hydrolysis of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and circulating VLDL
Prevent PCSK9-mediated degradation of hepatic LDL receptors → increased receptor recycling and faster LDL clearance
Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis → upregulate LDL receptors → reduced LDL
Bind bile acids within the gut lumen → interrupted enterohepatic circulation and increased faecal bile acid excretion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis → upregulate LDL receptors → reduced LDL
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates LDL receptors and lowers LDL.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Why are statins taken at night?
options: To reduce gastrointestinal side effects
To improve adherence only
To avoid interaction with food
Because LDL receptors are most active in the morning
Because hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Because hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Statins are taken at night because hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: In the cholesterol synthesis pathway, which conversion do statins block?
options: Mevalonate to lanosterol
7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol
Lanosterol to cholesterol
Acetyl-CoA to HMG-CoA
HMG-CoA to mevalonate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: HMG-CoA to mevalonate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, blocking the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate and reducing downstream cholesterol production.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What baseline investigations are checked before starting a statin?
options: Fasting lipid profile measurement only
Fasting lipids, LFTs, CK, TFTs, HbA1c
A resting 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram
QRISK3 cardiovascular risk score only
U&E with eGFR renal function testing only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Fasting lipids, LFTs, CK, TFTs, HbA1c
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Baseline checks before starting a statin are fasting lipids, LFTs, CK, TFTs and HbA1c.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: At the 3-month statin review, what LFT result mandates stopping the statin?
options: Any rise in ALT/AST
ALT/AST >3× ULN
ALT/AST >1.5× ULN
Mild transaminase rise
A normal LFT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: ALT/AST >3× ULN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: At 3 months, fasting lipids + LFTs are checked; if ALT/AST is >3× ULN, stop the statin (a mild rise is acceptable).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: A patient on a statin develops muscle pain. Which CK level indicates rhabdomyolysis and the need to stop immediately?
options: CK >1× ULN
CK >5× ULN
CK >3× ULN
CK >2× ULN
CK >10× ULN only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: CK >5× ULN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: If muscle pain occurs, check CK; CK >5× ULN = rhabdomyolysis → stop immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which symptom in a statin-related myopathy signals an emergency?
options: Mild aching after exercise
Joint swelling
Transient stiffness
Tingling in the hands
Dark urine (myoglobinuria)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Dark urine (myoglobinuria)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: In statin myopathy progressing to rhabdomyolysis, dark urine (myoglobinuria) signals an emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: How is the modest increase in diabetes risk from statins reconciled with prescribing?
options: The benefit vs CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients
Statins are strictly avoided in all patients with established diabetes
Statins are discontinued immediately if the HbA1c rises by any amount
The new-onset diabetes risk clearly outweighs any cardiovascular benefit
Statins are reserved only for non-diabetic patients at high CVD risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: The benefit vs CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: There is a modest increase in diabetes risk, but the benefit versus CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Why should a statin be held while a patient takes clarithromycin?
options: Clarithromycin markedly reduces gastrointestinal absorption of the statin
The combination causes dangerous hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrhythmia
CYP3A4 inhibition raises statin levels → increased myopathy risk
It precipitates acute pancreatitis through raised serum triglycerides
It suppresses hepatic LDL receptor expression, reducing statin efficacy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: CYP3A4 inhibition raises statin levels → increased myopathy risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Macrolides such as clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4, raising statin levels and increasing myopathy risk, so the statin is held.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the mechanism of ezetimibe?
options: Inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase to reduce cholesterol synthesis
Lowers triglycerides by activating the PPARα nuclear receptor
Prevents PCSK9-mediated LDL receptor degradation in hepatocytes
Activates circulating PCSK9 to enhance LDL particle clearance
Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 inhibitor)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 inhibitor)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption as an NPC1L1 inhibitor; it is used as add-on to a statin or in statin-intolerant patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: How do PCSK9 inhibitors work, and who are they for?
options: Inhibit hepatic HMG-CoA reductase to cut cholesterol synthesis; indicated first-line for all patients with any hyperlipidaemia
Block intestinal cholesterol absorption at the brush border; reserved for mild, diet-responsive cases not needing a statin
Monoclonal antibodies that prevent LDL receptor degradation → profound LDL reduction; for FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia
Lower serum triglycerides by activating PPARα; used mainly to prevent recurrent hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis
Bind bile acids in the gut lumen to interrupt recycling; used chiefly in patients who are fully intolerant of statin therapy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Monoclonal antibodies that prevent LDL receptor degradation → profound LDL reduction; for FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) are subcut monoclonal antibodies that prevent LDL receptor degradation, giving profound LDL reduction for FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which agent is used for severe hypertriglyceridaemia?
options: Fibrates (fenofibrate)
PCSK9 inhibitor
Ezetimibe
High-dose statin alone
Aspirin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Fibrates (fenofibrate)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Fibrates (fenofibrate) are used for severe hypertriglyceridaemia; omega-3 fatty acids are an adjunct for triglyceride lowering.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What are the key features of familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)?
options: Autosomal recessive inheritance, characteristically low serum cholesterol, with a first MI only in advanced old age
X-linked inheritance, markedly raised triglycerides, presenting with recurrent acute pancreatitis rather than early MI
Autosomal dominant LDL receptor mutation, very high cholesterol from birth, untreated MI in 4th–5th decade
An acquired dietary disorder with normal cholesterol levels and no measurable increase in cardiovascular risk
Polygenic inheritance causing only mild dyslipidaemia that remains asymptomatic and event-free throughout life
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Autosomal dominant LDL receptor mutation, very high cholesterol from birth, untreated MI in 4th–5th decade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: FH is autosomal dominant (LDL receptor mutation, or ApoB/PCSK9 variants) with very high cholesterol from birth and untreated MI in the 4th–5th decade.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Under Simon Broome criteria, what total cholesterol or LDL level is part of the diagnosis of FH?
options: Total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L (or LDL >4.9)
Total cholesterol >5 mmol/L (or LDL >3)
Total cholesterol >10 mmol/L (or LDL >7)
Triglycerides >10 mmol/L
HDL <1 mmol/L
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L (or LDL >4.9)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Simon Broome criteria include total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L (or LDL >4.9), tendon xanthomata, FHx premature CVD, and a DNA mutation = definite diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Under Simon Broome criteria, what confirms a definite diagnosis of FH?
options: Total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L alone
A DNA mutation in the LDL receptor/ApoB/PCSK9
Tendon xanthomata alone
A positive family history alone
Premature corneal arcus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: A DNA mutation in the LDL receptor/ApoB/PCSK9
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: A DNA mutation in the LDL receptor, ApoB or PCSK9 gives a definite diagnosis under Simon Broome criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What does management of familial hypercholesterolaemia involve?
options: Urgent specialist referral, genetic testing, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), ezetimibe if target not met, PCSK9 for refractory cases, cascade screening
Lifestyle and dietary measures alone, with saturated-fat restriction and exercise, deferring all drug therapy unless a cardiovascular event later occurs
A low-intensity statin such as simvastatin 10 mg used on its own, without ezetimibe, PCSK9 therapy, specialist referral or cascade screening of relatives
Fibrates such as fenofibrate as sole first-line therapy to lower LDL, reserving statins only for those who fail to reach target on the fibrate alone
Watchful observation with periodic lipid monitoring until the first myocardial infarction occurs, after which a high-intensity statin is finally begun
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Urgent specialist referral, genetic testing, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), ezetimibe if target not met, PCSK9 for refractory cases, cascade screening
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: FH management: urgent specialist referral, genetic testing, atorvastatin 80 mg, ezetimibe if target not met, PCSK9 inhibitor for refractory cases, and cascade screening of first-degree relatives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is cascade screening in familial hypercholesterolaemia?
options: Repeated lipid testing of the index patient
Genetic testing of the general population
Annual ECGs for the patient
Testing all first-degree relatives
Screening only if symptoms develop
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Testing all first-degree relatives
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Cascade screening means testing all first-degree relatives of the FH patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which examination signs are grouped as lipid deposition signs in the exam pearls?
options: Clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes
Malar flush, giant V waves, tapping apex
Xanthelasma, corneal arcus, tendon xanthomata
Papilloedema, cotton-wool spots, flame haemorrhages
Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Xanthelasma, corneal arcus, tendon xanthomata
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: The exam pearl groups xanthelasma, corneal arcus and tendon xanthomata as lipid deposition signs in the examination.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: A 45-year-old man has LDL 4.8 mmol/L and family history of premature MI. He has no other risk factors. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?
options: A fibrate such as fenofibrate as first-line
Low-intensity statin such as simvastatin 10 mg
High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg)
Ezetimibe alone blocking cholesterol absorption
Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation alone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) are first-line for high CV risk — aim for ≥50% LDL reduction. Low-intensity statins are insufficient for high-risk individuals.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the mechanism of action of ezetimibe?
options: Fibrate-like PPARα activation lowering circulating triglyceride-rich lipoproteins
HMG-CoA reductase inhibition reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis and raising LDL uptake
PCSK9 inhibition preventing LDL receptor degradation and boosting hepatic LDL clearance
Bile acid sequestration interrupting the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts
Inhibits cholesterol absorption at the intestinal brush border (NPC1L1 transporter)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Inhibits cholesterol absorption at the intestinal brush border (NPC1L1 transporter)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 transporter at the intestinal brush border — reduces cholesterol absorption by ~50%, lowers LDL by ~15–20%. Used as add-on to statin or if statin-intolerant.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What class of drug is most effective for reducing triglycerides?
options: Beta-blockers
Statins
Ezetimibe
PCSK9 inhibitors
Fibrates (e.g. fenofibrate)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Fibrates (e.g. fenofibrate)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: Fibrates (PPARα agonists) reduce triglycerides by 30–50% and modestly raise HDL — used for hypertriglyceridaemia (TG >10 mmol/L = pancreatitis risk) and mixed hyperlipidaemia. Statins mainly lower LDL.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: Which inherited lipid disorder causes tendon xanthomata and premature coronary artery disease in young adulthood?
options: Fredrickson Type V dyslipidaemia
Type 2 familial hypertriglyceridaemia
Secondary hyperlipidaemia
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)
Chylomicronaemia syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: FH = LDL receptor mutation — severely elevated LDL, tendon xanthomata (Achilles, extensor tendons), corneal arcus, xanthelasma, premature CAD. Autosomal dominant. Treat with high-intensity statin ± PCSK9 inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: What is the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors (e.g. evolocumab)?
options: Activate the PPARα receptor to lower serum triglyceride levels
Inhibit hepatic HMG-CoA reductase to reduce cholesterol synthesis
Block intestinal cholesterol absorption at the NPC1L1 transporter
Increase biliary bile acid secretion into the intestinal lumen
Prevent PCSK9 from degrading LDL receptors — increasing LDL clearance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: Prevent PCSK9 from degrading LDL receptors — increasing LDL clearance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: PCSK9 normally degrades LDL receptors. PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) block this — more LDL receptors remain on hepatocytes, clearing LDL by 50–70%. Used for FH or statin-intolerant high-risk patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the target LDL for very high cardiovascular risk patients (established atherosclerotic CVD)?
options: <2.6 mmol/L for moderate cardiovascular risk patients
<1.4 mmol/L (or ≥50% reduction) per ESC 2021 guidelines
<3.0 mmol/L as a general population lipid target
<4.0 mmol/L for low-risk primary prevention patients
<1.8 mmol/L applied uniformly across all patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.answer: <1.4 mmol/L (or ≥50% reduction) per ESC 2021 guidelines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disord.explanation: ESC 2021: very high CV risk (established CVD, diabetes with organ damage, CKD 3–4, FH) = LDL <1.4 mmol/L AND ≥50% reduction. Achieved with high-intensity statin ± ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: How does dry gangrene differ from wet gangrene?
options: Dry gangrene causes florid systemic sepsis and shock; wet gangrene stays localised without any toxaemia
Dry = bacterial infection without ischaemia, warm and pus-filled; wet = pure arterial ischaemia only, cold and dry
Both are clinically identical, spreading at the same rate and treated the same, told apart only by biopsy
Dry = ischaemia without infection, mummified, demarcated; wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, septic
Dry gangrene always requires urgent same-day amputation, whereas wet gangrene can be safely observed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Dry = ischaemia without infection, mummified, demarcated; wet = ischaemia + infection, swollen, septic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene: ischaemic necrosis, mummified, well-demarcated, no systemic upset. Wet gangrene: ischaemia + infection, malodorous, poorly demarcated, systemic sepsis — a surgical emergency.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which organism causes gas gangrene and what is its hallmark sign?
options: Clostridium perfringens — crepitus from gas in tissues
Group A Streptococcus — necrotising fasciitis
E. coli — urinary source
Staph aureus — skin abscess
Bacteroides — intra-abdominal sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clostridium perfringens — crepitus from gas in tissues
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens (Gram-positive anaerobe) — alpha-toxin destroys cell membranes, producing gas (CO₂ + H₂) → crepitus on palpation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the treatment of gas gangrene?
options: Oral antibiotics with outpatient wound review in the community clinic
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, without any surgical debridement or amputation
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone as the sole definitive treatment, avoiding surgery
Conservative management with regular wound dressings and limb elevation only
Emergency surgical debridement/amputation + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Emergency surgical debridement/amputation + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is a surgical emergency: wide debridement/amputation + high-dose IV penicillin G (± metronidazole) + hyperbaric oxygen as an adjunct.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is Fournier's gangrene?
options: Wet gangrene of the diabetic foot with infected, malodorous, swollen tissue and surrounding cellulitis
Clostridial gas gangrene of the lower limb muscles, producing crepitus and subcutaneous gas on X-ray after trauma
Dry ischaemic gangrene of the toes and digits caused by chronic atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease
Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva — polymicrobial, affects diabetics, emergency debridement required
Ischaemic necrosis of the small bowel due to mesenteric arterial occlusion, causing severe abdominal pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum/vulva — polymicrobial, affects diabetics, emergency debridement required
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia, most common in diabetic/immunocompromised men — emergency debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the hallmark clinical sign of necrotising fasciitis?
options: Pain out of proportion to appearance, with 'dishwater' fluid on incision
A black, mummified, clearly demarcated digit with absent distal pedal pulses
Palpable crepitus, which occurs only in gas gangrene and never in this condition
A well-localised fluctuant abscess with overlying pointing and warmth
Superficial erythema strictly limited to the skin surface, sparing deeper fascia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Pain out of proportion to appearance, with 'dishwater' fluid on incision
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Pain out of proportion + grey/brown dishwater fluid on incision = necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise. Requires immediate surgical exploration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: At what ABPI is critical ischaemia with tissue loss/gangrene expected?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: ABPI <0.5 = severe ischaemia; ABPI <0.3 = critical ischaemia with rest pain, non-healing ulcers, and gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the commonest precipitant of lower limb gangrene in clinical practice?
options: Aortic dissection with distal extension occluding the iliac arteries
Acute arterial embolism from atrial fibrillation lodging at a limb artery bifurcation
Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) in young male heavy smokers
Diabetic foot — neuropathy + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia causing arterial thrombosis and limb ischaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Diabetic foot — neuropathy + peripheral arterial disease + impaired immunity
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: The diabetic foot triad — peripheral neuropathy (unnoticed injury), peripheral arterial disease (impaired healing), and impaired immunity (infection) — is the commonest cause of limb gangrene.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the definitive management of established limb gangrene?
options: Revascularisation if viable tissue remains; amputation if not — with debridement and antibiotics for wet/gas gangrene
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, continued long-term without any surgical revascularisation or amputation
Conservative wound care only, with regular dressings and bedside debridement of slough without surgery
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone as the definitive treatment, avoiding any revascularisation or surgery
Systemic anticoagulation with heparin alone to restore limb perfusion, avoiding surgery or amputation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Revascularisation if viable tissue remains; amputation if not — with debridement and antibiotics for wet/gas gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Established gangrene: revascularisation (bypass/angioplasty) if viable tissue remains; amputation if not. Wet/gas gangrene require urgent debridement + antibiotics first.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What does the LRINEC score assess?
options: Severity of peripheral arterial disease, stratifying critical limb ischaemia to guide revascularisation
Laboratory risk of necrotising fasciitis — score ≥6 = high risk, prompts urgent surgical exploration
Prognostic scoring tool predicting mortality risk in patients with established septic shock on the ICU
Risk of major amputation in the diabetic foot, combining neuropathy, ischaemia and infection scores
Likelihood of clostridial gas gangrene, based on palpable crepitus and gas seen on plain radiographs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Laboratory risk of necrotising fasciitis — score ≥6 = high risk, prompts urgent surgical exploration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: LRINEC (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose) — score ≥6 suggests necrotising fasciitis and prompts urgent surgical exploration, not delay.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient presents with a black mummified fifth toe, clear demarcation, absent pedal pulses, no fever, ABPI 0.25. What is the type of gangrene and management?
options: Dry gangrene from critical ischaemia — urgent vascular review for revascularisation/amputation
Wet gangrene — urgent IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with surgical debridement of infected tissue
Gas gangrene — emergency IV penicillin G with radical surgical debridement of necrotic muscle
Fournier's gangrene — emergency perineal and scrotal surgical debridement with antibiotics
Necrotising fasciitis — urgent LRINEC scoring followed by surgical fascial exploration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Dry gangrene from critical ischaemia — urgent vascular review for revascularisation/amputation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene: mummified, demarcated, no infection, critical ABPI <0.3 → urgent vascular review for revascularisation; amputation if not feasible.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient has a rapidly spreading wound infection with severe pain, crepitus on palpation, and gas on X-ray. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) — emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric O₂
Dry gangrene — conservative management with dressings, awaiting spontaneous autoamputation of the digit
Wet gangrene — a short course of oral antibiotics with outpatient wound dressing and community review
Fournier's gangrene — localised perineal wound care with dressings and simple oral antibiotics
Necrotising fasciitis Type II — inpatient observation with IV antibiotics and delayed surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens) — emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin G + hyperbaric O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Crepitus + gas on XR + rapidly progressive pain = gas gangrene. Emergency: wide surgical debridement/amputation + high-dose IV penicillin G + hyperbaric oxygen.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 65-year-old diabetic presents with a 2-day history of severe perineal pain, swelling, and crepitus. He has a fever of 39.5°C and is haemodynamically unstable. What is the diagnosis and priority treatment?
options: Fournier's gangrene — emergency surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
Perianal abscess — theatre incision and drainage of the collection
Perineal cellulitis — IV antibiotics alone without any surgical intervention
Scrotal hydrocele — reassurance and conservative outpatient management
Inguinal hernia — elective outpatient mesh repair on a routine list
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Fournier's gangrene — emergency surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is necrotising fasciitis of the perineum — commonest in diabetics. Crepitus, systemic sepsis and rapid progression = emergency debridement. Delay is fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A patient sustained a penetrating wound and now has a wound with a 'sweetish' smell, crepitus, and bronzed discoloration of surrounding skin. He is confused and febrile. What organism is responsible?
options: Bacteroides fragilis
Staphylococcus aureus
Group A Streptococcus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Clostridium perfringens
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clostridium perfringens
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens — classically after penetrating wounds or surgery. Crepitus, rapid systemic toxicity, and distinctive smell point to clostridial myonecrosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the LRINEC score used for?
options: Predicting in-hospital mortality risk in patients with established septic shock
Risk stratifying suspected necrotising fasciitis using laboratory parameters
Grading the severity and depth of thermal burns to guide fluid resuscitation
Calculating the correct weight-based dose of VTE thromboprophylaxis heparin
Diagnosing and grading the severity of diabetic foot infection and ulceration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Risk stratifying suspected necrotising fasciitis using laboratory parameters
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: LRINEC uses CRP, WBC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose — score ≥6 = high risk for NF. However, high clinical suspicion should still prompt surgical exploration regardless of score.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 72-year-old woman with severe peripheral vascular disease has a dry, black, mummified 2nd toe with a clear demarcation line. She has no fever and no systemic sepsis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Simple wound dressings alone with watchful observation in the community clinic
Emergency wide surgical debridement of the toe with excision of tissue
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics alone without vascular assessment or surgery
Vascular assessment + elective amputation if revascularisation not possible
Long-term warfarin anticoagulation to restore perfusion to the ischaemic toe
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Vascular assessment + elective amputation if revascularisation not possible
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene = ischaemic mummification — stable without systemic sepsis. Assess revascularisation potential (Doppler, ABI, arteriography). If not salvageable, elective digital amputation at appropriate level.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the key clinical feature distinguishing necrotising fasciitis from severe cellulitis?
options: Superficial erythema and warmth of the skin only, without deep tissue involvement
Disproportionate severe pain with woody-hard induration and systemic sepsis
Isolated unilateral leg swelling and calf tenderness, as seen in deep vein thrombosis
A markedly elevated serum D-dimer level as the single key diagnostic marker
A positive blood culture being the defining feature that confirms the diagnosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Disproportionate severe pain with woody-hard induration and systemic sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: NF hallmarks: disproportionate pain (nerves involved), woody induration (fascial involvement), rapid spread, skin necrosis/crepitus, systemic sepsis. Cellulitis is softer and more contained.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which imaging finding on CT confirms necrotising fasciitis?
options: Soft tissue calcification
Subcutaneous oedema alone
Gas tracking along fascial planes
Cortical bone destruction
Fluid in joint spaces
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Gas tracking along fascial planes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas along fascial planes on CT = necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise — pathognomonic of gas-forming organisms. Does not exclude NF if absent; surgical exploration is definitive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What antibiotic combination is used for clostridial gas gangrene?
options: Flucloxacillin alone
High-dose IV penicillin + clindamycin
Piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin
Metronidazole alone
Ceftriaxone + amikacin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: High-dose IV penicillin + clindamycin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Penicillin G kills Clostridium; clindamycin inhibits toxin production by blocking protein synthesis. This combination is the antibiotic backbone for gas gangrene alongside emergency surgical debridement.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Why is clindamycin added to penicillin in gas gangrene?
options: It broadens cover against Gram-negative organisms missed by penicillin
It inhibits toxin production by blocking bacterial protein synthesis
It penetrates bone and necrotic muscle much better than penicillin does
It prevents the emergence of clostridial resistance against penicillin
It adds essential anaerobic cover that penicillin lacks in this setting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: It inhibits toxin production by blocking bacterial protein synthesis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Even after penicillin kills the bacteria, pre-formed alpha-toxin continues to cause tissue destruction. Clindamycin (protein synthesis inhibitor) turns off toxin production — critical in severe clostridial infections.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 78-year-old with dry gangrene of the right foot refuses surgery. What complication is most likely to develop without intervention?
options: Spontaneous healing
Wet gangrene with secondary infection and sepsis
Limb auto-amputation without infection
Progressive dry mummification only
Peripheral neuropathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Wet gangrene with secondary infection and sepsis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene is initially stable but can become infected (wet gangrene) — especially in diabetics with poor immunity. Secondary bacterial infection leads to systemic sepsis, which is life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 45-year-old intravenous drug user presents with a tender, erythematous, rapidly spreading arm swelling with skin necrosis and severe pain. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: CT scan and delay surgery
IV antibiotics and wait 24 hours
Incision and drainage as for abscess
Emergency surgical exploration and debridement
Amputation immediately
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Emergency surgical exploration and debridement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Clinical signs of necrotising fasciitis (IVDU + skin necrosis + rapid progression) = emergency surgical exploration. Do NOT delay for imaging when NF is strongly suspected — every hour increases mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the role of hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) in gas gangrene?
options: A definitive standalone cure that reliably avoids the need for surgery
First-line definitive treatment used instead of surgical debridement
Adjunct after surgical debridement — high O₂ inhibits anaerobe growth
Indicated only in wet gangrene and never in clostridial gas gangrene
Absolutely contraindicated in gas gangrene because of oxygen toxicity risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Adjunct after surgical debridement — high O₂ inhibits anaerobe growth
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Hyperbaric oxygen inhibits Clostridium (obligate anaerobe) and promotes tissue healing — used as an adjunct after surgical debridement + antibiotics in specialist centres. It does NOT replace surgery.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What percentage of necrotising fasciitis cases occur in diabetics?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Diabetes is the strongest risk factor for necrotising fasciitis and Fournier's gangrene — impaired immunity, neuropathy (unnoticed injuries), and vascular disease all contribute. Other risk factors: obesity, IVDU, immunosuppression.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which of the following is the key difference between Type 1 and Type 2 necrotising fasciitis?
options: Type 1 = gas-forming clostridial infection; Type 2 = no gas ever produced
Type 1 = mild superficial cellulitis; Type 2 = deep fulminant myonecrosis
Type 1 = polymicrobial; Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus)
Type 1 = confined to the limbs only; Type 2 = confined to perineum only
Type 1 = managed with antibiotics alone; Type 2 = requires surgery only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Type 1 = polymicrobial; Type 2 = monomicrobial (Group A Streptococcus)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Type 1 NF is polymicrobial (mixed aerobic/anaerobic), common in diabetics/elderly. Type 2 is monomicrobial, typically Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), can affect healthy young adults.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the triad of dry gangrene?
options: Palpable gas in tissue + florid systemic toxicity + audible crepitus
Moist swollen tissue + high fever + rapid proximal spread of infection
Black mummified tissue + clear demarcation line + ischaemic cause (PAD)
Perineal scrotal involvement + polymicrobial flora + diabetes mellitus
Warm erythematous swollen limb + deep vein thrombosis + pitting oedema
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Black mummified tissue + clear demarcation line + ischaemic cause (PAD)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Dry gangrene = ischaemic mummification from PAD. Key features: dry, black, shrunken tissue with a clear demarcation line. No systemic sepsis initially (unlike wet gangrene).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the classic risk factor combination for developing Fournier's gangrene?
options: Immunocompetent patient + penetrating injury
Female sex + hypertension + smoking
Young healthy athlete + minor wound
Male sex + diabetes + perineal trauma or local infection
Elderly woman + varicose veins
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Male sex + diabetes + perineal trauma or local infection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene predominantly affects men (10:1 M:F ratio) — classic risk factors: diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, perianal/urological procedures, or local infection as a trigger.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the gold standard for diagnosing necrotising fasciitis definitively?
options: Surgical exploration (biopsy + direct visualisation of necrotic fascia)
Contrast CT scan showing fascial thickening and subcutaneous gas tracking
MRI demonstrating deep fascial oedema with T2 hyperintense fluid signal
LRINEC score ≥8 combined with raised C-reactive protein and creatinine
Blood cultures growing Group A Streptococcus with positive Gram stain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Surgical exploration (biopsy + direct visualisation of necrotic fascia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Only surgical exploration can definitively confirm NF — finger sweep test (fascial planes separate without resistance) and grey necrotic fascia are diagnostic. No imaging has 100% sensitivity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 60-year-old with PAD presents with gangrene of the left big toe. ABI is 0.4. What should be considered before amputation?
options: Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) to improve perfusion
Immediate above-knee amputation without any vascular imaging beforehand
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and serial observation of the toe only
Systemic warfarin anticoagulation targeting an INR of 2 to 3 first
Compression bandaging of the limb to reduce oedema before surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) to improve perfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Before amputation, consider revascularisation to improve distal blood supply — successful bypass may allow a more distal (digit-only) amputation rather than a major limb amputation. ABI 0.4 = severe ischaemia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What skin finding is pathognomonic for gas gangrene?
options: Non-blanching purpuric petechial rash over the dependent limbs
Erythema migrans — an expanding annular rash with central clearing
Target lesion with concentric erythematous rings and dusky centre
Painless indurated ulcer with a rolled raised pearly heaped edge
Crepitus (crackling sensation) + bronze-brown discoloration of skin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Crepitus (crackling sensation) + bronze-brown discoloration of skin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Crepitus = gas in soft tissue from Clostridium fermentation — pathognomonic of gas gangrene when combined with bronze discoloration and systemic toxicity. X-ray may show gas in muscle planes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the most important prognostic factor in necrotising fasciitis?
options: The admission laboratory LRINEC risk score
Choice of first empirical antibiotic combination
Advancing chronological age of the patient
Presence of subcutaneous gas on the CT scan
Speed of surgical debridement (time to theatre)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Speed of surgical debridement (time to theatre)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Every hour of delay increases mortality in NF — early aggressive surgical debridement is the single most important intervention. Antibiotics alone cannot control the infection; surgery achieves source control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of wet gangrene?
options: Moist, swollen, oedematous discoloured tissue with blistering
Foul-smelling purulent discharge from the necrotic wound margins
Rapid uncontrolled proximal spread along the deep tissue planes
Overwhelming systemic sepsis with hypotension and organ failure
Clear demarcation line with mummified tissue (this is dry gangrene)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Clear demarcation line with mummified tissue (this is dry gangrene)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Wet gangrene has blurred margins, rapid spread, moist tissue, and foul odour. A clear demarcation line and mummified tissue are features of DRY gangrene (ischaemic origin, no infection initially).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) indication applies to necrotising fasciitis?
options: Clostridial gas gangrene with myonecrosis and tissue crepitus present
Every case of necrotising fasciitis routinely as first-line therapy
Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF (Group A Strep)
Fournier's perineal gangrene only, regardless of causative organism
MRSA-associated necrotising fasciitis confirmed on tissue culture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF (Group A Strep)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: IVIG neutralises superantigen exotoxins from Group A Streptococcus — used as adjunct in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome complicating NF. Not routine for all NF types.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the recommended amputation level when a patient has gangrene of toes with a non-reconstructable arterial supply?
options: Above ankle (below-knee or above-knee depending on blood supply)
Always above-knee regardless of the calf and thigh blood supply
Always digital ray amputation confined to the affected toes only
Knee disarticulation performed through the joint in every patient
Amputation exactly at the visible level of demarcated gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Above ankle (below-knee or above-knee depending on blood supply)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Amputation level depends on adequate blood supply at the stump for healing — typically BKA or AKA. Amputation through ischaemic tissue fails to heal. Doppler pressures and skin perfusion mapping guide level.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: A 58-year-old diabetic has a foot ulcer with surrounding crepitus and gas on X-ray but no systemic sepsis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Outpatient dressings and antibiotics
Urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
Observation only
Hyperbaric oxygen as sole treatment
CT scan and delay 24 hours
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas in soft tissue = gas-forming infection (possibly gas gangrene) even without obvious systemic sepsis — requires urgent surgical debridement and IV antibiotics. Gas in tissue = do not wait.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the mortality of untreated gas gangrene?
options: Zero mortality once hyperbaric oxygen therapy is commenced early
Around 10% mortality when the infection is left entirely untreated
Around 50% mortality even with surgery and intravenous antibiotics
Under 5% mortality when treated with intravenous antibiotics alone
Near 100% without treatment; ~20–30% with surgery + antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Near 100% without treatment; ~20–30% with surgery + antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Gas gangrene is rapidly lethal without surgical debridement. Even with optimal treatment, mortality is 20–30%. Alpha-toxin from C. perfringens causes massive haemolysis, multi-organ failure, and cardiovascular collapse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which population is at highest risk for non-clostridial gas gangrene (polymicrobial)?
options: Young healthy athletes
Diabetics with foot infections
Post-partum women
Immunocompetent post-surgical patients
Haemophilia patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Diabetics with foot infections
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Polymicrobial gas-forming infections in diabetic feet (E. coli, Klebsiella, Bacteroides) are more common than clostridial gas gangrene. Poorly controlled diabetics with peripheral neuropathy and vascular disease are highest risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What is the 'finger sweep' test in suspected NF?
options: Bedside test assessing capillary refill and perfusion in cold ischaemic toes distal to an occluded artery in peripheral vascular disease
Bedside test assessing the sharpness and clarity of the mummified demarcation line separating dead dry gangrenous tissue from viable skin
Surgical test: finger inserted through small incision — absence of resistance to blunt dissection along fascial planes confirms NF
Palpation test checking for subcutaneous crepitus and gas in the perineum and scrotum of a patient with suspected Fournier's gangrene
Handheld continuous-wave Doppler test assessing arterial flow signals within the digital vessels of the ischaemic gangrenous toes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Surgical test: finger inserted through small incision — absence of resistance to blunt dissection along fascial planes confirms NF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: The finger sweep test is intraoperative: a finger passed through a small fascial incision slides easily along necrotic fascial planes without resistance — confirms NF. Normal tissue resists blunt dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: What organisms are implicated in Fournier's gangrene (perineal necrotising fasciitis)?
options: Staphylococcus aureus alone acting as the sole causative organism spreading through the perineal soft tissues
Polymicrobial synergistic infection — aerobic Gram-negative rods + anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa alone as the single Gram-negative pathogen, without anaerobic or coliform co-infection
Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes only, driving the infection monomicrobially as in type 2 NF
Candida albicans as an invasive monomicrobial fungal pathogen destroying the perineal and scrotal soft tissue
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Polymicrobial synergistic infection — aerobic Gram-negative rods + anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is polymicrobial — synergistic infection by aerobic Gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella) and anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridia). The combination drives rapid tissue destruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: Which imaging is most useful for surgical planning in necrotising fasciitis (showing gas and spread along fascial planes) without delaying surgery?
options: Duplex USS
Plain X-ray
CT with IV contrast
MRI
PET scan
