conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: CT with IV contrast
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: CT with contrast shows gas tracking along fascial planes, the extent of infection, fluid collections and compartment involvement, and is fast — useful for surgical planning. Necrotising fasciitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis and imaging must NOT delay emergency surgical debridement. (MRI is more sensitive for soft-tissue extent but is slower and rarely appropriate acutely.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the 'hallmark' clinical finding of necrotising fasciitis that distinguishes it from all other soft tissue infections?
options: Disproportionately severe pain with anaesthesia of the skin (nerve destruction)
High swinging fever alone without any accompanying local skin change
A soft fluctuant swelling indicating a drainable subcutaneous abscess
Copious purulent discharge exuding from the surface of the wound bed
A positive wound swab culture growing the responsible pathogenic organism
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.answer: Disproportionately severe pain with anaesthesia of the skin (nerve destruction)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Gangrene.explanation: NF destroys nerve fibres as it spreads — early: disproportionate severe pain; late: paradoxical anaesthesia (nerves dead). This combination of pain then anaesthesia in rapidly progressing soft tissue infection = NF until proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: After confirming a tachycardia (HR >100 bpm), what is the first and most important ECG step?
options: Analyse the P waves
Assess the axis
Check the PR interval
Measure the QRS duration
Count the atrial rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Measure the QRS duration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The QRS width is the critical first fork: it determines whether the rhythm is narrow (supraventricular) or broad (ventricular until proven otherwise) and dictates the entire management pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A QRS duration <120 ms in a tachycardia implies which origin, and why?
options: Ventricular, because the impulse bypasses the His-Purkinje system
Supraventricular, because the impulse uses the normal His-Purkinje system
Either origin equally
Accessory pathway only
Sinus node only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Supraventricular, because the impulse uses the normal His-Purkinje system
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A narrow QRS means the ventricles are activated normally via the His-Purkinje system, guaranteeing a supraventricular origin ('narrow = safe').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the key rule for any broad-complex (QRS ≥120 ms) tachycardia?
options: Assume SVT with aberrancy
Assume it is benign if the patient is stable
Give verapamil first
Always perform vagal manoeuvres first
Treat as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: It is the QRS width, not the presumed origin, that triggers this rule. Never assume SVT with aberrancy without senior review.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which of the following is a cause of a REGULAR narrow-complex tachycardia?
options: Atrial fibrillation
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
AVNRT
Pre-excited AF
Torsades de pointes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AVNRT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Regular narrow-complex causes include sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia and atrial flutter with fixed block. AF and MAT are irregular; pre-excited AF and torsades are broad.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why is pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) particularly dangerous?
options: It invariably triggers immediate ventricular standstill and asystole, as the pathway abruptly ceases all conduction
It cannot be electrically cardioverted, because the accessory pathway keeps conducting despite a synchronised DC shock
It is completely resistant to every antiarrhythmic drug and to electrical therapy, so no intervention restores perfusion
It occurs exclusively in patients with underlying structural heart disease, never in those with a normal heart
It can produce a broad, irregular tachycardia that mimics VF; giving AV nodal blockers can precipitate VF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: It can produce a broad, irregular tachycardia that mimics VF; giving AV nodal blockers can precipitate VF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Blocking the AV node forces conduction down the accessory pathway, which can accelerate the ventricular rate and degenerate into VF. AV nodal blockers must be avoided.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: On a tachycardia ECG, a completely irregular rhythm with no pattern suggests which diagnosis?
options: Atrial flutter with fixed block
Sinus tachycardia
AVNRT
AF or multifocal atrial tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AF or multifocal atrial tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A completely irregular (no pattern) rhythm points to AF or MAT. Irregularity with a pattern (e.g. varying groups) suggests atrial flutter with variable block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In narrow-complex P-wave analysis, a sawtooth baseline at ~300 bpm indicates which rhythm?
options: Sinus tachycardia
Atrial flutter
Atrial fibrillation
AVNRT
Atrial tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Atrial flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm (best seen in II, III, aVF and V1) indicate atrial flutter.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A narrow-complex tachycardia shows a buried P wave producing a pseudo-R' in V1. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
options: AVNRT
AVRT
Atrial tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia
Atrial flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AVNRT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A pseudo-R' in V1 (or pseudo-S in II/aVF) from a P wave buried just after the QRS is characteristic of AVNRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why must you NOT proceed to P-wave analysis once you identify a broad QRS tachycardia?
options: P waves are never present in any tachycardia, so searching for them is futile
A broad QRS always means the patient is haemodynamically unstable and periarrest
P-wave analysis is only valid in bradycardia, never in any form of tachyarrhythmia
It wastes valuable time that is better spent giving IV verapamil to slow the rate
Broad QRS = VT until proven otherwise; you check for VT features instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Broad QRS = VT until proven otherwise; you check for VT features instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Step 2 (QRS width) is a hard fork: broad-complex rhythms go straight to the VT feature checklist, not to P-wave analysis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What ECG finding describes P waves marching through independently of the QRS complexes, and what does it indicate?
options: Concordance — indicates SVT
Sawtooth waves — indicates flutter
Capture beats — indicates aberrancy
Delta waves — indicates WPW
AV dissociation — diagnostic of VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation — diagnostic of VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AV dissociation means the atria and ventricles are beating independently, which is diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which set of ECG findings are all diagnostic features of VT in a broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Sawtooth flutter waves, delta waves, and a short PR interval
Irregular fibrillatory f-waves, absent P waves, and a narrow QRS
A pseudo-R' in lead V1, a short RP interval, and an abrupt onset
AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats, concordance
A prolonged QT, a twisting QRS axis, and waxing-waning amplitude
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats, concordance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats and concordance (all V leads deflecting the same direction) all favour VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Regardless of the rhythm diagnosis, what does haemodynamic instability in a tachycardia mandate?
options: Immediate IV adenosine given as a rapid 6 mg bolus to break the rhythm
Vagal manoeuvres such as the modified Valsalva or carotid sinus massage
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (or defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF)
Oral beta-blockade with bisoprolol to gradually slow the ventricular rate
Watchful waiting with continuous monitoring until the rhythm is identified
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (or defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The stability override: instability = immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. Do not delay to identify the rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which of the following counts as a feature of an UNSTABLE tachycardia?
options: Palpitations alone
Mild breathlessness
Anxiety
A heart rate of 110 bpm
Hypotension with SBP <90 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Hypotension with SBP <90 mmHg
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Instability features are hypotension (SBP <90), reduced consciousness, ischaemic chest pain and acute pulmonary oedema. Palpitations, mild breathlessness and anxiety do not constitute instability.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Do palpitations, anxiety, and mild breathlessness alone constitute haemodynamic instability in a tachycardia?
options: Yes, these symptoms always mandate urgent synchronised cardioversion
No, the threshold is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse
Only if the ventricular rate climbs above 150 beats per minute
Only in patients older than 65 years with these same symptoms
Yes, but only when the rhythm is a broad-complex tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: No, the threshold is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The threshold for instability is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse — not symptoms like palpitations, anxiety or mild breathlessness.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the central conceptual question that guides treatment of any stable tachycardia?
options: Is the QT interval prolonged?
Is the AV node in the circuit?
Is the patient over 65?
Is there a delta wave?
Is the rhythm regular?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Is the AV node in the circuit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Whether the AV node is part of the circuit determines whether AV nodal blocking agents will terminate, merely slow, or endanger the patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In which pair of rhythms do AV nodal blockers TERMINATE the arrhythmia because the node is part of the re-entry circuit?
options: AF and atrial flutter
AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT
Sinus tachycardia and atrial tachycardia
VT and pre-excited AF
MAT and torsades
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT the AV node is an essential part of the circuit, so nodal blockers terminate the rhythm. In AF/flutter/atrial tachycardia they only slow the rate; in VT/pre-excited AF they are dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In which rhythm are AV nodal blockers dangerous because the node is NOT in the circuit?
options: AVNRT
Pre-excited AF (WPW)
Orthodromic AVRT
Sinus tachycardia
Atrial flutter with fixed block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF (WPW)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In pre-excited AF, blocking the AV node forces all conduction down the accessory pathway, risking VF. Nodal blockers are also dangerous/useless in VT and antidromic AVRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which mnemonic summary correctly captures when adenosine is safe in a stable tachycardia?
options: Broad + irregular → AV node not involved → adenosine is safe and reliably terminates the rhythm
Irregular + narrow → AV-node-dependent → adenosine safely and reliably terminates the rhythm
Any tachycardia at all → adenosine is the universal first-line agent that safely terminates it
Broad + regular → give IV verapamil, which safely terminates the ventricular re-entry circuit
Narrow + regular + no pre-excitation → AV-node-dependent → adenosine safe and likely terminates
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Narrow + regular + no pre-excitation → AV-node-dependent → adenosine safe and likely terminates
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A narrow, regular tachycardia without pre-excitation is AV-node-dependent, so adenosine is safe and likely to terminate it. Any broad-complex rhythm is treated as VT; never give verapamil to a broad-complex rhythm.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In the Resus Council adult tachycardia algorithm, which is a recognised life-threatening (unstable) feature?
options: Palpitations
Isolated dizziness
Mild anxiety
A rate of 120 bpm
Syncope
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Syncope
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The four life-threatening features are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and severe heart failure. Their presence prompts synchronised DC shock up to 3 attempts.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In the Resus algorithm, an unstable tachycardia with life-threatening features is managed with synchronised DC shock up to 3 attempts. What is given if this is unsuccessful?
options: Adenosine 6 mg IV push, then repeat the shock if needed
Verapamil 5 mg IV over 2 min, then repeat the shock
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 10 min, then reshock
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min, then repeat the shock
Oral bisoprolol 5 mg, then repeat the shock once more
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min, then repeat the shock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: If up to 3 synchronised shocks fail, give amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min and then repeat the synchronised DC shock.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly ~150 bpm should raise suspicion of which rhythm until proven otherwise?
options: Sinus tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
AVNRT
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The 150 bpm trap: a regular narrow tachycardia at ~150 is atrial flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise; P (flutter) waves may be hidden in the T waves, and adenosine can unmask them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: As part of the ABCDE assessment of any tachycardia, which action is recommended?
options: Give IV amiodarone empirically to every patient regardless of the rhythm
Start oral anticoagulation first, before securing IV access or an ECG
Immediately cardiovert every patient before any further ABCDE assessment
Withhold supplemental oxygen regardless of the measured oxygen saturations
Obtain IV access and record a 12-lead ECG, and identify/treat reversible causes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Obtain IV access and record a 12-lead ECG, and identify/treat reversible causes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The ABCDE approach includes giving oxygen if SpO₂ <94%, obtaining IV access, monitoring and recording a 12-lead ECG, and identifying/treating reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte abnormalities, hypovolaemia causing sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What three features do all irregular narrow-complex tachycardias share?
options: Broad QRS complexes, a regular rhythm, and the AV node within the circuit
Narrow QRS complexes, a regular rhythm, and a fixed 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship
Narrow QRS, irregularly irregular rhythm, no consistent P–QRS relationship
Broad QRS complexes, an irregular rhythm, and pre-excitation delta waves
Narrow QRS complexes, sawtooth flutter waves, and a fixed AV conduction block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Narrow QRS, irregularly irregular rhythm, no consistent P–QRS relationship
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: All three (AF, variable-block flutter, MAT) share a narrow QRS, an irregularly irregular rhythm and no consistent P–QRS relationship; the AV node is a bystander, not part of the circuit.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG feature distinguishes multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) from atrial fibrillation?
options: ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead
Absent P waves with a chaotic baseline
Sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm
A fixed 2:1 block
A delta wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: MAT shows ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in one lead with varying PR intervals. AF has no P waves (chaotic f-waves); flutter has sawtooth waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the underlying electrical mechanism of atrial fibrillation?
options: Multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets with no single focus
A single ectopic focus firing rapidly
A macro re-entry circuit around the tricuspid annulus
Re-entry within the AV node
An accessory pathway bypassing the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets with no single focus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AF is disorganised atrial activity driven by multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets, with no single focus and no coordinated atrial contraction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: By approximately how much does AF increase stroke risk compared with the general population?
options: Five-fold
Three-fold
Two-fold
Ten-fold
No increase
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Five-fold
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Stasis in the left atrial appendage promotes thrombus formation, increasing stroke/TIA risk approximately five-fold (×5).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How is paroxysmal AF defined?
options: Continuous AF lasting more than 7 days that needs cardioversion to terminate
AF persisting beyond 12 months with rhythm control still being attempted
Self-terminating <7 days (usually <48h), sinus rhythm restored spontaneously
AF in which cardioversion is abandoned and only rate control is pursued
AF occurring in a patient with a prosthetic mechanical heart valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Self-terminating <7 days (usually <48h), sinus rhythm restored spontaneously
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Paroxysmal AF self-terminates within 7 days (usually <48h). Persistent is >7 days needing cardioversion; permanent is when cardioversion is abandoned.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which patient has valvular AF, mandating warfarin rather than a DOAC?
options: AF with well-controlled essential hypertension on a single agent
AF with mild, haemodynamically insignificant mitral regurgitation
AF with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus managed on metformin
AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve
AF with stable chronic ischaemic heart disease and prior stenting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Valvular AF = AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve, and requires warfarin (DOACs are contraindicated). All other AF is non-valvular → DOACs preferred.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In the SMITH mnemonic for AF causes, what does the 'T' represent, and what investigation does it prompt?
options: Thyroid (hyperthyroidism) — always check TFTs in new AF
Trauma — order an urgent CT of the head and chest
Thromboembolism — send a D-dimer and arrange a CTPA
Tamponade — order an urgent bedside echocardiogram
Toxins — send a urine and serum toxicology screen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Thyroid (hyperthyroidism) — always check TFTs in new AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The 'T' is Thyroid; hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause, so TFTs should always be checked in new AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the most common modifiable cause of AF worldwide?
options: Alcohol
Hypertension
Hyperthyroidism
Obesity
Caffeine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Hypertension is the most common modifiable cause of AF worldwide (the 'H' in SMITH).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A young patient develops paroxysmal AF after a weekend of heavy drinking. What is this called?
options: Holiday heart syndrome
Lone AF
Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
Permanent AF
Valvular AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Holiday heart syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Binge drinking triggering paroxysmal AF is known as holiday heart syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the hallmark ECG feature of atrial fibrillation?
options: Regular sawtooth-shaped atrial flutter waves at about 300 per minute
A slurred delta wave with a characteristically short PR interval
An irregularly irregular rhythm with no two R-R intervals equal
Regular narrow QRS complexes at a rate of about 150 per minute
Complete AV dissociation, with atria and ventricles beating separately
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: An irregularly irregular rhythm with no two R-R intervals equal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The irregularly irregular rhythm is the hallmark, with absent P waves replaced by fibrillatory f-waves (atrial rate 350–600 bpm).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why is the ventricular rate in AF (typically 100–160 bpm) slower than the atrial rate (350–600 bpm)?
options: The accessory pathway limits conduction
Beta-blockers are always present
The His-Purkinje system blocks most beats
The SA node overrides the atria
The AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The AV node acts as a gatekeeper, filtering the chaotic atrial impulses so only some conduct to the ventricles.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient with AF is haemodynamically unstable. What is the immediate management?
options: Anticoagulate for 3 weeks first, then cardiovert
Start oral bisoprolol
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of onset time
Perform a TOE before any intervention
Give IV digoxin and observe
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of onset time
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Unstable AF requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion; do not delay for anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which first-line rate-control agent for AF should be AVOIDED in decompensated heart failure?
options: Digoxin
Flecainide
Amiodarone
A beta-blocker
Adenosine
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A beta-blocker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Beta-blockers are first-line for rate control but should be avoided in decompensated HF. CCBs are avoided in HFrEF; digoxin suits sedentary patients or HF with AF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient presents with AF of unknown onset (likely >48h) and is stable. How should cardioversion be approached?
options: Perform a TOE to exclude LA appendage thrombus, OR anticoagulate ≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks after
Cardiovert immediately without any anticoagulation, as the rhythm is well tolerated and stable
Give IV adenosine to chemically cardiovert the AF back into sinus rhythm without any delay
Anticoagulate with a treatment-dose DOAC for just 24 hours, then proceed to cardioversion
Never attempt cardioversion in AF of unknown onset; commit to lifelong rate control instead
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Perform a TOE to exclude LA appendage thrombus, OR anticoagulate ≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks after
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: For AF >48h or unknown onset, either a TOE excludes an LA appendage thrombus, or the patient is anticoagulated for ≥3 weeks before and ≥4 weeks after cardioversion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which agent is used for chemical cardioversion of AF in a patient with NO structural heart disease?
options: Amiodarone
Adenosine
Digoxin
Verapamil
Flecainide
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Flecainide
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Flecainide is used when there is no structural heart disease; amiodarone is chosen if there is structural heart disease or HF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: On the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, how many points are awarded for age ≥75?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Age ≥75 scores 2 points, as does prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (S₂). Age 65–74 scores 1.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A male patient with AF has a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 2. What is the appropriate decision?
options: Anticoagulate — benefit clearly outweighs risk
No anticoagulation needed
Aspirin only
Repeat the score in 12 months
Cardiovert without anticoagulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Anticoagulate — benefit clearly outweighs risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A score ≥2 in males (or ≥3 in females) means anticoagulation is recommended as the benefit clearly outweighs the bleeding risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which anticoagulant is preferred for non-valvular AF?
options: A DOAC (e.g. apixaban, rivaroxaban)
Warfarin
Aspirin
Low-dose heparin indefinitely
Clopidogrel
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A DOAC (e.g. apixaban, rivaroxaban)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: DOACs are preferred for non-valvular AF. Warfarin is required for valvular AF (mechanical valve, moderate-to-severe MS).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the critical slow zone of the macro re-entry circuit in typical atrial flutter, and ablating it is curative?
options: The AV node
The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI)
The Bundle of Kent
The pulmonary vein ostia
The SA node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Typical flutter circulates around the tricuspid annulus; the cavotricuspid isthmus (between the tricuspid valve and IVC) is the critical slow zone, and CTI ablation is curative in ~95%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How does the energy required for cardioversion of atrial flutter compare with AF?
options: Flutter requires much higher energy than AF, typically 200 J or more biphasic
Flutter is often more cardioversion-responsive, needing lower energy (50–100 J)
They require identical energy, since both are atrial re-entry arrhythmias
Flutter cannot be electrically cardioverted and needs overdrive pacing instead
Flutter responds only to chemical cardioversion with IV flecainide, not shocks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Flutter is often more cardioversion-responsive, needing lower energy (50–100 J)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Flutter is often more responsive to cardioversion than AF and needs lower energy (50–100 J biphasic). Anticoagulation thresholds are the same as AF (stroke risk equivalent).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why is electrical cardioversion ineffective in multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
options: The rhythm is far too rapid for the defibrillator to synchronise onto
The broad QRS complexes prevent the shock from capturing the myocardium
MAT is caused by multiple ectopic foci, not a single re-entry circuit
The AV node absorbs and blocks the delivered shock before it reaches the atria
MAT is almost always a pulseless rhythm needing unsynchronised defibrillation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: MAT is caused by multiple ectopic foci, not a single re-entry circuit
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: MAT arises from multiple ectopic atrial foci firing chaotically — there is no single re-entry circuit for a shock to interrupt, so cardioversion is ineffective.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient with COPD develops MAT. What is the preferred rate-control agent, and what is avoided?
options: Beta-blocker preferred; avoid calcium-channel blockers, which worsen bronchospasm
CCB (verapamil/diltiazem) preferred; avoid beta-blockers in bronchospasm
Digoxin preferred; avoid amiodarone owing to its pulmonary toxicity in COPD
Adenosine preferred; avoid flecainide, which is contraindicated in lung disease
Amiodarone preferred; avoid magnesium, which precipitates bronchospasm in COPD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: CCB (verapamil/diltiazem) preferred; avoid beta-blockers in bronchospasm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In MAT (often associated with COPD), a CCB is preferred for rate control, and beta-blockers are avoided in bronchospasm. The cornerstone is treating the underlying cause.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Does multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) require routine anticoagulation?
options: No — it does not carry the same stroke risk as AF/flutter
Yes, exactly the same anticoagulation regimen as is used for AF
Yes, but with warfarin only, as DOACs are contraindicated in MAT
Only when the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score reaches 2 or greater
Yes, lifelong DOAC therapy is required in every single case
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: No — it does not carry the same stroke risk as AF/flutter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: MAT does not carry the same stroke risk as AF or flutter, so routine anticoagulation is not required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Into which three groups are regular narrow-complex tachycardias divided by their relationship to the AV node?
options: Fast, slow, and irregular, grouped purely by the ventricular rate
Stable, unstable, and pulseless, grouped by haemodynamic status
Atrial, junctional, and ventricular, grouped by their site of origin
Re-entry with AV node in circuit; AV node bystander; normal pacemaker
Pre-excited, aberrant, and idiopathic, grouped by conduction pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Re-entry with AV node in circuit; AV node bystander; normal pacemaker
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Group A = re-entry with AV node IN the circuit (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT); Group B = AV node bystander (atrial tachycardia, fixed 2:1 flutter); Group C = normal pacemaker (sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A regular narrow tachycardia is seen at exactly ~150 bpm. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
options: Sinus tachycardia
AVNRT
Atrial tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The 150 bpm trap: assume atrial flutter with 2:1 block. P (flutter) waves may be hidden in the T waves; adenosine can unmask them.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the most common paroxysmal SVT, and who does it most commonly affect?
options: Atrial tachycardia; elderly men
AVNRT; young adults, more commonly women
Orthodromic AVRT; older women
Atrial flutter; patients with COPD
Sinus tachycardia; athletes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AVNRT; young adults, more commonly women
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AVNRT is the most common paroxysmal SVT, affecting young adults and more commonly women, with abrupt onset and offset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the most useful single ECG sign of AVNRT?
options: A delta wave
AV dissociation
Sawtooth waves in II/III/aVF
A pseudo-R' in V1
A long RP interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A pseudo-R' in V1
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In AVNRT the P wave is buried in or just after the QRS, producing a pseudo-R' in V1 (the most useful sign) or a pseudo-S in II/III/aVF, with a short RP interval.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the first-line manoeuvre in the acute treatment of stable AVNRT?
options: Adenosine 6 mg by rapid IV bolus into a large proximal vein
Amiodarone 300 mg IV infused over ten to twenty minutes
Verapamil 5 mg IV given slowly over two to three minutes
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under conscious sedation
Vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva or carotid sinus massage)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva or carotid sinus massage)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Step 1 is vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva with legs elevated, or carotid sinus massage), which terminate ~25% of episodes. Adenosine is Step 2 if these fail.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient is given adenosine for AVNRT. What should they be warned about, and in which condition is it contraindicated?
options: Warn of flushing, chest tightness and brief asystole; contraindicated in asthma and high-degree AV block
Warn of throbbing headache and lightheadedness; contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension and stable angina
Warn of transient limb weakness and paraesthesia; contraindicated in poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
Warn of a widespread urticarial rash; contraindicated in chronic kidney disease and renal impairment
Warn of transient blurred vision; contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma and raised intraocular pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Warn of flushing, chest tightness and brief asystole; contraindicated in asthma and high-degree AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node, causing flushing, chest tightness and brief asystole (seconds). It is contraindicated in asthma and high-degree AV block.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the curative long-term treatment for recurrent AVNRT?
options: Lifelong amiodarone
ICD implantation
Permanent pacemaker
Slow-pathway catheter ablation
Accessory pathway ablation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Slow-pathway catheter ablation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Slow-pathway catheter ablation is curative (>95% success, low risk of AV block). Flecainide or a beta-blocker can be used for prevention beforehand.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In orthodromic AVRT, what is the path of conduction that results in a narrow QRS?
options: Down the accessory pathway, up the AV node
Entirely within the AV node
Around the tricuspid annulus
Down the AV node, up the accessory pathway
Down both pathways simultaneously
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Down the AV node, up the accessory pathway
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Orthodromic = conduction down the AV node (normal ventricular activation → narrow QRS) and retrograde up the accessory pathway.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How does the P-wave position in orthodromic AVRT typically differ from AVNRT?
options: P wave is buried within the QRS complex in AVRT but clearly visible before the QRS in AVNRT (short PR)
P waves are completely absent in both AVRT and AVNRT because the atria never depolarise during the tachycardia
P wave is clearly visible after the QRS in AVRT (longer RP), but buried in/just after the QRS in AVNRT
AVRT shows sawtooth flutter waves whereas AVNRT shows chaotic fibrillatory f-waves scattered between the QRS complexes
There is no reliable difference in P-wave position between AVRT and AVNRT on the surface ECG at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: P wave is clearly visible after the QRS in AVRT (longer RP), but buried in/just after the QRS in AVNRT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In orthodromic AVRT the retrograde P is clearly visible after the QRS (longer RP, though still RP < PR), whereas in AVNRT it is buried in or just after the QRS (very short RP).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What are the ECG hallmarks of WPW seen in sinus rhythm?
options: A prolonged PR and a U wave
A long QT interval
Sawtooth flutter waves
An irregularly irregular rhythm
A short PR interval and a delta wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A short PR interval and a delta wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In sinus rhythm, the accessory pathway pre-excites the ventricle, producing a short PR and a delta wave (δ) — the diagnostic hallmark of pre-excitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why does orthodromic AVRT produce a narrow QRS while antidromic AVRT produces a broad QRS?
options: Antidromic uses the His-Purkinje system to depolarise both ventricles rapidly and evenly, while orthodromic bypasses it, so the QRS width simply reflects which system is used
Antidromic AVRT is always faster than orthodromic, and this higher ventricular rate is what mechanically broadens the QRS complex seen on the surface ECG
They are determined by the heart rate alone, faster rates always narrowing the QRS and slower rates always widening it, regardless of the conduction pathway used
Orthodromic AVRT occurs only in structural heart disease, which narrows the QRS, whereas antidromic arises in structurally normal hearts and therefore broadens it
Orthodromic conducts down the AV node (normal activation → narrow); antidromic conducts down the accessory pathway, bypassing His-Purkinje → broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Orthodromic conducts down the AV node (normal activation → narrow); antidromic conducts down the accessory pathway, bypassing His-Purkinje → broad
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Orthodromic (~95%) activates ventricles via normal wiring → narrow QRS. Antidromic (~5%) goes antegrade down the accessory pathway into ventricular muscle, bypassing His-Purkinje → abnormal spread → broad QRS (mimics VT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In a WPW patient in sinus rhythm with orthodromic AVRT, what should be avoided long-term, and why?
options: Beta-blockers, because they cause bronchospasm
Statins, because of myopathy
AV nodal blockers, because of the risk of pre-excited AF
Anticoagulation, because of bleeding
Vagal manoeuvres, because they are ineffective
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV nodal blockers, because of the risk of pre-excited AF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: If WPW is present in sinus rhythm, AV nodal blockers are avoided long-term because of the risk that, should AF develop, blocking the node forces conduction down the accessory pathway (pre-excited AF → VF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the shared principle for Group B (AV node bystander) regular narrow tachycardias regarding adenosine?
options: Adenosine reliably terminates them by breaking the re-entry circuit within the AV node with a single rapid bolus
Adenosine is absolutely contraindicated because it dangerously accelerates conduction down the accessory pathway
Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction to unmask atrial activity (diagnostic) but does not terminate
Adenosine permanently cures them by ablating the abnormal atrial focus after just one or two intravenous boluses
Adenosine accelerates them by enhancing AV nodal conduction and markedly shortening the atrial refractory period
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction to unmask atrial activity (diagnostic) but does not terminate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In Group B the AV node conducts but is not part of the sustaining circuit, so adenosine unmasks the underlying atrial activity diagnostically but does not terminate the rhythm; management is rate control.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What feature of onset distinguishes atrial tachycardia from AVNRT/AVRT?
options: A gradual 'warm-up' (rate accelerates at the start)
An abrupt, instantaneous onset at full rate every time
Onset occurring exclusively during deep sleep at night
Onset triggered only by strenuous physical exertion
It characteristically has no identifiable onset at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A gradual 'warm-up' (rate accelerates at the start)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Atrial tachycardia shows a 'warm-up' phenomenon (gradual acceleration), distinguishing it from AVNRT/AVRT, which have an abrupt onset.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient on digoxin develops atrial tachycardia. What is a key management step?
options: Treat the underlying cause — suspect digoxin toxicity and stop digoxin
Increase the digoxin dose to regain adequate rate and rhythm control
Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to terminate the tachycardia
Perform immediate synchronised DC cardioversion without any delay
Start IV amiodarone promptly while continuing the current digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat the underlying cause — suspect digoxin toxicity and stop digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Atrial tachycardia is often caused by digoxin toxicity; the key step is to treat the cause (stop digoxin), alongside rate control with beta-blockers or CCBs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the ECG signature of atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block?
options: Atrial rate ~300 with 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150, regular; sawtooth waves (may hide in T waves)
Atrial rate ~150 with 1:1 AV conduction → ventricular rate ~150, regular, with clearly separate upright P waves
Irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves and a chaotic, constantly varying ventricular response
Broad QRS complexes with clear AV dissociation and independent atrial and ventricular rates marching apart
Short PR interval with a slurred delta wave at the very start of a broadened QRS complex on every beat
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Atrial rate ~300 with 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150, regular; sawtooth waves (may hide in T waves)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Fixed 2:1 flutter has an atrial rate ~300 conducting 2:1 → regular ventricular rate ~150, with sawtooth flutter waves (inverted in II/III/aVF; upright in V1) that may be hidden in the T waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the key principle when managing sinus tachycardia?
options: Always rate-block it immediately with an intravenous beta-blocker to bring the heart rate safely under control
It is always a response to something — identify and treat the cause rather than blindly slowing the rate
Perform urgent synchronised DC cardioversion whenever the ventricular rate climbs above 150 beats per minute
Start long-term oral anticoagulation guided strictly by the patient's calculated CHA₂DS₂-VASc stroke score
Give a rapid intravenous bolus of adenosine to block the AV node and promptly terminate the tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: It is always a response to something — identify and treat the cause rather than blindly slowing the rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is physiologically appropriate; rate-blocking without addressing the underlying driver can be dangerous.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG feature is characteristic of sinus tachycardia rather than another regular narrow tachycardia?
options: A normal upright P wave before every QRS with identical morphology, and gradual onset/offset
P waves completely buried within each QRS complex and never visible anywhere on the surface ECG
Sawtooth flutter waves seen best in the inferior leads at an atrial rate of around 300 per minute
A slurred delta wave preceding a broadened QRS with a characteristically short PR interval
An abrupt on-off pattern, with the tachycardia starting and stopping instantaneously at full rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A normal upright P wave before every QRS with identical morphology, and gradual onset/offset
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sinus tachycardia has a normal upright P before every QRS (identical morphology), a normal PR interval, and gradual (not abrupt) onset and offset, with the rate varying with respiration and activity.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In the PIRATES mnemonic for sinus tachycardia causes, what does the 'A' represent?
options: Anaemia, Anxiety, Alcohol withdrawal
Arrhythmia, Aneurysm, Asthma
Aortic stenosis, Angina, Ascites
Acidosis, Apnoea, Allergy
Atrial flutter, AVNRT, AVRT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Anaemia, Anxiety, Alcohol withdrawal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: PIRATES: Pain/PE/Pneumothorax, Infection/Sepsis/Inflammation, Respiratory failure (hypoxia), Anaemia/Anxiety/Alcohol withdrawal, Thyrotoxicosis/Tamponade, Exercise/Electrolyte imbalance, Shock/Stimulants.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the unifying question that determines management across all regular narrow-complex tachycardias?
options: Is the QT prolonged?
Is the AV node part of the circuit?
Is the patient young or old?
Is there structural heart disease?
Is the rhythm broad or narrow?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Is the AV node part of the circuit?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Yes → terminate (Group A: vagal/adenosine/ablation). No, but conduction via it → rate control (Group B; adenosine is diagnostic only). No, physiological → treat the cause (Group C: sinus tachycardia).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the 'Golden Rule' for any regular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Assume SVT with aberrancy and give IV verapamil to block the AV node and terminate the tachycardia
Treat as VT until proven otherwise — misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker can be fatal
Treat it as sinus tachycardia and focus on identifying and correcting the underlying physiological cause
Always give a rapid intravenous bolus of adenosine first to unmask and terminate the underlying rhythm
Only bother treating the rhythm at all once the patient becomes haemodynamically unstable or collapses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat as VT until proven otherwise — misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker can be fatal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Treating SVT as VT is always safe, but misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker (verapamil/diltiazem) can be fatal.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which of the following is one of the three causes of a regular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Atrial fibrillation
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
SVT with aberrancy (bundle branch block)
Torsades de pointes
Sinus tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: SVT with aberrancy (bundle branch block)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three causes are VT (most common, default assumption), SVT with aberrancy (SVT + BBB), and SVT with pre-excitation (antidromic AVRT).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why does ventricular tachycardia produce a wide QRS?
options: The impulse originates below the His bundle and spreads cell-to-cell (not via His-Purkinje), causing slow abnormal depolarisation
The impulse travels through the His-Purkinje system extremely rapidly, activating both ventricles at once and widening the QRS
An accessory pathway pre-excites the ventricle early, so the impulse bypasses the AV node and produces a broad slurred complex
The AV node conducts far too quickly, overwhelming the His-Purkinje system and forcing slow abnormal ventricular depolarisation
The atria depolarise the ventricles directly across the valve rings, bypassing the conduction system and broadening the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The impulse originates below the His bundle and spreads cell-to-cell (not via His-Purkinje), causing slow abnormal depolarisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: VT arises below the His bundle in ventricular myocardium and spreads cell-to-cell rather than via the fast His-Purkinje system, producing slow depolarisation and a wide QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the most common substrate for ventricular tachycardia?
options: An accessory pathway conducting antegrade to pre-excite the ventricle
A prolonged QT interval triggering early afterdepolarisations
Re-entry around scar from a prior MI / ischaemic heart disease
An automatic ectopic atrial focus firing faster than the sinus node
Enhanced automaticity within the AV node driving the ventricles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Re-entry around scar from a prior MI / ischaemic heart disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Re-entry around scar tissue from a prior MI or ischaemic heart disease is the most common substrate for VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In a patient with known ischaemic heart disease, what is the approximate pre-test probability that a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT?
options: About 25%
About 50%
Over 95%
About 75%
Under 10%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Over 95%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In a patient with known IHD or prior MI, the scar provides the re-entry substrate, raising the pre-test probability of VT to >95%. It is VT until definitively proven otherwise.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in a regular broad-complex tachycardia is haemodynamically stable and chatting comfortably. What does this tell you about the diagnosis?
options: Haemodynamic stability does NOT rule out VT — a common, dangerous trap
It confirms SVT with aberrancy conducting through an intact His-Purkinje system
It reliably rules out VT, since true VT always causes haemodynamic collapse
It means the underlying rhythm is entirely benign and needs no urgent treatment
It indicates the AV node forms part of the re-entry circuit driving the rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Haemodynamic stability does NOT rule out VT — a common, dangerous trap
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Patients can be in VT and remain haemodynamically stable. Stability does not exclude VT and must not be used to downgrade the diagnosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG finding has HIGH specificity for VT (rather than merely supporting it)?
options: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS marching independently)
An extreme north-west (superior) frontal QRS axis
A broad QRS duration measuring greater than 140 ms
A documented history of previous myocardial infarction
An atypical bundle branch block QRS morphology pattern
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS marching independently)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AV dissociation, capture beats, fusion beats and concordance are high-specificity (near-diagnostic) features. A very broad QRS, extreme axis, prior MI and atypical BBB are supportive but less specific.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is a capture beat, and what does it indicate?
options: A hybrid intermediate QRS formed when two impulses collide and merge together — indicates simple SVT
A beat carrying a slurred delta wave and short PR interval — indicates underlying Wolff-Parkinson-White
A QRS that widens further only at faster ventricular rates — indicates rate-dependent aberrant conduction
An occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles — diagnostic of VT
A completely dropped beat with a missing QRS after a P wave — indicates underlying high-grade AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: An occasional narrow QRS when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles — diagnostic of VT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A capture beat is a rare narrow QRS amid the broad complexes, occurring when a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles. With fusion beats, it is diagnostic of VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in stable, sustained monomorphic VT is to be treated pharmacologically (first-line UK). Which drug and regimen is used?
options: Adenosine 6 mg by rapid intravenous bolus, then 12 mg
Verapamil 5 mg by slow intravenous injection over 2 min
Flecainide 2 mg/kg intravenously over 10-30 minutes
Magnesium sulphate 2 g intravenously given over 10 min
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: First-line UK treatment of stable VT is amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24h maintenance, with electrolyte correction. Procainamide or lidocaine are alternatives.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A patient in VT becomes hypotensive and confused (unstable). What is the immediate management?
options: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20-60 minutes via central line
Synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious)
Adenosine 12 mg by rapid intravenous bolus into a large vein
Vagal manoeuvres such as carotid sinus massage or Valsalva
Oral beta-blockade with bisoprolol for urgent rate control
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Unstable VT requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (sedate first if conscious). If pulseless, treat as VF with unsynchronised defibrillation and CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the mechanism of SVT with aberrancy?
options: A ventricular focus firing below the His bundle and spreading cell-to-cell through myocardium, giving a broad abnormal QRS
A markedly prolonged QT interval triggering early afterdepolarisations and degenerating into polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
An accessory pathway conducting antegrade to pre-excite the ventricle ahead of the AV node, producing a broad slurred QRS
Multiple chaotic atrial wavelets bombarding the AV node irregularly and conducting down with variable aberrancy → broad QRS
A supraventricular rhythm conducting normally to the AV node, then blocked/delayed in one bundle branch below it → broad QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A supraventricular rhythm conducting normally to the AV node, then blocked/delayed in one bundle branch below it → broad QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In SVT with aberrancy the supraventricular impulse reaches the AV node normally, but below it conduction is blocked/delayed in one bundle branch, so the ventricle depolarises via the opposite bundle → slow spread → broad QRS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which feature would favour SVT with aberrancy rather than VT?
options: Clear AV dissociation with P waves marching through the QRS
Intermittent capture beats and fusion beats during the run
Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology with P waves 1:1 to the QRS
Positive concordance across all six precordial chest leads
QRS duration over 140 ms with an extreme north-west axis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology with P waves 1:1 to the QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Classic RBBB/LBBB morphology, 1:1 P:QRS, no AV dissociation/capture/fusion, identity to a prior ECG with BBB, and termination with adenosine all favour SVT with aberrancy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Adenosine is being considered to help diagnose a broad-complex tachycardia. When is this acceptable?
options: In all broad-complex tachycardias, since adenosine is a safe universal first-line agent whatever the mechanism
Only if the patient is haemodynamically unstable, when adenosine works faster and more safely than a DC shock
Only if you are confident it is NOT VT (old ECG showing BBB, no structural disease, stable, classic SVT history)
Never under any circumstances, because adenosine is absolutely contraindicated in every broad-complex rhythm
Only when the ventricular rate exceeds 200 bpm, as adenosine is ineffective at any slower tachycardia rate
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Only if you are confident it is NOT VT (old ECG showing BBB, no structural disease, stable, classic SVT history)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Adenosine can be diagnostically useful in suspected SVT with aberrancy, but only when you are confident it is not VT. When in doubt, treat as VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which describes the classic RBBB vs LBBB morphology used to identify aberrancy?
options: RBBB: rS in V1, R in V6; LBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6
RBBB: AV dissociation; LBBB: capture beats
Both show a delta wave in V1
Both show concordance across V1–V6
RBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6; LBBB: rS in V1, R in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: RBBB: rSR' in V1, qRs in V6; LBBB: rS in V1, R in V6
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Classic RBBB shows rSR' in V1 and qRs in V6; classic LBBB shows rS in V1 and R in V6. Atypical morphology that doesn't fit these patterns favours VT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: In antidromic AVRT, what is the path of conduction and the resulting QRS?
options: Antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the His-AV node → very broad, slurred QRS
Antegrade down the AV node and His-Purkinje, retrograde up the accessory pathway → narrow, normal QRS
Macro-re-entry circling the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium → sawtooth flutter waves at ~300 bpm
Re-entry confined within the compact AV node using dual pathways → narrow QRS with a pseudo-R' in V1
Impulse arising entirely within ventricular myocardium below the His → broad QRS with AV dissociation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the His-AV node → very broad, slurred QRS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Antidromic AVRT conducts antegrade down the accessory pathway (maximal pre-excitation of the ventricle → very broad, slurred QRS) and retrograde up the His-AV node. It is the opposite of orthodromic AVRT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why are AV nodal blockers dangerous in antidromic AVRT / pre-excited WPW?
options: They block retrograde AV conduction and may force all conduction antegrade down the accessory pathway → risk of VF
They markedly prolong the QT interval and trigger polymorphic torsades de pointes by blocking cardiac potassium channels
They cause only profound sinus bradycardia and prolonged asystole from excessive AV nodal suppression, with no other harm
They are simply pharmacologically ineffective at the accessory pathway and carry no real danger whatsoever to the patient
They precipitate severe bronchospasm and acute respiratory compromise through beta-2 receptor blockade in the airways
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: They block retrograde AV conduction and may force all conduction antegrade down the accessory pathway → risk of VF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) block retrograde AV conduction, potentially forcing all conduction down the accessory pathway and risking VF. Use flecainide or procainamide (or DC cardioversion).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which clue on the baseline ECG points towards antidromic AVRT as the cause of a broad-complex tachycardia?
options: A markedly prolonged QT interval on the baseline ECG
Sawtooth flutter waves seen in the inferior leads
A history of WPW or a delta wave on the baseline ECG
An irregularly irregular rhythm with no clear P waves
A pathological Q wave from a previous old infarct
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: A history of WPW or a delta wave on the baseline ECG
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: A history of WPW or a δ-wave on the baseline ECG is a diagnostic clue. Antidromic AVRT shows no AV dissociation, as the AV node is part of the circuit retrogradely.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which set of features all FAVOUR VT in the VT-vs-SVT decision?
options: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance, QRS >140 ms, known IHD
Classic RBBB/LBBB, 1:1 P:QRS, terminates with adenosine, young patient
Short PR, delta wave, narrow QRS, no structural disease
Sawtooth waves, fixed block, rate ~150
f-waves, no P waves, irregular rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, concordance, QRS >140 ms, known IHD
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Features favouring VT include AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, precordial concordance, QRS >140 ms, extreme/north-west axis, known IHD/prior MI, structural heart disease and atypical BBB morphology.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: You cannot confidently exclude VT in a stable broad-complex tachycardia. What is the safest approach?
options: Treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex rhythm
Give IV verapamil to test the response and terminate the rhythm if it is a supraventricular tachycardia
Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to unmask atrial activity and terminate it if it is truly supraventricular
Discharge home the same day with routine outpatient cardiology follow-up and an ambulatory Holter monitor
Start regular oral flecainide as a pill-in-the-pocket to chemically suppress the broad-complex rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Treat as VT (amiodarone IV); never give verapamil/diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex rhythm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Doubt = VT. If you cannot confidently exclude VT, treat it as VT and never give verapamil or diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex tachycardia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What are the three safety rules summarising the VT-vs-SVT approach?
options: Rate-control the ventricular response, anticoagulate to prevent thromboembolic stroke, then electively cardiovert
Adenosine first to break the circuit, verapamil second for rate control, then amiodarone third if both fail
Stability first (unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion); doubt = VT; the unifying question 'Could this be VT?'
Always attempt vagal manoeuvres first, then a trial of IV adenosine, and finally a synchronised DC shock
Identify buried P waves, measure the PR interval, and assess the frontal-plane QRS axis to reach a diagnosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Stability first (unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion); doubt = VT; the unifying question 'Could this be VT?'
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three rules: (1) stability first — unstable → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of diagnosis; (2) doubt = VT — treat as VT if VT cannot be excluded; (3) the unifying question — 'Could this be VT?' If yes, treat as VT and step down only with clear evidence and specialist input.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the danger instinct to apply to any irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: Assume ordinary AF with a rate-related bundle branch block and give an IV beta-blocker for rate control
Assume it is simply sinus tachycardia with aberrancy and focus solely on treating the underlying cause
Think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise; never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers
Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to terminate the re-entrant circuit and restore sinus rhythm promptly
Treat every case as torsades de pointes and empirically give IV magnesium sulphate to all such patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise; never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Irregular + broad narrows to a short list of high-risk rhythms; reflexively giving AV-nodal blockers can be fatal (especially in pre-excited AF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which are the three causes of an irregular broad-complex tachycardia?
options: VT, SVT with aberrancy, antidromic AVRT
Sinus tachycardia, atrial tachycardia, flutter
AF, atrial flutter, MAT
AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia
Pre-excited AF, polymorphic VT/torsades, AF with BBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF, polymorphic VT/torsades, AF with BBB
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: The three causes are 5A pre-excited AF (WPW+AF), 5B polymorphic VT/torsades, and 5C AF with BBB.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why are the ventricles bombarded at near-atrial rates in pre-excited AF?
options: The AV node abnormally conducts far faster than normal, losing its decremental delay and passing every atrial impulse straight through
The sinoatrial node itself fires at an extremely rapid rate and drives the ventricles directly at near-atrial frequencies throughout
The His-Purkinje conduction system fails and depolarises passively, letting the rapid atrial impulses flood the ventricles unchecked
The chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating
The patient's regular oral beta-blockers have worn off, removing the pharmacological brake that normally slows AV nodal conduction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: The chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node's protective rate-limiting gating
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: In WPW, AF impulses bypass the AV node's gating and conduct directly down the accessory pathway, so the ventricles are bombarded at near-atrial rates (often >200 bpm ventricular).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which ECG features are characteristic of pre-excited AF?
options: Perfectly regular rhythm, narrow QRS complexes, and clear sawtooth flutter waves between the beats
QRS complexes that twist and rotate around the baseline on a background of a markedly prolonged QT
Irregular R-R, broad QRS, very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, no organised P waves
Regular 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship with a classic broad left bundle branch block morphology throughout
Regular broad complexes at a fixed rate with clear AV dissociation and occasional capture beats seen
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Irregular R-R, broad QRS, very fast (>200 bpm), varying QRS width beat-to-beat, no organised P waves
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Pre-excited AF shows irregular R-R (underlying AF), broad QRS (via the accessory pathway), a very fast ventricular rate (>200 bpm), beat-to-beat varying QRS width (fusion), and no organised P waves.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which drugs must NEVER be given in pre-excited AF?
options: AV-nodal blockers — adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin
The class I antiarrhythmic drugs flecainide, procainamide and disopyramide
Electrolyte replacement with IV magnesium sulphate and potassium chloride
The class III agent amiodarone together with the class Ib drug lidocaine
Supplemental high-flow oxygen together with intravenous crystalloid fluids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: AV-nodal blockers — adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: These block the AV node and force all conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme rate acceleration → VF.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: A stable patient with pre-excited AF and no structural heart disease needs pharmacological treatment. What is first-line?
options: Verapamil IV
Metoprolol IV
Digoxin IV
Adenosine IV
Flecainide IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Flecainide IV
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Flecainide IV is first-line if there is no structural heart disease; procainamide is the alternative (safe with structural disease). Both slow accessory pathway conduction rather than blocking the AV node.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How is unstable pre-excited AF managed?
options: A rapid IV adenosine bolus of 12 mg via a large-bore cannula to break the accessory-pathway circuit
A loading dose of oral flecainide as a pill-in-the-pocket to chemically restore sinus rhythm
Slow IV verapamil 5 mg for rate control, repeated to 10 mg if the fast ventricular rate persists
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF)
Vagal manoeuvres such as carotid sinus massage and a modified Valsalva to terminate the tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR if it degenerates to VF)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Unstable pre-excited AF requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion; if it degenerates to VF, give unsynchronised defibrillation and CPR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What specifically defines torsades de pointes (as opposed to other polymorphic VT)?
options: Polymorphic VT arising on a background of an entirely normal QT interval
Pre-excited AF conducting down an accessory pathway in WPW syndrome
Monomorphic VT occurring in a patient with structural heart disease
Irregularly irregular AF conducting with a broad bundle-branch QRS
Polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Polymorphic VT occurring on a background of a prolonged QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT (continuously varying QRS morphology/axis, 'twisting around the baseline') occurring on a background of prolonged QT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What corrected QT (QTc) values are considered prolonged?
options: >400 ms (men) / >420 ms (women)
>440 ms (men) / >460 ms (women)
>480 ms (men) / >500 ms (women)
>350 ms in both
>500 ms in both
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: >440 ms (men) / >460 ms (women)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: QT is measured from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave; a QTc >440 ms in men or >460 ms in women is prolonged.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which is a recognised drug cause of a prolonged QT predisposing to torsades?
options: The cardioselective beta-blocker bisoprolol given once daily
The ACE inhibitor ramipril used widely in hypertension
Macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin, clarithromycin)
The dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker amlodipine
Low-dose aspirin used for cardiovascular prevention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g. erythromycin, clarithromycin)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: High-yield QT-prolonging drugs include antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antipsychotics, antidepressants (citalopram, TCAs), macrolides, antiemetics (ondansetron) and antimalarials.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which is the MOST common electrolyte cause of a prolonged QT?
options: Hyperkalaemia
Hypokalaemia
Hypernatraemia
Hypercalcaemia
Hypermagnesaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Hypokalaemia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Hypokalaemia is the most common electrolyte cause; hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia also prolong the QT by impairing repolarisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the first-line treatment for stable torsades de pointes, and the key point about it?
options: IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20-60 min as the definitive first-line rhythm control
IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — given even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal
A rapid IV adenosine 6 mg bolus to break the re-entrant circuit and restore sinus
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation as the first-line treatment
IV flecainide as a class Ic agent to chemically terminate the arrhythmia at once
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — given even if the serum Mg²⁺ is normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min is first-line, given even with a normal serum Mg²⁺ because it stabilises cardiac membranes. Do not wait for a low level before giving it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which drug should be AVOIDED in torsades de pointes, and why?
options: Magnesium, because it lowers the heart rate
Potassium, because it worsens repolarisation
Amiodarone, because it itself prolongs the QT
Lidocaine, because it is ineffective
Atropine, because it causes tachycardia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Amiodarone, because it itself prolongs the QT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Amiodarone is avoided in torsades because it prolongs the QT, which is the underlying problem. Stop all QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolytes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Why is sotalol an important exception when considering beta-blockers in long QT?
options: Sotalol usefully shortens the QT interval, making it the safest beta-blocker to use in patients with congenital long QT
Sotalol works mainly by blocking conduction through the accessory pathway, which is why it is favoured in long QT syndrome
Sotalol is the recommended first-line drug for actively terminating torsades de pointes and preventing its recurrence
Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, unlike other beta-blockers which are safe and used in congenital LQTS
Sotalol is absolutely contraindicated in every arrhythmia and must never be used for rhythm or rate control at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, unlike other beta-blockers which are safe and used in congenital LQTS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Sotalol prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, so it must not be confused with other beta-blockers, which are QT-safe and actually used in congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Which device intervention can be used acutely in torsades because it shortens the QT?
options: A permanent pacemaker set to a slow rate
Temporary (overdrive) pacing
An implantable loop recorder
CRT
A defibrillator vest only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Temporary (overdrive) pacing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Temporary overdrive pacing increases the heart rate, which shortens the QT and can suppress torsades. An ICD is used for recurrent or congenital LQTS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: What is the mechanism of AF with bundle branch block?
options: Fibrillatory AF impulses conduct rapidly down an accessory pathway, bypassing the AV node and pre-exciting the ventricles broadly
Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB providing the broad QRS, with the AV node intact
A single irritable ventricular ectopic focus firing irregularly and driving the ventricles independently of any atrial activity
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arising on a background of a markedly prolonged QT interval producing broad varying complexes
Macro-re-entry circling the tricuspid annulus with variable AV block giving irregular broad conducted complexes at the ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) plus a pre-existing or rate-related BBB providing the broad QRS, with the AV node intact
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: AF provides the irregularity and the BBB provides the broad QRS. The AV node remains intact and rate-limiting (ventricular rate rarely >180 bpm) — it's 'just AF that looks broad'.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: How can pre-excited AF be distinguished from AF with BBB?
options: AF with BBB is the faster of the two, consistently exceeding 200 bpm with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width, whereas pre-excited AF stays slower with a fixed morphology
Pre-excited AF is very fast (>200 bpm) with varying beat-to-beat QRS width and a WPW/δ-wave history; AF with BBB is slower (<180 bpm) with fixed BBB morphology
Both conditions show completely identical ventricular rates and identical fixed QRS morphology, so they simply cannot be told apart on the surface ECG at all
Pre-excited AF characteristically shows a single fixed bundle branch block morphology at a slow rate, while AF with BBB varies its QRS width markedly beat to beat
AF with BBB reliably shows a slurred delta wave and a short PR on the baseline tracing, which is the key feature separating it from pre-excited AF conduction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.answer: Pre-excited AF is very fast (>200 bpm) with varying beat-to-beat QRS width and a WPW/δ-wave history; AF with BBB is slower (<180 bpm) with fixed BBB morphology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.explanation: Pre-excited AF: rate >200, varying QRS width, WPW/δ-wave history, treat with flecainide/DC. AF with BBB: rate <180, fixed BBB morphology, known BBB/structural disease, treat with rate control + anticoagulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Tachycardia.question: Once pre-excited AF is confidently excluded, how is AF with BBB managed?
options: Give a rapid IV adenosine bolus to terminate the rhythm and restore normal sinus conduction
Use IV flecainide to slow conduction through the accessory pathway and safely narrow the QRS
Give IV magnesium sulphate and institute overdrive pacing to suppress the irregular broad rhythm
Manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker/CCB/digoxin) and anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc
