A sudden arterial occlusion presenting acutely with the classic six P's of the limb
An ABPI greater than 1.2 in a diabetic due to heavily calcified incompressible vessels
Painless neuropathic ulcers over the pressure points of the sole with intact foot pulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Any of: rest pain >2 weeks requiring opiates, ischaemic ulceration, gangrene, ABPI <0.5
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: CLI is defined by any of: rest pain >2 weeks requiring opiates, ischaemic ulceration, gangrene, or ABPI <0.5.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Why is the rest pain of critical limb ischaemia worse at night, and what gives relief?
options: The colder night air causing arterial vasospasm; relieved by actively warming the foot
Loss of gravity-assisted perfusion when supine; hanging the foot off the bed
Increased muscular activity during sleep; relieved by resting the leg still
Pooling of venous blood in the dependent calf; relieved by elevating the leg
Compression of the tibial nerve while lying flat; relieved by massaging the sole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Loss of gravity-assisted perfusion when supine; hanging the foot off the bed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: CLI rest pain is worse at night because lying supine loses gravity-assisted perfusion; the patient hangs the foot off the bed for relief, and opiates are required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: When is amputation indicated in critical limb ischaemia?
options: Routinely for all patients with critical limb ischaemia regardless of whether the limb is salvageable
If the limb is unreconstructable, or there is extensive necrosis/sepsis/limited life expectancy
Whenever the ABPI falls below 0.9, since this level always signals unsalvageable dead tissue
As the first-line intervention offered before any attempt at angioplasty or bypass grafting
Only when the patient specifically requests it, never on clinical or surgical grounds at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: If the limb is unreconstructable, or there is extensive necrosis/sepsis/limited life expectancy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Amputation in CLI is reserved for an unreconstructable limb or extensive necrosis/sepsis/limited life expectancy; revascularisation is otherwise attempted.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is the cardinal warning combination in acute limb ischaemia that indicates irreversible ischaemia is imminent?
options: Pain + pallor
Pallor + perishing cold
Pulselessness + perishing cold
Paralysis + paraesthesia
Pain + pulselessness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Paralysis + paraesthesia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: In acute limb ischaemia, paralysis + paraesthesia together mean irreversible ischaemia is imminent — act immediately.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Within the 6 P's of acute limb ischaemia, which is described as a LATE sign of irreversible ischaemia?
options: Pain
Paralysis
Pulselessness
Paraesthesia
Pallor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Paralysis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Paralysis (motor loss) is the LATE sign of irreversible ischaemia in the 6 P's and mandates urgent surgery; paraesthesia is the earlier sign of a threatened limb.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What does 'perishing cold' (poikilothermia) mean in acute limb ischaemia?
options: The limb is warmer than the body
The limb is numb only
The limb is hot and swollen
The limb temperature fluctuates rapidly
The limb temperature equals the environment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: The limb temperature equals the environment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Perishing cold means poikilothermia — the limb temperature equals the environment.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: How is an embolic cause of acute limb ischaemia distinguished from thrombosis in situ by onset and prior history?
options: Embolus: gradual onset with prior claudication; thrombosis: sudden, no claudication
Embolus: prior claudication; thrombosis: no symptoms
Both: sudden with no prior history
Embolus: sudden (<24h), no prior claudication; thrombosis: prior claudication with acute deterioration
Both present identically
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Embolus: sudden (<24h), no prior claudication; thrombosis: prior claudication with acute deterioration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: An embolus causes sudden (<24h) onset with no prior claudication, while thrombosis in situ presents with prior claudication and acute deterioration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Which sources are typical of an embolic acute limb ischaemia?
options: Rupture of a chronic atherosclerotic plaque in situ
AF, mural thrombus post-MI, AAA, prosthetic valve
Long-standing deep venous valvular insufficiency
Peripheral diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy
Tight four-layer compression bandaging of the limb
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: AF, mural thrombus post-MI, AAA, prosthetic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Embolic sources include AF, mural thrombus post-MI, AAA and prosthetic valve; thrombosis in situ arises from atherosclerotic plaque rupture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: How do the contralateral leg pulses differ between embolus and thrombosis in acute limb ischaemia?
options: Embolus: reduced from diffuse disease; thrombosis: normal with a healthy contralateral limb
Embolus: completely absent pulses; thrombosis: abnormally bounding, easily palpable pulses
Both remain entirely normal, so the pulses cannot help distinguish the two causes at all
Both are equally reduced because widespread atherosclerosis is invariably present in each
Embolus: normal (localised disease); thrombosis: reduced (widespread atherosclerosis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Embolus: normal (localised disease); thrombosis: reduced (widespread atherosclerosis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: In embolus the other leg has normal pulses (localised disease); in thrombosis the other leg has reduced pulses (widespread atherosclerosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Which medication is given in acute limb ischaemia to prevent clot propagation?
options: IV clopidogrel
IV penicillin
IV atorvastatin
IV naftidrofuryl
IV heparin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: IV heparin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: IV heparin is given in acute limb ischaemia to prevent propagation of the clot; IV opioids are used for pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What findings in acute limb ischaemia indicate an irreversible limb requiring amputation?
options: Mottled non-blanching skin + woody hard muscles
Marked pallor of the foot with reduced ankle pulses
Mild paraesthesia of the toes as the only sign
A perishingly cold foot on palpation as the sole sign
A crisp, normal handheld arterial Doppler signal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Mottled non-blanching skin + woody hard muscles
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Mottled non-blanching skin plus woody hard muscles indicate an irreversible limb requiring amputation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is reperfusion injury after revascularisation, and what does it cause?
options: Rapid re-occlusion of the freshly opened artery by fresh propagating thrombus within hours
A massive saddle pulmonary embolism thrown off from the reperfused deep limb veins
Immediate full-thickness gangrene of the revascularised foot developing within minutes
A retrograde aortic dissection propagating up from the treated arterial segment
Compartment syndrome (→ fasciotomy), hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuria → AKI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Compartment syndrome (→ fasciotomy), hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuria → AKI
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Reperfusion injury after revascularisation causes compartment syndrome (needing fasciotomy), hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and myoglobinuria leading to AKI.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: An ulcer is deep, 'punched-out', well-defined with a necrotic base, located distally on the toes/heel, and painful (worse on elevation). Which type is it?
options: Venous ulcer
Malignant ulcer
Neuropathic ulcer
Pressure ulcer
Arterial ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Arterial ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Arterial ulcers (PAD/ischaemia) are deep, punched-out, well-defined with a necrotic base, located distally (toes, heel, pressure points), and painful and worse on elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: A shallow, irregular ulcer with a granulating base at the gaiter area (medial malleolus), with surrounding haemosiderin staining, is which type?
options: Arterial ulcer
Dry gangrene
Neuropathic ulcer
Gas gangrene
Venous ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Venous ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Venous ulcers (venous insufficiency, 80% of ulcers) are shallow and irregular with a granulating base at the gaiter area, with haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema and lipodermatosclerosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: A painless punched-out ulcer surrounded by callus on the sole/metatarsal heads in a diabetic is which type?
options: Arterial ulcer
Venous ulcer
Pressure sore
Wet gangrene
Neuropathic ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Neuropathic ulcer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Neuropathic ulcers (neuropathy from diabetes or B12 deficiency) are painless, punched-out and surrounded by callus, at pressure points such as the sole and metatarsal heads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is the key management of a venous ulcer, and the precaution before it?
options: Revascularise; check renal function
IV antibiotics; check cultures
Offloading; glycaemic control
Amputation; check life expectancy
Compression bandaging; check ABPI ≥0.8 first
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Compression bandaging; check ABPI ≥0.8 first
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Venous ulcers are managed with compression bandaging, but ABPI must be checked (≥0.8) first to exclude arterial disease; arterial ulcers are revascularised and neuropathic ulcers are offloaded with glycaemic control and foot care.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is safety rule 2 regarding a deep neuropathic ulcer?
options: Always apply firm compression bandaging directly over the open ulcer
Take the patient straight to theatre for immediate limb revascularisation
X-ray for osteomyelitis — if bone is visible, osteomyelitis is confirmed
Never debride the wound, as removing dead tissue always spreads infection
Apply compression as soon as the ABPI has been checked and documented
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: X-ray for osteomyelitis — if bone is visible, osteomyelitis is confirmed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Safety rule 2: X-ray any deep neuropathic ulcer for osteomyelitis — if bone is visible, osteomyelitis is confirmed.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Which type of gangrene is ischaemic, aseptic, dehydrated, mummified and black with a well-defined demarcation line?
options: Wet gangrene
Gas gangrene
Dry gangrene
Necrotising fasciitis
Venous gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Dry gangrene
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Dry gangrene is ischaemic and aseptic — dehydrated, mummified, black, with a well-defined demarcation line; it is the classic PAD endpoint, typically affecting digits.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Wet gangrene is which combination, and how is it managed?
options: Pure ischaemia with no infection present; simply allow the dry toe to auto-amputate
Blunt limb trauma alone; manage with simple observation and elevation only
Infection alone with good perfusion; treat with a short oral antibiotic course
Ischaemia + infection; urgent debridement + IV antibiotics + revascularisation
Diabetic neuropathy alone; manage purely with pressure-offloading footwear
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Ischaemia + infection; urgent debridement + IV antibiotics + revascularisation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Wet gangrene is ischaemia + infection — moist, swollen, foul-smelling with no clear demarcation, a surgical emergency common in diabetics, managed with urgent debridement, IV antibiotics and revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Gas gangrene is caused by which organism, and what are its hallmark signs?
options: Staphylococcus aureus; thick yellow pus and abscess formation
Pseudomonas aeruginosa; a foul green-blue discharge from the wound
Group A streptococcus; a spreading erythematous cellulitis of the skin
Escherichia coli; a walled-off deep collection forming an abscess
Clostridium perfringens; crepitus on palpation + gas on X-ray
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Clostridium perfringens; crepitus on palpation + gas on X-ray
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens (post-trauma/contaminated wound), with crepitus on palpation and gas on X-ray, extremely rapid spread and life-threatening.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is the management of gas gangrene?
options: A course of oral antibiotics with watchful observation and simple daily wound dressings
Firm four-layer compression bandaging over the limb to control the spreading infection
Emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin/clindamycin + fasciotomies + hyperbaric O₂
Urgent arterial revascularisation alone, with no debridement or antibiotic cover needed
Simply allow the infected limb to demarcate and auto-amputate slowly over several weeks
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin/clindamycin + fasciotomies + hyperbaric O₂
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Gas gangrene is managed with emergency surgical debridement, IV penicillin/clindamycin, fasciotomies and hyperbaric O₂.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: Which is a listed primary indication for amputation in PAD?
options: A moderately reduced resting ABPI of 0.7
A shallow chronic venous gaiter ulcer
Stable intermittent calf claudication
Uncontrolled sepsis from an infected limb
A Buerger's angle of 30° on elevation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Uncontrolled sepsis from an infected limb
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Primary amputation indications include extensive weight-bearing necrosis, uncontrolled sepsis from an infected limb, paresis/irreversible ischaemia, limited life expectancy (palliation), and failed/impossible revascularisation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: A 62-year-old smoker presents with cramping calf pain on walking 200 metres that resolves with rest. ABI is 0.65. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
options: Musculoskeletal gastrocnemius strain — localised tenderness worse on the first steps, treat with rest, ice and oral analgesia
Venous claudication from outflow obstruction — bursting calf pain relieved by elevation, treat with compression stockings
Deep vein thrombosis — a hot swollen tender calf with a raised D-dimer, treat with low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulation
Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis — leg pain eased by bending forward, treat with physiotherapy and analgesia
Peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication) — supervised exercise programme + antiplatelet + statin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication) — supervised exercise programme + antiplatelet + statin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Intermittent claudication: exertional calf pain, ABI 0.5–0.9. First-line: supervised exercise (best evidence for improving walking distance), antiplatelet (aspirin/clopidogrel), statin. Revascularisation for lifestyle-limiting disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What ABI value is consistent with critical limb ischaemia?
options: ABI <0.5 (or ankle pressure <50 mmHg)
ABI 0.5–0.9 indicating mild claudication
ABI 0.9–1.2, the normal healthy range
ABI >1.3 from calcified stiff arteries
ABI 0.7–0.9 with only mild symptoms
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: ABI <0.5 (or ankle pressure <50 mmHg)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Critical limb ischaemia = rest pain + ABI <0.5, or tissue loss. Indicates severely compromised perfusion — risk of limb loss without revascularisation. Requires urgent vascular surgical referral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: A 70-year-old with diabetes presents with rest pain in the right foot, non-healing ulcer, and ABI 0.4. What is the management priority?
options: Start lifelong warfarin anticoagulation aiming for an INR of 2 to 3 to clear the block
Oral antibiotics with regular wound dressings only, avoiding any vascular intervention
Encourage a supervised walking exercise programme to build up collateral circulation
Urgent vascular surgical review for revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass)
Proceed straight to primary below-knee amputation as the very first step of care
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Urgent vascular surgical review for revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Critical limb ischaemia with tissue loss = vascular emergency — urgent revascularisation (angioplasty if suitable, bypass if not) to prevent limb loss. Wound care and antibiotics are adjuncts but revascularisation is the priority.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: What is Leriche's syndrome?
options: Superficial femoral artery occlusion causing isolated calf claudication with preserved femoral pulses
Aortoiliac occlusion causing buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses
A popliteal artery aneurysm shedding distal emboli that produce blue-toe syndrome in the foot
Takayasu large-vessel arteritis in young women causing absent upper-limb pulses and bruits
Subclavian steal syndrome, with arm exercise diverting vertebral flow and causing dizziness
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.answer: Aortoiliac occlusion causing buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Leriche's syndrome = bilateral aortoiliac occlusion: triad of buttock/thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction (internal iliac involvement), and absent femoral pulses. Treated by aortoiliac bypass or endovascular reconstruction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the ankle-brachial index (ABI) range for normal?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral A.explanation: Normal ABI = 0.9–1.2. <0.9 = PAD; 0.5–0.9 = intermittent claudication; <0.5 = critical ischaemia; >1.3 = non-compressible arteries (medial calcification in diabetes — falsely elevated, use toe-brachial index instead).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Why does the location of a thoracic aortic aneurysm matter so much?
options: It precisely reveals the patient's chronological age and predicts life expectancy
It drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds
It reliably alters the full blood count and clotting profile in a diagnostic way
It solely dictates the ultrasound surveillance interval and nothing else clinically
It carries no clinical relevance and never influences symptoms or management at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: It drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Location matters because it drives both the symptoms (compression syndromes) and the repair thresholds.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What proportion of TAAs occur at the ascending aorta/root, and what are the most common causes?
options: 10% — atherosclerosis
60% — Marfan's, bicuspid AV, syphilis
40% — dissection
10% — extends into abdomen
20% — Takayasu's
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: 60% of TAAs are at the ascending aorta/root, most commonly caused by Marfan's, bicuspid AV and syphilis, with a repair threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower in CT disease).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which TAA location has the highest repair threshold and a preference for TEVAR?
options: Ascending aorta — ≥5.5 cm
Aortic arch — ≥5.5 cm
Descending aorta — ≥6 cm, prefer TEVAR
Thoracoabdominal — ≥4 cm
Root — ≥4.5 cm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The descending aorta (40% of TAAs) has a higher threshold of ≥6 cm and prefers TEVAR; it is associated with posterior thoracic pain and atherosclerosis/dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How does TAA differ from AAA in aetiology and screening?
options: Both arise chiefly from atherosclerosis and both have national screening programmes
TAA: CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis, no national screening; AAA: atherosclerosis
TAA is caused by atherosclerosis, whereas AAA arises from Marfan's connective disease
Both share an identical atherosclerotic aetiology and identical screening pathways
TAA has a national ultrasound screening programme, whereas AAA has no screening at all
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: TAA: CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis, no national screening; AAA: atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TAA and AAA share definition and Laplace physics, but TAA has different aetiology (CT disease/bicuspid/syphilis vs atherosclerosis) and no national screening programme, unlike AAA.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is best described as what?
options: Intima + media rupture, blood contained only by adventitia
All 3 layers intact but dilated
Blood entering between the intima and media
Dilatation of all layers from atherosclerosis
A normal anatomical variant
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Intima + media rupture, blood contained only by adventitia
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: A false aneurysm involves rupture of intima and media with blood contained only by adventitia, caused by trauma, surgery or infection; a true aneurysm has all 3 layers intact but dilated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the mechanism of TAA formation?
options: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation
Acute thrombosis of the aortic lumen occludes flow, and the trapped high-pressure clot balloons the wall outward into an aneurysm
Progressive calcification of the intima stiffens the inner wall, which then bulges outward under arterial pressure to form the aneurysm
Immune complex deposition in the aortic wall drives inflammation that weakens the media and lets the vessel dilate into an aneurysm
Spasm of the vasa vasorum chokes the wall's blood supply, causing ischaemic injury that weakens the media and dilates the aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Tunica media degeneration → loss of tensile strength → dilatation → increased wall tension (Laplace) → further dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TAA forms by tunica media degeneration causing loss of tensile strength and dilatation, which increases wall tension (Laplace) and drives further dilatation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Approximately what proportion of people with a bicuspid aortic valve develop aortopathy (ascending aortic dilatation)?
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Around 50–70% of people with a bicuspid aortic valve develop some degree of aortopathy (ascending aortic dilatation) over time, from the shared connective-tissue/haemodynamic abnormality — hence the need for lifelong aortic surveillance. (Conversely, BAV underlies roughly 20–30% of ascending TAAs.)

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which cause is described as the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite?
options: Atherosclerosis
Trauma
Takayasu's arteritis
Tertiary syphilis
Marfan's syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Tertiary syphilis is the classic ascending aneurysm and an exam favourite.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is 'the discriminator' between TAA and AAA aetiology?
options: TAA → atherosclerosis; AAA → Marfan's and connective tissue disease
TAA → chronic infection such as syphilis; AAA → blunt traumatic injury
Both TAA and AAA → atherosclerosis as the shared underlying cause
TAA → Marfan's/EDS/bicuspid AV/syphilis; AAA → atherosclerosis
There is no reliable discriminator between TAA and AAA aetiology
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The discriminator: TAA points to Marfan's/EDS/bicuspid AV/syphilis, while AAA points to atherosclerosis — a frequently tested contrast.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How do most TAAs present?
options: With severe tearing chest pain radiating through to the back at onset
With haemoptysis from erosion of the aneurysm into the adjacent lung
Asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging
With sudden collapse and syncope from a transient fall in cardiac output
With progressive dysphagia from oesophageal compression by the aneurysm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Asymptomatic — found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Most TAAs are asymptomatic and found incidentally on CXR or cross-sectional imaging; there is no national screening programme.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which pain location corresponds to a descending aorta TAA?
options: Anterior chest pain
Neck pain
Left arm pain
Epigastric pain
Posterior thoracic/back pain
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Descending aorta TAA causes posterior thoracic/back pain; ascending → anterior chest pain; arch → neck pain.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A patient with a TAA develops a hoarse voice. Which structure is being compressed?
options: Trachea
Spinal cord
Oesophagus
SVC
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression causes a hoarse voice.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Distended neck veins and facial oedema in a TAA indicate compression of what?
options: SVC
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Oesophagus
Trachea/left bronchus
Spinal cord
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: SVC compression causes distended neck veins, facial oedema and SVC obstruction syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which compression effect produces dysphagia in TAA?
options: Trachea/left bronchus
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Aortic valve
SVC
Oesophagus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Oesophageal compression causes dysphagia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Aortic valve involvement in TAA leads to what?
options: Inspiratory stridor from tracheal compression
Aortic regurgitation → heart failure signs
A hoarse voice from recurrent laryngeal palsy
Dysphagia from external oesophageal compression
Interscapular back pain from local expansion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Aortic valve involvement causes aortic regurgitation, leading to heart failure signs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which of the following is a listed key differential for TAA?
options: Renal colic
Pneumothorax
Appendicitis
Diverticulitis
Ovarian torsion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Key differentials for TAA are PE, ACS, pneumothorax and aortic dissection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the role of ECG in the work-up of TAA?
options: Excludes ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN
Confirms the diagnosis of TAA
Measures aneurysm size
Assesses valve involvement
Detects mediastinal widening
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Excludes ACS; may show LVH from chronic HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: ECG is used to exclude ACS and may show LVH from chronic hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which CXR findings are characteristic of a TAA?
options: A boot-shaped cardiac silhouette with an upturned, uplifted cardiac apex
Inferior rib notching from enlarged, tortuous intercostal collateral vessels
Kerley B lines with upper-lobe pulmonary venous diversion and interstitial oedema
Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation
An isolated large left-sided pleural effusion with no other mediastinal changes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob, tracheal deviation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CXR shows a widened mediastinal silhouette, enlarged aortic knob and tracheal deviation — often the incidental finding.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which is the preferred/definitive imaging modality in TAA, and what does it provide?
options: CXR — incidental detection of a widened mediastinum
ECG — exclude acute coronary syndrome as the pain cause
CT angiogram — anatomy, size, extent, TEVAR suitability
TOE — valve assessment and proximal root imaging only
Routine bloods — baseline renal function and crossmatch
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: CT angiogram — anatomy, size, extent, TEVAR suitability
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CT angiogram is the preferred/definitive modality, giving anatomy, size, extent and TEVAR suitability for surgical planning.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: TOE is done in all of which patient group with TAA, and what does it assess?
options: All elderly patients — assesses aortic wall atherosclerotic plaque burden
All Marfan's patients — assesses valve involvement, AR, dissection
All hypertensive patients — assesses left ventricular hypertrophy severity
All smokers — assesses aneurysmal involvement of the adjacent lung tissue
All diabetics — assesses resting cardiac output and ejection fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: All Marfan's patients — assesses valve involvement, AR, dissection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TOE assesses valve involvement, AR and dissection, and is done in all Marfan's patients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which medical measure is the key modifiable factor for all TAA patients?
options: Statin
Antiplatelet
Weight loss
BP control
Smoking cessation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: BP control is the key modifiable factor; medical management also includes statin + antiplatelet, smoking cessation and optimising diabetes, hyperlipidaemia and weight.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the surgical threshold and procedure for an ascending/root TAA?
options: ≥6 cm; TEVAR stent graft deployed across the ascending aorta
≥5.5 cm; Dacron graft replacement, Bentall if root involved
≥4 cm; multi-limbed branched graft with valve sparing
≥5.5 cm; open repair only, never with a Bentall root graft
≥7 cm; continued observation with interval CT surveillance
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: ≥5.5 cm; Dacron graft replacement, Bentall if root involved
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Ascending/root TAA: threshold ≥5.5 cm (lower ~4.5–5 cm in Marfan's/bicuspid/CT disease); Dacron graft replacement, with a Bentall procedure if the root is involved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the procedure and key risk for an aortic arch TAA repair?
options: TEVAR stent graft across the arch; main risk is a type I endoleak with continued sac filling
Open repair via thoracotomy; main risk is spinal cord ischaemia causing paraplegia
Dacron tube graft replacement of the arch; carries no specific procedure-related risk
Bentall procedure with composite valved conduit; main risk is prosthetic valve failure
Multi-limbed graft (allows great vessel branching); high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Multi-limbed graft (allows great vessel branching); high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Aortic arch TAA (threshold ≥5.5 cm) is repaired with a multi-limbed graft allowing great vessel branching, carrying a high cerebral ischaemia/embolism risk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Why is the repair threshold lower (~4.5–5 cm) in Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos and bicuspid AV?
options: Because the aorta is inherently smaller in these patients
Because the wall is structurally weaker — operate earlier
Because these patients are younger with a longer life expectancy
Because TEVAR is absolutely contraindicated in these disorders
Because these connective tissue disorders cause atherosclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Because the wall is structurally weaker — operate earlier
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The threshold is lower in Marfan's/EDS/bicuspid AV because the wall is structurally weaker, so you operate earlier.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the Bentall procedure?
options: Aortic root replacement + prosthetic valve
Aortic arch multi-limbed graft
Endovascular stent across the descending aorta
Dacron tube graft of the descending aorta
Repair of a false aneurysm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The Bentall procedure is aortic root replacement plus a prosthetic valve — a key eponym.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: How is TEVAR performed?
options: Open chest on cardiopulmonary bypass, with the diseased descending segment excised and replaced by a sewn-in Dacron tube graft
A covered femoral stent graft advanced up into the abdominal aorta to line and exclude the diseased infrarenal segment from flow
Replacement of the aortic root with a mechanical valve and coronary reimplantation to restore flow through the ascending aorta
A multi-limbed branched graft sewn into the arch, allowing each great vessel to be reattached to a separate limb of the prosthesis
A stent graft delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: A stent graft delivered via catheter and deployed across the descending TAA, excluding the aneurysm from circulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TEVAR delivers a stent graft via catheter, deploying it across the descending TAA to exclude the aneurysm from circulation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: When a TAA ruptures, where does it bleed and what determines the clinical picture?
options: Into the peritoneal cavity; the clinical picture is determined by the patient's age
Into the retroperitoneum; the picture is determined solely by the blood pressure
Into the pleural space only; the clinical picture is always exactly the same
Into the pericardium only; the presentation never varies between patients
Into the mediastinum; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Into the mediastinum; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Rupture causes bleeding into the mediastinum with high mortality; the site of bleeding determines the clinical picture.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A ruptured TAA bleeding into the pericardial cavity produces what?
options: Haematemesis
Haemoptysis
Cardiac tamponade
Dysphagia
Stridor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Rupture into the pericardial cavity causes cardiac tamponade; into the oesophagus causes haematemesis, and into the airway/lungs causes haemoptysis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which signs accompany a ruptured TAA?
options: Reflex bradycardia with sustained hypertension, plus a bounding pulse and warm peripheries from raised cardiac output
Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension), signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension)
A malar flush with a loud first heart sound and an opening snap, pointing to coexisting rheumatic mitral stenosis
Bilateral papilloedema with cotton-wool spots and flame haemorrhages on fundoscopy from malignant hypertension
A pulsatile enlarged liver with giant V waves in the JVP, indicating severe tricuspid regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension), signs of tamponade (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Signs of a ruptured TAA include haemodynamic instability (tachycardia + hypotension) and tamponade signs (raised JVP, muffled sounds, hypotension).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the management of a ruptured TAA?
options: Emergency open surgical repair with synthetic graft replacement of the affected segment
TEVAR stent grafting alone in every case, regardless of the rupture site or the patient's stability
Permissive hypotension with fluid restriction and watchful observation, avoiding any surgery
Conservative management with tight blood pressure control and beta-blockade, deferring operation
A Bentall procedure with valved root conduit regardless of the rupture site
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Emergency open surgical repair with synthetic graft replacement of the affected segment
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: A ruptured TAA is managed with emergency open surgical repair and synthetic graft replacement of the affected segment; mortality is high.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A 45-year-old with Marfan syndrome has an ascending aortic aneurysm of 4.6 cm on CT. At what diameter should prophylactic surgery be offered?
options: Only once the aneurysm becomes symptomatic, irrespective of its measured diameter on imaging
≥6.0 cm, using the same fixed threshold for everyone regardless of Marfan's or connective disease
≥5.5 cm for all patients regardless of any underlying genetic or connective tissue disorder present
≥4.5–5.0 cm (or at smaller diameters if rapid expansion or genetic connective tissue disorder)
Only if the aneurysm extends to involve the arch vessels, irrespective of its diameter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: ≥4.5–5.0 cm (or at smaller diameters if rapid expansion or genetic connective tissue disorder)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Marfan syndrome and other connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve) have lower surgery thresholds (≥4.5–5.0 cm vs ≥5.5 cm for sporadic aneurysms) due to higher risk of dissection/rupture at smaller sizes.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the most common genetic condition associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm?
options: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation)
Turner syndrome
Down syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (classical type)
Loeys-Dietz syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation) causes cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall — predisposing to ascending aortic aneurysm and dissection. Also associated: bicuspid aortic valve, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Turner syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the surgical repair of ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm called?
options: Bentall procedure (if aortic root involved) or tube graft replacement
EVAR — an endovascular stent graft deployed within the ascending aorta
TEVAR (thoracic EVAR) — a stent graft placed across the ascending aorta
Insertion of an intra-aortic balloon pump to support the ascending aorta
Carotid endarterectomy to relieve pressure on the ascending aorta
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Bentall procedure (if aortic root involved) or tube graft replacement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Ascending aortic aneurysm repair: tube graft replacement (aortic body only) or Bentall procedure (root + ascending aorta + valve composite graft). TEVAR is for DESCENDING thoracic aorta; ascending repairs require open sternotomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the most appropriate treatment for descending thoracic aortic aneurysm >6 cm?
options: Open surgical repair via thoracotomy as first choice
TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair)
Medical management (beta-blockers)
EVAR
Emergency surgery only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Descending TAA: TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) has replaced open surgery as first-line for anatomically suitable aneurysms — lower mortality and morbidity than open thoracotomy. Open repair is reserved for complex anatomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which drug class is used for medical management of aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome?
options: Statins
CCBs
ACE inhibitors alone
Beta-blockers (and losartan — ARB)
Anticoagulation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Beta-blockers reduce aortic wall stress by reducing dP/dt (rate of pressure rise). Losartan (ARB) blocks TGF-β signalling — reduces aneurysm expansion in Marfan syndrome. Both recommended for Marfan aortic aneurysm management.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What complication is specific to TEVAR for descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (not EVAR)?
options: Endoleak with persistent sac perfusion
Spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia)
Acute renal failure from contrast use
Groin access-site haematoma formation
Acute lower limb ischaemia distally
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TEVAR covers intercostal arteries including the artery of Adamkiewicz (major anterior spinal artery) — risk of spinal cord ischaemia/paraplegia. Cerebrospinal fluid drainage can reduce this risk by lowering spinal cord perfusion pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: A 55-year-old presents with a hoarse voice. CT shows a 5.5 cm left-sided thoracic aortic aneurysm. What is the cause of hoarseness?
options: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the aneurysm
Direct involvement of the left common carotid artery by the aneurysm
External compression of the trachea and larynx by the expanding aneurysm
Compression of the left phrenic nerve as it runs beside the aneurysm
Extension of an aortic dissection flap up into the left carotid artery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.answer: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the aneurysm
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the aortic arch — compression by a thoracic aneurysm or mass causes hoarse voice (left vocal cord palsy). This is an indication for urgent CT and surgical referral.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: What is the annual risk of rupture or dissection for a thoracic aortic aneurysm >6 cm?
options: ~10–14% per year
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: TAA >6 cm has high annual rupture risk (~10–14%) — surgical threshold is ≥5.5 cm for sporadic aneurysms and ≥4.5 cm for Marfan/connective tissue disorders. Ruptured TAA has >50% mortality.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: Which imaging modality is best for ongoing surveillance of thoracic aortic aneurysms?
options: Plain CXR
CT aortography (CTA)
TTE
Duplex USS
MRI in all cases
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: CT aortography is gold standard for TAA measurement, planning intervention, and surveillance — 3D reconstruction allows precise diameter measurement. MRI is an alternative (no radiation) but less available and slower. CXR shows widened mediastinum but cannot measure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.question: EXAM PEARL: What CXR finding suggests a thoracic aortic aneurysm?
options: Widened mediastinum (>8 cm)
Cardiomegaly
Bilateral pleural effusions
Upper lobe blood diversion
Kerley B lines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Thoracic Aor.explanation: Widened mediastinum on CXR is the key screening finding for aortic pathology (aneurysm or dissection) — must be followed up with CT aortography. Also: tracheal deviation, loss of aortic knuckle, left pleural effusion (haemothorax in rupture).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A murmur is ejection systolic and crescendo-decrescendo, heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space, and radiates to the carotids. Which lesion is this?
options: Mitral regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation
Mitral stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Aortic stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The murmur master table lists AS as ejection systolic, crescendo-decrescendo, best heard at the right 2nd ICS with radiation to the carotids.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which valve lesion produces a pansystolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla?
options: Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Mitral stenosis
Tricuspid regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MR is pansystolic, blowing and high-pitched, heard at the apex with radiation to the axilla.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap is loudest at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position on expiration. Which lesion?
options: Tricuspid regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation
Mitral stenosis
Aortic stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MS gives a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, best heard at the apex in left lateral decubitus on expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which lesion gives an early-diastolic, blowing, high-pitched murmur heard at the left sternal edge, best with the patient sitting forward in expiration?
options: Mitral stenosis
Tricuspid regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Aortic regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AR is early diastolic, blowing and high-pitched at the left sternal edge, best heard sitting forward in expiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge becomes louder on inspiration. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Tricuspid regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Mitral stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Tricuspid regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TR is pansystolic at the lower left sternal edge and, being right-sided, is louder on inspiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which combination of added features points specifically to aortic stenosis?
options: Soft S1, S3, displaced apex beat
Loud S1, opening snap, malar flush, AF
Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft S2, S4
Wide PP, collapsing pulse, displaced apex
Giant V waves, pulsatile liver, raised JVP
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft S2, S4
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The master table gives the AS added features as a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft S2 and an S4.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Loud S1, an opening snap, malar flush and AF are the key added features of which lesion?
options: Mitral stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Tricuspid regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: These four added features are listed against MS in the murmur master table.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Giant V waves in the JVP, a pulsatile liver and a raised JVP are the added features of which lesion?
options: Tricuspid regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Tricuspid regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The master table lists giant V waves, a pulsatile liver and raised JVP as the added features of TR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: The mnemonic 'My Slaves Might Die' is used to remember which group of murmurs?
options: Systolic murmurs
Continuous murmurs
Right-sided murmurs
Innocent murmurs
Diastolic murmurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Diastolic murmurs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: 'My Slaves Might Die' (MS, AR, etc.) is the mnemonic given for diastolic murmurs; ASSES is the one for systolic murmurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: According to the 'MAPT' mnemonic, in what order does rheumatic fever affect the valves?
options: Aortic → Mitral → Pulmonary → Tricuspid
Mitral → Aortic → Pulmonary → Tricuspid
Mitral → Pulmonary → Aortic → Tricuspid
Pulmonary → Aortic → Mitral → Tricuspid
Tricuspid → Aortic → Mitral → Pulmonary
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral → Aortic → Pulmonary → Tricuspid
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MAPT: Mitral (most common) → Aortic → Pulmonary → Tricuspid.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: On a murmur-timing diagram, a continuous 'machinery' murmur spanning both systole and diastole indicates which lesion?
options: Aortic stenosis
Mitral regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation
Mitral stenosis
Patent ductus arteriosus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Patent ductus arteriosus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The timing diagram labels PDA as a continuous machinery murmur across both systole and diastole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which murmur appears on a timing diagram as a uniform band of sound occupying the whole of systole between S1 and S2?
options: Mitral regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Mitral stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Patent ductus arteriosus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral regurgitation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MR is pansystolic, shown as sound filling all of systole between S1 and S2 on the timing diagram.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: According to RILE, why are right-sided murmurs louder on inspiration?
options: Inspiration increases pulmonary venous return to the left heart
Inspiration increases afterload
Inspiration brings the apex closer to the chest wall
Inspiration decreases preload
Inspiration increases venous return, raising right heart flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Inspiration increases venous return, raising right heart flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: RILE: inspiration increases venous return → increased right heart flow → louder right-sided murmurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which set of murmurs is louder in expiration?
options: AS, MR, MS and AR
TR, TS and pulmonary murmurs
PDA only
Right-sided murmurs only
Innocent flow murmurs only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: AS, MR, MS and AR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Left-sided murmurs (AS, MR, MS, AR) are loudest in expiration; right-sided murmurs are louder in inspiration.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Beyond expiration, which extra manoeuvre maximises the mitral stenosis murmur, and why?
options: Sitting forward — brings the aortic root closer to the anterior chest
Valsalva strain — decreases preload and reduces flow across the valve
Left lateral decubitus — brings the apex closer to the chest wall
Squatting — increases preload and afterload, augmenting systemic flow
Standing — decreases venous return and preload, diminishing the murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Left lateral decubitus — brings the apex closer to the chest wall
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The notes state MS is also louder in left lateral decubitus because it brings the apex closer to the chest wall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How do Valsalva and squatting affect HOCM and MVP murmurs?
options: Valsalva makes them louder; squatting makes them quieter
Both make them louder
Valsalva makes them quieter; squatting makes them louder
Both make them quieter
Neither has any effect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Valsalva makes them louder; squatting makes them quieter
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The 'other manoeuvres' note: Valsalva increases HOCM & MVP murmurs (decreased preload); squatting decreases them (increased preload).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which heart sound is generated by mitral and tricuspid valve closure at the start of systole?
options: S2
S1
S3
S4
Opening snap
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: S1
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: S1 is mitral and tricuspid closure, marking the start of systole.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In which condition is S1 louder, and in which is it softer?
options: Louder in MS; softer in MR
Louder in AS; softer in AR
Louder in MR; softer in MS
Louder in AR; softer in AS
Louder in TR; softer in MS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Louder in MS; softer in MR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: S1 is loud in MS (rigid but mobile valves snapping shut) and soft in MR (valve doesn't close properly).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A wide fixed split of S2 is characteristic of which condition?
options: Severe aortic stenosis
Heart failure
Pulmonary hypertension
Mitral stenosis
Atrial septal defect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Atrial septal defect
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The S2 card notes a wide fixed split in ASD; S2 is soft/absent in severe AS and loud in pulmonary HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: S3 represents rapid ventricular filling. In which situation is it physiological rather than pathological?
options: The young, athletic, and pregnancy
Severe mitral regurgitation
Heart failure with LV dilatation
Aortic stenosis
Hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: The young, athletic, and pregnancy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: S3 is physiological in the young/athletic and in pregnancy; it is pathological in HF (LV dilatation) and severe MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why is S4 always pathological?
options: It is caused by rapid passive ventricular filling in early diastole, like S3
It results from turbulent systolic regurgitation of blood back into the atrium
It is produced by aortic and pulmonary semilunar valve closure at end-systole
It is the opening snap of a stenotic mitral valve early in diastole
It reflects atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: It reflects atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: S4 is atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle — never normal. Heard in AS, HCM, hypertension and ischaemic disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In mitral stenosis, what does an opening snap that occurs earlier after S2 indicate?
options: Lower LA pressure and milder stenosis
Constrictive pericarditis
Coexisting aortic regurgitation
A physiological S3
Higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Higher LA pressure and more severe stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The earlier the snap occurs after S2, the higher the LA pressure and the more severe the stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A sound resembling S3 but occurring earlier and louder, caused by abrupt halting of ventricular filling, describes which finding?
options: Pericardial knock
Opening snap
Ejection click
S4 gallop
Austin Flint murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Pericardial knock
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The pericardial knock of constrictive pericarditis sounds like S3 but is earlier and louder, from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the mechanism of the slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse in aortic stenosis?
options: Regurgitation lowering aortic diastolic pressure and widening the pulse
Obstruction to LV outflow giving a slow, low-amplitude upstroke
Systolic regurgitation of blood back into the right atrium each beat
Fixed valvular obstruction reducing overall resting cardiac output
LV dilatation from chronic volume overload lowering ejection force
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Obstruction to LV outflow giving a slow, low-amplitude upstroke
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The pulse table attributes the slow-rising AS pulse to LV outflow obstruction producing a slow, low-amplitude aortic upstroke.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which lesion produces a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, and by what mechanism?
options: AS — reduced stroke volume through a fixed narrowed valve gives a slow weak pulse
AR — regurgitation lowers diastolic pressure with compensatory raised stroke volume
MS — fixed obstruction at the mitral valve limiting left atrial emptying into the LV
TR — systolic regurgitation into the right atrium producing prominent giant JVP waves
MR — eccentric LV dilatation from volume overload with a large regurgitant fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: AR — regurgitation lowers diastolic pressure with compensatory raised stroke volume
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In AR, regurgitation drops diastolic pressure while compensatory increased stroke volume raises systolic — a wide PP and collapsing pulse.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A low-volume pulse with malar flush is characteristic of which lesion, and why the flush?
options: AR — wide pulse pressure
AS — concentric LV hypertrophy
MS — chronic low CO plus pulmonary HTN
TR — hepatic venous congestion
MR — raised LA pressure
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: MS — chronic low CO plus pulmonary HTN
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In MS, fixed obstruction lowers cardiac output (low-volume pulse) and the malar flush reflects chronic low CO plus pulmonary HTN.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Giant V waves in the JVP are produced by which mechanism?
options: Reduced forward stroke volume from a fixed outflow obstruction lowering the pulse
Atrial contraction against a stenosed, obstructed tricuspid valve giving giant a waves
LV outflow tract obstruction raising left-sided pressures and cardiac workload
Rapid early ventricular filling producing a normal venous descent in diastole
Systolic regurgitation into the right atrium producing a large venous V wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Systolic regurgitation into the right atrium producing a large venous V wave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In TR, systolic regurgitation into the RA generates a large V wave in the venous waveform.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which two lesions cause a displaced, thrusting apex beat, and why?
options: AS and MS — pressure overload
MR and AR — volume overload with LV dilatation
TR and TS — right heart overload
AS and AR — mixed lesion
MS and MR — atrial dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: MR and AR — volume overload with LV dilatation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Both MR and AR are volume-overload states; LV dilatation pushes the apex down and out, giving a displaced thrusting apex.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What explains the heaving, non-displaced apex beat of aortic stenosis?
options: Eccentric LV dilatation from volume overload displacing the apex laterally
Concentric LV hypertrophy producing a forceful, non-displaced heave
Right ventricular pressure overload producing a left parasternal heave
Left atrial enlargement from raised filling pressures behind the ventricle
Systolic regurgitation of blood back into the left atrium each systole
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Concentric LV hypertrophy producing a forceful, non-displaced heave
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AS causes concentric LV hypertrophy (pressure overload) — a forceful, non-displaced heaving apex, distinct from the displaced apex of volume-overload lesions.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the underlying mechanism of the narrow pulse pressure seen in aortic stenosis?
options: Increased stroke volume raising systolic and lowering diastolic
Regurgitation lowering diastolic pressure
Reduced stroke volume lowering systolic, with raised LVEDP raising diastolic
Hepatic venous congestion
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Reduced stroke volume lowering systolic, with raised LVEDP raising diastolic
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: The pulse table: in AS reduced stroke volume lowers systolic BP while raised LVEDP raises the diastolic, narrowing the pulse pressure.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the most common overall cause of aortic stenosis, and who does it typically affect?
options: Bicuspid aortic valve — middle age (40–60 yrs)
Senile calcific — elderly (>65 yrs)
Rheumatic fever — post-streptococcal
Supravalvular AS — Williams syndrome
Subvalvular AS — fibromuscular shelf
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Senile calcific — elderly (>65 yrs)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Senile calcific AS is the most common overall cause: calcium deposits on a normal tricuspid valve in the elderly (>65 yrs).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A 50-year-old presents with aortic stenosis. Which congenital cause is most likely, and what else can it cause?
options: Senile calcific — also causes MR
Rheumatic fever — also causes MS
Aortic sclerosis — also causes TR
Bicuspid aortic valve — also causes AR
Supravalvular AS — also causes PS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Bicuspid aortic valve — also causes AR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve presents in middle age (40–60 yrs), is congenital, and can also cause aortic regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How does HOCM differ from true aortic stenosis on examination?
options: Murmur increases with Valsalva, decreases with squatting, and does NOT radiate to carotids
Murmur increases with squatting and passive leg raising, and radiates to the carotids
Murmur is unchanged by all bedside manoeuvres and radiates towards the left axilla like MR
Murmur is early diastolic, best heard sitting forward in held expiration at the left sternal edge
Murmur is accompanied by a widely fixed split second heart sound that is unaffected by respiration
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Murmur increases with Valsalva, decreases with squatting, and does NOT radiate to carotids
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: HOCM is a dynamic obstruction: louder with Valsalva, quieter with squatting, and it does not radiate to the carotids — unlike true AS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A patient has calcification of the aortic valve without obstruction, a normal S2 and no symptoms. What is this?
options: Supravalvular AS
Subvalvular AS
Severe aortic stenosis
Aortic sclerosis
Bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Aortic sclerosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Aortic sclerosis is calcification without obstruction — it gives a normal S2 and no symptoms, distinguishing it from true AS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which mimic of AS is a coarctation-type lesion above the valve associated with Williams syndrome?
options: Supravalvular AS
Subvalvular AS
Aortic sclerosis
HOCM
Bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Supravalvular AS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Supravalvular AS is a coarctation-type lesion above the valve, associated with Williams syndrome.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In the pathophysiology of AS, why does the LV undergo concentric hypertrophy?
options: To accommodate a large regurgitant volume returning to the ventricle
Due to progressive left atrial dilatation raising ventricular filling load
Because of eccentric volume overload stretching the ventricular walls
Compensatory response to pressure overload that preserves wall stress
Because of established subendocardial infarction remodelling the ventricle
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Compensatory response to pressure overload that preserves wall stress
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Fixed outflow obstruction forces the LV to generate higher pressure; concentric hypertrophy is the compensatory response that preserves wall stress.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How can aortic stenosis cause angina even when the coronary arteries are normal?
options: Coronary artery spasm transiently reducing epicardial blood flow
Aortic dissection propagating back into a coronary artery ostium
Coronary embolism from calcific valve debris occluding a vessel
Subendocardial ischaemia from increased demand and reduced supply
Pulmonary hypertension raising right heart demand and myocardial work
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Subendocardial ischaemia from increased demand and reduced supply
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AS produces subendocardial ischaemia (increased O2 demand from hypertrophy plus reduced supply), causing angina even with normal coronaries.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Within the SAD triad of aortic stenosis, which symptom carries the worst median survival of around 2 years?
options: Syncope
Dyspnoea
Angina
Palpitations
Haemoptysis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Dyspnoea
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Dyspnoea (from LV failure and raised LVEDP) has the worst median survival of ~2 years; syncope ~2–3 years and angina ~5 years.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the mechanism of exertional syncope in aortic stenosis?
options: Fixed cardiac output plus vasodilation leading to cerebral underperfusion
AF with loss of atrial kick causing an abrupt fall in cardiac output
Pulmonary venous congestion reducing oxygenation and cerebral delivery
Hepatic venous congestion from right-sided backpressure lowering output
Subendocardial infarction acutely impairing left ventricular ejection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Fixed cardiac output plus vasodilation leading to cerebral underperfusion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: On exertion the fixed CO cannot rise to match peripheral vasodilation, so cerebral perfusion drops and syncope occurs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the key prognostic principle in aortic stenosis once symptoms develop?
options: Asymptomatic AS carries a far worse prognosis than symptomatic AS and needs urgent surgery
The onset of symptoms has no bearing on prognosis, which depends solely on echo valve area
Prognosis is poor without surgery; symptomatic AS does far worse than asymptomatic AS
Medical therapy with statins and ACE inhibitors reliably slows progression of stenosis
Severity graded on echocardiography does not affect the timing or need for valve surgery
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Prognosis is poor without surgery; symptomatic AS does far worse than asymptomatic AS
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Once symptoms develop, prognosis is poor without surgery; asymptomatic AS (even if severe) has a much better prognosis than symptomatic AS.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: When is the aortic stenosis murmur preceded by an ejection click?
options: When the valve is calcified
When the valve is valvular (not calcified)
Only in severe AS
Only when there is coexisting AR
When AF is present
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: When the valve is valvular (not calcified)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: An ejection click precedes the murmur if the valve is valvular (not calcified).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why is S2 soft or absent in aortic stenosis?
options: A calcified immobile valve cannot produce a crisp closure sound
Atrial contraction against a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle
Rapid early diastolic ventricular filling producing a third sound
Reduced venous return lowering the flow available for closure
Systolic regurgitation of blood back into the dilated left atrium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A calcified immobile valve cannot produce a crisp closure sound
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: In AS the calcified, immobile aortic valve cannot close crisply, so S2 becomes soft or absent.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why might the AS murmur become quieter as the disease becomes very severe?
options: A failing LV reduces stroke volume, lowering turbulence
The stenotic valve area increases and relieves the obstruction
Coexisting aortic regurgitation completely masks the murmur
New-onset AF lowers the transvalvular pressure gradient
The murmur shifts to become early diastolic in timing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A failing LV reduces stroke volume, lowering turbulence
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: As the LV fails, stroke volume falls and there is less turbulence, so the murmur softens — do not be reassured by a soft murmur in a sick patient.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which echo findings define severe aortic stenosis?
options: Peak gradient >30 mmHg, AVA <3 cm²
Mean gradient >10 mmHg, MVA <1.5 cm²
Mean gradient >20 mmHg, AVA <2 cm²
Mean gradient >40 mmHg / peak >64 mmHg, AVA <1 cm²
Mean gradient >5 mmHg, AVA <0.5 cm²
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mean gradient >40 mmHg / peak >64 mmHg, AVA <1 cm²
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Severe AS on echo: mean gradient >40 mmHg / peak >64 mmHg and aortic valve area <1 cm².

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What ECG findings are typical of aortic stenosis?
options: P mitrale from left atrial enlargement with atrial fibrillation
Saddle-shaped ST elevation with widespread PR depression of pericarditis
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy and RV strain
A slurred delta wave with a short PR interval of pre-excitation
LVH (tall R in V5–6, deep S in V1–2) with a lateral strain pattern
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: LVH (tall R in V5–6, deep S in V1–2) with a lateral strain pattern
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: AS shows LVH (tall R in V5–6, deep S in V1–2) and a strain pattern — ST depression with T-wave inversion in the lateral leads.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How is BNP useful in aortic stenosis?
options: It confirms the diagnosis of aortic stenosis directly
A rising BNP in asymptomatic AS predicts symptom onset
It precisely quantifies the aortic valve orifice area
It reliably distinguishes AS from aortic regurgitation
It directly measures the transvalvular pressure gradient
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A rising BNP in asymptomatic AS predicts symptom onset
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: A rising BNP in asymptomatic AS predicts the onset of symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Which is the gold-standard treatment for most patients with aortic stenosis, and a valid indication?
options: TAVI — reserved only for young, low surgical-risk patients who also have a bicuspid aortic valve
Surgical AVR (SAVR) — symptomatic severe AS, or severe AS with mean gradient >40 mmHg or EF <50%
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty — a definitive, durable treatment that permanently relieves the obstruction
Vasodilators such as ACE inhibitors — given long-term to slow the progression of valve stenosis
Loop diuretics such as furosemide — given to mechanically reverse the fixed valvular obstruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Surgical AVR (SAVR) — symptomatic severe AS, or severe AS with mean gradient >40 mmHg or EF <50%
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: SAVR is the gold standard for most patients; indicated for symptomatic severe AS (SAD), or severe AS with mean gradient >40 mmHg or EF <50%.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: A frail, elderly patient with multiple comorbidities needs aortic valve replacement but is high surgical risk. What is most appropriate?
options: Surgical AVR with a mechanical valve
Balloon valvuloplasty as definitive treatment
TAVI (transcatheter aortic valve implantation)
Vasodilators and nitrates
No intervention
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: TAVI (transcatheter aortic valve implantation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: TAVI is a transfemoral catheter-based valve implantation for high surgical risk patients (frail, elderly, comorbidities); no open-chest surgery required.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the role of balloon aortic valvuloplasty in aortic stenosis?
options: A definitive, curative procedure for severe calcific AS that restores a normal valve area for good
Used only in asymptomatic patients with mild aortic stenosis to prevent progression to severe disease
The recommended first-line treatment in all symptomatic patients regardless of surgical risk or age
A temporary measure with a high restenosis rate, used as a bridge to AVR/TAVI in unstable patients
A durable alternative that permanently replaces the need for SAVR or TAVI in younger, low-risk patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: A temporary measure with a high restenosis rate, used as a bridge to AVR/TAVI in unstable patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Balloon valvuloplasty is temporary with a high restenosis rate; it bridges to definitive AVR/TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients and is not definitive.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: Why are vasodilators and nitrates relatively contraindicated in aortic stenosis?
options: They accelerate calcium deposition and worsen the leaflet calcification directly
The obstruction is fixed, so dropping afterload can cause severe hypotension
They precipitate atrial fibrillation by shortening the atrial refractory period
They act on the valve to increase the transvalvular pressure gradient directly
They cause dangerous rebound hypertension and reflex tachycardia on withdrawal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: The obstruction is fixed, so dropping afterload can cause severe hypotension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: With a fixed obstruction the heart cannot increase output to compensate, so dropping afterload with vasodilators/nitrates risks severe hypotension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation in the developed world, and what is its characteristic murmur?
options: Rheumatic fever — pansystolic murmur
Infective endocarditis — early diastolic murmur
Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) — click + late systolic murmur (Barlow's)
Functional MR — continuous murmur
Ischaemic papillary muscle rupture — ejection systolic murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) — click + late systolic murmur (Barlow's)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: MVP is the most common cause of MR in the developed world; from myxomatous degeneration, it gives a click plus a late systolic murmur (Barlow's).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: What is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation worldwide?
options: Rheumatic fever
Functional MR
Mitral valve prolapse
Infective endocarditis
Connective tissue disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Rheumatic fever
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Rheumatic fever is the most common cause of MR worldwide, causing fibrosis plus commissural fusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: How does ischaemia cause acute versus chronic mitral regurgitation?
options: Annular dilatation → acute MR; fibrosis → chronic MR
Papillary muscle rupture → acute MR; ischaemia → chronic functional MR
Leaflet perforation → acute MR; calcification → chronic MR
Commissural fusion → acute MR; myxomatous change → chronic MR
Chordal rupture → chronic MR; ischaemia → acute MR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: Papillary muscle rupture → acute MR; ischaemia → chronic functional MR
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Papillary muscle rupture (post-STEMI) causes acute MR, while ongoing ischaemia causes chronic functional MR.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.question: In functional mitral regurgitation, why does the valve leak despite normal leaflets?
options: Leaflet perforation from infective endocarditis destroying valve tissue
Commissural fusion and leaflet thickening from chronic rheumatic disease
Myxomatous thickening of the chordae causing leaflet prolapse in systole
Calcific degeneration and rigidity of the mitral valve annulus with age
LV dilatation (any cause of DCM) → annular dilatation; leaflets are normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.answer: LV dilatation (any cause of DCM) → annular dilatation; leaflets are normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Valvular Hea.explanation: Functional MR arises when LV dilatation (any cause of DCM) stretches the annulus; the leaflets themselves are normal.
