Stop the combined OCP permanently (switch to progesterone-only or barrier method)
Switch to a lower-dose combined oestrogen pill which is safe after a first DVT
Prescribe anticoagulation and simply continue the combined OCP unchanged
Make no change at all to her current combined hormonal contraception method
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Stop the combined OCP permanently (switch to progesterone-only or barrier method)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Combined OCP (oestrogen-containing) significantly increases VTE risk — must be stopped after DVT. Progesterone-only pill or non-hormonal contraception is safer. This also constitutes a provoked DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the Wells DVT score for a patient with: swelling of entire leg (+1), tenderness along deep veins (+1), active cancer (+1)?
options: 0 — very low
2 — moderate probability
1 — low probability
3 — high probability
4 — maximum score
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Wells DVT: score ≥2 = high probability → proceed directly to compression USS. This patient scores 3 (swelling + tenderness + cancer), so D-dimer is not needed — image directly.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: What is the role of an IVC filter in DVT management?
options: First-line treatment for every DVT in place of standard anticoagulation
Prevents PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding)
Inserted to monitor the response of the clot to anticoagulation therapy
Mandatory in all cancer-associated DVT regardless of bleeding risk
Reliably prevents recurrent DVT in every patient once it is inserted
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Prevents PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: IVC filter is a temporary or permanent mechanical barrier placed in the inferior vena cava to prevent pulmonary embolism when anticoagulation is contraindicated — not routine for all DVTs.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: Which clotting factor is deficient in Factor V Leiden thrombophilia?
options: Factor X is congenitally deficient, impairing the common coagulation pathway and raising thrombosis risk
Factor V is completely absent, producing a haemorrhagic bleeding tendency rather than a thrombotic state
Factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (no deficiency — gain-of-function mutation)
Protein C is deficient, abolishing its normal anticoagulant role and permitting unopposed clot formation
Factor VIII levels are markedly elevated, driving excessive thrombin generation and pathological clotting
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: Factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (no deficiency — gain-of-function mutation)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Factor V Leiden = point mutation making Factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C — leads to hypercoagulability. It is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Europeans.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: A 68-year-old presents with a first unprovoked DVT. What does current NICE guidance recommend to look for occult cancer?
options: A focused review — history, examination, bloods, CXR and urinalysis (no routine CT)
Routine CT chest/abdomen/pelvis in all patients
Whole-body PET-CT as standard
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
A tumour-marker panel (CA-125, CEA, CA19-9) in all patients
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.answer: A focused review — history, examination, bloods, CXR and urinalysis (no routine CT)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Current NICE (NG158) does NOT recommend routine extensive cancer screening after unprovoked VTE. Perform a focused assessment — history, examination, baseline bloods, CXR and urinalysis — and investigate further only if this points to a cause. This replaced older advice (routine CT abdomen/pelvis) after the SOME trial showed no benefit from routine CT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the most common inherited thrombophilia and what is its inheritance?
options: Antithrombin deficiency — autosomal recessive
Protein C deficiency — X-linked
Factor V Leiden — autosomal dominant
Prothrombin G20210A — autosomal recessive
Protein S deficiency — X-linked
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__DVT.explanation: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia (~5% of Europeans are heterozygous). Autosomal dominant. Homozygous = much higher thrombosis risk. Accounts for ~50% of inherited thrombophilia cases.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which statement best defines a cardiomyopathy?
options: Myocardial dysfunction caused directly by coronary artery disease
A primary disorder of the heart muscle not explained by coronary, valve, hypertensive or congenital disease
Inflammation of the pericardial layers
Fibrosis and calcification of the cardiac valves
Ischaemic damage confined to the conduction system
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: A primary disorder of the heart muscle not explained by coronary, valve, hypertensive or congenital disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Cardiomyopathy is a primary disease of the myocardium itself, by definition not attributable to coronary, valvular, hypertensive or congenital heart disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which is the commonest type of cardiomyopathy?
options: Hypertrophic
Restrictive
Dilated
Takotsubo
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the commonest pattern, producing a dilated, poorly-contracting ventricle and systolic heart failure (HFrEF). HCM is the commonest INHERITED disorder but not commonest overall.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathies primarily cause which type of ventricular dysfunction?
options: Systolic with reduced EF
Diastolic with impaired filling and preserved EF
Isolated valvular dysfunction
Pure conduction dysfunction
No measurable dysfunction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Diastolic with impaired filling and preserved EF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM (stiff, hypertrophied) and RCM (rigid walls) impair filling → diastolic dysfunction with preserved EF; dilated cardiomyopathy causes systolic dysfunction (HFrEF).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A 33-year-old woman develops heart failure with a dilated, poorly-contracting LV in the last month of pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Peripartum (dilated) cardiomyopathy
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Constrictive pericarditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy of the last month of pregnancy or early postpartum period with LV dilatation and systolic dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which drug characteristically causes a dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy, prompting EF monitoring?
options: Ramipril
Doxorubicin
Bisoprolol
Atorvastatin
Furosemide
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin (and trastuzumab) cause dose-dependent cardiotoxicity leading to dilated cardiomyopathy; serial echo/EF monitoring is used.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which is the commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: Lamin A/C (LMNA)
Titin (TTN)
Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7)
Plakophilin (PKP2)
Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Truncating variants in titin (TTN) are the commonest genetic cause of DCM. LMNA is associated with conduction disease and malignant arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A dilated cardiomyopathy caused by which genotype is associated with conduction disease and malignant arrhythmia, warranting a lower threshold for an ICD?
options: Titin (TTN)
Lamin A/C (LMNA)
MYH7
MYBPC3
PKP2
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Lamin A/C (LMNA) dilated cardiomyopathy carries a high risk of conduction disease and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A young man with dilated cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation. Which therapy most importantly prevents a common complication?
options: Aspirin alone
Anticoagulation to prevent thromboembolism
A long-acting nitrate
Calcium supplementation
Prophylactic antibiotics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: The dilated, akinetic ventricle predisposes to mural thrombus and systemic embolism; anticoagulate when there is AF or intracardiac thrombus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which is the correct standard therapy for the heart failure of dilated cardiomyopathy?
options: Nitrate plus digoxin only
ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor
Calcium-channel blocker monotherapy
Aspirin and a statin only
No pharmacological therapy is indicated
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: DCM causes HFrEF, treated with the standard quadruple therapy (ACEi/ARB or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) plus diuretics; ICD/CRT where indicated.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the inheritance pattern and gene type in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: Autosomal recessive; ion-channel genes
X-linked; dystrophin gene
Autosomal dominant; sarcomere protein genes
Mitochondrial
Autosomal dominant; desmosomal genes
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM is autosomal dominant with sarcomere-gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3). Desmosomal genes cause ARVC; dystrophin causes Duchenne-associated DCM.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in a young athlete?
options: Aortic dissection
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary embolism
Acute myocarditis
Atherosclerotic coronary disease
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young people/athletes via ventricular arrhythmia; exertional syncope is a red flag.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: How does the murmur of obstructive HCM change with the Valsalva manoeuvre?
options: Softer, because preload increases
Louder, because reduced preload shrinks the LV cavity and worsens outflow obstruction
Unchanged
Becomes early-diastolic
Disappears
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Louder, because reduced preload shrinks the LV cavity and worsens outflow obstruction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Reducing preload (Valsalva/standing) increases dynamic LVOT obstruction, making the murmur louder — the opposite of aortic stenosis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which drug should be AVOIDED in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: Bisoprolol
Verapamil
Glyceryl trinitrate (nitrate)
Disopyramide
Intravenous fluids when hypotensive
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Nitrates (and ACE inhibitors, diuretics, digoxin) reduce preload/afterload and worsen dynamic obstruction; negative inotropes (beta-blocker/verapamil) are used instead.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment of symptomatic obstructive HCM?
options: A nitrate
A beta-blocker (or verapamil)
An ACE inhibitor
A loop diuretic
Digoxin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Negative inotropes — a beta-blocker or verapamil — reduce the outflow gradient and relieve symptoms.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which echocardiographic finding is characteristic of HCM?
options: Four-chamber dilatation with global hypokinesia
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
Large pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse
Mitral valve vegetations
Bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve and a dynamic LVOT gradient ('MR SAM ASH').

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which ECG changes are typical of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: Delta wave and short PR
LVH with deep T-wave inversion and dagger-like septal Q waves
Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation
Low voltage with electrical alternans
Epsilon wave in V1-V3
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: LVH with deep T-wave inversion and dagger-like septal Q waves
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM shows LVH, deep T-wave inversion and narrow 'dagger' septal Q waves. Saddle ST elevation = pericarditis; electrical alternans = large effusion; epsilon = ARVC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which feature is used to guide ICD implantation in HCM?
options: Mild concentric LVH
A family history of sudden cardiac death
Sinus bradycardia
Left-axis deviation
First-degree AV block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: A family history of sudden cardiac death
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: HCM Risk-SCD factors include FHx of sudden death, unexplained syncope, massive LVH (≥30 mm), non-sustained VT and abnormal exercise BP response.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What invasive procedure relieves refractory LV outflow obstruction in HCM?
options: Coronary artery bypass grafting
Septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation
Mitral valve replacement
Pericardiectomy
Catheter ablation of the AV node
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Refractory LVOT obstruction is treated by surgical septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation to reduce septal bulk.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the commonest cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
options: Sarcoidosis
Amyloidosis
Haemochromatosis
Radiation
Endomyocardial fibrosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Amyloidosis (AL and ATTR) is the commonest cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Restrictive cardiomyopathy closely mimics which surgically curable condition?
options: Aortic stenosis
Constrictive pericarditis
Mitral regurgitation
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Cardiac tamponade
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: RCM and constrictive pericarditis both cause diastolic right heart failure; constriction shows pericardial thickening/calcification and is curable by pericardiectomy.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which histological finding confirms cardiac amyloidosis?
options: Non-caseating granulomas
Apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining
Aschoff bodies
Multinucleated giant cells
Fibrofatty replacement
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Amyloid stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Granulomas = sarcoid; giant cells = giant-cell myocarditis; fibrofatty = ARVC.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which echo finding suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy?
options: Dilated ventricles with low EF
Non-dilated, non-hypertrophied ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved EF
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
Flail mitral leaflet
Bicuspid aortic valve
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Non-dilated, non-hypertrophied ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved EF
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: RCM shows normal-sized, non-hypertrophied ventricles with big atria and preserved EF, reflecting diastolic dysfunction.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: A 68-year-old woman develops chest pain, anterior ST elevation and a raised troponin after her husband's death; angiography is normal and echo shows apical ballooning. What is the diagnosis?
options: STEMI
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy
Acute myocarditis
Prinzmetal angina
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: catecholamine-driven transient apical ballooning after stress that mimics ACS but with unobstructed coronaries; usually recovers fully.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the typical outcome of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
options: Progressive irreversible heart failure
Full recovery of LV function over days to weeks with supportive care
Immediate need for transplantation
Conversion to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Permanent complete heart block
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Full recovery of LV function over days to weeks with supportive care
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Takotsubo is usually reversible: supportive management (treat as heart failure, avoid catecholamines) with recovery of LV function in weeks.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: Which ECG finding is characteristically associated with ARVC?
options: Delta wave
Epsilon wave
Prominent U wave
J (Osborn) wave
Short PR interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: ARVC classically shows an epsilon wave with T-wave inversion in V1–V3. Delta wave = WPW; J wave = hypothermia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the underlying pathology of ARVC?
options: Sarcomere disarray
Amyloid deposition
Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium
Myocardial iron overload
Granulomatous inflammation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: ARVC is an autosomal-dominant desmosomal disorder with fibrofatty replacement of the RV, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the key first-line/bedside investigation for suspected cardiomyopathy?
options: Coronary angiography
Echocardiography
Endomyocardial biopsy
Chest X-ray
24-hour urinary catecholamines
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Echocardiography is the key bedside test (with ECG, CXR, BNP), assessing chamber size, wall thickness, EF, diastolic function and gradients.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.question: What is the main role of cardiac MRI in cardiomyopathy?
options: To measure serum troponin
Tissue characterisation with late gadolinium enhancement for phenotyping and prognosis
To replace echocardiography for EF only
To screen for coronary disease
To guide anticoagulation dosing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.answer: Tissue characterisation with late gadolinium enhancement for phenotyping and prognosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiomyopat.explanation: Cardiac MRI provides tissue characterisation (LGE) for phenotyping and risk/prognosis and is increasingly the gold-standard imaging test.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Acute rheumatic fever typically develops after which infection, and after how long?
options: A skin infection, within 24 hours
A group A streptococcal throat infection, 2–4 weeks later
A viral gastroenteritis, 3 months later
A urinary tract infection, 1 week later
A dental abscess, 6 weeks later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: A group A streptococcal throat infection, 2–4 weeks later
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: ARF is a multisystem immune-mediated disease that develops 2–4 weeks after a group A β-haemolytic streptococcal (Strep pyogenes) throat infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Rheumatic fever characteristically follows streptococcal infection at which site?
options: The skin
The throat (pharyngitis)
The urinary tract
The middle ear
The lungs
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: The throat (pharyngitis)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows strep PHARYNGITIS (throat), unlike post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can follow throat or skin infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the underlying mechanism of tissue damage in rheumatic fever?
options: IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity
Molecular mimicry — cross-reactive antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein
Direct bacterial invasion of the myocardium
Immune-complex deposition in glomeruli
Granuloma formation from mycobacterial infection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Molecular mimicry — cross-reactive antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Molecular mimicry (a type II hypersensitivity reaction): antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with human antigens in the heart, joints, brain and skin.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the pathognomonic histological finding of rheumatic carditis?
options: Non-caseating granulomas
Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells
Psammoma bodies
Apple-green birefringence
Owl-eye inclusions
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Aschoff bodies — granulomatous nodules containing Anitschkow (‘caterpillar’) macrophages — in the myocardium are pathognomonic of rheumatic carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: According to the Jones criteria, what is needed to diagnose rheumatic fever?
options: Any single major criterion
Evidence of preceding strep PLUS 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor criteria
Three minor criteria alone
A positive throat swab alone
Raised ESR plus fever
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Evidence of preceding strep PLUS 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor criteria
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Diagnosis requires evidence of a preceding group A strep infection PLUS either 2 major criteria or 1 major + 2 minor criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which of the following is a MAJOR Jones criterion?
options: Fever
Arthralgia
Sydenham’s chorea
Raised ESR/CRP
Prolonged PR interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Sydenham’s chorea
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Sydenham’s chorea is a major criterion (JONES: Joints, Carditis, Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham’s chorea). Fever, arthralgia, raised markers and prolonged PR are minor criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which of the following is a MINOR Jones criterion?
options: Migratory polyarthritis
Carditis
Subcutaneous nodules
Prolonged PR interval
Erythema marginatum
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Prolonged PR interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A prolonged PR interval is a minor criterion. Migratory polyarthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum are major criteria.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Because rheumatic fever presents weeks after the sore throat, which investigation best confirms preceding streptococcal infection?
options: Throat swab culture
Raised/rising ASO titre and anti-DNase B
Blood cultures
CRP
Chest X-ray
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Raised/rising ASO titre and anti-DNase B
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Swabs are often already negative by presentation, so raised/rising anti-streptococcal antibody titres (ASO and anti-DNase B) are the more reliable evidence of recent infection.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which best describes the arthritis of rheumatic fever?
options: A symmetrical small-joint arthritis with erosions
A migratory (‘flitting’) large-joint polyarthritis, responsive to aspirin, leaving no damage
A monoarthritis with a hot, red joint and crystals
A chronic deforming arthritis of the hands
A seronegative sacroiliitis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: A migratory (‘flitting’) large-joint polyarthritis, responsive to aspirin, leaving no damage
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The arthritis is a migratory polyarthritis of large joints, hot and tender, dramatically responsive to aspirin/NSAIDs, and leaves no permanent joint damage.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which single manifestation of rheumatic fever is responsible for its long-term sequelae?
options: Migratory polyarthritis
Carditis
Sydenham’s chorea
Erythema marginatum
Subcutaneous nodules
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Carditis (a pancarditis) is the only manifestation with lasting sequelae, leading to chronic rheumatic heart disease (classically mitral stenosis).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: A soft mid-diastolic murmur of acute mitral valvulitis in rheumatic carditis is known as:
options: Graham Steell murmur
Carey Coombs murmur
Austin Flint murmur
Still’s murmur
Gibson murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Carey Coombs murmur
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The Carey Coombs murmur is the soft mid-diastolic murmur of active mitral valvulitis; the commonest acute murmur overall is mitral regurgitation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which statement about Sydenham’s chorea is correct?
options: It presents in the first 48 hours of infection
It is a late feature (1–6 months) and may be the only manifestation
It causes permanent movement disorder
It only occurs in boys
It is a minor Jones criterion
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: It is a late feature (1–6 months) and may be the only manifestation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Sydenham’s chorea is a late feature (1–6 months), can be the sole manifestation, is commoner in girls, and is self-limiting; it is a MAJOR criterion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which description matches erythema marginatum?
options: A malar (butterfly) facial rash
Pink rings with central clearing on the trunk/proximal limbs, sparing the face
A vesicular rash along a dermatome
Palpable purpura on the legs
A target lesion on the palms
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Pink rings with central clearing on the trunk/proximal limbs, sparing the face
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Erythema marginatum is pink rings with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs, characteristically sparing the face.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Subcutaneous nodules in rheumatic fever are associated with:
options: Mild disease with a good prognosis
Severe carditis
Renal involvement
Isolated arthritis
Skin infection
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Severe carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The painless, firm subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces are associated with severe carditis.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Which ECG finding is recognised as a minor Jones criterion in rheumatic fever?
options: Delta wave
Prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block)
ST elevation
Epsilon wave
Short QT interval
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block) is a minor Jones criterion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the role of echocardiography in suspected rheumatic fever?
options: It is not indicated
It is recommended in all suspected cases to detect valvulitis and subclinical carditis
It replaces the Jones criteria
It is only used after 6 months
It is used solely to measure ejection fraction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: It is recommended in all suspected cases to detect valvulitis and subclinical carditis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Echocardiography is recommended in all suspected cases; it detects valvulitis/regurgitation and subclinical carditis, plus any pericardial effusion.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the recommended antibiotic to eradicate the streptococcus in acute rheumatic fever?
options: Oral metronidazole
A single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (or 10 days oral penicillin V)
IV vancomycin
Oral ciprofloxacin
No antibiotic is needed
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: A single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (or 10 days oral penicillin V)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: A single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (or a 10-day course of oral penicillin V) eradicates the organism; a macrolide is used if penicillin-allergic.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: Rheumatic fever is one of the few paediatric settings where which drug is deliberately used despite the usual Reye’s syndrome caution?
options: Ibuprofen
Aspirin
Paracetamol
Codeine
Prednisolone
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Aspirin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: High-dose aspirin is deliberately used for the arthritis/fever of rheumatic fever (as in Kawasaki disease), despite the usual caution about Reye’s syndrome in children.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: What is the mainstay of secondary prevention after rheumatic fever?
options: A single course of antibiotics only
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis (IM benzathine every 3–4 weeks, or oral penicillin V)
Lifelong aspirin
Annual influenza vaccination
No specific prophylaxis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Long-term penicillin prophylaxis (IM benzathine every 3–4 weeks, or oral penicillin V)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: Long-term penicillin prophylaxis — IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks (or oral penicillin V twice daily) — prevents recurrence and further valve damage; duration depends on carditis and residual valve disease.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.question: In rheumatic heart disease, which valve and lesion are classically involved?
options: Aortic stenosis
Mitral stenosis
Tricuspid regurgitation
Pulmonary stenosis
Mitral valve prolapse
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.answer: Mitral stenosis
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Rheumatic Fe.explanation: The mitral valve is most commonly affected, classically producing mitral stenosis; the aortic valve is the next most involved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What are varicose veins?
options: Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins from incompetent valves and venous hypertension
Thrombosed deep veins of the calf
Dilated arteries of the lower limb
Inflamed lymphatic channels
Congenital arteriovenous malformations only
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins from incompetent valves and venous hypertension
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins (>3 mm) caused by incompetent venous valves and venous hypertension.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Normal venous return from the leg depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Competent venous valves
The calf muscle pump
Patent deep veins
High arterial pressure driving venous flow
(all three of the others are required)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: High arterial pressure driving venous flow
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Venous return relies on competent valves, the calf muscle pump and patent deep veins; failure of any of these causes venous hypertension. Arterial pressure is not the mechanism.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which vein and junction are most commonly involved in varicose veins?
options: Small saphenous vein at the saphenopopliteal junction
Great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction
Femoral vein at the common femoral vein
Popliteal vein
Perforators of the foot
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: The great saphenous vein (medial), refluxing at the saphenofemoral junction, is most commonly involved.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which is the commonest type of varicose veins?
options: Secondary to previous DVT
Primary (idiopathic valve/vein-wall weakness)
Secondary to a pelvic tumour
Congenital (Klippel-Trénaunay)
Secondary to arteriovenous fistula
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Most varicose veins are primary (idiopathic valve/vein-wall weakness); risk factors include age, female sex, family history, pregnancy, obesity and prolonged standing.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which is an important SECONDARY cause of varicose veins to ask about?
options: Previous deep vein thrombosis
Hypertension
Hypercholesterolaemia
Type 1 diabetes
Asthma
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: A previous DVT (post-thrombotic syndrome) damages the deep valves and is a key secondary cause — always ask about it.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: How do the symptoms of varicose veins typically behave?
options: Worse on elevation, better on standing
Worse on standing/at the end of the day, relieved by elevation
Present only at rest overnight
Unrelated to posture
Worse after exercise, better on standing
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Worse on standing/at the end of the day, relieved by elevation
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Aching, heaviness and throbbing are worse on standing/at the end of the day and are relieved by leg elevation.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: The 'inverted champagne bottle' leg of chronic venous insufficiency is due to:
options: Lymphoedema
Lipodermatosclerosis
Cellulitis
Deep vein thrombosis
Compartment syndrome
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Lipodermatosclerosis (fibrosis of the skin/subcutaneous tissue) produces the 'inverted champagne bottle' appearance; other CVI signs include haemosiderin, venous eczema and atrophie blanche.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Where do venous ulcers characteristically occur?
options: Over the toes
In the gaiter area, above the medial malleolus
On the sole of the foot
Over the sacrum
On the anterior shin
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: In the gaiter area, above the medial malleolus
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Venous ulcers characteristically occur in the gaiter area, above the medial malleolus.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: A lump at the saphenofemoral junction gives a cough impulse and disappears on lying down. What is it?
options: Femoral hernia
Saphena varix
Inguinal lymph node
Femoral artery aneurysm
Psoas abscess
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: A saphena varix (a dilatation at the SFJ) gives a cough impulse and disappears on lying — an important mimic of a femoral hernia.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What is the investigation of choice for varicose veins?
options: Venography
Duplex ultrasound
CT venogram
Plain radiograph
D-dimer
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice — it confirms reflux, localises the incompetence and excludes deep venous obstruction/DVT.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What must be checked before applying compression therapy to a leg?
options: Serum D-dimer
Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI)
Full blood count
Chest X-ray
Blood cultures
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: ABPI must be measured first to exclude significant arterial disease — compression on an ischaemic leg is harmful.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: According to NICE, what is the first-line interventional treatment for varicose veins?
options: Surgical ligation and stripping
Endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser)
Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy
Compression stockings alone
Sclerosant tablets
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser) is first-line; foam sclerotherapy is second-line and surgery third-line.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: If endothermal ablation is unsuitable, what is the next interventional option for varicose veins?
options: Amputation
Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy
Immediate surgery as first choice
Long-term antibiotics
No further options
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: The NICE interventional ladder is: endothermal ablation → ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy → surgery (ligation/stripping ± avulsions).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which of the following is a NICE criterion for referral of varicose veins to a vascular service?
options: Asymptomatic reticular veins only
A venous leg ulcer (active or healed)
Isolated calf cramps at night
A single spider vein
A normal duplex scan
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: A venous leg ulcer (active or healed)
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Referral criteria include symptomatic primary/recurrent varicose veins, CVI skin changes, superficial vein thrombosis with suspected incompetence, and a venous leg ulcer (active or healed).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for a venous leg ulcer (once arterial disease is excluded)?
options: Systemic antibiotics
Compression bandaging plus wound care
Bed rest with the leg dependent
Skin grafting first-line
Diuretics
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Compression bandaging (after excluding arterial disease with ABPI) plus wound care is the mainstay; treating venous incompetence reduces recurrence.

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which set of features best describes a VENOUS ulcer?
options: Punched-out, deep, very painful, ABPI <0.8
Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
On the toes, dry, with weak pulses
Over the sacrum with necrotic base
On the sole, neuropathic, painless
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Venous ulcers are in the gaiter area, large/shallow/exudative, with surrounding haemosiderin/eczema and a normal ABPI (≥0.8).

conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.question: Which set of features best describes an ARTERIAL ulcer?
options: Gaiter area, shallow, exudative, ABPI normal
Punched-out, deep, very painful, ABPI <0.8, on toes/pressure points
Above the medial malleolus with haemosiderin
Painless with good pulses
Only occurs after DVT
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.answer: Punched-out, deep, very painful, ABPI <0.8, on toes/pressure points
conditions__CARDIOVASCULAR__Varicose Vei.explanation: Arterial ulcers are small, deep and 'punched-out', very painful (worse on elevation), on the toes/pressure points, with cold hairless skin and a reduced ABPI (<0.8).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Which layer of an artery wall contains the endothelium and the internal elastic lamina?
options: Tunica adventitia
Tunica media
Tunica intima
Vasa vasorum
External elastic lamina
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: The tunica intima comprises the endothelium (simple squamous), subendothelial connective tissue and the internal elastic lamina at its outer edge. The media is muscle/elastic; the adventitia is connective tissue.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Which artery type has a media packed with fenestrated elastic laminae and performs the windkessel function?
options: Muscular artery
Elastic (conducting) artery
Arteriole
Capillary
Venule
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Elastic (conducting) arteries such as the aorta have abundant elastic laminae in the media; they expand in systole and recoil in diastole (windkessel), smoothing flow and maintaining diastolic pressure.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: A medium-sized named artery (e.g. the radial) shows a thick smooth-muscle media and a striking wavy internal elastic lamina. This is a:
options: Elastic artery
Muscular (distributing) artery
Arteriole
Large vein
Lymphatic
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: A prominent internal (and external) elastic lamina bounding a thick, predominantly smooth-muscle media is characteristic of a muscular (distributing) artery, which regulates regional blood flow.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Which vessels are the principal site of resistance and thus the main regulators of systemic blood pressure?
options: Elastic arteries
Muscular arteries
Arterioles
Capillaries
Large veins
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Arterioles, with 1–3 smooth-muscle layers, are the main resistance vessels; because resistance ∝ 1/radius⁴, small calibre changes strongly influence systemic vascular resistance and diastolic BP.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: The windkessel effect of elastic arteries functions to:
options: Increase resistance to flow
Convert pulsatile ejection into continuous flow and maintain diastolic pressure
Filter the blood
Actively pump blood forward
Prevent backflow with valves
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Elastic recoil in diastole maintains forward flow and diastolic pressure between heartbeats, smoothing the pulsatile output of the left ventricle. Valves (backflow) are a venous feature.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Which stain best identifies an elastic artery and demonstrates the internal/external elastic laminae?
options: H&E alone
An elastic stain (Verhoeff–Van Gieson / orcein)
Congo red
Periodic acid–Schiff
Ziehl–Neelsen
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: An elastic stain turns elastic laminae black, making it the key stain to identify elastic arteries and to visualise the IEL/EEL. H&E shows the IEL only as a faint wavy pink line.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Atherosclerosis is fundamentally a disease of which arterial layer?
options: Tunica adventitia
Tunica media
Tunica intima
Vasa vasorum
External elastic lamina
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Atherosclerotic plaques (lipid, foam cells, fibrous cap) develop in the tunica intima of elastic and muscular arteries. Aneurysm/dissection and arteritis primarily involve the media.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: A hypertensive diabetic patient's renal biopsy shows arterioles with pink, glassy wall thickening. This is:
options: Atherosclerosis
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Giant cell arteritis
Mönckeberg sclerosis
Aortic dissection
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis — homogeneous pink (hyaline) thickening of arteriolar walls — is characteristic of hypertension and diabetes, narrowing the lumen and contributing to end-organ damage.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: In aortic dissection, blood enters which layer through an intimal tear?
options: Adventitia
Media
Vasa vasorum
Lumen only
Intima only
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: In dissection an intimal tear allows blood to split the tunica media, creating a false lumen; the leading risk factor is hypertension (in younger patients, cystic medial degeneration as in Marfan syndrome).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Which feature reliably distinguishes an artery from its accompanying vein on a slide?
options: The artery has a thinner wall and larger lumen
The artery has a thicker media, smaller round lumen and more elastic/muscle
Only veins have endothelium
Only arteries have valves
Veins have a thicker media
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Arteries have a thicker, more muscular/elastic media and a smaller, rounder lumen; veins have thin walls, large often-collapsed lumina and valves.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Rod-shaped endothelial granules that store von Willebrand factor and P-selectin are:
options: Nissl bodies
Weibel–Palade bodies
Birbeck granules
Zymogen granules
Russell bodies
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Weibel–Palade bodies are endothelium-specific storage granules for von Willebrand factor (platelet adhesion) and P-selectin (leukocyte rolling).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Flow into a capillary bed is controlled by smooth-muscle rings called:
options: Internal elastic laminae
Precapillary sphincters
Vasa vasorum
Volkmann's canals
Intercalated discs
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Precapillary sphincters at the ends of metarterioles regulate whether blood enters a given capillary bed.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Nitric oxide released by the endothelium causes:
options: Vasoconstriction
Vasodilation
Thrombosis
Basement-membrane thickening
Elastic-lamina formation
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Endothelial nitric oxide is a potent vasodilator (relaxing medial smooth muscle); endothelin is the opposing vasoconstrictor.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Why do large elastic arteries possess vasa vasorum?
options: To conduct the cardiac impulse
Because their walls are too thick for luminal diffusion to nourish the outer layers
To store calcium
To produce blood cells
To filter plasma
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: The thick walls of large vessels cannot be supplied by diffusion from the lumen alone, so vasa vasorum in the adventitia/outer media nourish the outer wall.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: A giant cell (temporal) arteritis biopsy characteristically shows:
options: Lipid plaque in the intima
Granulomatous inflammation of the media with fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina
Hyaline thickening of arterioles
Medial calcification
Fenestrated endothelium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is a transmural granulomatous vasculitis of large/medium arteries centred on the internal elastic lamina, with giant cells and IEL destruction; start high-dose steroids urgently to prevent blindness.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: A 72-year-old with a new temporal headache, jaw claudication and an ESR of 90 is at immediate risk of permanent visual loss. The priority is to:
options: Wait for temporal artery biopsy before treating
Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately
Start aspirin only
Arrange routine outpatient review
Give antibiotics
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Giant cell arteritis threatens sight via anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy; start high-dose steroids on clinical suspicion — the biopsy stays positive for 1–2 weeks and skip lesions mean a negative biopsy does not exclude it.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: Endothelium of the pulmonary vasculature is a major site of which enzyme?
options: Renin
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
Carbonic anhydrase
Alkaline phosphatase
Cathepsin K
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Pulmonary capillary endothelium expresses ACE, converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II and inactivating bradykinin.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.question: A young heavy smoker develops distal digital ischaemia and gangrene with a segmental thrombosing vasculitis of small and medium vessels. The key treatment is:
options: Corticosteroids
Smoking cessation
A statin
Lifelong warfarin
Temporal artery biopsy
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Arteries (ela.explanation: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) affects distal small/medium arteries and veins in young smokers; strict smoking cessation is the only effective treatment.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: The wall of a capillary consists of:
options: Three tunics like an artery
A single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane (plus pericytes)
Smooth muscle and elastic laminae
Stratified squamous epithelium
Endothelium and a thick media
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Capillaries are reduced to endothelium on a basement membrane (with pericytes) — no media or adventitia — minimising the diffusion distance for exchange.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Which capillary type has tight junctions and a complete basement membrane, and forms the blood–brain barrier?
options: Fenestrated
Sinusoidal
Continuous
Discontinuous
Lymphatic
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Continuous capillaries have unbroken endothelium sealed by tight junctions; in the CNS these tight junctions (with astrocyte foot processes) create the blood–brain barrier. They are also the commonest type.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Fenestrated capillaries are found in all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Gut mucosa
Endocrine glands
Renal glomerulus
Skeletal muscle
Choroid plexus
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Skeletal muscle has continuous capillaries. Fenestrated capillaries (with pores for rapid small-solute exchange/filtration) occur in gut mucosa, endocrine glands, choroid plexus and the glomerulus.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Which capillary type has large inter-cellular gaps and a discontinuous basement membrane, allowing whole cells and proteins through?
options: Continuous
Fenestrated
Sinusoidal (discontinuous)
Metarteriole
Precapillary sphincter
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are the leakiest — wide irregular lumina, large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane — found in liver, spleen and bone marrow, where blood cells and proteins must cross.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Sinusoidal capillaries lined by resident macrophages (Kupffer cells) are characteristic of which organ?
options: Kidney
Liver
Skeletal muscle
Brain
Lung
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: The liver has sinusoids (discontinuous capillaries) — fenestrae grouped in sieve plates with no diaphragm and little/no basement membrane — lined by Kupffer cells (resident macrophages). Spleen and bone marrow also have sinusoids.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: The glomerular filtration barrier is formed by fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane and:
options: Kupffer cells
Podocyte foot processes
Pericytes
Tight junctions only
Mesothelium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Filtration across the glomerulus occurs through fenestrated endothelium → glomerular basement membrane → the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes. The glomerular fenestrae notably lack diaphragms.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: How are the three capillary types most reliably distinguished?
options: By H&E staining
By electron microscopy
By their smooth-muscle content
By Congo red staining
By their valves
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Fenestrae and inter-endothelial gaps are below the resolution of light microscopy, so electron microscopy is needed to classify capillaries; H&E cannot reliably type them.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Increased basement-membrane thickening of capillaries, causing retinopathy and nephropathy, is characteristic of:
options: Sepsis
Diabetes mellitus (microangiopathy)
Multiple sclerosis
Atherosclerosis
Marfan syndrome
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Diabetic microangiopathy thickens the capillary basement membrane, underlying diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Histamine released during inflammation increases capillary permeability, leading to:
options: Vasoconstriction and pallor
Fluid leak into the tissues (oedema)
Basement-membrane thickening
Angiogenesis
Thrombosis
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Histamine increases capillary/venular permeability, allowing plasma to leak into the interstitium — producing the oedema and swelling of acute inflammation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Which molecule is the key driver of new capillary formation in tumours and wound healing?
options: EPO
VEGF
PTH
Histamine
Cathepsin K
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) drives angiogenesis; anti-VEGF agents are used to limit tumour vascularisation and in retinal disease.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: The main route of exchange across a continuous capillary with tight junctions is:
options: Large inter-cellular gaps
Transcytosis and small intercellular clefts
Fenestrae without diaphragms
Discontinuous basement membrane
Active pumping by pericytes
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: With tight junctions limiting paracellular flow, continuous capillaries rely on transcytosis (vesicular transport) and narrow intercellular clefts for exchange.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages lining which structure?
options: Renal glomerulus
Hepatic sinusoids
Pulmonary alveoli
Splenic arterioles
Cerebral capillaries
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Hepatic sinusoids (discontinuous capillaries) have fenestrated endothelium in sieve plates (no diaphragm, scant basement membrane) plus Kupffer cells that clear portal blood; beneath them lies the space of Disse.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: The postcapillary venule is the principal site of:
options: Gas exchange only
Leucocyte emigration and fluid leak during inflammation
Impulse conduction
Bone remodelling
Filtration of urine
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Postcapillary venules, with their loose junctions and pericytes, are where leucocytes exit and plasma leaks (oedema) during inflammation, partly under histamine control.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: In the CNS, the blood–brain barrier is reinforced around continuous capillaries by:
options: Kupffer cells
Astrocyte foot processes
Podocytes
Mesangial cells
Pericytes only
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Astrocyte end-feet ensheath CNS capillaries and induce/maintain the tight-junction barrier, together forming the blood–brain barrier.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: The glomerular filtrate passes, in order, through:
options: Podocytes → basement membrane → endothelium
Fenestrated endothelium → glomerular basement membrane → podocyte slit diaphragms
Continuous endothelium → mesothelium → tubule
Sinusoid → Kupffer cell → duct
Tight junction → adventitia → lumen
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Filtration crosses fenestrated endothelium → glomerular basement membrane → the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Capillaries are efficient exchange vessels chiefly because they have:
options: Thick muscular walls
A thin (single-cell) wall, huge total surface area and slow flow
Valves
Elastic laminae
A discontinuous media
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: A single endothelial-cell wall, an enormous aggregate surface area and slow blood flow together optimise diffusion of gases and solutes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome develops generalised oedema. The principal mechanism is:
options: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia
Lymphatic obstruction
Increased capillary permeability
Increased blood viscosity
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Heavy urinary protein loss lowers plasma albumin and thus plasma oncotic pressure, so less fluid is reabsorbed and oedema develops; the four broad mechanisms are raised hydrostatic, low oncotic, raised permeability and lymphatic obstruction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.question: Activation of the hepatic stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse leads to:
options: Increased vitamin A storage
Liver fibrosis (cirrhosis)
Bile secretion
Kupffer-cell proliferation
Closure of the fenestrae only
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Capillaries (.explanation: Quiescent Ito cells store vitamin A; on activation they become myofibroblast-like and deposit collagen in the space of Disse, driving hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The cardiac conducting system is composed of:
options: Peripheral nerves
Modified (specialised) cardiomyocytes
Smooth muscle
Fibroblasts
Purely fibrous tissue
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The conduction system is made of specialised cardiomyocytes, not nervous tissue; the heartbeat is therefore myogenic, with autonomic nerves only modulating the rate.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which structure is the normal pacemaker of the heart?
options: AV node
SA node
Bundle of His
Purkinje fibres
Bundle of Kent
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The SA node (right atrium near the SVC) has the fastest intrinsic rate (~60–100/min) and sets the pace; it is the dominant pacemaker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The physiological delay at the AV node serves to:
options: Speed up the ventricles
Allow the atria to finish emptying before the ventricles contract
Insulate the atria
Generate the resting potential
Prevent Purkinje conduction
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The ~0.1 s AV nodal delay separates atrial from ventricular systole, allowing the ventricles to fill fully before they contract.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which part of the conducting system is the only electrical connection between the atria and ventricles?
options: SA node
AV node
Bundle of His
Left bundle branch
Purkinje fibres
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The Bundle of His penetrates the fibrous skeleton, which otherwise electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles — so it is their sole normal electrical link.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: On a slide, subendocardial cells that are larger and paler than working cardiomyocytes with peripheral myofibrils are:
options: SA nodal cells
Purkinje fibres
Fibroblasts
Endothelial cells
Smooth muscle cells
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Purkinje fibres are large, pale (glycogen-rich) subendocardial cells with myofibrils displaced to the periphery — specialised for rapid conduction to the ventricular myocardium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: If the SA node fails, which is the expected escape rate from the AV node?
options: 0 (asystole always)
150/min
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The pacemaker hierarchy is SA (60–100) > AV (40–60) > His–Purkinje (20–40). An AV junctional escape rhythm is typically ~40–60/min.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Stimulation of the vagus nerve on the conduction system will:
options: Increase SA firing and speed AV conduction
Slow SA firing and slow AV conduction (lower heart rate)
Have no effect
Cause a delta wave
Block the Bundle of His permanently
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Parasympathetic (vagal) activity slows SA node firing and AV nodal conduction, lowering the heart rate; sympathetic activity does the opposite.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which stain best demonstrates the abundant glycogen of Purkinje fibres?
options: Congo red
Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)
Ziehl–Neelsen
Elastic stain
Perls' Prussian blue
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: PAS stains glycogen magenta, highlighting the glycogen-rich cytoplasm of Purkinje fibres (which appears clear on routine H&E because the glycogen is dissolved).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: An abnormal accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node causes:
options: Complete heart block
Wolff–Parkinson–White pre-excitation and re-entry tachycardia
Sick sinus syndrome
Bundle branch block
Asystole
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The Bundle of Kent directly connects atrium to ventricle, bypassing the AV nodal delay — producing pre-excitation (delta wave) and a substrate for AV re-entrant tachycardia (WPW).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Complete (third-degree) heart block results from disease of which structures?
options: SA node only
The AV node / Bundle of His conduction
Purkinje fibres only
The atrial myocardium
The coronary sinus
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Third-degree AV block reflects failure of conduction through the AV node/His bundle, so atria and ventricles beat independently; the ventricles are driven by a slow escape pacemaker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Spontaneous pacemaker depolarisation in the SA node is generated by the:
options: Fast sodium current
'Funny' current (If)
Delayed rectifier potassium current alone
Chloride current
Sodium–potassium pump only
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The funny current (If) is a slow inward cation current that drives the gradual diastolic depolarisation giving nodal cells their automaticity.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The AV node lies within which anatomical landmark?
options: The crista terminalis
The triangle of Koch
The membranous septum only
The coronary sinus lumen
The fossa ovalis
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The AV node sits in the floor of the right atrium within the triangle of Koch — a key landmark to identify (and avoid) during catheter ablation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Which cells are small, pale and ovoid with very few myofibrils, specialised for impulse generation?
options: Purkinje fibres
SA/AV nodal (P) cells
Working ventricular myocytes
Endothelial cells
Fibroblasts
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Nodal (P) cells are small, pale, spindle-shaped cells with sparse myofibrils, specialised for impulse generation rather than contraction. Purkinje fibres are large and pale.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The SA and AV nodes are most commonly supplied by which artery, explaining nodal block in inferior MI?
options: Left anterior descending
Right coronary artery
Circumflex artery
Left main stem
Internal thoracic artery
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: In most individuals the right coronary artery gives the SA and AV nodal branches, so inferior (RCA-territory) MIs can produce sinus or AV nodal dysfunction/block.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Ventricular contraction begins at the apex and moves toward the base because:
options: The base depolarises first
Purkinje fibres deliver the impulse to the apex first
The AV node is at the apex
The SA node is ventricular
Gap junctions are absent
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The His–Purkinje system carries the impulse rapidly to the ventricular apex, so contraction starts there and sweeps toward the outflow, ejecting blood efficiently.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Unlike a ventricular myocyte, the upstroke of the SA-node action potential is generated mainly by:
options: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
L-type (slow) Ca2+ channels
Chloride channels
The Na+/K+ ATPase
Rapid K+ efflux
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Nodal cells lack functional fast Na+ channels; their slow upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels, which is why they conduct slowly and are sensitive to calcium-channel blockers. Phase-4 automaticity is driven by the funny current (If, HCN channels).

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: The PR interval on the ECG corresponds chiefly to conduction delay in the:
options: SA node
AV node
Bundle branches
Purkinje network
Ventricular myocardium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: The PR segment reflects the slow conduction (delay) through the AV node; the P wave is atrial depolarisation and the QRS is His-Purkinje/ventricular activation.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.question: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block usually reflects disease in the:
options: AV node
His-Purkinje (infranodal) system
SA node
Atrial myocardium
Coronary sinus
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Condu.explanation: Mobitz II block is infranodal (His-Purkinje), often with a broad QRS and a high risk of progression to complete heart block — a pacemaker indication; Mobitz I (Wenckebach) is AV-nodal and usually benign.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Which layer of the heart wall is the equivalent of the tunica intima of a blood vessel?
options: Myocardium
Endocardium
Epicardium
Fibrous pericardium
Parietal pericardium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: The endocardium (endothelium + subendothelial CT + subendocardial Purkinje layer) is continuous with, and equivalent to, the tunica intima. Myocardium ≈ media; epicardium ≈ adventitia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: The epicardium is the same structure as the:
options: Fibrous pericardium
Parietal layer of serous pericardium
Visceral layer of serous pericardium
Endocardium
Myocardial mesothelium only
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: The epicardium IS the visceral layer of the serous pericardium — mesothelium over connective tissue and fat, carrying the coronary vessels.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Which histological feature is unique to cardiac muscle?
options: Peripheral nuclei
Intercalated discs
Absence of striations
Multinucleate unbranched fibres
Spindle-shaped cells
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Intercalated discs (with desmosomes/fascia adherens and gap junctions) joining branching, centrally-nucleated striated cells are unique to cardiac muscle.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Intercalated discs allow the myocardium to act as a functional syncytium because they contain:
options: Tight junctions
Gap junctions
Hemidesmosomes
Basement membrane
Elastic fibres
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Gap junctions within the intercalated discs electrically couple adjacent cardiomyocytes, letting the impulse pass cell-to-cell so the myocardium contracts as one unit.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: A striated muscle shows branching fibres with single central nuclei and dark cross-lines between cells. This is:
options: Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Purkinje fibres only
Dense regular connective tissue
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Branching + central nuclei + intercalated discs (dark cross-lines) identify cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle is unbranched with peripheral nuclei; smooth muscle is non-striated.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: A heart valve is best described histologically as:
options: A muscular flap
A core of dense fibrous connective tissue covered by endothelium, and avascular
Cartilage covered by mesothelium
A fold of myocardium
Elastic cartilage
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Valves have a dense fibrous connective-tissue core covered by endocardium/endothelium; they are avascular and anchored to the fibrous skeleton — which is why infective vegetations are hard to clear.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: The pericardial cavity lies between which two layers, and what does its fluid do?
options: Endocardium and myocardium; lubricates valves
Parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium; allows frictionless beating
Fibrous pericardium and bone; cushions
Myocardium and epicardium; nourishes muscle
Two layers of myocardium; conducts impulses
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: The serous fluid in the pericardial cavity between the parietal and visceral (epicardial) serous layers lubricates the beating heart. Excess fluid causes tamponade.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: The fibrous skeleton of the heart electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. Which structure is the only normal electrical connection across it?
options: The SA node
The Bundle of His
The coronary sinus
The Purkinje network of the atria
The tricuspid valve
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Only the Bundle of His penetrates the fibrous skeleton, so it is the sole normal electrical link between atria and ventricles.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: After a myocardial infarction the dead myocardium is replaced by:
options: Regenerated cardiomyocytes
A fibrous (collagenous) scar
New cartilage
Adipose tissue only
Smooth muscle
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Cardiac muscle is a permanent tissue that cannot regenerate meaningfully, so infarcted myocardium heals by fibrous scarring, predisposing to aneurysm and arrhythmia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Where are the Purkinje fibres located within the heart wall?
options: In the epicardial fat
In the subendocardial layer of the endocardium
Within the fibrous pericardium
In the valve cusps
In the tunica media of the coronary arteries
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Purkinje fibres lie subendocardially (in the deep endocardium), from where they rapidly deliver the impulse to the ventricular myocardium.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Which cells line both serous surfaces of the pericardium?
options: Endothelium
Mesothelium (simple squamous)
Cuboidal epithelium
Cardiomyocytes
Chondrocytes
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: The serous pericardial layers (parietal and visceral/epicardial) are lined by mesothelium — the simple squamous epithelium of serous membranes.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: T-tubules in cardiac muscle are located at the ______ and function to ______.
options: A-band; store calcium
Z-line; spread the action potential deep into the fibre
M-line; anchor actin
Intercalated disc; couple cells electrically
Sarcolemma surface; secrete hormones
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Cardiac T-tubules invaginate at the Z-line, carrying the action potential into the cell interior for synchronous calcium release and contraction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Cardiac muscle's heavy dependence on aerobic metabolism (many mitochondria) makes it especially vulnerable to:
options: Cold
Ischaemia/hypoxia
Stretch
Alkalosis
Dehydration
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Because cardiomyocytes contract continuously and rely on aerobic ATP, interruption of oxygen supply (ischaemia) rapidly impairs function and causes infarction.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: The main load-bearing layer of a heart-valve cusp, on its outflow surface, is the:
options: Spongiosa
Fibrosa
Ventricularis
Endocardium
Atrialis
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: The fibrosa (dense collagen on the outflow/downstream side) provides the valve's strength; the spongiosa is a loose GAG-rich shock-absorber and the ventricularis/atrialis is elastin-rich on the inflow side.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Fibrous, sometimes calcified thickening of the pericardium that restricts ventricular filling causes:
options: Cardiac tamponade
Constrictive pericarditis
Myocarditis
Infective endocarditis
Atherosclerosis
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Chronic pericardial fibrosis/calcification produces a rigid sac that limits diastolic filling — constrictive pericarditis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Why is infective endocarditis on a heart valve difficult to eradicate?
options: Valves are highly vascular
Valves are avascular, so antibiotics and immune cells reach them poorly
Valves regenerate rapidly
Valves are made of cartilage
Valves have no connective tissue
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Heart valves are avascular dense fibrous structures, so the blood-borne antibiotics and immune cells penetrate vegetations poorly — hence prolonged IV therapy is needed.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: A healed myocardial infarct is a non-contractile fibrous scar, which predisposes to all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Ventricular aneurysm
Mural thrombus
Re-entry arrhythmia
Myocardial regeneration to normal
Heart failure
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Cardiac muscle cannot regenerate to normal; the infarct heals by scar, which can cause aneurysm, mural thrombus, re-entrant arrhythmia and contractile failure.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Membrane-bound natriuretic-peptide granules that promote natriuresis are found chiefly in:
options: Ventricular Purkinje fibres
Atrial cardiomyocytes
Valve fibroblasts
Pericardial mesothelium
Coronary endothelium
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Atrial cardiomyocytes contain atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) granules released on stretch, promoting natriuresis, diuresis and vasodilation; BNP (mainly ventricular) is the heart-failure biomarker.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.question: Subacute infective endocarditis on a previously rheumatic mitral valve is most often caused by:
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus viridans
Candida albicans
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Sterile immune complexes
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Heart Wall (e.explanation: Subacute IE on abnormal/damaged valves is classically Streptococcus viridans; acute IE on normal or prosthetic valves (and IVDU tricuspid disease) is typically Staphylococcus aureus.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A vessel on a histology slide has a large, flattened lumen full of red cells, a very thin wall in which the outermost collagenous layer is clearly the thickest, and no distinct elastic laminae. It is most likely a:
options: Muscular artery
Vein
Elastic artery
Arteriole
Lymphatic capillary
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: A large collapsed lumen, thin wall with a dominant (thickest) adventitia and absent elastic laminae are classic for a vein. Arteries have a thick media and defined elastic laminae.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the layers of arteries and veins?
options: The media is thickest in both
The adventitia is thickest in both
The media is thickest in arteries; the adventitia is thickest in veins
The intima is thickest in veins
Veins lack an adventitia
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The defining contrast: arteries have the thickest tunica media, veins have the thickest tunica adventitia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Venous valves are formed by folds of which layer?
options: Tunica adventitia
Tunica media
Tunica intima
Vasa vasorum
External elastic lamina
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Valves are paired semilunar folds of the tunica intima (endothelium over a thin CT core), with cusps directed toward the heart.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: In which vessel do leukocyte rolling, adhesion and diapedesis predominantly occur during acute inflammation?
options: Elastic artery
Capillary
Postcapillary venule
Large vein
Arteriole
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The postcapillary venule is the principal site of leukocyte emigration and of histamine-mediated increased permeability.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Venous valves are normally ABSENT from which of the following?
options: Great saphenous vein
Femoral vein
Inferior vena cava
Popliteal vein
Cephalic vein
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: The venae cavae (like the portal, dural and most visceral veins) lack valves; limb veins such as the saphenous, femoral, popliteal and cephalic are richly valved.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A large vein near the heart shows prominent longitudinally arranged smooth-muscle bundles in its outer coat. This vessel is most likely the:
options: Radial artery
Vena cava
Muscular venule
Aorta
Dorsalis pedis artery
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Large veins such as the venae cavae characteristically have longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles in the tunica adventitia.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Why is venous return highly dependent on the skeletal-muscle and respiratory pumps?
options: Veins have thick muscular walls that need assistance
Venous pressure is high and pulsatile
Venous pressure is low and the wall is thin/compliant, so blood needs external propulsion
Veins have no endothelium
Valves actively pump blood
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Because venous pressure is low and the wall is thin and compliant, blood is moved mainly by external compression (muscle and respiratory pumps) and venous tone rather than by the wall itself.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: Which best describes the elastic-stain appearance of a vein compared with an artery?
options: A vein has a thicker internal elastic lamina
A vein has crisp internal and external elastic laminae
A vein has sparse, scattered elastic with no distinct laminae
A vein has no elastic tissue at all
A vein has more elastic than an elastic artery
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Veins contain only sparse, scattered elastic fibres and lack the discrete internal/external elastic laminae that arteries display on elastic stains.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: A patient develops a DVT after a long flight. Which component of Virchow's triad is most directly related to prolonged immobility?
options: Hypercoagulability
Endothelial injury
Venous stasis
Increased platelet count
Valve calcification
histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.explanation: Immobility causes venous stasis (loss of the muscle-pump effect), one of the three arms of Virchow's triad predisposing to venous thrombosis.

histology__CARDIOVASCULAR__Veins & Venul.question: High endothelial venules (HEVs) are distinguished by tall cuboidal endothelium and are the site where lymphocytes enter lymphoid tissue. They are found in:
options: Skeletal muscle
Lymph nodes and Peyer's patches
The renal medulla
Cardiac muscle
The epidermis
